### C. Part 2 — finishing the outside-title search (gap-discovery source 4)

Every item below was searched statute-wide and every landlord-relevant hit read section-open. **Boundary: statutes only** — the Nebraska Administrative Code, municipal codes and case law were not searched, so each absence is "no Nebraska *statute*" and nothing more.

#### C.1 Found: a four-section meth-lab scheme, with duties and a fast termination right

**§§71-2432 to 71-2435**, Chapter 71, cited nowhere in the library. Found by `clandestine` after `methamphetamine laboratory` returned zero. All four read verbatim.

- **§71-2433 — you must report.** "A property owner with knowledge of a clandestine drug lab on his or her property shall report such knowledge and location as soon as practicable to the local law enforcement agency or to the Nebraska State Patrol." The Patrol then forwards its report to the owner among others, so an owner may also *learn* of a lab this way.
- **§71-2434(3) — you must not re-rent, and it has teeth.** The owner "shall not permit the human habitation or use of such property until the rehabilitation ... has been completed and the property has been released." Knowing violation: **civil penalty up to $1,000**, enforced by DHHS.
- **§71-2434(2) — you pay for the oversight.** The local public health department "may charge and collect fees from the owner or owners of contaminated property to cover the costs directly associated with monitoring the rehabilitation."
- **§71-2435 — three days, no cure, overrides everything.** "Notwithstanding any other provision of law, if leased property contains a clandestine drug lab, an owner may terminate the lease agreement upon three days' written notice for the purpose of rehabilitating the contaminated property."

New row **`edu-clandestine-drug-lab-ne`** (REQUIRED, education). **No new lease clause** and **no clause edit owed**: §71-2435 operates notwithstanding any other law so the right does not depend on lease text, and the **instruction 33 check came back clean** — `default-by-tenant-ks-ne` already reads "except where applicable law permits Landlord to proceed without giving Tenant an opportunity to cure," so the no-cure right is not contractually surrendered. Currency (instruction 34): §71-2433 was amended by **Laws 2025, LB317, §375**, which only substituted the renamed Department of Water, Energy, and Environment among the report's recipients; the owner's duty is unchanged. **Not read:** the DHHS rehabilitation rules under §71-2434(1) — administrative code, flagged under instruction 16 as needing rulemaking rather than bill-tracking monitoring.

#### C.2 Found: an entire radon act, in Chapter 76 itself

**Radon Resistant New Construction Act, §§76-3501 to 76-3507**, cited nowhere in the library. `radon` returned 20 sections.

- **§76-3504** — new construction built **after 1 September 2019** "intended to be regularly occupied by people" **shall** be built using radon-resistant new construction, with specified minimum standards: gasketed or sealed sump lids; a passive subslab depressurisation system with a ≥3-inch vent pipe terminating ≥12 inches above the roof and ≥10 feet from any opening; separate vent pipes where interior footings divide the subslab material; interior pipes labelled "Radon Reduction System" on each floor and in accessible attics; and an electrical circuit in an approved box near the anticipated fan location so an active system can be added later.
- **§76-3505** — three exemptions, but **only two reach a rental**: a licensed architect's or professional engineer's design, or a county whose average radon concentration is below **2.7 pCi/L** as determined by the department. The third, a local building official's determination, is expressly unavailable "other than for any residential dwelling unit."

New row **`edu-radon-new-construction-ne`** (CONDITIONAL, education). `edu-no-radon-tenant-disclosure-ne` amended to point to it: its conclusion was right but its framing left the impression that Nebraska does not legislate on radon at all. **This is the sharpest illustration of instruction 7's limit**: the act sits in **Chapter 76, the URLTA's own chapter**, so "check adjacent chapters" has to mean adjacent *articles* too. The 2.7 pCi/L county list is a departmental determination and **no county is named as exempt**.

#### C.3 Found: four uncited sections inside the URLTA, from the `landlord` diff

- **§76-1429 Fire or casualty damage** — tenant may vacate immediately and give written notice within **fourteen days** thereafter, terminating **as of the date of vacating**; or, if continued occupancy is lawful, vacate the unusable part with rent reduced in proportion to the loss in **fair rental value**. On termination the landlord returns all prepaid rent and deposit recoverable under §76-1416, accounting **as of the date of the casualty**; the tenant stays liable for damage from their own negligence. → new `casualty-termination-ne` and `edu-casualty-damage-ne`. **Instruction 18 mattered here**: Kansas runs on a 5-day notice, Nebraska on 14 days after vacating. Nebraska was the **only one of the 14 states with no fire/casualty clause** — KS, ND, SD, MN, CA, NV, TX, FL and AZ all have one.
- **§76-1420 Limitation of liability** — the release on sale, and the Nebraska analog of A.R.S. §33-1325 (the gap Arizona's own screen found). Release runs only to events **after written notice to the tenant** of the conveyance, on a good-faith sale to a bona fide purchaser, and **does not cover the deposit** unless deposits and prepaid rents are **assigned to the purchaser with written notice**. Subsection (2) is the manager analog. Opens "Unless otherwise agreed." → new `edu-selling-rented-property-ne`.
- **§76-1422 Rules and regulations** — six conditions for a house rule to be enforceable, plus the mid-tenancy test: reasonable notice **and** no "substantial modification of his bargain." Enforcement runs through §76-1431. → new `edu-rules-regulations-enforceability-ne`. The NE-active set carries at least six clauses that *are* house rules within this section and none cited it; KS, NV and AZ already had the analog row.
- **§76-1428 Landlord's noncompliance as defense** — the counterclaim, pay-into-court and netting mechanics, and **"If the defense or counterclaim by the tenant is without merit and is not raised in good faith, the landlord may recover reasonable attorney's fees."** → new `edu-eviction-process-ne`; `edu-statutory-attorney-fee-actions-ne` amended to add the award. **An omission in the landlord's favour**: a row whose job was to list statutory fee awards listed the ones running against them and left this one out.

Also newly cited: **§76-1405** — "The aggrieved party has a duty to mitigate damages." `default-by-tenant-ks-ne` already promised mitigation "to the extent required by applicable law," so the clause was correct by deference; this supplies the basis rather than fixing an error.

#### C.4 Found: a Chapter 60 towing scheme, including a prohibition aimed at the landlord

`towing` returned 61 sections. Read: §§60-2401, 60-2401.01, 60-2402, 60-2403, 60-2409, 60-2410, 60-2411.

**Nebraska conditions a lawful private tow on posted signs** — the same shape as Arizona's finding, but split by class of city. Outside Omaha and Lincoln, parking in a **properly posted** restricted lot without the owner's or authorised tenant's consent is an **infraction** and the vehicle may be towed at their request (§60-2401.01). In Omaha (metropolitan class) and Lincoln (primary class), absent a conforming local ordinance, towing is available "if the lot is properly posted" (§60-2401). **§60-2402** sets the sign contents: readily visible, stating the purpose(s) of parking, the **hours** of restriction, and **who to contact** about a towed vehicle. And **§60-2411** points straight at the landlord: an owner or tenant causing a tow "shall not solicit or accept therefor a commission, gift, gratuity, or any form of compensation or wealth" from the tower.

New row **`edu-towing-ne`**. No clause conflict — `parking-vehicle-rules` and `parking-ne` already defer to law, so the exposure is operational, not textual. **No penalty section was located for a §60-2411 violation** and the row asserts none. The Omaha/Lincoln class identifications are general knowledge, not read from the classification statute; the metropolitan/primary split itself is in the statutory text, which is what the row turns on.

#### C.5 Found: medical cannabis is now lawful in Nebraska

**§71-24,105** (Initiative Law 2024, No. 437, §3 — enacted, in the official compilation with an initiative-law source line, satisfying instruction 17). Qualified-patient and caregiver conduct is "not an offense under state or local law" and is removed from the Uniform Controlled Substances Act.

New row **`edu-medical-cannabis-ne`**. **`smoking-policy` is fine and no edit is proposed** — it is a contractual ban and the act imposes no landlord duty. The real exposure is different and is **instruction 33 in reverse**: not a shared clause giving away a state right, but a state law quietly narrowing what an existing clause's *enforcement theory* can reach. A registered patient's use is no longer illegal, so it cannot support §76-1431's drug-related-criminal-activity fast track; enforce it as a smoking or house-rules breach instead. The no-landlord-duty negative is **strong but not exhaustive**: §71-24,105 imposes none on its face and the statute-wide `landlord` sweep returned no section in the 71-24,1xx range, but §71-24,104's definitions and the rest of the Patient Protection Act were not read, and that is stated in the row.

### D. The error found in a shipped VERIFIED row — and it was a correction to a self-correction

**`edu-smoke-detector-scope-ne` was wrong, and the wrong part was the re-audit's own fix.**

The history matters more than the error. The original NE pass stated the smoke-detector duty unconditionally. The re-audit created this row at `NEEDS_REVIEW` carrying a caveat that a pre-1982, never-remodelled building might fall outside the mandate — then, in the same session, **self-corrected that caveat away**, asserting that §81-5,142(3) swept in pre-1982 dwellings with "compliance deadlines now decades expired" and that coverage was "effectively universal" *because of subsection (3)*. That note was written up as a methodology win: the over-include-and-flag discipline catching an error before it shipped.

Reading §81-5,142 verbatim today shows **the second step was also wrong**. Subsection (3) contains **no deadline of any kind**. Its trigger is "at the time of their **remodeling or sale**." A pre-1982 dwelling unit never remodelled and never sold has no §81-5,142(3) installation trigger at all, so "all the deadlines are decades past" was fiction, and the note's "residual gap: subsection (3)'s exact compliance deadline was truncated" was chasing a deadline that does not exist. Only subsection (2), for lodging-house guest rooms and dormitories, ever carried the 1984 date.

**The row's bottom line survives, for a different reason.** §81-5,144(1) puts the supply-install-maintain-test duty on the owner of **every** apartment house, dwelling, hotel, lodging house, dormitory or mobile home, and §81-5,144(3) says "This section shall apply **solely to rental property**" — with no construction-date qualifier anywhere. **That**, not §81-5,142(3), is the real source of universal rental coverage. So a Nebraska landlord should still assume the duty applies regardless of build date, and `smoke-detector-duty-ne` — which tracks §81-5,144 and was re-read against primary text today — **needs no change**.

**The methodology datum, which is the actual finding.** This is the same failure mode the project has now named repeatedly — reading part of a multi-section statute and generalising — committed **three times on one statute**: in the original pass, again by the re-audit's correction of it, and caught only on a third reading, by a session whose remit was not smoke detectors at all. Two things follow. **An over-correction is as wrong as the error it replaced**, and it is more dangerous, because it arrives wearing the credibility of a fix. And **"self-corrected" in a note is not evidence the second answer was checked** — the re-audit's note is detailed, confident, explicitly reasoned, and wrong. Nothing in its tone distinguishes it from a correct correction.

**New material added to the row, all read verbatim:** §81-5,143 (mounting per State Fire Marshal rules; the alarm must sound inside the unit) — previously uncited; **§81-5,145** (a political subdivision may not set less stringent standards, **must** require hardwiring to a centralised power source in post-1982 buildings, and **may not** require hardwiring in a pre-1982 building) — previously uncited and directly useful, since it tells an owner of an older building what a city cannot demand; §81-5,142(3)'s **seller-only, non-assignable** duty on sale; and §81-5,146's Class V misdemeanor.

#### D.1 Cross-state question for Taylor — not acted on

**`no-alterations` (tagged all 14 states) has no reasonable-modification carve-out.** Its self-limiting sentence defers to law for "any repair, installation, or rekeying that applicable law entitles Tenant to perform" — but a disability **modification** (grab bars, a ramp, a widened doorway) is none of those three things. Nebraska makes it discrimination to refuse "to permit, at the expense of the person with a disability, reasonable modifications of existing premises" where necessary for full enjoyment, subject to a restoration condition (§20-319(2)(a), already on `edu-no-modification-duty-ne`).

The clause does not **waive** the tenant's right, so it is not a prohibited provision, and Nebraska's education row covers the duty — which is why the scenario is scored Covered. But the lease text reads as unfettered landlord discretion where state and federal fair-housing law constrains it. **This is a shared row across 14 states and is a product decision, so no edit was made.** If Taylor wants it, the fix is one clause: extend the existing carve-out to "any repair, installation, rekeying, or **reasonable modification** that applicable law entitles Tenant to perform," which is true in every state and would be a **uniform** edit under §5a.1 — but it needs paste-ready propagation notes for all 14 logs, which are not written here.

## Propagated shared-row edit, 2026-09-29 (from the Pennsylvania pass)

Not a re-audit; nothing else in this state was reviewed.

**Propagation note (from the Pennsylvania pass, 2026-09-29): `severability` rewritten.** Old: 'If any provision of this Agreement shall be held or made invalid by a court decision, statute or rule, or shall be otherwise rendered invalid, the remainder of this Agreement shall not be affected thereby.' New: 'If a court decision, statute or rule makes any part of this Lease invalid or unenforceable, the rest of this Lease still applies.' §5a.1 judgment: UNIFORM. No state-specific review owed. `last_checked` reset to 2026-09-29 (PA log §3.1, §9).

### The 14 rules

**Rule 41 — just cause. Checked; no clause defect; absence row extended.** Nebraska has no tenure-based just-cause rule, and `edu-no-for-cause-eviction-ne` already carried the `for-cause-eviction` key rule 41b requires (so 41b was already satisfied, consistent with the conformance table). Wording screen run on the clauses the prompt named — `surrender-end-of-term-ks-ne`, `holdover`, `security-deposit-use`, `no-alterations`, `keys`, `early-termination-ne`: in a state with no just-cause rule, "the end of the term ends possession" wording is not a defect, so **no clause change is owed**. But rule 41 also asks the absence row to record situational for-cause limits, and **Nebraska has one the library had never cited: §76-886** (Condominium Act) — during the 60-day conversion window a tenant may be required to vacate only for nonpayment, waste, or disturbing other tenants' peaceful enjoyment, the tenancy's terms may not be altered, and failure to give the notice "is a defense to an action for possession." Found by searching `condominium conversion` after the rule's own text named a conversion notice as the example; the URLTA has no `conversion` or `escrow` hit, so it sits outside the act. No rent-escrow bar and no tenants'-association protection exist. **Rows: `edu-no-for-cause-eviction-ne` (changed), `edu-condo-conversion-tenant-rights-ne` (new).**

**Rule 42 — required text inside a shared clause. Checked, no issue.** The whole-act battery for `shall be included / shall set forth / shall state / shall contain / must state|contain|include` returned **exactly two hits, both court process**: §76-1441 (what the complaint for restitution must contain) and §76-1442 (what the summons must state). The `in writing` battery returned only §76-1417 (the disclosure duty, already a `REQUIRED_DISCLOSURE` row) and §76-1419(2)–(3) (the delegation writings, rule 48). **No Nebraska statute forces a sentence into a fee, deposit or other clause.** Recorded in `edu-no-statutory-forms-ne`.

**Rule 43 — cure promises. Checked; the right is preserved; a drafting improvement is proposed, not made.** §76-1431 read section-open. Nebraska has **three** no-cure routes: §76-1431(4) — five days' written notice "and without the right of the tenant to cure the default" for violent criminal activity, illegal controlled-substance sale, or activity threatening health or safety; §76-1431(1)'s recurrence route — 14 days' notice with no cure where substantially the same breach recurs within six months; and §71-2435 (meth lab, three days, "notwithstanding any other provision of law"). `default-by-tenant-ks-ne` **does** preserve them: its rent limb is self-limiting ("within the time period specified by applicable law", and §76-1431(2) sets seven calendar days), and the carve-out "except where applicable law permits Landlord to proceed without giving Tenant an opportunity to cure" attaches to the non-rent limb immediately before it. `application-of-payments` is clean and expressly preserves any statutory cure right. **Nothing is forfeited, so no override is written.** Under AL 4's refinement the carve-out should nonetheless be its own sentence reaching every limb; that is a shared row across KS, NE, OH and NC, so it is **proposed below under rule 62, not made**.

**Rule 44 — terms the statute turns into landlord duties. Checked, no issue.** The whole-act battery for `as agreed` and `agreed in the rental agreement` returned **no hit**; the only `rental agreement provides`-family hit is §76-1414(4) (the lease fixing a definite term). So no generous lease term is converted into a mandatory duty. The adjacent risk is real but points the other way and is already held: §76-1413(10) expressly says the electronic-notice section "does not affect any requirement related to the content or timing of any notice", and §76-1413(9) **forbids** requiring a tenant to accept electronic delivery as a lease term — a prohibition, not a duty-conversion, already carried by `edu-electronic-notice-regime-ne`.

**Rule 45 — electronic notices. Checked and extended; the state's electronic-transactions act had never been read.** §76-1413(5) routes e-delivery through the UETA, so its exclusions decide whether default, cure and eviction notices can go electronically. **§86-630(2) read section-open: the only exclusions are wills/codicils/testamentary trusts and the UCC other than articles 2 and 2A.** Nebraska's UETA has **no** carve-out for default, cure, acceleration, foreclosure or eviction notices and none for a primary residence — so unlike the state that put this question on the topic reference, Nebraska's regime is not undercut. Two **unwaivable** constraints found and added: §86-635(3) makes an electronic record **unenforceable** against a recipient whose ability to print or store it was inhibited, and §86-635(4) says that cannot be varied by agreement — which bites directly on §76-1413(4)(b)'s portal-posting method; and §86-632(3) gives an unwaivable right to refuse electronic delivery for other transactions, reinforcing §76-1413(9). **Federal flag (rule 21):** §76-1413(16) preserves E-SIGN "as such act existed on January 1, 2025"; E-SIGN's own treatment of residential default and eviction notices was **not read** — federal, outside this search, identified not resolved. **Row: `edu-electronic-notice-regime-ne` (changed, body and notes).**

**Rule 46 — the lease as the required notice. Checked, confirmed absent.** No provision lets a lease paragraph serve as a statutory notice: every notice section (§§76-1425, 76-1431, 76-1437) requires a separate written notice specifying the breach and the termination date. The nearest thing is §76-886(d), where a **conversion notice** doubles as a notice to vacate — a statutory document doing double duty, not a lease paragraph, so the absence stands. Nothing to reconcile in the shared clauses that promise a separate notice.

**Rule 47 — penalties for knowingly using a prohibited term. Checked; the penalty exists; no prohibited term found.** §76-1415 read section-open. **§76-1415(2):** a prohibited provision "is unenforceable", and "If a landlord deliberately uses a rental agreement containing provisions known by him or her to be prohibited, the tenant may recover actual damages sustained by him or her and reasonable attorney's fees." So rule 47 applies here and a savings sentence does not rescue a void term — now said in the row, which previously stated the penalty but drew no drafting conclusion from it. The four clauses the prompt named were each read against §76-1415(1): **`notices`** clean and better than neutral (it defers to statutory method, form, timing and content and disclaims designating an alternative delivery method — the right posture given §76-1413(9)); **`common-area-use`** clean, and its waterbed restriction was the live question, since the topic reference records a statutory flotation-bedding right elsewhere — a Nebraska search found no flotation-bedding or waterbed right, so nothing is blocked; **`early-termination-ne`** clean, because its fee could offend §76-1415(1)(a) only if charged on a statutory termination and the clause expressly carves out the SCRA, uninhabitability and Nebraska's DV rights; **`late-fee-ne`** clean on §76-1415, with its acceptance-reservation already handled by `edu-late-rent-reservation-fix-ne`. Also added: **§76-1415(1)(c) runs both ways** — it voids a term that the tenant "Agrees to pay the landlord's **or tenant's** attorney's fees", so a mutual fee clause is prohibited too. **Row: `edu-prohibited-lease-terms-ne` (changed).**

**Rule 48 — separate-document requirements. CHECKED, DEFECT FOUND, FIXED.** The whole-act battery found **exactly one** separate-writing requirement: **§76-1419(3)**. For a dwelling unit *other than* a single-family residence, an agreement that the tenant perform specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations or remodeling binds only if it "is set forth in a **separate writing** signed by the parties and supported by adequate consideration" and "does not diminish or affect the obligation of the landlord to other tenants"; §76-1419(2) lets the lease itself be the writing for a single-family residence. **`snow-removal` and `landscaping-irrigation` are both tagged NE and both assign tasks in the lease, so in a Nebraska duplex or apartment they do not bind the tenant** — and §76-1419(1)(c) makes keeping "all common areas of the premises in a clean and safe condition" the landlord's own duty, so snow on a shared walk or entrance is the landlord's regardless, while §76-1419(3)(b)'s other-tenants proviso independently blocks shifting a common-area task however it is papered. The consequence is **ineffectiveness, not voidness**: the duty stays with the landlord, §76-1415(1)(a) is not obviously engaged, and the §76-1415(2) penalty is not the primary risk — the risk is a landlord who believes the tenant must shovel. **Treatment (Taylor, 2026-09-30): match Arizona.** The NE tags stay, scoped by an NE note on each, because the defect and remedy are identical to A.R.S. §33-1324(C)/(D) and S.C. Code Ann. §27-40-440(c)/(d), and a per-state applicability condition is one product gap rather than a drafting fork. **Flagged for Claude Code:** the same applicability condition AZ already logged, so these rows are suppressed for non-single-family NE properties. **Rows: `snow-removal`, `landscaping-irrigation` (NE note segment only — no text, state, type or basis change, so no §5a.1 propagation is owed), `edu-habitability-duty-delegation-ne` (changed).**

**Rule 49 — collection-cost bans. Checked, no issue.** §76-1415(1)(c) bans only **attorney's fees**; (1)(d)'s "or the costs connected therewith" is tethered to the negligence-exculpation limb, not to collection costs generally. There is no Nebraska collection-cost ban, so `default-by-tenant-ks-ne`'s "reasonable costs and expenses" is lawful as written. **One construction risk recorded, not fixed:** in a state that voids *any* attorney-fee clause, "costs and expenses" could be argued to sweep in fees. That is a shared row and a reading, not a defect — flagged below rather than changed.

**Rule 50 — "the lease controls" wording. Checked; every choice accounted for.** The whole-act battery found six places: **§76-1414(3)** twice — rent payable at the time and place agreed, and "Unless otherwise agreed, rent shall be uniformly apportionable from day to day" (both exercised by `rent-payment` and the Basic Terms); **§76-1414(4)** — the lease fixing a definite term, else week-to-week for a weekly roomer and month-to-month otherwise (exercised by the Term); **§76-1420(1) and (2)** — the release on sale and on a management change, already held by `edu-selling-rented-property-ne`; **§76-1424** — "Unless otherwise agreed, the tenant shall occupy his dwelling unit only as a dwelling unit", exercised by `residential-use-only`, plus the extended-absence hook (rule 54 below); and **§76-1433** — acceptance of rent with knowledge of a breach waives the right to terminate for it "unless otherwise agreed **after the breach has occurred**". That last one is a choice the lease **cannot** make: the contrary agreement must post-date the breach, so no advance reservation works, which is exactly what `edu-late-rent-reservation-fix-ne` already records (log §3). **No change owed.**

**Rule 51 — plain-language and consumer-contract statutes. Checked, confirmed absent.** Nebraska has **no** plain-language consumer-contract statute reaching residential leases (`plain language` returned 101 loosely-matched hits with no such act; the §76-1419 hit is a false positive). Both consumer statutes were read: **§87-302** (Uniform Deceptive Trade Practices Act) enumerates fifteen-plus practices — passing off, confusion, geographic origin, false representations, advertising, pyramid and referral schemes — and contains **neither** a blank-space-filled-after-signing nor a copy-at-signing practice; **§59-1602** (Consumer Protection Act) is a general standard with no enumerated list. The rule 40 formatting battery was run on 2026-09-27 and found nothing conditioning a Nebraska lease term, consistent with this. **Not resolved and labelled unread doctrine (rule 76):** whether either act reaches a residential lease at all — Nebraska's CPA carries a public-interest requirement in the case law and no case was read, so the new row describes the general standard as a backstop rather than asserting it applies. **Row: `edu-no-lease-completeness-rule-ne` (new).**

**Rule 54 — optional clauses, general screen. Checked; every candidate listed with its verdict.** Full list, as the rule requires:

| Optional clause | Citation | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| Extended-absence notice | §76-1424 ("The rental agreement **may require**…"), remedy at §76-1432(1) only "If the rental agreement requires…" | **Already offered** — `extended-absence-notice-ne`. Genuinely load-bearing: silent lease forfeits the remedy |
| DV lock-change cost recovery | §76-1431.04(4) — "The landlord may require the tenant to pay for the actual and reasonable cost incurred by the landlord in changing the locks" | **Added as education** — statutory, needs no lease text, and was missing from `edu-dv-tenant-rights-ne`, now the only place NE's DV rules live |
| Stipulated holdover rate | §76-1437(3) measures only a holdover that is "willful and not in good faith", and is a **lump** measure, not a daily rate | **Offerable, recorded not drafted.** Nebraska sets no measure for a non-willful holdover, so a lease rate could fill it; offering it means untagging NE from shared `holdover` and writing an override — beyond a scalpel retro, so it goes to Taylor. Liquidated-damages-not-penalty doctrine **not read** |
| Landlord casualty termination | §76-1429 gives the **tenant** rights only; nothing bars a landlord right that leaves §76-1429 intact | **Offerable, recorded not drafted** — same reason. CO was judged likely void; Nebraska is not CO |
| Crime-free / criminal-activity clause | §76-1431(4) already supplies a five-day no-cure statutory termination for violent crime, drug sales and health-or-safety threats | **n** — the statute already does the work, as in UT and IL |
| Statutory waiver (conversion rights) | §76-886(f) — a tenant may waive, but only "by a written instrument executed **after the date of notice**" | **n** — the lease cannot capture it, by the statute's own timing |
| Statutory waiver (Act rights generally) | §76-1415(1)(a) voids any waiver of Act rights; §76-1434 prohibits landlord liens and distraint | **n** — no waiver or exemption clause serves a Nebraska landlord |
| Eviction / notice-service fee | §76-1415(1)(c) voids attorney-fee clauses; no notice-service-fee statute exists | **n** — unauthorised and sitting against the (1)(c) and unconscionability backdrop |
| Landlord self-cure billed as rent | No URLTA §4.105 analogue (whole-act battery: no hit) | **n** — no statutory mechanism; see `edu-no-landlord-self-cure-ne` |

**Rule 54t — tenant-caused damage. Checked; each provision screened separately; education row added, no clause offered.** Each abatement and exit provision was checked for **its own** fault exception, as SC 4 now requires, and they do not match: **§76-1425** — "The tenant may not terminate for a condition caused by the deliberate or negligent act or omission of the tenant…" (has one); **§76-1427** — remedies do not arise "if the condition was caused by the deliberate or negligent act or omission of the tenant…" (has one); **§76-1429 — has none.** It makes the tenant "responsible for damage caused by his negligence" but does **not** bar the termination right at (1)(a) or the proportional rent reduction at (1)(b). **That asymmetry is the finding**, and it decides the rule: a no-abatement or no-termination-if-at-fault term would take away a right the Act gives, void under §76-1415(1)(a) with §76-1415(2) exposure on top. What Nebraska *does* give the landlord: repair-cost liability by statute (§76-1429(2)) and by contract (`tenant-duties-ne`), and on termination "a claim for rent and a separate claim for actual damages for breach" (§76-1435), which can reach lost rent subject to §76-1405's mitigation duty. **`tenant-caused-damage-tn` was read and deliberately not tagged or copied:** its limb (1) ("Rent will not abate or be reduced while the property is repaired") and its bar on the tenant leaving are precisely the two things §76-1429 forbids here, so the clause would be void in Nebraska in exactly the respects that make it worth having in Tennessee, while its limb (2) is already statutory under §76-1435. **Case-law flag (rule 21):** the annotations printed under §76-1429 record *SFI Ltd. Partnership 8 v. Carroll*, 288 Neb. 698, 851 N.W.2d 82 (2014), holding both that the Act "expressly upholds tenants' liability for negligent fire damage" and that because a specific statute does so, a lease provision doing the same cannot be void against public policy or unconscionable. Quoted from the annotation; **the opinion itself was not read**, so it needs case-law monitoring, not a bill watch. **Row: `edu-tenant-caused-damage-ne` (new).**

**Rule 27 — the seven topics no state had a row for. All seven answered; none had an NE row before today.**

| Topic | NE verdict | New row |
|---|---|---|

| `fees-as-rent` | **PRESENT** — §76-1410(13): "Rent means all payments to be made to the landlord under the rental agreement." No designation wording needed; the definition already does it | `edu-fees-as-rent-ne` |
| `landlord-self-cure` | **Confirmed absent** — no URLTA §4.105 analogue; whole-act battery (`charge … as rent`, `added to the rent`, `may cause the work to be done`) returns nothing | `edu-no-landlord-self-cure-ne` |
| `lease-completeness` | **Confirmed absent** — no blank-space rule (the single `blank` hit is the case name *Blankenau*), no lease-copy duty, and neither consumer statute lists those practices | `edu-no-lease-completeness-rule-ne` |
| `quiet-possession` | **Confirmed absent** as a lease covenant — §76-207 governs covenants "in conveyances of real property" breached by a paramount title holder, not landlord and tenant. Common-law covenant left open as unread doctrine | `edu-no-quiet-possession-covenant-ne` |
| `statutory-forms` | **Confirmed absent** — no prescribed lease or notice form; §§76-1441 and 76-1442 prescribe court documents only | `edu-no-statutory-forms-ne` |
| `tenant-security-cameras` | **Confirmed absent** — no installation right, no restriction. "in camera" is the dominant false positive, so every hit was reviewed | `edu-no-tenant-camera-rule-ne` |

**Rows: seven new education rows, one per topic key (rule 57).** The `fees-as-rent` row carries a product consequence, flagged not fixed: given §76-1410(13), an unpaid late fee **is** rent in Nebraska, so `default-by-tenant-ks-ne`'s sentence that failure to pay a late fee alone will not support termination gives away a route Nebraska law allows. Lawful — a landlord may always ask for less — but it should be a decision rather than an accident.

### Findings for other states or the product (flagged, not fixed)

1. **Fourteen dangling pointers in shared rows, belonging to other states' segments.** The same scan that found fix 15 turned these up; each sits in another state's `NE:`-style segment, so under the prompt's shared-row rule they were not touched. For their states' retros: `returned-payments` → `nsf-fee-limit-co`; `due-at-signing` → `security-deposit-cap-az`, `-nc`, `-ga`; `application-of-payments` → `application-of-payments-nj`; `security-deposit-use` → `security-deposit-return-va`, `-sd`; `existing-condition` → `move-in-inspection-az`; `no-alterations` → `portable-solar-va`, `tenant-use-rights-ca`; `entire-agreement` → `rent-increase-notice-ca`; `keys` → `dv-lease-termination-nc`, `-nv`; `common-area-use` → `flag-display-oh`. This is larger than the 11 the SOP 1.10 change log recorded from SC 5, so **the notes scan is worth re-running library-wide**.
2. **`application-of-payments-nj` supersedes `application-of-payments` while overlapping it on FL and NJ** — a live display collision, reported on 2026-09-27 and still present. Not Nebraska's to fix.
3. **Rule 62 proposal, not made — `default-by-tenant-ks-ne` (KS;NE;OH;NC).** Under AL 4 the no-cure carve-out should be its own sentence reaching every limb. Proposed text: keep the two limbs as they are and append as a separate sentence — *"Landlord need not give Tenant an opportunity to cure any breach, including a failure to pay Rent, where applicable law permits Landlord to proceed without one."* Nebraska-safe (it only tracks §76-1431(4), §76-1431(1)'s recurrence route and §71-2435), and I believe uniform, but I can vouch for it in Nebraska only — so under rule 62 it needs KS, OH and NC checked before any merge.

### Proposed SOP changes

1. **Rule 78 should say to scan every row in the state, not only the rows a prompt names.** The prompt named one dangling pointer; scanning all 120 NE-active rows found a second, plus fourteen in shared rows for other states. Cheap, mechanical, and it finds what a hand-built list misses.
2. **Rule 78 should distinguish a coverage pointer from a provenance note.** "See `id`" / "covered by `id`" dangles and must be repointed; "Moved from `id` by the three-bucket scrub" is accurate history and rewriting it destroys the audit trail. Four NE rows fell on the right side of that line and should not be "fixed".
3. **A library-wide pass that rewrites a shared clause should reset `last_checked` on every state row that DESCRIBES that clause, not only the clause itself.** `edu-holdover-ne` described "double the Monthly Rent" for four weeks after the figure was removed. A state row quoting a shared clause's text is a dependency, and nothing currently flags it.
4. **Rule 45 should say to read the state's electronic-transactions act itself, not just the landlord-tenant notice section.** Nebraska's §76-1413 is detailed and was already in the library, but its incorporation of the UETA meant two unwaivable constraints (§86-635(3) print-or-store, §86-632(3) refusal) sat unread. The exclusion list is where a state can quietly knock out eviction notices.
5. **Rule 54 should ask whether the statutory measure is conditional and what shape it takes.** §76-1437(3) looks like a complete holdover answer until you notice it applies only to a willful bad-faith holdover and is a lump rather than a daily rate — which is exactly where an optional lease clause earns its place. "Is there a statutory measure?" is the wrong question; "for which cases, and in what shape?" is the right one.

### Rule 35c — constitution screen

**Not already covered: NE's log says so explicitly** ("The SOP 1.11 constitution screen (row 35c) postdates this prompt and is due in NE's end-of-run circle-back", sync note 2026-09-30). Run now.

**The official search does not index the constitution, and rule 35's control test is what proved it.** The control term `Legislature` returned **2,678 results and every one was a statute section** — not a single constitution article among them. So a constitutional absence taken from that search would have been a clean negative proving nothing, exactly as the rule warns. Read article by article instead: **all 239 sections** (Preamble, Articles I–XVIII) fetched individually from `/laws/articles.php`, zero failures, **671,243 characters raw / 120,392 characters of operative text** once case annotations were stripped, normalised SHA-256 prefix **`bb04a3c123de07049a580dd743ccb464`**. Controls inside the corpus: `Legislature` 207, `Governor` 76.

| Target | Result |
|---|---|
| **Cannabis** | **ZERO hits** on `cannabis`, `marijuana`, `marihuana` in the operative text of all 239 sections. Nebraska has no constitutional cannabis provision, so **Missouri's art. XIV problem does not arise** and shared `smoking-policy`'s ban on vaping marijuana needs no NE override. Nebraska's medical-cannabis law came as an **initiative statute** (Initiative Law 2024, No. 437 → §§71-24,105 etc.), not an amendment, and an initiative statute creates no constitutional right against a private landlord. Recorded on `edu-medical-cannabis-ne` |
| **Firearms** | **FOUND — art. I-1.** A right to keep and bear arms "for security or defense of self, family, **home**, and others… and such rights shall not be denied or infringed **by the state or any subdivision thereof**" (Amended 1988, Initiative Measure No. 403). **New row `edu-firearms-ne`** |
| **Signs and speech** | **art. I-5** — "Every person may freely speak, write and publish on all subjects". Binds the state. `common-area-use`'s restriction on signs visible from outside is private action and already carves out displays the law entitles the tenant to make. **No conflict** |
| **Privacy** | **ZERO hits** on `privacy`, `private affairs` in the operative text. Art. I-7 (search and seizure) does not use the word and binds government. **No reach into a private lease** |
| **Leases / property** | **art. XII-8** — corporate and syndicate ownership and **leasing** of farm or ranch land. See below |

**The firearms finding fixes nothing and that is the finding.** Art. I-1's right runs against "the state or any subdivision thereof", so it does not void a private lease term — a privately owned Nebraska rental may restrict firearms by lease, and no Nebraska statute makes such a term unenforceable against a permit holder. No NE-tagged clause restricts firearms, so there was nothing to fix or override. But Nebraska had **no firearms row while fourteen other states do**, and the "subdivision" wording has two real edges worth a landlord knowing: a city or county could not compel landlords to ban firearms, and a public housing authority *is* bound where a private owner is not. That is the screen's product.

**Art. XII-8 is the case rule 35 warns about — and Nebraska's site handles it properly.** Adopted 1982 by Initiative Measure No. 300, it restricts corporations and syndicates from acquiring an interest in, or leasing, farm or ranch land. The official page carries: *"Note: This section is unconstitutional as a violation of the dormant Commerce Clause. Jones v. Gale, 470 F.3d 1261 (8th Cir. 2006)."* So unlike South Dakota's art. XXX, the invalidity **is** annotated on the official text. Doubly out of reach anyway: void, and agricultural rather than residential. **No action.** Nebraska's constitution ends at **Article XVIII** — there is no late initiated article of the kind the rule flags.

### Targeted fixes

**Fix 3 — the two optional clauses NE's retro found but did not draft. Both drafted.**

- **`holdover-rate-ne` (new, CONDITIONAL, `CONSTRAINED_TERM`).** §76-1437 re-read. The gap is real: §76-1437(3)'s measure applies only "if the tenant's holdover is willful and not in good faith", and it is a **lump** figure, so for an ordinary holdover Nebraska sets **no measure at all** — rule 54's "measures the statute doesn't set". Drafted on the `holdover-rate-az`/`-ga`/`-sc`/`-va`/`-al`/`-pa`/`-in`/`-mi` pattern and **reusing the existing `{{holdover_daily_rate}}` variable** (rule 60 — 11 rows already use it, so no new variable). **One Nebraska-specific change to that pattern, and it is why the clause is safe here:** AZ's text preserves the statutory willful-holdover amount *alongside* the daily charge. Nebraska's §76-1437(3) figure is a **ceiling on the total**, so stacking a contractual daily charge on top could exceed the statutory maximum — this row makes the two **alternative, not cumulative, for the same period**. Shared `holdover` stays tagged (companion clause, as in ten other states; no collision).
- **`casualty-landlord-termination-ne` (new, CONDITIONAL, `SERVES_LANDLORD`).** §76-1429 confers rights on the **tenant** only and says nothing about the landlord, and nothing in the URLTA bars the lease supplying one — so this is contract territory (CO was judged likely void; Nebraska is not CO). Drafted on the `casualty-landlord-termination-az`/`-ks` pattern, with two Nebraska adjustments: the accounting date is **the date of the casualty** (§76-1429(2)), and the closing sentence expressly preserves **both** of §76-1429(1)'s limbs **"whether or not Tenant caused the damage"** — because, as `edu-tenant-caused-damage-ne` records, §76-1429 is the one Nebraska exit route with **no tenant-fault exception** (contrast §§76-1425 and 76-1427, which each have one). A clause that quietly cut off a negligent tenant's §76-1429 exit would be void under §76-1415(1)(a) with §76-1415(2) exposure — that sentence is load-bearing, not boilerplate.

**Fix 4 — LB80 traced, and it corrects this chat's own note.** LB80 is 109th Legislature (2025), DocumentID 59055, introduced by **Senator Hallstrom** 2025-01-09: *"Adopt the Protection Orders Act, … provide for domestic violence victims to change rental agreements and request the changing of locks, and change provisions related to landlords and tenants."* Source lines read individually: **§76-1431.02 is LB80 §48, §76-1431.03 is §49, §76-1431.04 is §50** — three different act sections. The 2026-09-30 note said both .03 and .04 were §50, which is the rule 79 failure shape (right citation, wrong subdivision) committed in a note. **Did LB80 change the substance `edu-dv-tenant-rights-ne` relies on? No — and the answer is cleaner than "no change":** all three sections carry **only** a 2025 LB80 source line with no earlier Laws citation, so LB80 **created** the perpetrator-removal and lock-change scheme rather than amending one. There is no prior version whose substance could have changed, and the flag is closed. **Effective date:** no emergency clause on the bill page, so Nebraska's default applies — the 2025 session's general effective date, **2025-09-03**, corroborated from inside the code rather than from a secondary source, because §76-1413(13) fixes that same date for LB185 of the same session. **Not read:** LB80's slip-law PDF, which is where an emergency clause or split effective date would appear.

**Fix 5 — scrub-switched-off required clauses. None was carrying a statutorily required notice; nothing to restore.** Rule 78's own test applied first: *does the statute require the notice before or at the start of the tenancy?*

| Switched off | Statute | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| `security-deposit-return-ne` | §76-1416(2) — written itemization delivered **within fourteen days after termination** | **Termination-time notice.** Rule 78: never lease text. Correctly moved |
| `dv-lease-release-ne` | §76-1431.01(2)(b) — written notice runs **tenant → landlord**, in-tenancy | Not a landlord notice at all. Correctly moved |
| `dv-perpetrator-removal-ne` | §76-1431.02 — tenant-initiated, in-tenancy | Correctly moved |
| `dv-lockchange-ne` | §§76-1431.03, 76-1431.04 — tenant-initiated; §76-1431.04(4) is a landlord **cost right**, not a notice | Correctly moved |
| `casualty-termination-ne` | §76-1429 — tenant's notice to landlord, post-casualty | Correctly moved |

Rule 78 also requires searching the state's **required-content provisions**, not just each clause's own citation. Nebraska's only at-or-before-tenancy written requirements are **§76-1417** (owner and manager name and address "in writing at or before the commencement of the tenancy") and **§76-1413(7)(b)** (the clear and conspicuous statement before electronic-delivery consent). Both are already held — by `landlord-disclosure-ne` (`REQUIRED_DISCLOSURE`) and `edu-electronic-notice-regime-ne`. **The contrast with Arizona is the point:** AZ had a notice to restore because A.R.S. §33-1321(C) requires a *move-in* notice of the right to attend the move-out inspection. §76-1416 read section-open today has **no move-out inspection right at all**, so Nebraska has no such notice to carry.

**Fix 6 — `returned-payments`, rule 62 vouch. The AZ wording is lawful in Nebraska.** Changing "during the Term" to "during any 12-month period" is safe here, and the underlying concern is real in Nebraska too: §76-1437(4)/§76-1414(4) mean a tenancy with no fixed term is week-to-week or month-to-month, so a month-to-month Nebraska tenancy genuinely has no "Term" for the sentence to count against. Rule 62's two questions: (1) **can it drop a cure or notice Nebraska requires?** No — the clause governs replacing a failed payment method and charging a fee; no Nebraska statute attaches a cure or notice to either. (2) **does it change what the clause promises in Nebraska?** No — the NE note segment records only "generic mechanics, no NE-specific statutory language or number", with none of the "gives up" or "kept on purpose" language rule 62 says to look for first. **No Nebraska statute speaks to the counting period.** The near-misses, both read section-open: **§28-611** is criminal bad-check restitution ($10 plus any reasonable handling fee, on conviction) — not a civil cap; and **§45-918.01** does cap a returned-check charge at **fifteen dollars**, but only for a **licensee** on a **"delayed deposit transaction"**, i.e. payday lending, so it does not reach a landlord. **Vouched, no change needed.** Per rule 62 this verdict is recorded here, not in the shared row's notes, so `returned-payments` is untouched.

### Errors corrected in rows that shipped VERIFIED — both written by this chat

1. **`edu-no-statutory-forms-ne` (created 2026-09-30) was wrong.** It said Nebraska "supplies no statutory form for a residential lease, a disclosure, or **any notice a landlord gives a tenant**" and that "There is no prescribed wording you must copy." **§69-2304** provides that a notice under §69-2303 "shall contain one of the following statements, as appropriate" and then sets out **two statements verbatim** — one for property going to public sale with the surplus to the State Treasurer, one for property believed worth under two thousand dollars. That is prescribed text a landlord must copy. **How it happened matters more than the fix:** the row's notes recorded the boundary honestly ("Patterns run against the full URLTA text"), but the landlord-facing sentence was written as an unbounded statewide claim, and §69-2304 sits in **Chapter 69, outside the URLTA**. A correctly-scoped battery produced a correctly-scoped note and an over-broad claim, and the note stating the boundary did not stop the body from overreaching. Found by rule 79's re-read of a *different* row's citations, not by any forms search.
2. **`edu-dv-tenant-rights-ne`'s section attribution** — see fix 4.

### Findings for other states or the product (flagged, not fixed)

1. **The 29 research-pass rows with no basis on the row** (listed above) are a standing gap in NE, and the shape is unlikely to be Nebraska-only. Worth a library-wide count before it is screened state by state.
2. **§45-918.01's fifteen-dollar returned-check cap applies only to payday "delayed deposit" licensees.** Any state whose NSF row cites a general returned-check statute should check it is not a lender-only provision — this is the same trap as the "$10 is a civil cap" conflation already recorded for §28-611.
3. **A rate-limited search returns a clean zero.** The site served HTTP 429 mid-session and two batteries came back as 0 results. Any state whose absences were recorded in a long search session without a control term run *in the same batch* could be carrying a false negative.

### Integrity checks on the delta

### Proposed SOP changes

1. **Rule 19 should require the control term in the same batch as the battery, not once per session.** A rate-limited search (HTTP 429) returns 0 results, which is indistinguishable from a true absence. Two of today's batteries came back empty for that reason and would have shipped as absences. A control run an hour earlier proves nothing about the query that just returned zero.
2. **Rule 79's basis vocabulary should include "statute-wide search with terms and hit counts" as a first-class basis.** For an absence there is no section to read open, so the artifact *is* the search — and a keyword screen looking only for "section-open" miscounts those rows as having no basis. My own first count was inflated by seven rows for exactly this reason.
3. **Rule 19 (or 36) should say that a bounded battery licenses only a bounded claim.** `edu-no-statutory-forms-ne` recorded its boundary correctly ("the full URLTA text") and still shipped a statewide denial, which §69-2304 — one chapter away — falsified. Where a row's claim is broader than the corpus searched, the body must name the corpus, not just the notes.
4. **Rule 54 should say that where a statute caps the TOTAL recoverable, an optional lease charge must be alternative to the statutory remedy, not additional.** The house holdover-rate pattern preserves the statutory willful-holdover amount alongside the daily charge, which is right where the statute sets a floor or an independent remedy and wrong where §76-1437(3)-style wording caps the total.

## 1. Sources, channel and currency

Run 2026-10-29. Nebraska's second visit for this pass, after the first lost its output (below). 244
listed topics plus the named Nebraska items. Rows added, no existing row's text changed.

### What happened to the first pass, and what this one inherits

The pass of 2026-10-25 answered all 244 topics and built a 249-row delta. It never sent that delta
out of its workspace, and the workspace — a temporary cloud container — was reclaimed during a
four-day usage-limit pause. The corpus, the fourteen answer files, every drafted row, the research
file and the scripts went with it.

What survived is `NE-gaps-salvage.md`: the statutes the first pass verified section-open with their
Source lines, its currency findings, its findings on existing rows, its proposed topic questions and
its method lessons. **No drafted row text survived, so every row in this delta is written fresh.**
The salvage record is used as a map of where the law is, never as a citation: **every section relied
on here was re-opened in the corpus before being quoted** (rule 59).

Two procedural changes follow from the loss, and both are in force here. **The delta and this log are
written to `/mnt/user-data/outputs/` and delivered after every batch**, each delivery replacing the
last, so the workspace never holds the only copy. And a short running record goes to the Project
after each batch, where it survives the container entirely.

### Channel

**Primary channel — a local corpus of official text, verified before use.** Downloaded by Claude Code
from nebraskalegislature.gov on 2026-10-24 and extended on 2026-10-29 at the first pass's request.
It holds every section each chapter index lists for **twelve chapters — 18, 20, 25, 28, 29, 36, 40,
59, 69, 76, 86, 87 — 7,208 sections**, plus the **Nebraska Constitution** and the **363 slip laws** of
the 109th Legislature's 2025 and 2026 sessions. Sections are read whole, Source line included;
batteries run over the corpus text.

| Chapter | Sections | Chapter | Sections |
|---|---|---|---|
| 18 Cities and Villages | 807 | 59 Monopolies; Consumer Protection Act | 240 |
| 20 Civil Rights; Fair Housing Act | 166 | 69 Personal Property; Disposition Act | 446 |
| 25 Courts; forcible entry and detainer | 1,560 | 76 Real Property; URLTA and Mobile Home Act | 1,152 |
| 28 Crimes and Punishments | 797 | 86 Telecommunications and Technology | 677 |
| 29 Criminal Procedure | 1,066 | 87 Trade Practices | 202 |
| 36 Fraud and Voidable Transactions | 76 | 40 Homesteads | 19 |

**The six chapters added for this restart — 18, 28, 29, 36, 40 and 86 — are there because the first
pass found, by accident, that the law deciding whether a lease exists at all sat outside the six
chapters it had fetched.** § 36-105 makes a lease for longer than one year **void** without a writing
signed by the lessor; § 40-104 makes an instrument encumbering a married person's homestead **void**
without both spouses executing *and* acknowledging it. No Nebraska row in the library cites either.
That is recorded as a proposed SOP change: a corpus assembled from the subject matter of the
questions keeps missing the law of formation.

**Not held, and named in every row that touches them:** chapters 31, 45, 52, 66, 70, 71, 75, 77 and
**81** (state administrative departments, including the State Fire Marshal — left out for size at
3,837 sections) and the rest of the Revised Statutes; the Nebraska Administrative Code; Supreme Court
rules and court forms; case law (the annotations printed with a section are **leads only**, rule 1);
and city ordinances, which are flagged and not resolved (rule 3).

**Second channel — the official keyword search, for anything outside those twelve chapters.** The
shell cannot reach the statute endpoint (`curl` → 403 from the agent proxy; WebFetch →
`URL_NOT_ON_ALLOWLIST`), so out-of-corpus text is fetched centrally through the browser pane and
relayed. Canvassing agents have no route of their own: they file a request and the coordinator runs
it.

**Three properties of that search govern how its figures are read in §3, all verified directly rather
than assumed.** It **ANDs its words and ignores quotation marks**, so adding a word can only narrow a
result set and a five-word query returning zero proves very little on its own — every out-of-corpus
absence therefore pairs its targeted query with a **bare-term known-positive control**, and both
counts are recorded. It renders no result as "**No matches were found for your search**" rather than
"0 results", so a missing count is a true zero and not a failed page load. And a **small non-zero
count is frequently all false positives**, so every non-zero figure in §3 names its hits and says why
they do not answer the topic.

**Controls re-established for this corpus**, because the first pass's figures were measured on six
chapters and do not all carry over: `landlord` all twelve chapters → **137** sections; `landlord`
chapter 76 → **111**; `security deposit` → **3**; `zzqqxyzzy` → **0**. The chapter-76 figure matches
the first pass exactly, which is independent evidence the corpus text is the same.

**A figure from one channel is never quoted as a control for the other.** The first pass relayed
`water meter` → 9 as a local control; locally it is **0**, because those nine hits are in chapters
the corpus does not hold. A control that cannot be reproduced in the channel it is quoted in destroys
the only thing a control is for.

### Currency

Every row records the Source line of each section it relies on, plus a 2025/2026 slip-law check.
Four method points govern how those checks are read, each of which corrected work in the first pass:

**1. A slip-law search returns a false zero for a newly created section.** An act that *amends* a
section recites its number, so a text search finds it; an act that *creates* one enacts it as
"Sec. N." with no codified number. Worked example: searching the slip corpus for `76-1431\.0[234]`
returns **0 files**, yet § 76-1431.04's own Source line reads "Laws 2025, LB80, § 50" and LB80 is in
the corpus. **The Source line is the authority; the slip search is a supplement.** No absence here
rests on a slip-law zero alone.

**2. A slip-law hit is not an amendment.** Finding a section number in an act's text usually means a
cross-reference. Verified: `slip '76-1422'` returns LB185, but § 76-1422's Source line still ends
"Laws 1974, LB 293, § 22".

**3. The "landlord" keyword sweep has a blind spot, and in the first pass it fired three times.** It
finds acts using the word "landlord"; an act binding an **owner** without ever saying it is invisible.
Confirmed instances: **§ 81-503.01** (State Fire Code) amended by Laws 2025, **LB434**, § 4;
**§ 71-2518** amended by Laws 2025, **LB376**, § 23; and **§ 76-2711** ("Homeowner, defined") amended
by Laws 2025, **LB474**, § 109 — which changed the trigger term for both of chapter 76's translation
sections. So the eight-act table is reliable for *landlord-tenant* amendments and unreliable as a
general currency screen for owner-facing regulation. Where a topic turns on a regulatory duty rather
than a lease term, the section's own Source line is the only safe check.

**4. One section in the corpus carries text that is not yet in force.** A section page can show the
version an amendment will install, under an "Operative Date" notice, so reading it today can state a
rule that does not yet apply. The single forward-dated one is **§ 87-302 (Deceptive trade practices;
enumerated), operative January 1, 2027**, amended by Laws 2026, LB838, § 27. **Any row citing
§ 87-302 says which version it states.** This matters because § 87-303.07 makes a lease induced by a
violation of § 87-302 or § 87-303.01 "unenforceable by the seller or lessor" — the strongest
consumer-protection feature found in Nebraska — and its trigger is the section that changes.

## 3. Batteries for every absence

**124 of the 255 rows are confirmed absences.** Each battery ran the statute's own term of art and the everyday word, singular and plural, `\b`-anchored, with a known-positive control and a nonsense control **in the same command** — a broken pattern and a true absence both return zero, so a battery without both controls proves nothing. Every figure names the channel that produced it: the **local corpus** (12 chapters, listed in §1) or the **official site search**. A figure from one channel is never a control for the other.

### `accessory-dwelling-unit` — edu-no-accessory-dwelling-unit-rule-ne

Fisher, 32 Neb. 107, 48 N.W. 821 (1891)' — a debtor's-exemptions case from 1891, not a housing provision. Institutional student housing is regulated, if anywhere, in the University and state-college chapter, and an absence battery over the twelve held chapters proves nothing about it — which is why this row's claim is confined to a PRIVATE landlord and why § 76-1408(1) is quoted as the Act's own answer for institutional residence rather than a chapter-85 search being reported as one. Chapter 77 IS NOT HELD locally, so § 77-202 was readable only this way. slip '77-202' -w -> 7 files, 5 OF WHICH AMEND IT — LB209 (2025), LB647 (2025), LB1010 (2026), LB1114 (2026) and LB901 (2026) — so the round-ten caution that more than one act may amend the same section is understated here at FIVE, and subdivision (1)(d)(iv) appears identically in all five, which is why it can be stated. slip '\bdormitor' -> 4 files: LB1071 and LB261 (appropriations language, "dormitory rentals, dormitory operations and maintenance"), LB1072 (revenue from "the dormitories, residence halls, single-dwelling units, multiple-dwelling units", a cross-reference), and LB320 (2026), which defines "[h]otel" for the human-trafficking poster scheme to exclude "dormitories or facilities operated by an educational institution and regularly used to house students" — all four read at the match, none a landlord duty.

The word 'sunset' appears in exactly ONE section of the held corpus - '\bsunset\b' -> 1, s 25-21,185, where it is the 1992 contributory-negligence transition and nothing to do with landlord law. Where a doctrine would have to live, it does not: the Act's own applicability section, s 76-1448, read section-open, is a commencement provision in one sentence - 'The Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act applies to rental agreements entered into or extended or renewed after July 1, 1975' (Source: Laws 1974, LB 293, s 49; Laws 2001, LB 7, s 20) - and the Mobile Home Act's twin catchline is s 76-14,111 'Applicability of act'. A TITLE sweep confirms there is no other candidate: index 'exempt|exclusion|applicability|not governed' --ch 76 -> 28 sections, the landlord-tenant ones being ss 76-1408, 76-1430, 76-1431.02, 76-1448, 76-14,100 and 76-14,111. SLIP-LAW CHANNEL, as a cross-check and not as the proof. First, the figure corrected 2026-10-29: slip 'Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act' -> 2 FILES (LB185 with 4 occurrences, LB80 with 1), not the 0 this row and the brief's trap list both carried; the zero was a hard-wrap artefact and nesec.py gained soft-wrap repair at 19:51 on 2026-10-29. Both files are cross-references, not amendments of a section matching the pattern, and nothing in either is a sunset - LB185 is electronic delivery and LB80 is the domestic-violence set. Nothing in this row rests on that figure either way: a slip zero cannot prove an absence in the code, because the slip corpus holds only the 2025 and 2026 sessions and the Act dates from 1974. Second: slip '76-1449' -w -> 1 file (LB80, 2025) whose AMENDS line reads 'AMENDS 30 section(s) -- NONE matching the pattern, so this is a CROSS-REFERENCE', and the matched context is LB80's amended s 76-1401 - 'Sections 76-1401 to 76-1449 and sections 48 to 50 of this act shall be known and may be cited as' - i.e. the Act being EXTENDED, not sunset. Per the brief, note that the comma-anchoring subtlety matters here: the slip anchor rejects a comma only when a digit follows, precisely so that outright-repeal LISTS (where a repealed section would be named) are not suppressed, and no 76-14xx section appears in any 2025 or 2026 repeal list.

## 4. Decisions, and questions asked of Taylor

### 4.1 No questions were asked of Taylor in this pass, and that was deliberate

**Rule 76 asks that an uncertain point be put to Taylor with a recommendation. Nothing in this pass met
that bar, and the reason is worth stating rather than leaving as an absence.**

The restart instruction (Nebraska item 0) was explicit about method: use the salvage as a starting
point, re-open each section in the corpus before quoting it, follow Part 5's method lessons, do not
re-report Part 3's findings, carry Part 4 into the proposed topic questions. The scope fence was
equally explicit: add rows, tag shared rows, change nothing else, report problems rather than fix them.
Between those two instructions there was no point at which a wrong guess could not be undone by editing
a row that had not yet been synced.

Where a legal question could not be settled, the standing instruction is **not** to ask Taylor — it is
to write the row as `NEEDS_REVIEW`, name the open question precisely with both readings, and state the
cautious course. That is what happened **17 times**, listed in § 2. Those are not deferred questions
for Taylor; they are questions for a source this session cannot reach, almost always Nebraska case law
(rule 1) or a chapter outside the corpus.

Two further constraints removed the usual reasons to ask. The prompt forbids asking Taylor for landlord
experience outside Colorado or to buy a lease, which rules out the two questions a canvass of this kind
would otherwise generate. And the work ran unattended for most of its length, where a question would
simply have stalled it.

**The one thing that would have been worth asking, had Taylor been present, is recorded in § 4.3 as a
recommendation instead:** whether the two shared-clause defects found in this pass should be fixed
across all their states rather than only noted for Nebraska. That is a library-wide editorial decision,
it is reversible, and it is Taylor's to make — so it is put as a recommendation with the evidence
attached, not as a blocking question.

### 4.2 Decisions taken without asking

**On the restart itself.**

1. **The first pass's tooling was rebuilt from scratch rather than reused.** Four faults from the first
   pass are designed out of `nesec.py` by construction rather than fixed on discovery: comma-style
   section numbers (320 of 3,766 sections had printed as "None", § 76-14,109 among them), silently
   ignored flags, unlabelled channel, and the absence of a title sweep. The cost was perhaps an hour;
   the first pass lost more than that to each of those faults individually.
2. **The delivery pipeline was built and proved before the first batch landed, not after.** The first
   pass's 249-row delta was built, validated, and never sent out of the container, which is why it is
   gone. `deliver.sh` existed and had been run end-to-end before batch 01 produced a single row.
3. **Every agent correction is re-run or re-opened by the coordinator before it is written into shared
   briefing material.** This was adopted after the third batch offered a correction that did not
   survive checking — an agent had read a per-file occurrence count as a file count and concluded that
   the slip-law false zero reaches amended sections. Had that gone into the brief unchecked, every
   later batch would have inherited a wrong currency rule. **Of the corrections offered across thirteen
   batches, the great majority held; three did not**, and all three are retracted in place in the brief
   with the output that disproves them rather than silently dropped.
4. **Two of my own errors are recorded the same way**, because a log that only catches agents' mistakes
   is not an audit. I wrote a battery figure into a row without running it (`'construction lien'` → 0;
   it returns 5). And my § 28-826 entry gave the cross-reference range without identifying it, next to
   chapter-28 drug material — §§ 28-807 to 28-829 is the **obscenity** article, so anyone reading that
   entry as covering drug use in a rental would have overstated it badly. Both are corrected in place.
   Three further errors of mine were in the agent-facing instructions themselves and are at § 4.4.

**On scope and method.**

5. **Rule 62 was applied strictly: not one existing row was edited.** The pass found **88** problems in
   existing rows and fixed none of them. Several are errors running in the landlord's favour, which is
   the dangerous direction — `edu-violent-crime-eviction-ne` would have a landlord use a five-day route
   the statute forbids; `edu-alt-housing-self-help-ne` overstates a ceiling roughly fourfold in a
   weekly tenancy; `edu-eviction-process-ne` describes the forcible-entry article as a parallel route
   when § 25-21,219 excludes URLTA premises outright. Each is quoted against the statute in § 6 for
   Claude Code to fix at sync. **Tagging a shared row with NE was treated as the only permitted edit**,
   and done 22 times.
6. **Where a lawful option was considered and declined, it still earned an education row** (rule 54),
   and where research turned up a genuinely separate subject, it was filed as an extra row rather than
   crowded into the topic's row (rule 7). Five extra rows resulted.
7. **An absence was never reported without a battery.** 118 of 118 confirmed absences carry one, each
   naming its channel, and each run with a known-positive and a nonsense control in the same command.
   The validator rejects an ABSENT row whose battery does not name its channel.
8. **Figures from the two channels were never mixed.** `water meter` → 0 in the local corpus against 9
   on the official site search is the clearest case: both are correct for their channel and neither is
   a control for the other.

**On the agents.**

9. **Two at a time, thirteen batches, each saving to its answer file after every topic.** The cap is
   the prompt's. The save-after-every-topic rule is the lesson of the lost first pass, and it earned
   itself back: batches re-appended corrected lines throughout, and nothing had to be redone.
10. **The agent brief became the authoritative artefact, with corrections appended as dated rounds that
    override earlier text.** It reached **thirteen rounds and about 133 KB**. Appending rather than
    editing was chosen so that a later reader can see what was believed and when it changed; the one
    exception is where leaving the original text in place would mislead, and there the original was
    corrected in place with a forward pointer to the round that corrected it.

### 4.3 Recommendations that need Taylor's decision

These are library-wide and reversible, so they are recommendations rather than questions. Each has its
evidence in § 6 or § 7.

1. **The door-posting delivery option should probably come out of `scheduled-services-entry-la` in
    every URLTA state, not just be noted for Nebraska.** Uniform URLTA § 1.202's receipt list excludes
    posting, as Neb. § 76-1413(2)(c) does, so the option is defective in all eight of that row's
    states, not only this one. **Recommendation: remove it library-wide.**
2. **`showing-notice-la` should be rewritten as a standing-schedule clause** — one proper notice
    covering a defined series of showings, with stated purpose and window — rather than patched. It
    currently has four independent defects in Nebraska, and **Colorado and Kansas are on its tag list
    and both have entry statutes**, so the defects are not Nebraska-specific. A standing-schedule
    clause is lawful in a mandatory-content state and depends on no waiver. **Recommendation: rewrite,
    then re-tag.**
3. **The figure taxonomy should carry five shapes, not three**, and the reading test that produces
    them — *read the five words before any statutory figure* — should go into the SOP. It repaired
    three mis-sorted Nebraska figures in one batch. **Recommendation: adopt both** (proposed SOP change
    at the end of this log).
4. **`late-fee-ne` carries `lease_clause_basis` = CONSTRAINED_TERM while no Nebraska statute constrains
    a residential late fee.** The row is shared, so the basis may have been set correctly for another
    state. **Recommendation: check the other states before changing it; for Nebraska alone the basis
    would be SERVES_LANDLORD.**
5. **`entire-agreement` needs a scope note, not an edit.** Against § 76-1410(14)'s "all agreements,
    written or oral", it is either an ordinary integration clause or a term removing a § 76-1425
    remedy. **Recommendation: add the scope note; do not resolve the tension in the clause text.**
6. **`inspection-rights` needs three words.** "Tenant will allow Landlord to perform periodic
    inspections" against § 76-1423(1)'s "shall not **unreasonably** withhold consent".
    **Recommendation: restore the qualifier.**
7. **Run a library-wide screen for attorney-fee and collection-cost shifts in NE-tagged clauses before
    sync.** § 76-1415(1)(c) bars the fee-shift in **both** directions, so such a clause is partly
    unenforceable with § 76-1415(2) damages plus fees on deliberate use. The screen was not run in this
    pass and is not aimed at a named row. **Recommendation: run it at sync.**

### 4.4 Three errors in my own instructions to the agents, and what they cost

Recorded because they are the pass's most reproducible failure mode, and all three were mine rather
than any agent's.

1. **The validator command in the agent instruction file was wrong** — it named a single answer file
   where `validate.py` takes a topic list and a directory, and dies with `IndexError`. **Two agents
   diagnosed a tool they had no reason to distrust** before it was corrected. The command had never
   been run as written.
2. **The instructions told agents to "report" findings and never said to file them.** Two numbered
   sections of this log are generated from the JSONL fields `findings_existing_rows` and
   `findings_other_states`. One batch reported four findings on existing rows and filed none; all four
   would have been dropped from this deliverable and lost with the session. Fixed in the instructions,
   and the batch was asked to file them. **The pipeline summary now reports findings filed per batch,
   because the whole-pass total cannot show a zero contribution** — which is why this went unnoticed
   for a batch.
3. **The brief's trap list was carried forward from a six-chapter corpus into a twelve-chapter one, and
   every entry was provisional without saying so.** Five entries needed their figures repaired
   (`\bcarpets?\b` 7→8, `background check` 2→3→4, `\bmaster key` 7→9, `\bresort` 7→16, `\bwells?\b`
   69→137), and **twice an entry concealed a chapter-28 criminal duty that was the whole substance of a
   topic** — `\bresort` hid § 28-417(1)(e), `\bmaster key` hid § 28-1316. One entry's stated **reason**
   was wrong rather than its figure (`\bvacation`, explained as employment leave when the dominant
   sense is judicial), which is the worse defect: a plausible wrong explanation is a standing
   instruction to skip the hit list.
