## 5. The independent check

Rule 80, scaled to this pass as the prompt directs: **at most two rounds, one agent at a time**, the
second re-checking only rows edited after the first.

### 5.1 How round one was set up

The checker was given the answer files, the row schema, the corpus tool and the delta, and was **told
not to read `AGENT-BRIEF.md`** — the briefing every canvassing agent worked from. That was deliberate:
a checker reading the brief would re-verify the canvass against its own premises and produce an echo
rather than a check. It was asked to get any fact it needed from the corpus instead, and to be
adversarial but to quote the statute wherever it thought something was wrong, on the ground that a
false alarm costs as much as a miss.

It ran three exhaustive automated passes over all 333 JSONL lines before opening a single statute —
attributed-quote presence against the whole 7,589-file corpus (1,326 fragments), figure reproduction
(1,156 claims re-executed), and anchoring-trap detection — then used that output to choose where to
read. **1,056 of 1,156 figure claims reproduced exactly on the first pass.** It re-ran all 100
non-reproducing claims individually; 86 were artefacts of its own parser and **14 were real**.

### 5.2 What it found, and the most important finding is the coordinator's

**The headline defect is mine, and it is the one I had already written an SOP proposal about.** I
changed the corpus tool's matching semantics **twice in the middle of the pass** — adding soft-wrap
repair, and making the chapter filter key on the section number rather than the file's directory — and
I re-ran the **statute controls** afterwards but **not the figures already written into rows**. File
times confirm the shape exactly: `nesec.py` last changed at 19:51; batches 01–09 and the coordinator's
own file were written between 17:16 and 19:47, batches 10–13 between 20:46 and 21:41.

So **fourteen figures in already-written rows went stale**, and the two rows the checker reported as
"contradicting each other" — one saying `background check` → 3, another → 4 — were each correct when
written, with my fix landing between them. The conclusions resting on those figures survive; the
figures as printed do not reproduce. This is precisely the failure that proposed SOP change 32 exists
to prevent ("when a shared helper changes, re-run the commands that depend on it against known-good
output"), committed by the person who wrote it.

**And it falsified one of my own briefing rules on its own evidence.** Round seven of the brief told
every later agent that "a slip-law zero on an act NAME proves nothing", citing
`slip 'Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act'` → **0 files** against `'Medical Assistance Act'`
→ 15. Re-run now: **2 files and 19 files.** The zero was a **hard-wrap artefact of my own unfixed
tool** — the sessions did name the URLTA, in LB185 and LB80 — not evidence that a session corpus can
fail to name an act. The *rule* survives for a better reason, which is the one round fourteen gives: a
session-law corpus covers only the sessions it holds, so a zero there can never establish absence in
law. But the evidence offered for it was wrong, and a row (`tpa-sunset`) had reasoned from the bad
figure.

**The one defect that materially exposes a landlord** was a genuine drafting error, found by reading the
statute: **`criminal-activity` dropped a condition precedent from § 76-1431(4)(c)**. The statute makes
"possession of a controlled substance" a five-day no-cure ground only "**if the tenant knew or should
have known of the possession**"; the row carried the medical-order exception and silently dropped the
scienter element, while telling the landlord it may terminate "on five days' written notice with no
right for Tenant to cure". A landlord acting on the row would use the no-cure route where the statute
requires knowledge.

**Also found:** thirteen `battery` fields in one batch with their backslashes stripped (`bfines?b` for
`\bfines?\b`), so the patterns as printed return 0 and the batteries are not re-runnable — for one
absence row, three of the five supporting zeros were, as printed, zeros no literal string could avoid;
**`holding-deposit`** calling § 76-1416(3)'s "an amount equal to … whichever is less" a **ceiling**
when it is a fixed sum, an error in the landlord's favour and inconsistent with `statutory-caps`;
**twenty-three rows** quoting a scope string the tool does not print, in the generous direction, some of
which then list as unread chapters whose stray sections were in fact swept; and three unmarked
quotation defects, including three sentences of § 25-2803(3) presented as contiguous with their order
inverted and four sentences excised, plus the omission of § 25-2803(4), which bars a successor landlord
from suing in Small Claims on the predecessor's rent.

### 5.3 What held

Reported because the coverage of a check is part of its result, and because "I checked X and it holds"
is a finding.

- **The five-words-before-a-figure test holds throughout.** All 33 rows using a "whichever is" formula
  get it right. § 76-1430 is correctly a fixed sum with willfulness correctly attached to only the
  diminution limb; § 76-1438(2) is called a **floor** in every row that touches it; § 76-1427(1)'s
  ceiling is correctly flagged as available only on a deliberate failure. The sole exception is
  `holding-deposit` above.
- **No understated notice requirement anywhere.** Every statement of § 76-1431(1) across 24 rows, and
  of § 76-1431(2)'s seven calendar days, is right. Across 47 mentions of the § 76-1423(3)(a) entry
  notice, **none** states twenty-four hours as a ceiling, and two expressly call it a floor.
- **§ 76-1439's landlord-favouring provisos are carried where they matter** — every rent-increase row
  carries (2)'s savings clause, every possession row carries (3)(a)–(c).
- **All 124 ABSENT rows have a battery naming its channel with both controls**, checked
  programmatically, zero gaps. The two documented anchoring traps are **not** present: no row uses a
  trailing `\b` after a two-word phrase, and no row uses a bare `cable`.
- **The checker tried independently to break four ABSENT verdicts and could not**, running its own
  probes (`\bbonds?\b --ch 76` → 21, `supersedeas|stay of (execution|proceedings)` --ch 76 → 1) and
  surfacing nothing the rows had missed.
- **Structure is clean on all 255 rows:** every education row has an empty `lease_clause_basis`, every
  LEASE_CLAUSE row has one of the three, every `rule_type` token is permitted, every row carries NE, no
  `states` cell contains a comma, and all 22 tagged rows have NE appended semicolon-delimited with an
  `NE:` segment. It also confirmed that `gen.py` correctly keeps the answer row for each of the 17
  topics whose **last** JSONL line is a `NEEDS_SECTION`.
- **Dollar and day figures check verbatim** across §§ 25-2802(4), 25-21,276(2)(b), 40-101, 69-2110,
  76-1416(2) and 76-1446.

### 5.4 What it could not reach, in its own terms

The checker had **no browser channel**, so it could neither confirm nor impeach anything sourced to the
OFFICIAL SITE SEARCH — every chapter-71 quote, the asbestos and lead material, the ADU figure. Those
rows are correctly labelled by channel, and the checker said so rather than treating them as suspect.

It did not reach **19 of the 22 tagged rows'** library `bodyText` against Nebraska law, and named that
as the likeliest remaining place for a landlord-adverse error, since a tag imports another state's
drafting wholesale; the three it did check were clean. It did not have the existing library to verify
the `findings_existing_rows` content against. And it flagged the limit of its own method honestly: it
treated quoted prose as in scope only where a quotation mark sat within 170 characters of a section
citation, so **a row that paraphrases a statute loosely without quoting it would pass unflagged.**

It also named two readings the project asserts that the text cannot settle: whether § 76-1431(1)'s
six-month recurrence route is genuinely "no cure" (asserted in about eight rows, textually tied to the
first sentence, no row flagging it), and whether a lease fee is "rent" so that § 76-1431(2)'s seven-day
route reaches it — which **`required-fees` expressly leaves open while two other rows state it as
settled.** Both are landlord-favouring. Neither is resolvable from the corpus; both are now flagged.

### 5.5 Round two

Round two was scoped, as the rule requires, to the rows edited after round one: the repair pass acting
on §§ 5.2's findings — the § 76-1431(4)(c) scienter restoration, the thirteen battery fields, the
figure-shape correction, the fourteen stale figures re-run at current tool semantics, the twenty-three
scope strings, and the three quotation defects. Each repaired figure was **re-run by the repairing
agent at the scope its row states** rather than copied from the check's report.

**Round two also corrected the check itself, twice.** The scope-string defect was **33 rows, not 23** —
twelve attributing the wrong string to the tool, twenty-one stating the same wrong form as the channel
without naming it. And one of the check's findings was **misattributed**: the dropped § 76-1433
fragment is not in `security-deposit-holding`, which contains no reference to § 76-1433 at all, but in
`rent-installments`. Finding the real row took a sweep of every answer file for the quoted sentence
rather than a spot-check. The check was right about the defect and wrong about its location, which is
the ordinary division of labour between a check and a repair.

**And round two found a defect that round one's premises concealed: the soft-wrap repair creates a new
class of false positive, and `\b` anchoring cannot suppress it.** With wraps repaired, an unanchored
multi-word pattern reaches across a line-broken hyphenated compound — `'day care'` now matches inside
"day-to-day\ncare" at § 29-2260.02 — and because a hyphen is a non-word character the anchored form
`'\bday care\b'` returns the same spurious hit. Nothing in the pattern can exclude it; only opening
the hit can. So the fix that recovered three understated figures introduced this, and **any figure that
ROSE after wrap repair needs its new hits opened before it is quoted.**

**Nothing in the check required a row to be withdrawn.** Every substantive conclusion survived; what
failed was reproducibility — figures that no longer re-run, batteries that cannot be re-executed as
printed, a scope string quoted wrongly — plus one dropped condition precedent and one mislabelled
figure shape. That distinction is worth recording, because reproducibility is the thing a later reader
actually tests, and it degraded silently while the substance held.

## 6. Findings on existing rows

This pass adds rows and changes none. Where research showed an existing row looked wrong or incomplete, the statute and the row's own words are quoted for Claude Code to act on. Defects already listed in Part 3 of `NE-gaps-salvage.md` are **not** repeated here — Claude Code is fixing those in parallel — so everything below is new.

### Found while answering `abandonment-and-mitigation`

NEW FINDING, not in the salvage record's Part 3, offered as a re-audit question rather than a flat error. `early-termination-ne` (NE, topic early-termination, LEASE_CLAUSE, SERVES_LANDLORD) says in its own words: 'Tenant will pay an early termination fee equal to one month's Rent ({{monthly_rent}}) or 30% of the remaining Rent due under the Term, whichever is greater, and remains responsible for Rent and other obligations up to the termination date.' Nebraska gives the landlord only an actual-damages measure once the agreement ends - § 76-1435: the landlord 'may have a claim for rent and a separate claim for actual damages for breach of the rental agreement' - subject to § 76-1405(1) ('The aggrieved party has a duty to mitigate damages'), and § 76-1432(3) makes re-letting terminate the agreement as of the date the new tenancy begins. A greater-of formula reaching 30% of the remaining term can therefore exceed anything the Act lets the landlord recover, and it is payable whether or not the unit is re-let the following week. Two things cut the other way and are why this is a question and not an assertion: § 76-1414(1) permits 'terms and conditions not prohibited by' the Act, and an early-exit option is a bargained right the Act does not give the tenant, so the fee may be consideration for a release rather than a waiver of a remedy. Neither this row's bodyText nor its notes names § 76-1432(3) or § 76-1435. Worth a re-audit against Nebraska's liquidated-damages-versus-penalty case law, which is not in the corpus. Separately and for the record, no defect found: `default-by-tenant-ks-ne`'s mitigation promise ('to the extent required by applicable law') is correct for Nebraska.

### Found while answering `accessory-dwelling-unit`

NEW FINDING, a gap rather than an error. No Nebraska row cites § 18-1758. A screen of the 140 NE-tagged rows for 'short-term rental' in bodyText returns exactly one, and it is the other way round: `no-sublet-assign` (49 states incl. NE) says 'Tenant will not rent the property, or any portion of the property, through any short-term rental program such as Airbnb, VRBO, or similar service, and doing so will be cause for termination of this Lease by Landlord.' That clause is lawful — § 18-1758 restrains MUNICIPALITIES, not landlords, and § 18-1758(7) expressly leaves private restrictions alone, while § 76-1414(1) permits the term — so no defect, but it means the library's only Nebraska mention of short-term rentals is a prohibition on the tenant and nowhere records the landlord's own statutory shield. That shield is a substantive omission beyond this topic: § 18-1758(2) is a state preemption of any municipal ordinance that 'expressly or effectively prohibits the use of a property as a short-term rental', § 18-1758(3) confines municipal regulation to measures whose primary purpose the municipality can demonstrate is public health and safety, § 18-1758(6) requires land-use rules to be applied to a short-term rental 'in the same manner as another similar property', and § 18-1758(5) lists the only five purposes for which use may be limited or prohibited. A Nebraska landlord letting by the night or the week has a statutory shield no row mentions, and the library has topics where it belongs. Also uncited by any row, and relevant here: § 76-1410(16)'s two-limb single-family-residence test, which the salvage record identifies as the gate on § 76-1419(2); the salvage record's Part 3 item 4 already records the § 76-1419(1) defects in the habitability rows and is not re-reported.

### Found while answering `association-obligations-disclosure`

NEW FINDING, a gap rather than a misstatement. `hoa-compliance` (50 states incl. NE) says in its own words: 'If the property is located within a homeowner or condominium association, Tenant will comply with the association's rules and regulations applicable to the property. Any fines incurred due to Tenant's violation of association rules will be Tenant's responsibility.' It is lawful in Nebraska, but it leans on rules the tenant may never have been given, and § 76-1422(6) makes a rule enforceable against the tenant 'only if ... the tenant has notice of it at the time he enters into the rental agreement', with a later-adopted rule enforceable only on reasonable notice and only if it 'does not work a substantial modification of his bargain.' A clause that promises compliance with an undisclosed rule book is not void - it is simply hollow for any rule the tenant was not given, so the fines limb may not be collectible. The clause also says 'rules and regulations' where § 76-1421(8) reaches 'bylaws, covenants, rules or regulations', so it claims less than Nebraska law gives the landlord. Both points are addressed in this row's bodyText rather than by editing the shared row (the fence). Separately, no Nebraska row cites § 76-868 or § 76-876, so the lessee-voting and lessee-records consequence of a declaration is new ground.

### Found while answering `criminal-activity`

NEW finding (not in salvage Part 3), on `edu-violent-crime-eviction-ne` [expedited-criminal-eviction]. Its bodyText states the § 76-1431(5) limit as: "you can't use this against a tenant who is themselves a domestic-violence victim if they've taken protective steps (a protective order, a police report, or DV certification from a qualified third party)." The statute is broader and differently structured. § 76-1431(5)(a) reads: "A landlord shall not take action under subsection (4) of this section if the violent criminal activity, illegal sale of any controlled substance, or other activity that threatens the health or safety of other tenants, the landlord, or the landlord's employees or agents, as set forth in subsection (4) of this section, is conducted by a person on the premises other than the tenant or a household member and the tenant or household member takes at least one of the following measures: (i) The tenant or household member seeks a protective order, restraining order, or other similar relief which would apply to the person conducting such activity; (ii) The tenant or household member reports such activity to a law enforcement agency in an effort to initiate a criminal action against the person conducting the activity; or (iii) If the activity is an act of domestic violence, the tenant or household member receives certification ..." Two consequences. First, measures (i) and (ii) are NOT domestic-violence-specific: the limit protects any tenant who seeks protective relief against, or reports to law enforcement, a third party's qualifying activity — the row's "a tenant who is themselves a domestic-violence victim" wrongly confines it, and a landlord relying on the row would believe the five-day route is available where § 76-1431(5)(a)(ii) forbids it. Second, the row omits the gating condition that the activity be "conducted by a person on the premises other than the tenant or a household member", which is what makes the limit coherent with (5)(b). The error runs AGAINST the tenant and in the landlord's favour, so it is the kind the fence's own-direction check asks for. Not fixed here (fence: add rows, do not change existing ones).

### Found while answering `dv-eviction-protection`

edu-violent-crime-eviction-ne (topic expedited-criminal-eviction, NE, VERIFIED) states Section 76-1431(5) too narrowly in two respects, in its landlord-facing bodyText. (1) IT DROPS THE GATE. The row's words: "Important carve-out: you can't use this against a tenant who is themselves a domestic-violence victim if they've taken protective steps (a protective order, a police report, or DV certification from a qualified third party)". The statute's words: "A landlord shall not take action under subsection (4) of this section if the violent criminal activity ... is conducted by a person on the premises OTHER THAN THE TENANT OR A HOUSEHOLD MEMBER and the tenant or household member takes at least one of the following measures" (Section 76-1431(5)(a)). The row makes the bar turn on the tenant's victim status plus protective steps; the statute makes it turn first on WHO conducted the activity. On the row's wording a landlord would believe the fast track is blocked where the tenant or a household member committed the conduct, which is the opposite of the statute. (2) IT TREATS THE WHOLE SUBSECTION AS DOMESTIC-VIOLENCE-SPECIFIC. Only (5)(a)(iii) is: (i) is "seeks a protective order, restraining order, or other similar relief which would apply to the person conducting such activity" and (ii) is "reports such activity to a law enforcement agency in an effort to initiate a criminal action against the person conducting the activity" - neither mentions domestic violence, so any tenant who takes (i) or (ii) against a third party's qualifying activity is protected. The row therefore understates the protection's reach while mislabelling it, and its "a police report" is looser than (ii)'s "in an effort to initiate a criminal action against the person conducting the activity". WORDING I WOULD USE, if the row were being edited: "Important carve-out, and read it precisely. If the violent criminal activity, drug sale or other health-or-safety-threatening conduct was conducted by someone on the premises OTHER than the tenant or a member of the tenant's household, and the tenant or household member either (a) seeks a protective or restraining order against the person who did it, (b) reports it to law enforcement in an effort to get that person charged, or (c) where the conduct was domestic violence, obtains certification from a qualified third party under federal VAWA, then you may not use the five-day route against that tenant - whether or not domestic violence is involved. If the tenant or a household member was the one who did it, this carve-out does not apply at all. And where the victim and the perpetrator are both on the lease, you must proceed against the perpetrator only (Section 76-1431(5)(b); Section 76-1431.02(3))." The row is otherwise accurate, and it does correctly confine the bar to the subsection (4) route rather than to the whole section.

### Found while answering `dv-lockchange`

`keys` (shared, 44 states incl. NE, LEASE_CLAUSE, topic keys). Read against Nebraska's fee rules and Sections 76-1431.03 and 76-1431.04 as asked. THE COST-MEASURE CONFLICT IS ALREADY ON RECORD and is not re-reported here. TWO FURTHER POINTS THAT ARE NOT. (1) THE CLAUSE IS OVERRIDDEN BY STATUTE AND SAYS NOTHING ABOUT IT. The row's words: "Tenant may not duplicate keys without Landlord's consent", and the clause reserves re-keying to Landlord ("Landlord may re-key the applicable locks and charge the cost to Tenant"). Section 76-1431.04(2)(a) provides that if a landlord fails to change the locks as required, the tenant "[m]ay change the locks in a workmanlike manner with locks of similar or better quality than the original lock", "[s]hall timely notify the landlord" and "[s]hall, by a reasonable method agreed upon by the landlord and tenant, provide the landlord with a new key or the entry code" - and Section 76-1431.04(2)(b) says in terms: "This subsection applies notwithstanding any provision in the rental agreement to the contrary." So where a tenant has made a Section 76-1431.03 request and the landlord misses the twenty-four hours in Section 76-1431.03(3), the tenant may lawfully change the lock without consent and is not in breach of the keys clause. A landlord relying on the clause as written would treat that as a lease violation. (2) THE CLAUSE LEAVES A LANDLORD RIGHT ON THE TABLE (rule 54 shape). Section 76-1431.04(3): "A landlord who installs a new lock pursuant to this section may retain a copy of the key or entry code that opens the new lock." The keys clause claims no such right for a statutory lock change, and the tenant-performed change under (2)(a)(iii) obliges the tenant to supply a key or code - so the landlord's key-holding position is better than the clause describes. WORDING I WOULD USE, as an added sentence rather than an edit to the existing text: "Where applicable law requires Landlord to change a lock at Tenant's request, Landlord will do so as that law requires, may retain a copy of the new key or entry code, and may charge Tenant only the actual and reasonable cost Landlord incurs; if Landlord does not change the lock when required to, Tenant may change it as that law permits without breaching this Section, and will promptly give Landlord a new key or entry code." One further note, not a conflict: Section 76-1415(1)(c) does NOT reach a re-key charge, because it voids only a term by which the tenant "[a]grees to pay the landlord's or tenant's attorney's fees" - a key charge is not a fee award. But Section 76-1410(13) defines rent as "all payments to be made to the landlord under the rental agreement", so the charge is rent in Nebraska, reachable by the Section 76-1431(2) seven-day nonpayment notice and swept into every figure the Act measures in rent.

### Found while answering `ev-charging-requirements`

`hoa-compliance` (shared, 50 states incl. NE, LEASE_CLAUSE, topic hoa-compliance). Read against Nebraska's fee rules including Section 76-1415(1)(c) and against Sections 76-1431.03 and 76-1431.04 as asked. NO CONFLICT WITH THE LOCK-CHANGE SECTIONS: nothing in Sections 76-1431.03 or 76-1431.04 touches association rules or fines, and an association rule cannot displace the twenty-four-hour duty, which Section 76-1431.04(2)(b) protects "notwithstanding any provision in the rental agreement to the contrary". THREE NEBRASKA POINTS ON THE FEE SIDE. (1) THE FINE PASS-THROUGH IS LAWFUL, BUT ITS BREADTH IS THE PROBLEM. The row's words: "Any fines incurred due to Tenant's violation of association rules will be Tenant's responsibility." A fine is not an attorney's fee, so Section 76-1415(1)(c) does not reach it on its face. But Nebraska condominium declarations commonly assess the unit owner the association's enforcement costs and counsel fees alongside the fine, and Section 76-873(b) lets the association charge interest on a past-due assessment "at the rate established by the association not exceeding eighteen percent per year". An undifferentiated "any fines incurred" therefore passes an attorney-fee component of the landlord's own liability to the tenant, which is what Section 76-1415(1)(c) voids - "[a]grees to pay the landlord's or tenant's attorney's fees" - with Section 76-1415(2) adding the tenant's actual damages and reasonable attorney's fees if the landlord "deliberately uses a rental agreement containing provisions known by him or her to be prohibited". (2) THE CLAUSE IS WIDER THAN THE STATUTORY DUTY IT TRACKS. Section 76-1421(8) already obliges the tenant to "[a]bide by all bylaws, covenants, rules or regulations of any applicable condominium regime, cooperative housing agreement, or neighborhood association NOT INCONSISTENT WITH LANDLORD'S RIGHTS OR DUTIES." The clause carries no such qualifier, so as written it binds the tenant to an association rule that cuts across the landlord's own obligations under the Act - and because Section 76-1415(1)(a) voids a term by which the tenant waives rights or remedies under the Act, the overbroad part is the part that fails. (3) THE FINE BECOMES RENT. Section 76-1410(13): rent is "all payments to be made to the landlord under the rental agreement." A fine the lease makes payable to the landlord is rent, so nonpayment is reachable by the Section 76-1431(2) seven-day notice - useful - and it is swept into the figures the Act measures in rent, including the Section 76-1416(1) "one month's periodic rent" ceiling, where the effect is unresolved in both directions. WORDING I WOULD USE: "If the property is located within a homeowner or condominium association, Tenant will comply with the association's rules and regulations applicable to the property, except to the extent a rule is inconsistent with Landlord's rights or duties under applicable law. Tenant will reimburse Landlord for the amount of any fine the association assesses against Landlord or the property because of Tenant's violation of those rules, excluding any attorney's fees, enforcement costs or interest included in the association's charge, and Landlord will give Tenant a copy of the association's assessment." Not changed; reported only.

### Found while answering `family-child-care`

NEW FINDING, not in salvage Part 3. § 29-4017 is a concrete, non-obvious landlord consequence of a licensed child care facility and it appears nowhere in the project's record. A political subdivision may enact a sex-offender residency restriction 'only if the restrictions are limited to sexual predators, extend no more than five hundred feet from a school or CHILD CARE FACILITY', and meet subsection (2); § 29-4017(2)(c) exempts a sexual predator who established residence after July 1, 2006 where the school or child care facility 'was established AFTER the initial date of the sexual predator's residence at that location'; and § 29-4017(3) makes any non-conforming restriction void 'regardless of whether such ordinance, resolution, or legal restriction was adopted prior to, on, or after July 14, 2006'. So a new child care home in a building creates a five-hundred-foot zone affecting future lettings in a municipality that has such an ordinance, while not displacing existing residents. The project's record covers § 29-4009 (sex offender registry information and the employer-name limitation) and concludes there is no owner or lessor notice duty, which is right; § 29-4017 is a separate provision with a separate effect and belongs with any Nebraska row on tenant screening, criminal history or occupancy restrictions. Second: § 20-318(5)'s inquiry ban (reported in full on my good-cause-notice row) bears directly here, because a landlord assessing a child care request must be careful not to turn it into an inquiry about familial status.

### Found while answering `foreclosure`

NEW FINDINGS, none in salvage Part 3 and none in its verified-statute parts. (1) The Nebraska Trust Deeds Act (§§ 76-1001 to 76-1018) is in chapter 76 and was in the corpus throughout, and § 76-1010(2) is the single most consequential Nebraska provision for a tenant of mortgaged property: a junior leasehold is terminated at the acceptance of the highest bid, without right of redemption. No section of the Act appears anywhere in the salvage record, and the salvage's conclusion that 'Nebraska has no tenant-protection-on-foreclosure statute of its own' is correct but incomplete - Nebraska has the opposite, written in terms. (2) § 25-1530(2) is the judicial-foreclosure twin and § 25-1530(1) confines redemption to 'the owners', which settles the Colorado-style question of tenant redemption rights in the negative. (3) § 76-1008 gives a tenant NO notice of default or sale unless the tenant has recorded a request under § 76-1008(1) before the notice of default is recorded - a real, usable step a tenant could take and almost certainly never does, confirmed by the First Neb. Ed. Credit Union annotation. (4) § 76-238(2)'s related-party possession rule (possession by a relative within the third degree is not notice, for a post-July 16, 2004 lease over one year that has not satisfied § 76-211, unless the creditor received a written copy) is recorded in salvage Part 5 as 'the only Nebraska provision found that turns on the landlord-tenant relationship being familial'; this row confirms that reading from the section text and adds its practical consequence in a foreclosure. Recommend: if the library has a subordination or attornment clause for Nebraska, § 76-1010(2) is its basis and should be cited there.

### Found while answering `foreclosure-disclosure`

NEW FINDING, not in salvage Part 3. § 76-2712's definition of 'residence in foreclosure' - 'a residence or dwelling that is occupied as the HOMEOWNER'S PRINCIPAL PLACE OF RESIDENCE and against which any type of foreclosure action, including, but not limited to, the filing of a notice of default of a deed of trust or the filing of a lawsuit to foreclose a mortgage or other lien, has been commenced' - settles something the salvage record leaves open. Salvage Part 1.5 and proposed topic 2 describe the Nebraska Foreclosure Protection Act as 'a complete landlord-tenant regime no topic owns' and 'the largest hole found', which is right about its importance; what should be added is that the Act's trigger is owner-occupancy, so the Act does NOT reach a rented investment property in foreclosure and does NOT create any landlord-to-tenant duty. The regime applies to a landlord only when the landlord is the equity purchaser in a sale-leaseback with the former owner-occupier. A row built on the salvage description without § 76-2712 could easily overstate the Act's reach. Note also that § 76-2711 ('Homeowner, defined') was amended by Laws 2025, LB474, § 109 per the project's own record and was not read here, so the trigger term should be re-read before the Act is applied.

### Found while answering `good-cause-notice`

NEW FINDINGS, not in salvage Part 3. (1) § 20-318(5) makes it unlawful to 'cause to be made any written or oral INQUIRY or record concerning the race, color, religion, national origin, disability, familial status, sex, or military or veteran status of a person seeking to purchase, rent, or lease any housing.' That is an inquiry ban, not merely a decision ban, and it is stronger than the way fair-housing limits are usually summarised. Any Nebraska screening, application-form or tenant-selection row should be checked against it, because a row that says only 'do not discriminate on these grounds' understates the rule: asking is itself unlawful. This also bears on any row that suggests a landlord verify citizenship, immigration status or national origin for any purpose. (2) § 20-318's protected-class list, as amended by Laws 2025, LB150, § 13, is 'race, color, religion, national origin, disability, familial status, sex, or military or veteran status' - repeated in each subdivision. Salvage Part 1.8 records LB150 as adding military or veteran status across the civil-rights statutes and records § 20-322(6)'s veteran-housing safe harbour, which is consistent; what should be added is that the amendment reached § 20-318 itself, so any Nebraska row quoting the protected-class list from before 2025 is now incomplete. (3) § 76-1441(1)(b) requires the possession complaint to plead 'the facts, with particularity' and (1)(a) 'the specific statutory authority under which possession is sought' - a pleading standard that limits the practical value of a no-cause termination and that I did not find reflected in any row title. I did not run the full CSV screen, so all three are offered as checks to run rather than located defects.

### Found while answering `government-fee-reimbursement`

NEW FINDING, not in salvage Part 3. § 18-1758 (Laws 2019, LB57, § 1) is a short-term-rental preemption statute that appears nowhere in the salvage record: a municipality 'shall not adopt or enforce an ordinance or other regulation that expressly or effectively prohibits the use of a property as a short-term rental' (subsection (2)); may regulate short-term rentals specifically 'only if the municipality demonstrates that the primary purpose of the ordinance or other regulation is to protect the public's health and safety', with an illustrative list covering fire and building codes, health and sanitation, traffic control, waste and pollution control, and an emergency contact designation (subsection (3)); may impose a sales or occupation tax (subsection (4)); may limit or prohibit short-term-rental use only for five named purposes - housing sex offenders, operating a structured sober living home or similar enterprise, selling illegal drugs, selling alcohol or other activity needing a Liquor Control Act permit, and operating a sexually oriented business (subsection (5)); must apply general land-use, nuisance and property-maintenance regulation 'in the same manner as another similar property' (subsection (6)); and the section does not affect private restrictions including a homeowners association under either condominium act (subsection (7)). 'Short-term rental' is defined as residential property 'rented wholly or partly for a fee for a period not longer than thirty consecutive days' (subsection (1)(b)). If the library has a short-term-rental, local-preemption or municipal-regulation topic for Nebraska, this is its statute, and it is a substantial landlord protection that no Nebraska row appears to carry. Second, smaller: § 18-1208 was amended by Laws 2025, LB647, § 22, adding the annual occupation-tax report for any new or increased occupation tax on or after June 5, 2025 - another 2025 act touching a landlord-relevant section without using the word 'landlord', which is the blind spot the brief's §14 counts instances of.

### Found while answering `governmental-fines`

NEW FINDING, not in salvage Part 3. § 76-1415(1)(c) bars a lease term by which the tenant 'agrees to pay the landlord's OR TENANT'S attorney's fees' - the prohibition runs in BOTH directions, so a Nebraska residential lease may not contain a prevailing-party or tenant-favourable fee-shifting clause either, and a 'mutual attorney's fees' clause written to look even-handed is still unenforceable under § 76-1415(2), with actual damages and the tenant's reasonable attorney's fees if the landlord deliberately uses a term known to be prohibited. Any Nebraska row, or any multistate row tagged NE, that offers a mutual or reciprocal fee-shifting clause should be screened against this. I did not run the full CSV screen, so this is offered as a check to run rather than as a located defect in a named row. No conflict found with any row listed as adjacent to this topic.

### Found while answering `rental-inspection`

**row_id** landlords-access

**topic_key** landlord-entry

**states** WY;KS;NE;OH;NV;TX;NJ;GA;NC;SC;PA;UT;IL;ID;MO;IN;OK;NY;WI;WV;MA;ME;LA;AR;MS;VI;AS;MP

**why** The row's own words: "Except in the case of an emergency, Landlord will provide Tenant at least 24 hours' notice, OR THE NOTICE PERIOD REQUIRED BY APPLICABLE LAW IF LONGER, prior to entry." The saving words reach only the PERIOD. Nebraska's statute, read section-open 2026-10-29, requires more than a period: § 76-1423(3) - "Except in case of emergency or if it is impracticable to do so, the landlord shall: (a) Give the tenant at least twenty-four hours' WRITTEN notice of the landlord's intent to enter. SUCH NOTICE SHALL BE PROVIDED TO EACH INDIVIDUAL UNIT AND INCLUDE THE INTENDED PURPOSE FOR ENTRY AND A REASONABLE PERIOD DURING WHICH THE LANDLORD ANTICIPATES MAKING ENTRY; and (b) Enter only at reasonable times." (Source: Laws 1974, LB 293, § 23; Laws 2021, LB320, § 4.) So the row is short of Nebraska law in three respects it does not save: it does not require the notice to be WRITTEN, it omits the two mandatory contents (purpose and anticipated window), and it omits the per-unit delivery requirement - all three added or confirmed by LB320 in 2021. A landlord who follows the clause as written and gives oral 24-hour notice has made an unlawful entry, and the price is a FLOOR rather than a ceiling: § 76-1438(2) gives the tenant, for an unlawful entry or a lawful entry in an unreasonable manner, injunctive relief or termination plus "actual damages NOT LESS THAN an amount equal to one month's rent and reasonable attorney's fees." Not changed, per rule 62 and because the row is shared across 28 states. NOT a duplicate: the brief's fifth round faults edu-entry-notice-content-ne for omitting § 76-1423(3)'s two prefatory exceptions, which is the opposite direction (that row over-warns); neither the salvage record's Part 3 nor any correction round names landlords-access.

**row_id** inspection-rights

**topic_key** inspection-rights

**states** shared; includes NE

**why** Raised as a question rather than asserted as an error, because the text can be read two ways and I will not resolve it (rule 76). The row's own words: "Tenant WILL ALLOW Landlord to perform periodic inspections of the property during the Term, and at move-out, upon reasonable notice consistent with this Lease's Access & Entry terms." Nebraska's § 76-1423(1) imposes a QUALIFIED duty: "The tenant shall NOT UNREASONABLY WITHHOLD CONSENT to the landlord to enter into the dwelling unit in order to inspect the premises..." READING ONE: "will allow" simply restates that duty in plain language and the qualifier is implicit, in which case the row is fine. READING TWO: it removes the word "unreasonably", so the tenant has promised to admit the landlord even where withholding consent would be reasonable - which is an agreement to forgo a protection the Act gives and so unenforceable under § 76-1415(1)(a), with § 76-1415(2)'s actual damages and attorney's fees if the provision is used deliberately knowing it is prohibited. The cautious fix, if the coordinator wants one, is three words: "Tenant will not unreasonably withhold consent to Landlord performing periodic inspections..." which tracks the uniform text and loses the landlord nothing. Separately, the row's reliance on "reasonable notice consistent with this Lease's Access & Entry terms" inherits whatever defect landlords-access has - see the finding above. Not changed (rule 62); shared row.

### Found while answering `required-fees`

**row_id** edu-no-all-in-pricing-law-ne

**topic_key** fee-transparency

**states** NE

**why** The row affirmatively directs the landlord: "You may advertise base rent and disclose mandatory fees separately in the lease." It then says "Three real limits still apply" and lists § 76-1412 unconscionability, § 76-1415(2)'s prohibited-provision penalty, and "federal unfair-and-deceptive-practices rules on fee disclosure". The list omits the Nebraska limit that bears most directly on ADVERTISED pricing, and it is a state limit rather than a federal one. § 87-302(a)(10) (read section-open 2026-10-29) makes it a deceptive trade practice to "[a]dvertise goods or services with intent not to sell them as advertised or advertise the price in any manner calculated or tending to mislead or in any way deceive a person", and (a)(12) reaches "false or misleading statements of fact concerning the reasons for, existence of, or amounts of price reductions". The consequence is not a fine: § 87-303.07 provides that "[i]f a buyer or LESSEE is induced by a violation of section 87-302 or 87-303.01 to enter into a sale or LEASE, the agreement is UNENFORCEABLE BY THE SELLER OR LESSOR and the buyer or lessee, at his or her option, may rescind the agreement or retain the merchandise delivered and the benefit of any services performed without any obligation to pay for them" (Source: Laws 1974, LB 327, § 9; Laws 2008, LB781, § 8). So the practice the row blesses - base rent advertised, mandatory fees disclosed only later in the lease - is exactly the fact pattern § 87-302(a)(10) describes, and the sanction is losing the ability to enforce the lease. Two caveats the coordinator should carry if this is fixed. (1) OPERATIVE-DATE TRAP: the § 87-302 page in the corpus carries "Operative Date: January 1, 2027" with its Source ending Laws 2026, LB838, § 27, so any row citing it must say which version it states; (a)(10) and (a)(12) trace to Laws 1969, c. 855, § 2 and are very likely unchanged, but that needs confirming against the currently operative page. (2) § 87-301 defines neither "goods" nor "services", so whether a residential lease is within (a)(10) is not settled by the text - though § 87-303.07 names a "lessee" and a "lease" without qualification and § 87-302(a)'s chapeau needs only a person acting "in the course of his or her business, vocation, or occupation". Either way the row's current three-limit list is incomplete in the direction that costs the landlord. Not changed, per rule 62. NOT a duplicate: the salvage record's Part 3 item 15 records § 87-303.07 as cited by no Nebraska row and its Part 4 proposes a home for it at topic consumer-protection-act, but no finding anywhere names edu-no-all-in-pricing-law-ne, and `grep` of the salvage record for "all-in-pricing" returns nothing.

### Found while answering `security-deposit-on-sale`

NEW FINDING -- Sec. 76-1420 is the whole answer to a sale of tenanted property and NO Nebraska row appears to cite it. The deposit set (`security-deposit-use`, `edu-security-deposit-cap-ne`, `edu-security-deposit-noncompliance-penalty-ne`, `edu-no-deposit-interest-ne`, `edu-security-deposit-return-ne`) carries the cap, the fourteen-day return, the itemization and the penalty, and none of them carries the transfer mechanism -- so a Nebraska landlord selling a rented building is told what the deposit duties are and not how they move. The statute, read section-open 2026-10-29: Sec. 76-1420(1) -- "Unless otherwise agreed, a landlord, who conveys premises that include a dwelling unit subject to a rental agreement in a good faith sale to a bona fide purchaser, is relieved of liability under the rental agreement and the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act as to events occurring subsequent to written notice to the tenant of the conveyance, but the landlord remains liable to the tenant for any property and money to which the tenant is entitled under section 76-1416, EXCEPT THAT ASSIGNMENT of any security deposits or prepaid rents to a bona fide purchaser WITH WRITTEN NOTICE TO THE TENANT shall serve to relieve the conveying landlord of any further liability under section 76-1416." Sec. 76-1420(2) does the same for a manager on written notice of termination of the management. Source: Laws 1974, LB 293, Sec. 20; Laws 2001, LB 7, Sec. 15. The omission costs the landlord in a specific way: relief from deposit liability requires TWO acts (assignment plus written notice), and a seller who simply hands the money over at closing without notifying the tenant stays liable under Sec. 76-1416, while Sec. 76-1416(5) binds the buyer as "[t]he holder of the landlord's interest in the premises at the time of the termination of the tenancy" -- so the tenant can have two defendants and the seller has bought nothing. Rule 62: filed, not fixed.

Read section-open 2026-10-29, the last sentence is: "This section shall not apply to actions for possession of any premises subject to the provisions of the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act or the Mobile Home Landlord and Tenant Act." Source: Laws 1929, c. 82, Sec. 117, p. 309; ... Laws 1984, LB 1113, Sec. 1; R.S.1943, (1985), Sec. 24-568; Laws 2021, LB320, Sec. 1. Paired with Sec. 76-1440 -- "An action for possession of any premises subject to the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act shall be commenced in the manner described by sections 76-1440 to 76-1447" (Source: Laws 1974, LB 293, Sec. 40; Laws 1991, LB 324, Sec. 2) -- that makes Secs. 76-1440 to 76-1447 the ONLY route for a residential tenancy, and makes the forcible entry and detainer article (Secs. 25-21,219 to 25-21,235) the wrong statute. Bearing on existing rows: `edu-eviction-process-ne` [and any Nebraska row, form or checklist that describes the possession action] should be checked for reliance on the forcible-entry article, because a filing or a notice built on it is built on a statute that disclaims the case; and note that Sec. 76-1431(4) itself says "[n]otwithstanding subsections (1) and (2) of this section or section 25-21,221", which shows the Act legislating against the forcible-entry article's notice section by name. Related and also uncited: Sec. 76-1428 ("Landlord's noncompliance as defense to action for possession") is the Act's ONLY defense/counterclaim section, and its gateway admits only a claim the tenant "may recover under the rental agreement or the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act". Rule 62: filed, not fixed.

### Found while answering `single-family-zone-lease-limit`

NEW FINDING -- Sec. 20-131.02(1) contains an owner-occupancy carve-out from the state disability housing provisions that no Nebraska row appears to carry, and it runs AGAINST the landlord. Read section-open 2026-10-29: "Housing accommodations means any real property which is used or occupied or is intended, arranged, or designed to be used or occupied as the home, residence, or sleeping place of one or more human beings. Housing accommodations DOES NOT INCLUDE any single-family residence IN WHICH THE OWNER LIVES and in which any room is rented, leased, or provided for compensation to persons other than the owner or primary tenant". Sec. 20-131.02(2) takes "[d]isability" from 42 U.S.C. 12102 "as such section existed on January 1, 2021". Source: Laws 1975, LB 83, Sec. 2; Laws 1997, LB 254, Sec. 6; Laws 2008, LB806, Sec. 9; Laws 2021, LB540, Sec. 10. Bearing on existing rows: `edu-fair-housing-classes-ne` [fair-housing] and `edu-esa-federal-only-ne` [assistance-animal-accommodation] both speak to disability in housing without the scope line that Secs. 20-131.01 to 20-131.04 carry -- the definition is SECTION-LOCAL ("[f]or purposes of sections 20-131.01 to 20-131.04"), so it does not shrink the Nebraska Fair Housing Act at Secs. 20-301 to 20-344, and a row must not read it as a general landlord exemption. The practical point is the direction of the carve-out: it depends on the owner ACTUALLY LIVING THERE, so renting the whole house out destroys it. That is the same trap as Sec. 71-6318.01(2) in the lead Act, whose do-it-yourself exemption is unavailable precisely because the dwelling is "occupied by a person or persons other than the owner or the owner's immediate family". A landlord's instinct that owner-occupancy language helps them is backwards in both. Also worth pairing: Sec. 20-322(3)'s own-home rooms exception stops applying to "any person who makes available for rental or occupancy MORE THAN FOUR SLEEPING ROOMS". Rule 62: filed, not fixed.

### Found while answering `smart-access`

NEW FINDING -- Sec. 76-1431.04 is the ONLY statutory reference to electronic access in a Nebraska residential tenancy and no Nebraska row cites its electronic provisions. Read section-open 2026-10-29. Sec. 76-1431.04(1): a landlord required to change locks under Sec. 76-1431.02 or Sec. 76-1431.03 shall do so by either "(a) Replacing the entire locking mechanism with a locking mechanism of equal or better quality than the lock being replaced; or (b) If the lock is in good working condition: (i) Rekeying the lock; or (ii) IN THE CASE OF A KEYLESS ELECTRONIC LOCK, RESETTING THE ENTRY CODE." Sec. 76-1431.04(2)(a) gives the tenant self-help if the landlord fails -- change the locks in a workmanlike manner with locks of similar or better quality, notify the landlord timely, and "by a reasonable method agreed upon by the landlord and tenant, provide the landlord with a new key OR THE ENTRY CODE" -- and (2)(b) makes that "appl[y] notwithstanding any provision in the rental agreement to the contrary." Sec. 76-1431.04(3): "A landlord who installs a new lock pursuant to this section MAY RETAIN A COPY OF THE KEY OR ENTRY CODE that opens the new lock." Sec. 76-1431.04(4): the landlord "may require the tenant to pay for the actual and reasonable cost incurred by the landlord in changing the locks under this section." Source: Laws 2025, LB80, Sec. 50. Bearing on existing rows: the three Nebraska domestic-violence rows the brief records as INACTIVE after the 2026-09-29 three-bucket scrub -- `dv-lockchange-ne`, `dv-lease-release-ne` and `dv-perpetrator-removal-ne` -- predate LB80, and `edu-dv-protections-procedure-ne` [dv-qualifying-documents] addresses documentation and landlord costs; none of them appears to carry (1)(b)(ii), (2)(b), (3) or (4), which are the four provisions a landlord actually needs: the keyless compliance method, the un-draftable-around tenant self-help, the express right to retain the entry code, and the cost-recovery right. Rule 62: filed, not fixed. Separately, and this is why it sits on the smart-access row: (1)(b)(ii) and (3) are the only places Nebraska law treats an "entry code" as the functional equivalent of a key, which is the textual hook for the open question this row leaves on Secs. 28-1315 and 28-1316.

### Found while answering `smoke-drift-waiver`

NEW FINDING -- Nebraska's Clean Indoor Air Act imposes an affirmative, criminally enforced, daily-accruing duty on a landlord as "proprietor" of a rental building's enclosed common areas, and NO Nebraska row carries it. CHANNEL: OFFICIAL SITE SEARCH (browser pane); the section pages were read by the coordinator on 2026-10-29 and the wording below is quoted from that reading. This agent did not open the pages; chapter 71 is not in the local corpus. (1) § 71-5726 defines "public place" as "an indoor area to which the public is invited or in which the public is permitted, whether or not the public is always invited or permitted" and draws its carve-out inside the definition — "A private residence is not a public place" — at "a private residence" and NOT at a residential building, so an apartment building's enclosed hallways, lobbies, laundry rooms and leasing office are NOT exempt, while the dwelling unit is. (2) § 71-5730(1)'s exemption list is closed and has no residential entry. (3) § 71-5725 makes an "owner" a "proprietor" expressly -- the status the Act's duties attach to. (4) § 71-5731 in full: a proprietor "shall take necessary and appropriate steps to ensure compliance with the act at such place" -- affirmative and open-ended. (5) § 71-5733 puts real consequences behind it: (2) proprietor failure is a Class V misdemeanor for the first offence and a Class IV misdemeanor for the second and any subsequent; (3) "[e]ach day that a violation continues to exist shall constitute a separate and distinct violation"; (4) an employee's or agent's act or omission "is deemed to be the act or omission of such proprietor", at the same penalty -- so a landlord is criminally liable for the on-site manager's omission and the exposure compounds daily. (6) § 71-5732 carries injunctive enforcement by the Department of Health and Human Services or a local public health department, a prohibition on retaliation, and an express provision on waiver of the act, which is the direct answer to a lease term purporting to permit common-area smoking. Currency is established and all five Source lines are carried verbatim: § 71-5725 (Laws 2008, LB395, § 10), § 71-5726 (Laws 2008, LB395, § 11), § 71-5731 (Laws 2008, LB395, § 16) and § 71-5733 (Laws 2008, LB395, § 18) are UNAMENDED 2008 text, while § 71-5730 (Laws 2008, LB395, § 15; Laws 2009, LB355, § 6; Laws 2010, LB861, § 82; Laws 2015, LB118, § 10; Laws 2020, LB840, § 7) has been AMENDED FOUR TIMES — so whoever encodes point (2) above must cite Laws 2020, LB840, § 7 for the closed exemption list, not 2008, and must re-check § 71-5730 on any later currency pass, since it is the section through which a residential exemption would arrive; and a first-hand SESSION-LAW check (nesec.py slip, 363 acts of 2025-2026, -w anchored) returns 0 files for every one of §§ 71-5725 to 71-5733, with slip '76-1431' -w -> 1 file as the positive control and slip 'zzqqxyzzy' -w -> 0 as the nonsense control. BEARING ON EXISTING ROWS: this is a real, affirmative, daily-accruing Nebraska landlord duty in the building-and-safety area, and the two Nebraska rows nearest to it do not reach it -- `edu-smoke-detector-scope-ne` [alarm-duties] covers the smoke DETECTOR mandate and says nothing about smoking, and `edu-confirmed-absences-outside-title-ne` [confirmed-absences-outside-title] lists subjects Nebraska has no statute for and (as read in the CSV on 2026-10-29) makes no claim about smoking either way, so neither row is WRONG -- the finding is that the duty is UNCITED, which is the shape this project has been recording for §§ 18-1737, 76-1442.01 and 28-1251. Two cautions for whoever encodes it: the common-area conclusion is a reading of § 71-5726's text and the closed exemption list, not a holding (no Nebraska decision applying § 71-5726 to apartment common areas was located, and case law is out of corpus), and § 71-5732's operative words were described rather than quoted, so that section must be opened before its text is used. Rule 62: filed, not fixed.

### Found while answering `statutory-caps`

TWO NEW FINDINGS ON `edu-alt-housing-self-help-ne` [alt-housing], both from reading § 76-1427 WHOLE for this row's ceiling taxonomy.

(1) THE ROW STATES THE CEILING AS "ONE MONTH'S RENT"; THE STATUTE SAYS "THE PERIODIC RENT". The row's words: "if your failure was deliberate — may also recover the actual cost of that substitute housing UP TO ONE MONTH'S RENT, plus attorney fees (§76-1427(1)(c))." The statute's closing sentence in § 76-1427(1), re-opened in the local corpus, reads: "In addition to the remedy provided in subdivisions (a) and (c), if the failure to supply is deliberate, the tenant may recover the actual and reasonable cost or fair and reasonable value of the substitute housing NOT IN EXCESS OF AN AMOUNT EQUAL TO THE PERIODIC RENT, and in any case under this subsection reasonable attorney's fees" (Source: Laws 1974, LB 293, § 27). "The periodic rent" is not "one month's rent": § 76-1414(4) makes the tenancy WEEK TO WEEK for a roomer who pays weekly rent where no definite term is fixed, and § 76-1437(1) confirms week-to-week tenancies exist in the Act, so in a weekly tenancy the periodic rent is one week's rent. The row therefore overstates the tenant's ceiling roughly fourfold in a weekly tenancy. The error is in the tenant's favour and so is not a landlord exposure, but the brief is explicit that an error in the tenant's favour is still an error, and the figure is the whole point of the row. A second, smaller point in the same sentence: the row attributes the recovery to § 76-1427(1)(c), but the deliberate-failure recovery sits in the UNNUMBERED closing sentence of subsection (1), which reaches "subdivisions (a) and (c)" together — so the substitute-housing cost is recoverable alongside the (a) procure-and-deduct remedy as well, which the row does not mention.

(2) THE ROW OMITS § 76-1427(2), WHICH IS AN ELECTION THAT FAVOURS THE LANDLORD. § 76-1427(2): "If the tenant proceeds under this section, he MAY NOT PROCEED UNDER SECTION 76-1425 as to that breach." So a tenant who takes the substitute-housing or procure-and-deduct route gives up the § 76-1425 route for the same breach — including § 76-1425(1) TERMINATION and § 76-1425(2) damages and injunctive relief. That is a real limit on the tenant's remedies and a real piece of information for a landlord deciding how to respond to an essential-services complaint, and the row (whose whole subject is the choice between Colorado's landlord mandate and Nebraska's tenant self-help) does not carry it. Both filed under rule 62, not fixed.

### Found while answering `stove-refrigerator`

ONE FINDING ON `appliances-included` (shared, active, tagged NE), filed as an ADDITION rather than an error, under rule 62. The row's Nebraska tagging note records it as "generic mechanics, no NE-specific statutory language or number, confirmed no conflict with NE findings from this project". The text is indeed generic — "The property includes the following appliances and equipment as of the Start Date, which Landlord will maintain as provided in this Lease and applicable law: {{appliance_list}}" — but in Nebraska the clause is NOT generic in EFFECT, and that is worth recording because it changes how it should be filled in. § 76-1419(1)(d) obliges the landlord to "[m]aintain in good and safe working order and condition all ... facilities and appliances ... SUPPLIED OR REQUIRED TO BE SUPPLIED by him or her" (Source: Laws 1974, LB 293, § 19; Laws 2001, LB 7, § 14). Listing an item in {{appliance_list}} is therefore the act that brings it inside a statutory maintenance duty, and the clause's own promise ("which Landlord will maintain") is not merely a restatement of the default — it is the trigger. Two consequences the row's notes do not carry. (a) An item left OFF the list is not thereby outside the duty: § 76-1410(14) defines "[r]ental agreement" as "all agreements, WRITTEN OR ORAL", so an oral promise at a showing can make an appliance "required to be supplied" whatever the list says — which means the list protects the landlord only if showing practice matches it. (b) The duty cannot be shifted back by a separate writing in a multi-unit building: § 76-1419(3) reaches only "specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations, or remodeling" and enumerates no subdivision, so a clause making the tenant responsible for the listed appliances as a class does not bind in anything other than a single-family residence (§ 76-1419(2)). Not a defect in the clause and no change proposed; offered because the row is tagged in states where the same uniform § 2.104(a)(4) language applies and the "generic" characterisation may be carried forward into further taggings.

### Found while answering `student-housing`

TWO NEW FINDINGS ON `edu-five-year-lease-exclusion-ne` [scope], both arising from reading § 76-1408 WHOLE for this row rather than reading subdivision (8) alone.

(1) THE ROW OMITS § 76-1408'S ANTI-AVOIDANCE CHAPEAU, AND THE OMISSION RUNS AGAINST THE LANDLORD. The row's words: "A lease of residential land for a term of five years or more is excluded from Nebraska's Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act ENTIRELY (§76-1408(8)) ... If you're drafting a lease with an initial term of 5 years or longer, NONE of the Act's protections or requirements (security deposit rules, notice-and-cure mechanics, habitability duties, etc.) apply by statute." But § 76-1408's opening words, re-opened in the local corpus, are: "UNLESS CREATED TO AVOID THE APPLICATION OF the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, the following arrangements are not governed by the act" (Source: Laws 1974, LB 293, § 8; Laws 2001, LB 7, § 7). The chapeau governs all eight subdivisions, so the exclusion is conditional on PURPOSE. A landlord who writes a five-year term in order to escape the Act is in the one case the chapeau was written for, and the row tells that landlord the opposite — that the escape is automatic and entire. The word "entirely" and the word "none" are both unqualified in the row and the statute qualifies both.

(2) FILED AS A QUESTION, NOT AN ASSERTION: THE ROW GENERALISES THE STATUTE'S OBJECT FROM LAND TO ANY LEASE. § 76-1408(8)'s own words are "[a] lease of improved or unimproved RESIDENTIAL LAND for a term of five years or more." The row states the rule accurately in its first sentence ("a lease of residential land") and then applies it to "a lease with an initial term of 5 years or longer" without qualification — i.e. to a five-year APARTMENT or house lease as readily as to a ground lease. Two readings are available on the text and nothing in the material read here chooses between them: "improved ... residential land" may mean land improved with a dwelling, in which case a five-year apartment lease is outside the Act; or the subdivision may be aimed at leases of LAND as such (ground leases), in which case a five-year lease of a dwelling unit stays inside the Act with all of its deposit, notice and habitability machinery. The consequences are large and opposite, and the row resolves the question silently. Chapter 76 carries no annotation on § 76-1408 in the material available and case law is out of corpus (rule 1). Both filed under rule 62, not fixed.

### Found while answering `tenancy-at-will`

A NEW FINDING ON `edu-eviction-process-ne` [eviction-process], and it runs in the direction that could cost a Nebraska landlord a possession case. THE ROW'S OWN WORDS: "Nebraska has TWO possession procedures, and which one you are in matters. ... Separately, Nebraska's older forcible entry and detainer statutes, sections 25-21,219 to 25-21,235, supply a PARALLEL ROUTE with their own jurisdiction, notice-to-leave, trial, restitution and appeal-bond mechanics, and section 25-21,220 says expressly that those provisions are NOT EXCLUSIVE." THE STATUTE: § 25-21,219's final sentence, re-opened in the local corpus, reads "This section shall not apply to actions for possession of any premises subject to the provisions of the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act or the Mobile Home Landlord and Tenant Act." (Source: Laws 1929, c. 82, § 117, p. 309; ... Laws 1974, LB 293, § 48; ... Laws 2021, LB320, § 1.) § 25-21,219 is the article's JURISDICTION section — it is what confers jurisdiction on the district and county courts over forcible entry and detainer complaints and directs restitution. So for residential premises inside the Act the forcible entry and detainer article is NOT a parallel route the landlord may elect; its jurisdictional foundation is switched off for exactly those premises. TWO FURTHER PRECISIONS. (a) The row attributes the "not exclusive" proposition to § 25-21,220, but that section's closing sentence reads "This section shall not be construed as limiting the provisions of sections 25-21,219 to 25-21,235" — an INTERNAL non-limitation clause saying the five-category list in § 25-21,220 does not limit the rest of the FED article. It says nothing about the FED article being non-exclusive as against the URLTA, and read the other way round it is the opposite of what the row uses it for. (b) § 76-1431(4) opens "Notwithstanding subsections (1) and (2) of this section or section 25-21,221", which shows the legislature treated § 25-21,221 as something to be displaced for a residential route rather than as a freely available alternative. THE FAIR QUALIFICATION, stated so the finding is not overclaimed: § 25-21,219's exclusion is worded "This section" and not "sections 25-21,219 to 25-21,235", so a narrow reading leaves the remainder of the article formally untouched; that does not rescue the row's characterisation, because § 25-21,220's own words key its proceedings to "sections 25-21,219 to 25-21,235" and the jurisdiction section is the one excluded. Filed under rule 62 and not fixed. DISTINCT FROM the brief's sixth-round finding on the same row (that it omits the § 76-1446 money-judgment bar); that finding concerns what the row leaves out, this one concerns what it affirmatively says. SEPARATELY, AND OFFERED AS AN ADDITION RATHER THAN AN ERROR: no Nebraska row in the library cites § 25-203, whose one-year limitation on a forcible entry and detainer action is the shortest possession deadline in Nebraska law and applies precisely to the non-URLTA premises for which the FED article IS the route.

Two things the row therefore does not tell its reader: the sale to an innocent purchaser for value is NOT unwound once the deed is recorded with the compliance statement - so the title risk is bounded - but the seller's exposure in DAMAGES to the tenant survives the recordation entirely. Salvage Part 3 does not fault this row (grep of NE-gaps-salvage.md for '76-886' returns only the Part 1 note on s 76-886(f) and a Part 5 method lesson), so this is new.
