That is a criminal exposure sitting directly on the landlord who restores service after a shutoff, and no row in the library mentions it. It is also the only provision in the twelve held chapters that names the disconnection article at all, so it is the route by which §§ 70-1601 to 70-1615 can be found from a landlord-tenant starting point.

### Found while answering `utility-disconnection-notice-authorization`

`edu-municipal-sewer-charge-lien-ne` (batch 07, topic `municipal-utility-lien`) states the sewer-lien half correctly and carries none of the water half. It cites §§ 18-509(1), 18-509(2), 18-3522(5), 18-1748, 76-1410(13), 76-1431(2), 76-1416(1), 76-1416(2) and 70-1601 - and not § 16-682, § 17-538 or § 18-503. Two things are missing as a result: the first-class-city owner's sixty-day notice and written-discontinuance route, which is the only deadline in Nebraska law a landlord can act on to cap a utility lien; and § 18-503's printed annotation that an 'Ordinance authorizing water supply to be shut off for nonpayment of delinquent sewer charges is not in conflict with this section' (Michelson v. City of Grand Island, 154 Neb. 654, 48 N.W.2d 769 (1951)), which is how a tenant's unpaid sewer bill becomes a water shutoff and therefore a § 76-1419(1)(f) problem for the landlord. Zero of the library's 11,634 rows cite § 16-682 or § 18-503.

### Found while answering `utility-interruption-submeter`

Neb. Rev. Stat. § 76-14,100 is cited by ZERO of the library's 11,634 rows. It is the Mobile Home Landlord and Tenant Act's counterpart to § 76-1430 and it differs in BOTH directions - 'an amount not to exceed one and one-half months' periodic rent' (a ceiling, and half the size) but with the added remedy that the tenant may 'require the restoration of essential services'. Any Nebraska row describing § 76-1430's three months as the measure for all Nebraska tenancies is wrong for a mobile home park, and the restoration remedy is the sharpest available proof that the URLTA's omission of it was deliberate.

### Found while answering `utility-interruption-submeter`

Neb. Rev. Stat. § 28-515.02 is cited by ZERO of the library's 11,634 rows; a screen on the bare string '28-515' returns two rows, `tenant-caused-damage-tn` and `edu-termination-notices-tn`, both Tennessee citation collisions of the kind the brief warns about (Tenn. Code 66-28-515 and neighbours), not this section. Two existing rows reason about metering exposure and have only the CIVIL half: `edu-no-submeter-disclosure-ne` (batch 03) and `edu-no-meter-conservation-charge-ne` (batch 06) both cite §§ 25-21,276(1) and 25-21,276(2) and correctly carry the damages gate and the willfulness gate - but § 28-515.02 has NEITHER gate, is a Class III misdemeanor, and adds a prima facie evidence rule against 'the person in possession of the premises'. Both rows' reassurance that a downstream submeter 'should not expose you' is right about the civil action and silent about the criminal one.

### Found while answering `utility-landlord-account`

Neb. Rev. Stat. §§ 70-1601 to 70-1615 are cited by ZERO of the library's 11,634 rows (screened anchored as '70-160[0-9]|70-161[0-5]', counting stdout lines, because the unanchored '70-16' returns three Montana and Guam collisions). Two consequences for the eight existing `utility-landlord-account` rows and for Nebraska. § 70-1602's exclusion of 'businesses of any nature' from 'domestic subscriber' means a landlord-held account forfeits § 70-1605's seven-day notice (holidays and weekends excluded) and its cap on any discontinuance or reconnection fee at 'the reasonable costs of providing such service' - so a row presenting a landlord-held account as the controlling option has the trade-off backwards. And § 70-1607 makes a third-party notice procedure MANDATORY for every covered utility, which is the lawful substitute and which no row carries.

Neb. Rev. Stat. § 70-1601 is cited by exactly ONE line in this project's delta (the batch 07 `municipal-utility-lien` row, in its later version) and by ZERO of the library's existing rows. It is substantive and runs in the landlord's favour on this topic: 'No applicant for the services of a public or private utility company furnishing water, natural gas, or electricity at retail in this state shall be denied service because of unpaid bills for similar service which are not collectible at law because of statutes of limitations or discharge in bankruptcy proceedings.' With § 70-1602 behind it, that is what makes moving service into a problem tenant's own name both possible and desirable, and no row tells a landlord so. The corpus also holds two transfer stubs showing the article was consolidated out of the municipal chapters - § 18-417 'Transferred to section 70-1601' and § 19-2702 'Transferred to section 70-1605'.

### Found while answering `utility-shutoff-statute`

Neb. Rev. Stat. §§ 70-1601 to 70-1615 are cited by ZERO of the library's 11,634 rows - screened anchored, '70-160[0-9]|70-161[0-5]', counting stdout lines, because the unanchored '70-16' returns three Montana and Guam collisions (`mold-disclosure-mt`, `edu-no-statutory-forms-mt`, `edu-liquidated-damages-gu`). So no Nebraska row carries the seven-day notice, the capped reconnection fee, the § 70-1607 third-party designation, or the § 70-1602 'businesses of any nature' exclusion that decides whether any of it applies.

An item of the Nebraska confirmed-absence inventory must not be written, and this now has the text behind it. `edu-confirmed-absences-outside-title-ne` has already been faulted twice in this project's brief (item (4) on the rental registry, item (7) on typography); a third thing that cannot be said in any Nebraska row is that Nebraska has no utility-disconnection statute. §§ 70-1601 to 70-1615 exist, § 70-1605 fixes a seven-day notice period with holidays and weekends excluded and caps the reconnection fee at 'the reasonable costs of providing such service', and the corpus holds two transfer stubs proving the article was consolidated out of the municipal chapters (§ 18-417 'Transferred to section 70-1601', § 19-2702 'Transferred to section 70-1605').

### Found while answering `utility-submetering-disclosure`

The library's rows on this topic rest to a striking degree on a UTILITY REGULATOR rather than on a statute - `utility-billing-disclosure-az`, `water-submeter-disclosure-ca`, `edu-water-submeter-billing-ca`, `edu-water-submetering-tx` and `utility-submetering-disclosure-tx` among them, and the topic's own question list includes 'Water and electric submetering lease disclosures set by a utility regulator, with different unit thresholds (water: 5+ units; electric: more than 5)'. Nebraska cannot be answered on that axis from this corpus: chapter 75 is unheld and Nebraska's electric distribution is public power under chapter 70, so the regulator may not be a commission at all. The gap is named in this row and filed as a NEEDS_SECTION rather than resolved. It is a finding about the SHAPE of the library's coverage, not a defect in any one row: a topic whose answer is usually regulatory has been canvassed statute-first.

### Found while answering `utility-transfer`

`utility-service-continuity` (shared, 56 states and territories including NE) excludes the wrong services for a Nebraska tenancy, and the exclusion is in the clause's own text: 'This requirement does not apply to telephone, cable, or internet service.' Nebraska's essential-service provisions name 'electric, gas, water or other essential service' (§ 76-1430) and 'running water, hot water, or heat, or essential services' (§ 76-1427(1)), so the clause's listed services are right - but it omits HEAT, which § 76-1419(1)(f) makes the landlord's own duty and which is the service whose interruption by the tenant most often damages the building. A tenant who lets gas service lapse mid-winter is caught by the gas limb; a tenant who turns off a landlord-supplied heating system is not caught by the clause at all. Flagged under rule 62, not changed.

### Found while answering `veterans-incentive`

LAWS 2025, LB150 IS A LANDLORD-RELEVANT ACT MISSING FROM THE PROJECT'S ACT TABLE, and it amended at least four sections this library depends on. Verified by reading the Source lines and the act: § 20-318 (LB150, § 13), § 20-320 (LB150, § 14), § 20-322 (LB150, § 16) and § 76-1495 (LB150, § 129). `slip 'military or veteran status'` returns one file, LB150, at 68 occurrences, and the act's own title includes 'to prohibit discrimination based upon military or veteran status as prescribed'. The brief's '2025-26 acts touching landlords are eight' table does not carry it, and the running 'landlord-keyword blind spot' list does not either - LB150 is visible to a 'landlord' sweep only through § 76-1495, so it is a gap in the act table rather than a new instance of the blind spot. Any Nebraska row whose currency rests on that table is unverified as to LB150.

`edu-fair-housing-classes-ne` is the only Nebraska row that mentions § 20-322(6), and it mentions it in a single sentence - 'A related safe harbor at §20-322(6) lets you offer housing, favorable loan or lease terms, or other benefits LIMITED to veterans, servicemembers, or their family members without that being discrimination.' That is correct and is the right place for it, but it means the safe harbour exists in the library only as a note inside a protected-classes row, and NO row implements it as a term a landlord can use.

Neb. Rev. Stat. § 76-1495 is cited by ZERO of the library's 11,634 rows (screened on the bare number, counting stdout lines), and it was amended by Laws 2025, LB150, § 129 to add 'military or veteran status' to a mobile home park landlord's prohibited acts at § 76-1495(1). That is part of the wider Nebraska gap recorded on `utility-apportionment` in this batch: the library carries no Mobile Home Landlord and Tenant Act coverage for Nebraska at all.

### Found while answering `water-heater-temperature`

Neb. Rev. Stat. §§ 71-1569, 71-1570, 71-1571, 18-1920 and 18-1906 are cited by ZERO of the library's 11,634 rows (screened on the bare numbers, counting stdout lines). So no Nebraska row tells a landlord of a multi-unit building that delivered water at a tub or shower is capped at 115 degrees Fahrenheit by statute, that the trigger is the fixture's installation date rather than the building's age, that municipal plumbing inspectors are directed to check it, or that § 18-1920 makes a municipal plumbing permit or a § 18-1906 variance irrelevant to it. This belongs with §§ 18-1737, 76-1442.01, 28-1251, 18-2312 and the Clean Indoor Air Act as a real Nebraska landlord duty no active row carries.

A screening note for whoever reconciles this delta: this duty cannot be found by screening the library for temperature language either. 'water heater', 'degrees' and '115' will not locate the rows that need it; the rows that need it are every Nebraska habitability, repair and building-safety row, because § 76-1419(1)(a) and (1)(d) are the route by which a non-compliant fixture becomes a tenancy problem with no four-fixture threshold.

### Found while answering `waterbed`

Neb. Rev. Stat. § 76-1475(2) appears in exactly ONE of the library's 11,634 rows, and only in the NOTES of `edu-confirmed-absences-habitability-ne`, which records it as a contrast and warns 'do not read that as authority for the general rental case, and mobile homes are out of scope'. That caution is right about its scope and it has had an unintended effect: the subsection's DEFINITION is the only place a Nebraska legislature has written down what a landlord-protective tenant liability insurance requirement may cover - 'liability insurance shall mean insurance that protects the landlord from negligence on the part of the tenant and any invitees or guests of the tenant' - and no row in the library uses it as the FORM OF WORDS it is. Every renter's-insurance clause that requires a tenant to name the landlord as an insured needs that narrowing to survive § 76-1415(1)(d) in Nebraska, and the phrase is available from Nebraska's own statute book rather than having to be drafted. The distinction is between citing a sibling act as AUTHORITY, which the existing note rightly refuses, and borrowing its drafting, which nothing prevents.

### Found while answering `window-guards`

CORRECTION TO MY OWN FIRST SCREEN, recorded because the method matters: I initially read the Carbon Monoxide Safety Act as uncited in the library. It is not. `edu-carbon-monoxide-alarm-requirement-ne` and `carbon-monoxide-alarm-duty-ne` both exist, are active, and state § 76-606's two triggers correctly, including the change-of-tenant-occupancy trigger; § 76-606 is cited by 4 rows in all. The brief's fourth correction round is right that the Act is missing from the SALVAGE RECORD, and wrong by implication if read as saying it is missing from the library. The screening error was mine and is worth naming: piping a match-and-count helper through `tail -1` prints only the final line, which can be the stderr count or the last match depending on interleaving, and it silently turned a four-row result into a one-row one. Count the stdout lines.

Neb. Rev. Stat. § 81-502 and § 81-503.01 are cited by ZERO of the library's 11,634 rows (screened on the bare numbers '81-502' and '81-503.01', counting stdout lines). § 81-502(1)(c)'s closed list of premises subject to mandatory State Fire Marshal inspection excludes ordinary rental housing, so there is NO state fire-safety inspection of a Nebraska apartment building or rental house - a fact that bears on every building-safety row and that no Nebraska row states. And § 81-503.01(2) requires the Fire Marshal's rules only to 'conform generally' to NFPA 1 and NFPA 101 'but not when doing so would impose an unduly severe or costly burden without substantially contributing to the safety of persons or property', so any row quoting an NFPA requirement as the operative Nebraska standard is wrong.

`carbon-monoxide-alarm-duty-ne` is a LEASE_CLAUSE with basis SERVES_LANDLORD whose text restates § 76-606(1) to (4) almost clause for clause - Landlord will install, Landlord will replace before occupancy, Landlord will provide batteries, Tenant will keep test and maintain, Tenant will notify. On the three-bucket test a restatement of a landlord duty and a tenant duty is education, which is the ground on which the 2026-09-29 scrub switched off `dv-lockchange-ne`, `dv-lease-release-ne` and `dv-perpetrator-removal-ne`. There is a defensible SERVES_LANDLORD reading - the clause's value is that it documents the § 76-606(3)(b)/(4) allocation of ongoing maintenance to the tenant, which the statute permits but does not write into the lease - so this is flagged as a basis question under rule 62, not asserted as an error.

### Found while answering `written-notice-required`

Neb. Rev. Stat. § 76-1410(18) and § 76-1471.01 - both added by Laws 2025, LB185 - are cited by ZERO of the library's 11,634 rows (screened on '76-1410\(18\)' and '76-1471.01', counting stdout lines). They are the definition that decides whether every statutory 'written notice' in a Nebraska tenancy can be given electronically, so any Nebraska row that states a written-notice requirement without them is stating pre-September-2025 law on the question landlords actually ask.

A screening consequence worth stating for whoever reconciles this delta: a row can cite § 76-1413 and still be out of date, because § 76-1413 was amended by LB185 rather than created. The screen that finds the stale rows is on the SUBDIVISIONS - '76-1413\(9\)', '76-1413\(1[0-6]\)' and '76-1410\(18\)' - not on the bare section number.

## 7. Findings for other states

Nebraska features worth checking elsewhere, and cross-state questions raised. Nothing here was acted on: cross-state changes are product decisions for Taylor (rule 62).

### From `abandonment-and-mitigation`

The topic's framing line - 'Lease stays enforceable for rent for the remaining term despite notice or filing, alongside a mitigation duty' - is the opposite of Nebraska's rule and should not be assumed for any state that enacted 1974 URLTA § 4.203. That section's third limb (Nebraska's § 76-1432(3)) makes re-letting terminate the abandoned agreement by operation of law, so in every URLTA state a 'lease survives and rent keeps running' clause needs checking against the state's § 4.203 analogue rather than against its general-remedies section. Worth checking `continue-lease-remedy-ca` and `edu-landlord-remedies-after-breach-az` for whether the AZ row (URLTA state) carries the deemed-termination sentence.

### From `accessory-dwelling-unit`

Two points. (1) The ADU question is a ZONING question, and in Nebraska zoning sits outside the chapters a landlord-tenant corpus would naturally hold. Any state row on this topic that rests on a landlord-tenant or property-chapter search alone may be reporting a false absence; the state's municipal-zoning enabling chapters and any density or middle-housing act have to be searched by name. (2) More useful than the absence: Nebraska preempted municipal regulation for SHORT-TERM rentals in 2019 (§ 18-1758) and not for accessory dwelling units. Several states have done one, the other, or both, and the two statutes are usually drafted in the same preemptive shape. A state being checked for an ADU statute is worth checking for a short-term-rental preemption statute in the same pass, because the second is often easier to find and the library appears to have no topic recording it for Nebraska at all.

### From `actual-notice-method`

Section 76-1413 is 1974 URLTA § 1.302 as rewritten by Nebraska's Laws 2025, LB185. Two portable points. (1) The original uniform text's 'whether or not the other actually comes to know of it' survives in every URLTA state and is a landlord-favourable rule that the topic's existing rows do not appear to state - the twenty-two rows on this topic are framed around whether an ADDITIONAL method may be agreed, which is the narrower question. (2) Nebraska's LB185 rewrite is recent and elaborate (sixteen subsections, a bar on requiring electronic acceptance, a two-bounce fallback rule, and its own September 3, 2025 transition provisions). States that have adopted similar electronic-notice packages since 2023 should be re-checked for currency, because a row written before such a package will understate both the landlord's options and the consent conditions.

### From `adverse-proceeding-notice`

Nebraska's eminent domain definition of 'condemnee' - which reaches anyone 'in possession of or occupying' the property - is the mechanism that gives its tenants condemnation notice without any landlord duty, and it sits in the eminent domain chapter rather than the landlord-tenant act. The twenty-four rows on this topic are framed around foreclosure and attornment; none appears to ask whether the state's condemnation statute makes an occupant a party. That is worth a sweep, because the answer is likely yes in many states and it changes the row's conclusion from 'no notice' to 'notice, but from the condemner'. Second point: § 76-1487's mandatory park-transfer notice against the residential act's silence is the kind of sibling-act contrast that should be run in every state with a separate mobile-home tenancy act before an absence on this topic is finalised.

### From `alarm-tampering-fee`

FINDING ON A SHARED ROW, for the states that hold it. detector-care-la (LA, MS, PR, GU, VI, AS, MP) says flatly 'Tenant will not remove, disconnect, disable or cover any smoke or carbon monoxide detector in the Premises, or remove a working battery from one' with no exception for inspection, testing, maintenance, repair or replacement. Nebraska's analogue, § 76-606(5), carries that exception in terms - 'except as part of a process to inspect, maintain, repair, or replace the alarm or replace the batteries in the alarm' - and § 76-606(4)(a) separately obliges the tenant to 'Keep, test, and maintain all carbon monoxide alarms in good repair.' Model carbon-monoxide statutes in other states commonly carry the same pairing, so each of the seven jurisdictions holding detector-care-la is worth checking for whether its own alarm statute obliges the tenant to maintain or test the device, or carries a maintenance carve-out to its tampering prohibition. If it does, the clause as written puts the tenant in breach for complying with the statute. The fix is one phrase, not a redraft. Also: the row's notes say it 'recovers actual cost only, not a fixed fee (see edu-no-alarm-tampering-fee-la for why a fixed fee is not offered)' - that reasoning holds in Nebraska too and is the reason this row recommends actual cost.

### From `animal-care-access`

A caution about the clause family rather than a defect. `animal-care-access-vi` and `animal-care-access-la` both work by supplying the tenant's advance consent against a backdrop of NO statutory access section. In a URLTA state the backdrop is different: 1974 URLTA § 3.103 (Nebraska's § 76-1423) ends with an exhaustive 'the landlord has no other right of access except' sentence, and § 1.403 (Nebraska's § 76-1415(1)(a)) voids a tenant waiver of Act rights. Colorado holds `animal-care-access-vi`, and Colorado is a state with its own statutory entry framework - worth checking whether its access provision carries the same closed-list sentence, because if it does the clause is exposed there in the same way it would be in Nebraska. More generally, every URLTA state's § 4.203(b) analogue (Nebraska's § 76-1432(2)) gives an unrestricted entry right after an absence of more than seven days, which is a better answer to this topic than an advance-consent clause and is currently stated in no row the batch file listed.

### From `appliances-excluded`

FINDING ON A SHARED ROW. `appliances-excluded-la` (LA, MS, PR, AS, MP) rests on the premise its notes state - 'no statute governs the subject; the clause is a contract term' - and draws its liability carve-out at Louisiana's 'intentional or gross fault' line. Both are safe only outside a URLTA state. Every state that enacted 1974 URLTA § 2.104 has Nebraska's 'supplied or required to be supplied' phrase in its landlord-maintenance section, and 1974 URLTA § 1.403's prohibited-provisions section commonly voids limitation of landlord liability at a lower threshold than gross fault. Mississippi in particular is worth checking. The row's bracketed warning not to use it for 'a gas appliance or water heater' is good drafting and does not cure either point. Separately, `appliances-excluded-sc`, `appliances-excluded-wv` and `appliances-excluded-ri` are single-state rows in URLTA or URLTA-derived states and are worth the same check.

### From `application-fees`

Nebraska has no application-fee rule, so the only limit is whether the money is 'security, however denominated' under its deposit cap. That function-over-label test is the 1974 Uniform Act's own wording (URLTA § 2.101) and exists in every URLTA state, which means the forty-two rows filed under 'Rent & Payment' on this topic that report 'no cap' may be understating the position: a nonrefundable move-in or administrative fee can be caught by the deposit ceiling even where no fee statute exists. Worth checking in each state whose deposit section carries 'however denominated' or an equivalent. The Colorado framing question in this topic - whether the state sweeps any nonrefundable pre-tenancy fee into its application-fee rules, citing C.R.S. § 38-12-902(5) - is the explicit version of the same idea, and the implicit version via the deposit cap is the one to look for elsewhere.

### From `asbestos-hazards`

Two points. (1) The lease-with-option reach of a seller-disclosure statute is a trap worth checking in every state: Nebraska's § 76-2,120(1)(d) and (2) sweep 'lease with option to purchase' into a statute whose catchline and vocabulary are entirely about selling, and its contents list has an environmental-hazard catch-all. A library that files seller-disclosure statutes away as irrelevant to leases will miss that, and it is the same error the salvage record's Part 5 records for §§ 76-2718 and 76-2727 (characterised from their catchlines, verdict came out backwards). Any state with a rent-to-own or lease-option product is worth re-checking. (2) The nineteen rows on this topic should be checked for whether they state a federal asbestos LEASE disclosure. There is none analogous to the lead-based-paint rule, and the federal rules that exist attach to work rather than to tenancies - a row that implies otherwise would be wrong in every state.

### From `association-obligations-disclosure`

The § 76-1422(6) point is portable and is the most useful thing on this topic. Every state that enacted 1974 URLTA § 3.102 has the same condition - a rule is enforceable against the tenant only if the tenant had notice of it when the agreement was made - which means `hoa-compliance` is partly hollow in every URLTA state unless the association documents are actually delivered. That is worth checking across the fifty states the row is tagged in, and the fix is a delivery-and-receipt sentence rather than a legal change. Second, § 76-868(c) is 1980 UCA § 3-110(c) and will appear in substantially the same words in every Uniform Condominium Act and Uniform Common Interest Ownership Act state: where the declaration gives specified votes to lessees, the OWNER LOSES THE VOTE and the lessee gains notice and records rights. None of the twenty-nine rows on this topic appears to state it, and it is a direct cost to a condo landlord of letting the unit.

### From `automatic-renewal`

The Vermont framing question in this topic - whether a general consumer auto-renewal statute reaches leases because it is written around 'lessor' - is the right question to ask everywhere, and in Nebraska the answer is no because no such statute exists in its consumer chapters at all. Two portable points. (1) Any state row that reports 'no auto-renewal rule' should be checked against the state's 1974 URLTA § 4.301 analogue (Nebraska's § 76-1437(3)), because that section's closing cross-reference commonly routes a CONSENTED holdover into the month-to-month default rather than into a renewed term - which is a different and more useful answer than 'no rule'. (2) Separately, the sixty-day rent-increase notice in Nebraska's mobile-home act (§ 76-1490) against the residential act's silence is a contrast worth running in every state with a separate mobile-home tenancy act, because a renewal at a higher rent is how a rent increase usually arrives and a library that states no notice period may be wrong for mobile-home spaces.

### From `balcony-inspection`

One portable point worth more than the absence itself. In every Uniform Condominium Act and Uniform Common Interest Ownership Act state, the analogue of § 76-839(4) makes a balcony, porch, patio, stoop or exterior door serving a single unit a LIMITED COMMON ELEMENT rather than part of the unit - so a condo landlord's repair right, and therefore what they may promise a tenant, is set by the declaration and not by the lease. None of the twenty-three rows on this topic appears to make that distinction, and it affects both the balcony-inspection and the landlord-maintenance topics in every condominium rental. Second: the California and Maryland mandates both use the term 'exterior elevated element', which returns zero in Nebraska and is worth using as the search term in any state being checked, because a battery built on 'balcony' alone will miss a statute drafted around that phrase.

### From `bed-bug-cooperation`

FINDING ON A SHARED ROW. `pest-cooperation-la` (LA, MS, VI) bakes 'at reasonable times, after reasonable notice' into the clause. That is adequate only where the state has no statutory entry-notice standard, which is the Louisiana premise the row's notes state. Mississippi's and the Virgin Islands' entry provisions should be checked: if either prescribes a fixed notice period, a written form, or a statement of purpose, the clause understates it in the same way it would in Nebraska, and the fix is the one Puerto Rico already made - route entry through the lease's entry section instead of restating a standard. More broadly, every state holding `pest-cooperation-la` or `pest-cooperation-pr` alongside a URLTA-style entry section is a candidate for the Puerto Rico version, because 1974 URLTA § 3.103's twenty-four-hour notice (Nebraska's § 76-1423(3)(a), as amended by Laws 2021, LB320, § 4 to add the purpose and window requirements) is stricter than 'reasonable notice' everywhere it appears.

### From `binding-arbitration`

Two points of general reach. (1) Nebraska's constitutional voluntariness proviso (art. I, § 13, as amended 1996) is unusual and is the reason its statutory test reads 'entered into voluntarily and willingly' rather than tracking the Federal Arbitration Act. Any state row that treats a lease arbitration clause as valid because the state has adopted the Uniform Arbitration Act should be checked for a state constitutional open-courts or right-to-remedy proviso of this kind. (2) The Arkansas framing question in this topic - whether the state arbitration act excludes personal injury or tort claims, citing Ark. Code Ann. § 16-108-233(b)(1) - has a direct Nebraska analogue in § 25-2602.01(f)(1), and the two exclusions sit in the same place in the same uniform structure. That suggests the exclusion is a recurring feature of the 1997-era state arbitration acts rather than an Arkansas peculiarity, and is worth a sweep across the other states holding an arbitration row, especially the two that ship a clause (AK, WY).

### From `carpet-cleaning`

The drafting note above about a capped deposit is Nebraska-specific (§ 76-1416(1): all security 'however denominated' limited to one month's periodic rent), but the shape of the question is not: wherever `carpet-cleaning-ar` is tagged in a state with a statutory deposit ceiling, the clause's actual-cost charge has to fit inside that ceiling, and the clause does not say so. Kansas, which holds the row, has a deposit cap. Also see the ordering tension with `security-deposit-use` recorded under findings_existing_rows, which reaches AR, MS, PR, VI, AS and MP as well as Nebraska.

### From `carpet-cleaning`

§ 76-1485(2) - the Mobile Home Act's express 'burden of proving, by a preponderance of the evidence, the reason for withholding' on the landlord - has no counterpart in § 76-1416, and no Nebraska row cites § 76-1485 at all. Other states that enacted a separate mobile-home or manufactured-housing tenancy act are worth checking for the same asymmetry, because a library that states the deposit burden from the general act may be understating it for mobile-home spaces.

### From `casualty-and-mitigation-waivable`

The topic's existing single-state rows split on whether these rules are waivable (edu-casualty-and-mitigation-waivable-oh says waivable; MD, CT, RI, ME say non-waivable). Nebraska lands with the non-waivable group, and for a reason that is portable to every URLTA state with the 1974 § 1.403 prohibited-provisions section: the test is not whether the casualty section says 'non-waivable' but whether the state's prohibited-provisions section bars waiver of 'rights or remedies under the Act' generally. Any state row resting a waivability finding on the casualty section's own silence should be re-read against its § 1.403 analogue.

### From `certificate-of-occupancy-disclosure`

Two portable points. (1) Nebraska's answer to this topic is not 'no rule' but 'the rule is municipal', and the mechanism that makes the absence tolerable is § 18-1722.01's requirement that the municipality POST and RECORD an unfit determination - so the information reaches the tenant and the market without any landlord disclosure. Any state row concluding 'no certificate-of-occupancy disclosure' should be checked for an equivalent posting-and-recording statute before the absence is presented as leaving the tenant uninformed. (2) § 76-1416(4)'s second sentence is NOT in the 1974 Uniform Act - it is a Nebraska addition - so it should not be assumed in other URLTA states; conversely, states that have added something like it have a provision worth finding, because it answers who bears the loss when a unit is condemned, and that question is live in the twenty-three rows on this topic and in the condemned-premises-rent-bar topic.

### From `children-occupancy`

Nebraska's § 20-322(4)(a) preserves only 'reasonable LOCAL restrictions regarding the maximum number of occupants' - a state-law saving clause for municipal ordinances, not for a landlord's own policy. The federal Fair Housing Act's § 3607(b)(1) is worded the same way, and the twenty-eight rows on this topic are split between 'Compliance & Prohibited Terms' and 'Other / Miscellaneous' framings. Any row that states a numeric occupancy standard (the familiar two-per-bedroom figure) should be checked for whether that number comes from the state's statute, from a local ordinance, or only from HUD guidance - because in Nebraska it comes from none of the first two, and a row that presents it as state law would be wrong. Second point: Nebraska's § 20-318(5) ban on the INQUIRY and the RECORD, not merely the decision, is unusual and is the reason a Nevada-style required children clause cannot be ported here. Other states' fair-housing acts should be screened for an inquiry-and-record provision before any row recommends collecting household composition on an application.

### From `cold-weather-vacate-notice`

Minnesota's cold-weather notice is unusual, and the twenty-three rows on this topic mostly report its absence. The more useful finding for every URLTA state is that 1974 URLTA § 3.105 (Nebraska's § 76-1424) expressly authorises the lease to require notice of an anticipated absence over seven days, and § 4.203(a) and (b) (Nebraska's § 76-1432(1) and (2)) back it with actual damages for a willful failure and an entry right during the absence. That combination does the work Minnesota's statute does, applies year round, and is available in every URLTA state - but only if the lease actually contains the requirement, since the duty is opt-in. Any state row on this topic that reports a bare absence should be checked for whether the state's § 3.105 analogue is being used, and whether that state's lease carries the clause.

### From `collection-fee`

§ 76-1415(1)(c)'s bidirectional ban ("the landlord's or tenant's attorney's fees") is a Nebraska drafting change from 1972 URLTA § 1.403(a)(3), which barred only the landlord's fees. Every other URLTA state's prohibited-provisions row should be checked for whether its own text is one-way or two-way before a fee-shifting clause is tagged into it.

### From `common-area-lighting`

§ 76-873(c)(3) is worth a correction note wherever the project relies on it: the salvage record describes it as a rule that "requires utilities not separately metered to be assessed in proportion to usage," but subsection (c)'s chapeau is "To the extent required by the declaration", so the proportional-usage rule bites only where the condominium declaration calls for it. The same shape — a Uniform Condominium Act provision that reads as a mandate but is conditioned on the declaration — will appear in every UCA state.

### From `communal-land-lease-approval`

The question's real content for a mainland state is not communal tenure but APPROVAL-BEFORE-VALIDITY, and the states that have something in that family usually have it for a different reason — a state-land or school-land lease, a public-housing-authority lease, or a conservation easement. A canvass that searches only 'communal', 'tribal' and 'native' will return zero in every mainland state and prove nothing. The functional query used here ('approv... lease ... officer/secretary/governor') is the one worth carrying to the remaining states.

### From `condemned-premises-rent-bar`

§ 76-1416(4)'s closing sentence (no tenant liability for damages from a government-ordered removal caused by the landlord's negligence or neglect) is a Nebraska addition to 1972 URLTA § 2.101 and does NOT appear in the uniform text. Other URLTA states' deposit rows should not be assumed to carry it, and states that do carry an analogue may have it in their deposit section rather than their habitability section — the same placement surprise the salvage record flagged for § 76-1420.

### From `confession-of-judgment`

The library's confession-of-judgment rows for the other URLTA states should be checked against their own § 1.403 analogue: Nebraska's ban sits in the prohibited-provisions section of the Act (§ 76-1415(1)(b)), not in the civil-procedure chapter, and the civil-procedure machinery (§§ 25-1309 to 25-1312) is left fully intact. A row that says a state 'abolished' confession of judgment, rather than 'barred the lease term', would be wrong in Nebraska's shape.

### From `construction-liens`

The bidirectional attorney-fee bar at Neb. Rev. Stat. § 76-1415(1)(c) ("the landlord's OR tenant's attorney's fees") is a Nebraska change from 1972 URLTA § 1.403(a)(3), and it bears on this shared clause in every URLTA state tagged on it: "Tenant will ... pay Landlord's reasonable costs caused by it" is safe only while "costs" excludes counsel's fees. Worth checking AR, MS, GU, VI, AS, MP and WY for a one-way or two-way fee bar before relying on that sentence, and worth considering whether the shared text should say "costs, not including attorney's fees" so it is safe in both kinds of state. Separately: Nebraska has NO notice-of-non-responsibility statute, and § 52-145(5) lets a lien CLAIMANT record the notice of commencement when the owner has not — so an owner cannot keep the record clear by inaction. Any state row that tells a landlord to rely on posting or recording a disclaimer should be checked for whether that state actually provides one.

### From `consumer-protection-act`

§ 87-303.07's remedy shape — the agreement becomes UNENFORCEABLE BY THE LESSOR, and the lessee may keep what was delivered without paying — is unusual: most states' consumer acts give damages and fees rather than disabling the contract. Any state whose consumer-protection row says only 'damages and attorney's fees' should be re-checked for a parallel unenforceability section, which in Nebraska sits in the deceptive-trade-practices chapter and not in the consumer-protection chapter.

### From `criminal-activity`

Do NOT tag the shared row `criminal-activity-ky` (KY,AR,MS,PR,GU,VI,AS,MP) into Nebraska, and its carve-out should be re-examined in each tagged state. Its third sentence reads: "This Section does not apply to criminal activity in which Tenant or a member of Tenant's household is the victim, including conduct that is the subject of a protective order protecting them, or to any request for help from the police or other emergency assistance." Measured against Nebraska that fails in four ways, each giving away more than the statute requires — the same defect the earlier pass caught in a crime-free clause. (1) It switches the WHOLE Section off; § 76-1431(5) bars only the subsection (4) five-day no-cure route and leaves the § 76-1431(1) material-noncompliance route untouched. (2) Nebraska's limit is CONDITIONAL on the tenant or household member actually taking one of three named measures; the candidate's limit is unconditional on victim status. (3) Nebraska requires the tenant to SEEK a protective order (§ 76-1431(5)(a)(i)); the candidate is satisfied by conduct that is merely "the subject of a protective order protecting them." (4) The candidate carries no analogue of § 76-1431(5)(b): the limit does not apply to a tenant who is the perpetrator, and where victim and perpetrator are both parties the landlord "shall only take action under subsection (4) ... against the perpetrator" — which is a direction to the landlord, not merely a permission the clause can omit. The candidate also writes "on or near the property" where § 76-1431(4) is confined to activity "on the premises", though that widening is a contract term and not itself unlawful. Finally, the candidate's "any request for help from the police or other emergency assistance" has no Nebraska statutory source at all; several states have an emergency-assistance protection statute and Nebraska does not, so in Nebraska that sentence is a pure giveaway.

### From `defective-drywall-disclosure`

A drywall battery that searches only 'drywall' can return a false zero in a state that legislated by material rather than by trade name. The synonym set that matters is gypsum / wallboard / sheetrock / plasterboard plus the mechanism words sulfur, hydrogen sulfide and corrosive, and the near-hit to expect in any Uniform Condominium Act state is the unit-boundary definition (Nebraska's is § 76-839), which is a false positive and not a disclosure rule.

### From `deposit-cost-schedule`

Worth checking across the URLTA states: Nebraska's § 76-1416(2) uses "damages which the landlord HAS SUFFERED", the 1972 URLTA § 2.101(b) wording. A pre-set charge schedule is inconsistent with that wording wherever it was adopted verbatim, so a cost-schedule clause tagged into a URLTA state on the strength of silence alone may in fact be barred by the deduction measure itself.

### From `deposit-escheat`

The structural point is portable: a state can run its deposit dormancy off the LANDLORD-TENANT act rather than off the unclaimed-property act, with a much shorter period. Nebraska's one-year trigger in § 76-1416(2) displaces its own five-year catch-all in § 69-1308(a), and the unclaimed-property act never mentions security deposits. Any state row that states a dormancy period taken from the unclaimed-property act alone should be re-checked against that state's deposit-return section for a shorter, special trigger.

### From `deposit-last-month-rent`

Every URLTA state that adopted 1972 URLTA § 2.101(a) has the phrase "security, however denominated" and a section catchlined to cover prepaid rent as well, so the same unresolved question — is up-front last month's rent inside the cap? — exists in each of them unless that state added an express carve-out or has a decision on it. Nebraska's own answer to the question in a NEIGHBOURING act (§ 76-1469's "other than a deposit which is exclusively an advance payment of rent") is the kind of express carve-out to look for in each state's mobile-home or manufactured-housing act before concluding the main act is silent.

### From `deposit-surrender-notice`

A deposit statute that legislates the NO-FORWARDING-ADDRESS case (mail to the last-known address) is strong textual evidence that the same statute imposes no forwarding-address condition — the fallback would be surplus if the tenant's failure to give an address suspended the duty. That reasoning is portable to any state whose deposit section has such a fallback sentence, and is worth applying before a surrender-notice-condition row is written as a bare silence.

### From `designated-repairer`

§ 76-1492(2) is a ready-made designated-vendor rule — no exclusive-use condition unless necessary for health, safety, aesthetic value or welfare, and any resulting charge capped at "the actual cost incurred" — sitting in Nebraska's MOBILE HOME act rather than its URLTA. Most states' manufactured-housing or mobile-home-park acts have a provision in this family, and a designated-repairer canvass that looks only at the general residential act will miss it. Worth checking in every state that has a separate park act.

### From `disability-accommodation`

Nebraska's § 20-319 is the Fair Housing Amendments Act text adopted almost verbatim, including the covered-multifamily-dwelling definition and the ANSI A117.1 safe harbour, so most states' fair housing acts will match it closely. Two Nebraska-specific features are worth checking state by state rather than assumed: (1) the definition of disability is FROZEN to 42 U.S.C. 12102 as it existed on January 1, 2021 (§ 20-308.01), so a state that incorporates the federal definition dynamically will drift from Nebraska's; and (2) § 20-322(3)'s own-home exemption turns on MORE THAN FOUR SLEEPING ROOMS, not on the federal Mrs. Murphy four-unit line, and it is an exemption from the whole Act including the disability provisions. A row written to the federal four-unit line would be wrong in Nebraska.

### From `disaster-displaced-guests`

A 'displaced' keyword battery will return false positives in every state that has a Uniform Relocation Act analogue, because that act's duties fall on a government 'displacing agency' and its vocabulary is the same. Nebraska's hits were §§ 76-1220 and 76-1238. Worth adding to the project's mapped-trap list so a later state does not read a condemnation-relocation statute as a landlord sheltering duty.

### From `disaster-duties`

§ 76-1425(2)'s force-majeure sentence is 1972 URLTA § 4.101(b) and is far narrower than a drafter would expect: it removes CONSEQUENTIAL DAMAGES only, from the § 76-1425 claim only, and expressly preserves the essential-services remedy. Any URLTA-state row that describes it as an act-of-God excuse for the habitability duty, or that adds a general 'conditions beyond the landlord's control' excuse to a habitability clause, should be re-checked — the salvage record found exactly that error in Nebraska's own `edu-habitability-baseline-ne`.

### From `double-letting`

The library's double-letting rows should be re-checked in every URLTA state for the 1972 URLTA §§ 2.103 and 4.102 pair, which Nebraska carries as §§ 76-1418 and 76-1426. A state canvass that searched for 'double letting' would have found nothing, exactly as it did here, while the rule is fully present: the definitional phrase 'to the exclusion of others' plus the failure-to-deliver-possession section is the query that works. Also portable: these sections impose liability on 'a person' whose failure to deliver possession is willful, not only on the landlord, so a holdover occupant or a letting agent can be the defendant.

### From `drug-free-housing-addendum`

§ 28-417(1)(e)'s "knows or should know is resorted to by persons using controlled substances" is an owner-side criminal exposure with a CONSTRUCTIVE-knowledge standard and no landlord carve-out. Most states have a 'maintaining a drug house' or 'keeping a disorderly house' statute of this family, and the library's drug-free-addendum and criminal-activity rows for other states should be checked for whether the owner-side crime is stated at all — it is the real reason a private landlord wants the term, and it is not an eviction provision, so a canvass built around eviction grounds will miss it.

### From `dv-confidentiality`

Section 76-2406's definition of "confidential information" runs to the licensee's CLIENT. Any state whose real-estate agency act is built on the same 1990s limited-agency template (and many are) will have the same trap: a confidentiality duty that looks tenant-protective in the index and protects the landlord in the text. Worth checking before any state's row says a licensee owes a tenant confidentiality.

### From `dv-deposit-timing`

The Mobile Home Act's Section 76-1486 has no URLTA counterpart in Nebraska: a landlord who fails to furnish the written statement "shall forfeit all rights to withhold any portion of the rental deposit," and Section 76-1485(2) puts the burden of proving the reason for any withholding on the landlord by a preponderance. Any state that enacted the 1980s model mobile-home act alongside URLTA may have the same asymmetry - total forfeiture plus a reversed burden in the mobile-home act and neither in the general act. Worth a check where a state's row treats the two acts as parallel.

### From `dv-eviction-protection`

Section 76-1431(5)(a)(i) and (ii) are crime-victim protections of general application that happen to live inside a domestic-violence amendment. Any URLTA state that copied Nebraska's or a sibling state's "crime-free" carve-out should be checked for the same structure: the subsection will usually be indexed and summarised as a DV provision while two of its three triggers protect any tenant who seeks protective relief against, or reports, a third party's conduct. A library row that frames such a subsection as DV-only understates it.

### From `dv-lockchange`

Section 76-1431.04 separates the duty (change the lock) from the cost (the tenant may be made to pay the actual and reasonable cost) and from the key (the landlord may keep a copy). Colorado's C.R.S. 38-12-402(7)-(8), which the library's framing question names, pairs the lock-change right with a void-contrary-term rule AND a private action with statutory damages. Nebraska has the void-contrary-term rule for the tenant's self-help only (Section 76-1431.04(2)(b)) and NO damages provision anywhere in Sections 76-1431.02 to 76-1431.04 - a landlord who misses the 24 hours faces the tenant's self-help and the general Section 76-1425 noncompliance route, not a statutory penalty. Any state row that imports a Colorado-shaped "statutory damages" sentence into a Nebraska-shaped statute would overstate it.

### From `dv-protection-order-chapter-moved`

Nebraska's Section 76-1410(1) defines "act of domestic violence" entirely by cross-reference into two other chapters, one of which (Section 28-323) was amended in 2026. Any state whose landlord-tenant DV definition is a cross-reference rather than a self-contained definition carries the same silent-staleness risk, and a library row that quotes the borrowed definition's CONTENT rather than its citation will drift without warning. Recommend that state rows on DV definitions cite the landlord-tenant definition section and name the borrowed sections, without reproducing their text.

### From `electric-submetering-disclosure`

TWO CORRECTIONS TO THIS PROJECT'S OWN RECORD OF Sections 25-21,275 to 25-21,278, both from reading the sections. (1) The salvage record and AGENT-BRIEF Section 9 say "a landlord's own submeter installation is actionable by the utility: actual damages or $750 liquidated, plus ... costs" and describe "$750 liquidated damages against the master-meter landlord." That is too strong. Section 25-21,276(1) gives the action only "when such act results in damages to the utility," and Section 25-21,276(2) makes the actual-damages / $750 measures available only "upon proof of willful or intentional bypassing, tampering, or unauthorized metering." A submeter placed downstream of the utility's revenue meter, which does not alter what the utility measures or bills, satisfies neither condition on its face. The definition in Section 25-21,275(5) is broad; the liability is not. Section 25-21,277(2) is a presumption of KNOWLEDGE, not of liability, and attaches only where bypassing, tampering or unauthorized metering "is proven to exist." Any state row built on the Nebraska finding should carry those conditions. (2) Section 25-21,275(6) defines "Utility" as any person or entity "lawfully operating in whole or in part for the purpose of supplying electricity, gas, water ... to the public OR TO ANY PERSON" - wide enough on its face to include a submetering landlord. That definition serves a private civil-remedy act about diversion; it makes no claim about regulatory classification, and must not be cited as evidence that a landlord is or is not a regulated utility (AGENT-BRIEF Section 12). REFINEMENT TO BRIEF Section 14: its correction of Section 76-873(c)(3) is right that the subsection is gated on "To the extent required by the declaration"; (c)(3) carries a SECOND condition in its own words - "if reasonably determined" - so a row using it as a contrast should state both.

### From `emergency-contact`

TWO NEBRASKA PROVISIONS WORTH CHECKING FOR IN OTHER STATES. (1) Section 18-1758(3)(b) - a municipality may regulate short-term rentals only on a demonstrated health-and-safety purpose, and the authorised list includes "[r]equirements regarding the designation of an emergency contact for the property." So in Nebraska the emergency-contact duty, where it exists, is MUNICIPAL and attaches to short-term rentals, under an express state preemption statute that also forbids a municipality from prohibiting short-term rental use outright (Section 18-1758(2)). Other states with short-term-rental preemption acts (several passed one in the same 2018-2021 window) will likely have the same emergency-contact carve-out, and a state row that searches only the landlord-tenant act will miss it. (2) Section 87-1104(16) excludes from the Data Privacy Act "[d]ata processed or maintained as the emergency contact information of an individual ... that is used for emergency contact purposes" - a clean answer to the privacy objection to collecting a contact, and the kind of provision that appears verbatim in the many states that adopted the same comprehensive-privacy template. Nebraska's data-breach act is separate and ungated (Sections 87-801 to 87-808), and Section 87-802(5)'s "personal information" definition does not reach a bare name and telephone number.

### From `eminent-domain`

The Virgin Islands segment labels this clause's award-assignment proposition as resting on 28 V.I.C. ch. 19's "each and every separate estate and interest therein" assessment. Nebraska reaches the same place by a different route - Section 76-701(2) defines the tenant INTO the condemnee class and Section 76-710 has the appraisers assess each condemnee's own damages - so in both places the clause works as an inter-party assignment rather than as a statement of who may claim. Any state tagging this clause should check its own definition of condemnee before describing the clause as deciding who gets the award: it decides who gets it as between landlord and tenant, not whether the tenant may appear.

### From `employee-screening`

The productive technique here transfers: for any state's employee-screening row, sweep that state's own property chapter for fingerprint / criminal-history-record-check sections attached to a NEIGHBOURING occupation (appraisers, brokers, home inspectors, appraisal management companies). Nebraska has six such sections in chapter 76 and none for rental-property staff, which turns an unprovable silence into a demonstrated legislative choice. Also: Section 28-417(1)(e)'s "knows or should know is resorted to" standard, with no landlord safe harbour, is the strongest landlord-side criminal exposure found in Nebraska and it is reached only by a title sweep (its catchline is "Unlawful acts; violations; penalty"). Most states have a descendant of the same Uniform Controlled Substances Act provision; a state row that discusses drug activity only through the eviction statute is missing the criminal half.

### From `energy-data-release`

Section 87-802(5)'s closed list is the useful cross-state point: in every state that adopted the 2005-2007 data-breach template, utility usage data is almost certainly outside "personal information," so an energy-data row in any of those states can say so without a fresh search, provided the state's own list is checked for an added element. Separately, in an all-public-power state the operative rule is a district tariff rather than a statute - any state row asserting that a lease clause authorizes a utility release should name whose rules actually control the release.

### From `entity-landlord-court-representation`

Two cross-state points. (1) The Nebraska pair is worth looking for everywhere: a general county/justice-court statute forbidding non-attorney appearance for another, and a small-claims statute that MANDATES appearance by an entity's own employee and FORBIDS attorneys. Many states have both, and a library row that answers only one of them gives the landlord the wrong answer half the time. The decisive question for a row is which court hears possession. (2) Nebraska's Section 25-2803(6) claim-frequency cap - two per calendar week, ten per calendar year - and Section 25-2803(5)'s bar on assigned claims are the kind of limit that makes small claims unusable for a portfolio landlord, and they sit in the representation section rather than the jurisdiction section, so a search aimed at jurisdiction will miss them.

### From `environmental-event-termination`

The D & R Realty annotation printed with Section 76-1414 - rent apportionment where a substantial portion of the premises is rendered incapable of use, "in the absence of an expressed assumption of the risk of such destruction" - is a common-law rule, not a URLTA rule, and the same default almost certainly exists in other states that never codified it. Any state row that says "no environmental-event or casualty rent-abatement rule" should check whether the common-law apportionment default is doing the work instead, because its existence makes an express risk-allocation clause valuable rather than cosmetic.

### From `ev-charging-end-of-tenancy`

The Illinois segment ties this clause to 765 ILCS 1085/35(e) and Kansas to its own statute; Nebraska has no statute at all, so for Nebraska the clause is pure contract and the controlling interaction is the state's ABANDONED-PROPERTY act rather than an EV act. That is likely true of every state without a right-to-charge statute, and it suggests the generic version of this clause should cross-reference the lease's abandoned-property provision in all of them: a tenant who simply leaves the charger triggers the disposal statute, not the removal clause.

### From `ev-charging-requirements`

The deposit sentence in this clause ("Any money Landlord holds to secure Tenant's obligations for the system is part of the Security Deposit and counts toward its legal limit") is correct in Nebraska because of the two words "however denominated" in Section 76-1416(1). That phrase, or its absence, decides the point - any state tagging this clause should check whether its own deposit cap is drafted "however denominated" / "by whatever name" or is limited to a thing called a security deposit, because in the latter the sentence gives away a position the statute does not require. Second point: the "[a separate meter]" blank deserves a standing check against each state's utility-diversion / unauthorized-metering statute, which is almost always in the civil-remedies or criminal code rather than the landlord-tenant act and so is invisible to a chapter-limited search.

### From `ev-charging-shared-area`

Nebraska's Section 76-1410(13) - rent is "all payments to be made to the landlord under the rental agreement" - converts this clause's reservation fee into rent automatically, with knock-on effects on the nonpayment-notice route and on every figure the statute measures in rent. That definition is the 1972 URLTA text and is in most URLTA states verbatim, so the point generalises: in a URLTA state, an EV reservation fee, a submeter charge and a parking fee are all rent whether or not the lease says so, and a row that treats them as "fees" distinct from rent is wrong in those states. Also worth checking in every URLTA state: the "Premises" definition's "held out for the use of tenants generally" clause, which makes reserving a shared space a change to other tenants' bargain and routes it through the rules-and-regulations section.

### From `eviction-hardship-stay`

Section 25-21,235 - restitution enforceable in the court's discretion NOTWITHSTANDING the tenant's supersedeas bond, on the landlord's own bond - is an unusually landlord-favourable provision and it sits in an 1929-vintage forcible-entry-and-detainer chapter, not in the modern landlord-tenant act. Several states carry descendants of the same chapter. Any state whose eviction-stay row says "a proper appeal bond stays the writ" should check its forcible-entry chapter for a counterpart before that sentence ships. Second, transferable method note: the stay question is best answered by a TITLE sweep of the civil-procedure chapter, because the controlling sections are captioned by their stage in the action (continuance, writ of execution, supersedeas, restitution) and never by the word hardship or stay.

### From `eviction-penalty-clause-ban`

Section 76-1415(1)(c)'s symmetry - "the landlord's OR TENANT'S attorney's fees" - is the point to carry across. It is the 1972 URLTA Section 1.403(a)(3) text, which several states narrowed when they adopted it, and in the states that kept it a RECIPROCAL fee clause is prohibited, not cured. Any library row in a URLTA state that recommends making a fee clause mutual "so it is fair both ways" should be checked against that state's own wording. Second point: Section 76-1415(2) attaches the damages remedy to a landlord who "deliberately USES a rental agreement containing" the prohibited term, not to one who enforces it - a template-level exposure that recurs wherever the URLTA text was adopted unchanged.

### From `eviction-service-party`

The Nebraska pairing is worth testing in every state: a landlord-tenant NOTICE section that expressly honours a "place held out" by either party (so the lease can fix notice addresses), sitting beside a SERVICE statute whose methods are closed (so the lease cannot fix who takes the summons). Rows in this library that treat a lease-designated service party as generally available should be checked against the state's own service statute. Second, and more valuable: Nebraska's Section 76-1442.01 posted-service route is paired with Section 76-1446's bar on a money judgment. Any state with a posting-and-mailing alternative should be checked for the same trade-off, because a landlord who uses posted service to save time and then takes a default money judgment has a judgment that may be void.

### From `expedited-deposit-disposition`

Two transferable points. (1) Nebraska's Section 76-1416(3) penalty is "one month's periodic rent or two times the amount of the security deposit, WHICHEVER IS LESS" - the Act's only landlord-favourable greater-of/lesser-of formula, and the opposite of the "whichever is greater" wording in Sections 76-1426 and 76-1437(3). Any state row stating a deposit penalty should quote the connector, because the same statute reads as a doubling or as a cap depending on that one word. (2) Nebraska's Mobile Home Act carries a total-forfeiture rule its URLTA does not: Section 76-1486, "[a] landlord who fails to provide a written statement as required by section 76-1485 shall forfeit all rights to withhold any portion of the rental deposit," with Section 76-1485(2) putting the burden of proving any withholding on the landlord by a preponderance. States that enacted both acts should be checked for the same asymmetry before a row describes the two deposit regimes as parallel.

### From `family-child-care`

Two portable points. FIRST, the substantive one, and it is the kind of thing a landlord-tenant search never finds: in a state with a clean-indoor-air or smoke-free-workplace act, a licensed home child care program can convert the dwelling into a regulated 'place of employment' during operating hours, and the act's compliance duty may fall on the OWNER as a statutory 'proprietor' rather than only on the tenant who runs the business. Nebraska is the worked example (§§ 71-5724, 71-5725, 71-5729, 71-5731, against the general rule in § 71-5726 that 'a private residence is not a public place'). Every state row on this topic - including the states that require a landlord to allow a family child care home, where the landlord has no choice in the matter - should be checked against its clean-indoor-air act, because in a mandatory-allowance state the landlord acquires the compliance duty without the power to refuse. That is a worse position than Nebraska's and no row appears to mention it. SECOND, a screening point of the same shape: a sex-offender residency-restriction statute measured from a 'child care facility' (Nebraska § 29-4017) means a tenant's home child care business can change what the landlord may lawfully do with NEIGHBOURING units. Worth checking in every state with such a statute. THIRD, a drafting point for any state that permits refusal: the refusal must be framed as a prohibition on operating a business, applied uniformly, and never in terms of children or household composition, because familial status is a protected class under the federal Fair Housing Act in every state and some state acts (Nebraska § 20-318(5)) additionally make the INQUIRY unlawful.

### From `farmland-hunting-rights`

The Arkansas-style question this topic asks ('does a tenant of rented farmland have hunting or fishing rights unless the owner grants them in writing?') cannot be answered from a property code alone, and Nebraska shows why: the twelve chapters researched contain no allocation rule, while the chapter that would contain one - the game and parks chapter - was outside the corpus. Any state row on this topic should say which chapters it searched, and should search the game-and-wildlife chapter specifically, because several states place a landowner-or-tenant permit privilege there rather than in the property code. A row resting on a property-code silence alone is not safe. Second portable point, and a broader one: a residential landlord-tenant act's exclusions list decides whether any of the library's clauses apply at all, and agricultural occupancy is excluded in the 1972 URLTA text that Nebraska adopted (§ 76-1408(7)) and therefore in most URLTA states. A farmland clause drafted on residential assumptions - deposit caps, habitability, notice periods - will be wrong in every one of them. THIRD: in a URLTA state the agricultural exclusion is usually qualified by an anti-avoidance preamble (Nebraska: 'unless created to avoid the application of'), so a landlord cannot label a house lease agricultural to escape the act; a state row that states the exclusion without the qualifier invites exactly that attempt.

### From `fee-in-lieu-of-deposit`

The Nebraska mechanism is portable and is the cheapest test to run in any state with a deposit cap: look for the words 'however denominated' (or 'by whatever name called') in the cap sentence. Where they appear, a nonrefundable deposit-alternative fee collected BY THE LANDLORD is inside the cap and inside the itemized-return machinery no matter what the lease calls it, and no separate anti-avoidance statute is needed - which means a state row saying 'the state has no deposit-alternative statute, so the fee is unregulated' is wrong wherever the cap carries those words. The states listed on this topic include several with caps (MA, WA, OR, KY, VA, WI) and the TX and FL rows offer the fee affirmatively; each should be checked for the phrase. Second portable point: Nebraska's cap says 'demand or receive', which puts the dividing line at whose hands the money passes through, not at what the product is called - a premium the tenant pays direct to a third-party surety is outside a 'demand or receive' cap but would be inside a cap written in terms of what the tenant is required to pay. Rows offering an insurance-backed alternative should state which formula their state uses.

### From `fee-unprovided-service`

The Nebraska finding that travels is the remedy, not the prohibition. Many states answer this topic with a fee-specific ban and a refund or statutory-damages remedy. Nebraska has no ban at all, yet its consequence is harsher: § 87-303.07 makes a lease induced by a deceptive practice 'unenforceable by the seller or lessor', with the lessee free to 'rescind the agreement or retain the merchandise delivered and the benefit of any services performed without any obligation to pay for them.' Nebraska's § 87-303.07 is section 9 of the 1974 Uniform Deceptive Trade Practices Act adoption (Laws 1974, LB 327), so the same sentence is likely to sit in other 1970s UDTPA-adopting states' codes, where it has probably gone unnoticed in a landlord-tenant library because it is filed under trade practices rather than tenancies. That is a cheap, high-value check to run in every UDTPA state: search the trade-practices chapter for 'unenforceable by the seller or lessor'. Second portable point, for any state row written around a fee ban: a public-interest element in the state's general consumer-protection act (Nebraska's, per Nelson v. Lusterstone) can make a single-tenant fee dispute unactionable under that act while a portfolio-wide fee is squarely actionable - so a row should say which of the two routes it is describing.

### From `fire-code-standard`

FIRST, a method finding that bears on every state in this project: a state's fire code can be read from its SESSION LAWS even when the codified chapter is not in the research corpus, because an amendatory section prints the whole section as amended. Here §§ 81-503.01 and 81-502 were recovered from the 2025 and 2026 slip laws after a twelve-chapter sweep returned 'fire code' -> 0. Any state pass that reported a fire code as unread for want of the chapter should re-check its session laws before filing that as an absence - and conversely, an absence battery run only over selected chapters will produce false zeros on any subject the chapter plan excluded. SECOND, the substantive point that travels: Nebraska's fire code is not NFPA. § 81-503.01(2) requires the adopted rules to 'conform generally' to NFPA 1 and NFPA 101 (2012 editions) 'but not when doing so would impose an unduly severe or costly burden without substantially contributing to the safety of persons or property.' A state row that states the NFPA edition as the operative standard, without the 'conform generally' and the burden qualifier, overstates what the landlord must do and points at the wrong document - the binding text is the fire marshal's administrative rules. Rows for ND, WV, MD, MA, CT, RI, NH and ME should be checked for that distinction. THIRD, on the Louisiana framing question (2026 La. Acts No. 881 moving the construction code to a new title): Nebraska did not renumber its fire code this session. But Nebraska did renumber a different body of law landlords care about - the alien land law moved from §§ 76-402 to 76-415 to §§ 76-3701 to 76-3717 by Laws 2024, LB1301 - so a renumbering check is worth running state by state and not only on construction codes.

### From `fire-sprinkler-duty`

FIRST, the method point, which is the valuable one: a statutory sweep is the wrong instrument for this topic in most states, and Nebraska shows why cleanly - 'sprinkler' returns zero across 7,208 statutory sections and 363 session laws, yet § 81-503.01 delegates exactly this subject to the fire marshal's rules and requires them to conform generally to NFPA 101 (2012 edition). A row reading 'no sprinkler duty' from a statute search, without saying that the requirement lives in administrative rules and local building code, will be read by a landlord as permission. Every state row on this topic should state which of the three layers it searched - statute, administrative code, local ordinance - and the states listed here (MN, WI, WV, MD, MA, RI, NH) should be checked for that. SECOND, where a state's fire code is delegated with a 'conform generally ... but not when unduly severe or costly' qualifier, as Nebraska's is, the NFPA edition is not the operative standard and a row quoting an NFPA requirement as state law is wrong. THIRD, a drafting point that is portable to every URLTA state: a lease promise about a safety system is converted into a statutory maintenance duty by URLTA § 2.104(1)(d)'s 'supplied or required to be supplied' (Nebraska § 76-1419(1)(d)), and the damages limb of § 4.101 has no materiality threshold - so the tenant-obstruction clause is safe to offer and the landlord-promise clause is not. Any multistate sprinkler or fire-safety clause should be checked for a landlord-side promise that does this.

### From `flood-disclosure`

The method point here is worth more than the Nebraska answer and it is cheap to run in every state. For a disclosure topic, do not stop at a keyword sweep of the landlord-tenant act: find the state's PRESCRIBED seller-disclosure list and read it item by item. An absence from an enumerated statutory list is far stronger evidence than a zero from a keyword search, and the list also tells you which hazards that legislature has actually turned its mind to. Nebraska's § 76-2,120(4) lists eleven items including a carbon monoxide alarm compliance item and omits flood, which simultaneously confirms the flood absence and strengthens several other absence rows. The states on this topic that assert an absence (NC, and any other) should be re-checked that way. Second portable point: in a state whose seller-disclosure statute is triggered by a 'lease with option to purchase' or a ground lease coupled with improvements (Nebraska § 76-2,120(1)(d) and (2)), a landlord offering a rent-to-own or lease-option arrangement crosses into the seller-disclosure regime, and a flood-disclosure row written purely in tenancy terms will miss it. Third: where a state has no flood disclosure statute, the practical exposure usually runs through its deceptive-trade-practices act, and the strongest such remedy found in Nebraska makes the LEASE unenforceable by the lessor (§ 87-303.07) rather than imposing a penalty - a shape likely to recur in 1970s Uniform Deceptive Trade Practices Act states and worth searching for by the phrase 'unenforceable by the seller or lessor'.

### From `foreclosure`

A method point with wide reach, and a substantive one. METHOD: a keyword battery on tenancy-and-foreclosure terms returns nothing in Nebraska - 'bona fide tenant' 0, 'bona fide lease' 0, and only two proximity hits, both false - yet the statutes that decide the question are explicit. They are invisible because they never use the word 'tenant': §§ 76-1010(2) and 25-1530(2) speak of 'all persons claiming by, through, or under' the trustor or mortgagor. Any state pass that recorded 'no foreclosure tenant protection' from a tenant-keyword search should re-run on that phrase, or on its state's trustee's-deed and sheriff's-deed sections, before the absence is filed. The rows listed for this topic that assert an absence (KS, TN) are the first to check. SUBSTANTIVE: in a trustee's-sale state, the moment of extinguishment is often the acceptance of the bid rather than the deed or the confirmation, and that timing decides who is entitled to rent for the gap. Nebraska fixes it at acceptance of the highest bid in both routes, expressly. A state row that says the lease ends 'on the foreclosure sale' without naming the moment leaves the rent question open. THIRD: the recording-act interaction is the same everywhere and is the only thing that makes a lease survive - a lease senior to the encumbrance, or one of which the lender had notice, is not an interest 'acquired subsequent to the execution' of it. A multistate subordination-and-attornment clause would be well founded in every such state and the library does not appear to offer one.

### From `foreclosure-disclosure`

Two portable points. FIRST, and this is the one most likely to catch other states' rows: a 'foreclosure protection act' is usually a foreclosure-RESCUE statute aimed at consultants and equity purchasers, with an owner-occupancy trigger, and it creates no landlord-to-tenant disclosure duty at all. Nebraska's is exactly that shape (§ 76-2712). Any state row that cites such an act as the basis for a foreclosure disclosure to a tenant should be re-read against its definitions section; the mention of a 'rental agreement or lease' in the equity-purchase contract contents (Nebraska § 76-2720(1)(g)) is the sentence most likely to have been misread, because it is a buyer-to-homeowner disclosure. SECOND, a route to the same result without a disclosure statute: where a state's deceptive-trade-practices act makes a LEASE induced by a prohibited practice unenforceable by the lessor (Nebraska § 87-303.07, which is section 9 of the 1974 Uniform Deceptive Trade Practices Act adoption and is likely to have siblings in other 1970s UDTPA states), silence about a pending foreclosure while letting a fixed term is actionable even though no statute requires the disclosure. That gives a state with no disclosure statute a stronger practical rule than one with a disclosure statute whose only sanction is a fine, and it is worth checking in every UDTPA state by searching the trade-practices chapter for 'unenforceable by the seller or lessor'. THIRD, for any state row that offers a foreclosure disclosure clause: the most useful content is not the fact of the foreclosure but the mechanism by which the tenant can get notice of the sale - in Nebraska, recording a request under § 76-1008(1) before a notice of default is filed. Most trustee's-sale states have an equivalent request-for-notice provision, and no row in this library appears to mention one.

### From `foreign-ownership`

The topic's framing question asks about 'a foreign-ownership restriction with a lease-duration carve-out ... that exempts only leaseholds under one year, so a 12-month lease falls inside it.' Nebraska is the opposite case and the contrast is portable: § 76-3703(1)(a)'s carve-out is FIVE years, so an ordinary residential lease is outside the ban. Any multistate row on this topic that states or implies that a one-year lease falls inside a foreign-ownership prohibition must not be extended to Nebraska. Second portable point: Nebraska pairs the restriction with an express no-duty-to-inquire and no-liability-for-not-inquiring provision (§ 76-3715) that also names who IS responsible for making the determination. The state rows listed for this topic (TX, AZ, KS, ID, IN, OK, MI, IA) should be checked for an equivalent immunity, because a landlord-screening recommendation written for a state without one would be actively harmful in a state with one - here it would be unlawful in itself, because § 20-318(5) bans the INQUIRY and not merely the decision - a distinction any state row recommending citizenship or immigration screening must be checked against in its own state's fair-housing act. Third: Nebraska's exemption is geographic (inside city or village limits, or within three miles) rather than use-based, which is an unusual shape worth noting for any state whose statute is modelled on Nebraska's 1889 act.

### From `forfeiture-redemption`

Two portable points. FIRST, the sibling-act contrast used here is available in almost every state and is cheap to run: compare the state's trustee's-sale or mortgage-cure statute with its landlord-tenant act. Nebraska gives a defaulting borrower a statutory right to cure and have the security 'reinstated ... the same as if no acceleration had occurred' (§ 76-1012(1)) and gives a defaulting tenant nothing, which turns a silence into a demonstrated legislative choice. A state row asserting no relief from forfeiture should carry that contrast rather than resting on the landlord-tenant act's silence alone. SECOND, and this is the point most likely to matter to the library's clause set: the 'acceptance of rent is not a waiver' clause. Where a state has a URLTA § 4.207 analogue (Nebraska § 76-1433) whose only escape is an agreement made AFTER the breach, a lease-form non-waiver clause is both ineffective and, in a state with a § 1.403 prohibited-provisions section, affirmatively unenforceable with a damages exposure. Any multistate lease clause containing a non-waiver-of-rent-acceptance sentence should be screened against every URLTA state's § 4.207 analogue, and the clause rewritten as a direction to use a separate post-breach writing.
