THIRD, a scoping caution for any row of this kind: relief from forfeiture in practice often comes from the rules of court (a stay of the writ, an appeal bond) rather than from a statute, and a statute-only search cannot see it. Nebraska's court rules were outside this research and the row says so; other states' rows should say the same or search them.

### From `frozen-standard-incorporation`

Two portable methods. FIRST, a single-formula sweep finds half the frozen standards in a state's code, and Nebraska proves it: 'as such ... existed on' catches 101 sections here but catches nothing in the fire code, which instead names a pamphlet number and an edition year. Any state row on this topic that reports 'the state freezes standards as of [date]' from one phrase search should re-run with an edition-year pattern, and vice versa. SECOND, search the standards body's full name, not its initials. '\bNFPA\b' returns zero in Nebraska's statutes while 'National Fire Protection Association' finds the section that matters; a battery built on initials (NFPA, ICC, IBC, IRC, ASHRAE, UL) will produce false absences in any state whose drafters spell the body out. THIRD, and this is the substantive point worth carrying to every state row: freezing is not uniform within a single act. Nebraska's Carbon Monoxide Safety Act freezes the trade standard to 2015 in § 76-602(4) while adopting 'any building code adopted by the state or by the political subdivision' with no date at all in §§ 76-603, 76-604 and 76-606, and § 76-607 lets local authorities go stricter. A row that states a state's position as simply 'frozen' or 'dynamic' is likely to be wrong about half the references in the same statute.

### From `furnishings-included`

The clause is sound and portable, and the Nebraska reading suggests one addition the library might consider for every state that carries it. The clause creates an itemized inventory, which is exactly what a landlord needs on two later occasions: deducting from the deposit, and separating the landlord's furniture from the tenant's abandoned property. The second is the one the clause does not mention, and in Nebraska it matters because the abandoned-property statute's definition of personal property expressly includes 'furnishings' (§ 69-2302(6)). A sentence directing that the inventory be kept with the file for use under the state's abandoned-property procedure would improve the clause in every state. Second, a caution for the states already carrying it: in a URLTA state, listing a furnished appliance engages the landlord's § 2.104(1)(d) duty to maintain facilities and appliances 'supplied or required to be supplied' (Nebraska § 76-1419(1)(d)), and the damages limb of § 4.101 commonly has no materiality threshold - so in those states the clause has a landlord-side cost that the Louisiana Civil Code basis does not carry. CO is a URLTA-family state among the eleven on this row and should be checked. Third: the clause correctly avoids a separate furniture deposit, which would be unlawful in any state whose deposit cap reaches security 'however denominated' (Nebraska § 76-1416(1)); any state row that adds one should be screened against its cap's wording.

### From `good-cause-notice`

The distinction this row turns on is portable and is widely elided: a state can have no good-cause requirement for the NOTICE while imposing a particularity requirement on the COMPLAINT. Nebraska is the clean example - § 76-1437(2) needs no reason, § 76-1441(1)(b) demands 'the facts, with particularity'. Any state row that answers this topic with 'no good cause required' should check its state's possession-complaint statute or court rule, because the landlord still has to plead something and the row as written will be read as 'nothing to prove'. Second portable point, and a date trap rather than a length trap: Nebraska's month-to-month notice must be given at least thirty days before 'the periodic rental date specified in the notice' (§ 76-1437(2)), so the notice must point at a rental date, not at today-plus-thirty. Many URLTA states use the same formula and many rows state only the number of days. A row that gives a day count without the rental-date anchor will produce invalid notices. THIRD: retaliation provisions modelled on URLTA § 5.101 commonly list only two or three triggers - in Nebraska, a complaint to a government code-enforcement agency and tenants'-union membership (§ 76-1439(1)) - and notably do NOT protect a complaint made to the landlord. A state row describing retaliation protection in general terms overstates it; the trigger list should be quoted. Note also the apostrophe: Nebraska writes 'tenants' union', and a search for 'tenant union' returns nothing.

### From `government-fee-reimbursement`

The clause is sound and portable. Three notes for the four states carrying it and for any state considering it. FIRST, the clause's deliberate silence about attorney's fees is load-bearing in Nebraska, where § 76-1415(1)(c) voids a fee-shifting lease term in BOTH directions; a state row that adds a fee-recovery sentence to this clause would break it here and in any state with the same bar. SECOND, whether the reimbursement is 'rent' is decided by each state's definitions section and changes the clause's teeth: where rent means all payments to be made to the landlord under the rental agreement (the URLTA form, Nebraska § 76-1410(13)), non-reimbursement is a rent default with the summary notice period attached, so the '[number] days' blank should be set generously; where rent is defined as the consideration for occupancy only, it is an ordinary contract claim. A state row offering this clause should say which. THIRD, and the point most likely to matter: the pass-through this clause authorises is broader than what any Nebraska statute grants anyone. Nebraska's only statutory pass-through, § 76-14,102 in the Mobile Home Act, is conditioned on the TENANT'S failure to comply with a regulatory order, whereas this clause reaches a fee assessed merely because the property is rented. That asymmetry is worth naming in the clause's own guidance, because a landlord in a state with a tenant-fault-conditioned statute may read the clause as reflecting local law when it goes further. Separately, for any state row that asserts a jurisdiction has no rental-registration regime: Nebraska's statutes are silent but § 18-1758(3) and (4) presuppose municipal short-term-rental regulation and taxation, so a statute-only search will understate what a landlord actually faces, and the row should say that the search did not reach ordinances.

### From `governmental-fines`

The clause itself is sound and portable; two notes for the states that carry it (AS, MP, WY) and for any state considering it. FIRST, the closing promise 'Landlord will not deduct the amount from a Rent payment' interacts with each state's definition of rent. In a URLTA state whose definitions section says rent means all payments to be made to the landlord under the rental agreement (Nebraska § 76-1410(13) is the standard form), a lease-created reimbursement is rent, so the sentence is about payment allocation only and costs the landlord nothing; in a state where rent is defined narrowly as the consideration for occupancy, the same sentence can push the charge outside the summary nonpayment remedy. The row should not be read as a uniform concession. SECOND, the clause should be checked against each state's prohibited-provisions section for an attorney-fee bar: Nebraska's § 76-1415(1)(c) voids a fee-shifting term in both directions, which is unusual and which this clause happens to comply with by saying nothing about fees. A state row that adds a fee-recovery sentence to this clause would break it in Nebraska and in any state with the same bar. THIRD, for Colorado specifically, the framing question about C.R.S. § 31-15-402(4) has no Nebraska counterpart: Nebraska's nuisance provision (§ 18-1720) delegates everything to municipal ordinance and creates no statutory default liability of occupant to owner, so the 'unless the lease provides otherwise' trap the Colorado question describes cannot arise here.

### From `guarantor-renewal`

The clause is sound and portable, and one of its drafting choices turns out to carry a benefit its authors may not have intended. Its bracketed instruction 'use only if a guarantor signs this Lease' is what keeps it clear of the rule, present in many statute-of-frauds states and stated in Nebraska by Spittler v. Nicola, that a guaranty entered into INDEPENDENTLY of the original transaction needs consideration distinct from the original debt. Any state row that offers this clause for use on a separate form, or for adding a guarantor mid-tenancy, should check its own state's version of that rule - the CO and KS rows carrying this clause are both statute-of-frauds states and the point is worth confirming there. Second portable point, and the cheap test: on the Massachusetts framing question about whether a start-of-tenancy money cap also limits what may be demanded from a guarantor, the answer follows from how the cap sentence is written. Nebraska's § 76-1416(1) caps what the LANDLORD 'may demand or receive' as 'security, however denominated', which by its terms reaches money from a guarantor; a cap written instead as a limit on what the TENANT may be required to pay would not. Any state row on a deposit cap should say which formula it has before anyone concludes a guarantor deposit is available. Third: states should be screened for a cosigner rule sitting in a rent-to-own or consumer-leasing act rather than in the landlord-tenant act - Nebraska's is at § 69-2109(2) and is invisible to a landlord-tenant search.

### From `guest-rights`

The central Nebraska point is portable to every state with a Model Penal Code trespass article, which is most of them, and it is the kind of thing a landlord-tenant-only search never finds. Where the trespass offence is framed as entering or remaining 'knowing that he or she is not licensed or privileged to do so' (Nebraska §§ 28-520(1)(a), 28-521(1)) and the affirmative-defence section extends to a licence from 'the owner of the premises OR OTHER PERSON EMPOWERED TO LICENSE ACCESS' (Nebraska § 28-522(3)), a tenant with exclusive occupancy can license a guest into the leased unit and a landlord's ban cannot make that guest a trespasser there. Any multistate clause purporting to let the landlord bar a tenant's guest from the dwelling unit should be screened against the state's trespass article, not its landlord-tenant act - and the library already has at least one such clause, because the project's own record notes a trespass clause corrected for exactly this. Second portable point: a guest-policy clause's enforceability in a URLTA state usually turns on the rules-and-regulations section's notice condition (Nebraska § 76-1422(6): notice 'at the time he enters into the rental agreement'), so every guest-policy clause in the library should carry a delivery-and-receipt sentence in every URLTA state. Third: the everyday word 'guest' is the wrong search term in a URLTA state - the Act's phrase is 'person on the premises with his consent'. A state row reporting 'no guest provisions' from a guest-keyword search is probably wrong about its own state.

### From `habitability-materiality`

A drafting test that is portable to every URLTA state and is cheap to run: compare the state's § 4.101 analogue (tenant's remedy for landlord noncompliance) subsection (1) against its subsection (2). The 1972 URLTA text puts 'material' in the termination limb and omits it from the damages-and-injunction limb, so in a faithful-adoption state a non-material defect still supports damages. Nebraska is a faithful adoption (§ 76-1425), and Nebraska's own 1984 mobile-home-park statute proves the omission is readable as deliberate by inserting the word (§ 76-1498(2)). Any state row on this topic that states a single materiality threshold for 'habitability claims' without separating termination from damages should be re-read against its own subsection (2). Second portable point: an essential-services section modelled on URLTA § 4.104 (here § 76-1427) typically carries NO materiality threshold at all and only a written-notice gate, so a state row that folds heat and water into a general materiality test understates the tenant's position. The states listed on this topic (WY, MD, MA, NH, ME, VT, DE, AK) include several URLTA adopters where that check would apply.

### From `hoa`

association-approval-la's notes say the wording follows association-approval-fl and that the Florida version 'rest[s] on Florida's fee-cap and association-deposit statutes'. Nebraska has neither, and I did not open the Florida statutes, so this is not a finding about Florida - but it is a caution for any further state tagged onto this row: the row is safe to tag only where the tagging state either has no landlord-side cap on 'security, however denominated' or where the association rather than the landlord holds its own deposit. Nebraska's § 76-1416(1) cap is of that kind, and my NE segment states the condition. Any state whose deposit statute reaches money the landlord merely collects and remits should not be tagged onto this row without the same sentence.

### From `informal-dispute-resolution`

informal-dispute-resolution-or's notes state the clause is offered under rule 54 as 'a term the statute expressly lets the lease include', citing ORS 90.220(5). That justification is Oregon-specific and does not travel. For the ten states already on this row other than Oregon (AR, MS, DC, GU, VI, AS, MP, CO, WY, KS), the clause is presumably resting on general freedom of contract rather than on an express authorisation, as it now does for Nebraska - but I did not open any of those states' statutes and this is a flag for the next pass that touches the row, not a finding about them. The substantive risk to check in each is the same one Nebraska raises: a URLTA-family state with a § 76-1415(1)(a)-style blanket bar on waiving Act rights and remedies makes the clause's non-delay sentence the only thing keeping it lawful, so any state tagged here should confirm that sentence is present and unqualified before relying on the row.

### From `jury-waiver`

jury-waiver-possession-co (Colorado) is a LEASE_CLAUSE on this topic in the library and, on its id, is scoped to possession actions. I did not read it or Colorado law, so this is a flag rather than a finding: in Nebraska the equivalent clause would be pointless, because § 76-1446 removes the jury from the residential possession action by statute ('The action shall be tried by the court without a jury'). Any URLTA-family state being canvassed on this topic should check its own possession-procedure section for that sentence BEFORE writing or tagging a possession-specific jury-waiver clause - a clause waiving something the statute already withholds is dead weight, and if it is drafted broadly it can sweep in the money claim and the counterclaims, where a jury does exist.

### From `key-control-policy`

The shared clause keys (tagged NE, among many states) ends 'Tenant may not duplicate keys without Landlord's consent.' That is a contractual rule and is lawful everywhere I can see, but in Nebraska the landlord's own side of the same subject is CRIMINAL and stronger than the clause: § 28-1316(1)(c) makes it a Class III misdemeanor to duplicate a MASTER key without written permission from the person who has legal control of it, and requires every master key and every duplicate to be stamped DO NOT DUPLICATE, with § 28-1315(4) treating submaster, grand master, great grand master, emergency and overriding keys as master keys. Other states are likely to have a parallel provision in their criminal code rather than their landlord-tenant act - Nebraska's sits at §§ 28-1315 and 28-1316 under the catchlines 'Locks and keys; terms, defined' and 'Unlawful use of locks and keys; penalty; exceptions', which name neither landlords nor rentals - so any state canvassed on this topic should run a TITLE sweep of its criminal code for locks and keys rather than searching its landlord-tenant act. I did not read any other state's statute, so this is a search instruction, not a finding about them.

### From `knowing-use-penalty`

The Rhode Island question the topic poses - whether a later-added section's own voidness clause displaces the chapter's knowing-use penalty - has a mirror-image answer in Nebraska that is worth carrying to other URLTA states: here the later-added prohibition (§ 76-1413(9), Laws 2025, LB185) has NO voidness or penalty clause of its own, and the chapter's knowing-use penalty does not reach it either, because § 76-1415(2) is drafted as 'A provision prohibited by subsection (1) OF THIS SECTION'. Any URLTA state whose § 1.403-derived penalty is similarly self-referential should be checked the same way whenever a prohibited-term rule is added OUTSIDE that section - the new prohibition may carry no remedy at all. I did not read Rhode Island's sections or any other state's, so this is a method flag, not a finding about them.

### From `landlord-liability-insurance`

Two points for the twenty-two other states on this topic. (1) The question that separates the states is not 'is landlord liability insurance mandatory' - it is almost never mandatory outside New Jersey and a few municipalities - but 'what happens to the clause the landlord would use instead'. Nebraska's § 76-1415(1)(d) voids exculpation, limitation AND indemnity for the landlord's 'active and actionable negligence', and § 76-1415(1)(c) voids fee-shifting, so a Nebraska landlord has no contractual substitute for insurance at all. That is 1974 URLTA § 1.403(a)(4), so it exists in substantially those words in every URLTA state, and pairing it with the insurance question makes a far more useful row than either alone. The Nebraska annotation also fixes its boundary - the ban is residential only (Bedrosky v. Hiner) - which is worth checking state by state, because a mixed-use landlord's commercial leases are not covered. (2) The sibling contrast is likely to repeat everywhere: the Uniform Common Interest Ownership Act and the 1980 Uniform Condominium Act both make the ASSOCIATION carry liability insurance (Neb. § 76-871 is UCA § 3-113), so in nearly every state the statute books contain a residential liability-insurance mandate aimed at associations and none aimed at landlords. A row that states only the absence misses the demonstration that the silence is deliberate.

### From `landlord-registration`

The Retirement Subdivisions and Communities Act is a 1972 model (Laws 1972, LB 1311) of a kind several states enacted in the same decade, usually captioned 'retirement community', 'continuing care retirement community' or 'life care' registration and usually administered by a real estate commission or an insurance department rather than a housing agency. Two transferable points. (1) The trigger that matters is not retirement branding but a MINIMUM AGE LIMIT (Neb. § 76-1302(2)) - a library screening other states for landlord registration on the words 'register' or 'licence' will miss these acts entirely, because they are captioned as subdivision or community registration and the operative bar (§ 76-1305(1) here) does not use the word 'landlord'. (2) The entrance-fee definition (Neb. § 76-1302(13),(18)) is the usual gate, so in any state with a comparable act the question to ask is whether the act's 'lease' definition requires an entrance fee, which decides whether an ordinary age-restricted apartment complex is inside. Also worth carrying: Nebraska's short-term-rental preemption (§ 18-1758, Laws 2019, LB57) bars a municipality from 'expressly or effectively' prohibiting short-term-rental use and confines specific regulation to a demonstrated health-and-safety purpose - a landlord protection against municipal registration regimes that the states with short-term-rental rows should be screened for.

### From `landlord-remedies-termination`

Two transferable points. (1) § 76-1435 is 1974 URLTA § 4.201, and § 76-1436 is § 4.207, so every URLTA state should have a one-sentence answer to the 'possession, rent, or both' question in the same place - which is worth checking against the twenty-one other rows on this topic, several of which may be stating the answer from the general law of landlord and tenant when the act states it expressly. (2) The service-versus-money-judgment trade-off is the finding most likely to repeat and least likely to have been noticed. Nebraska's alternative service provision (§ 76-1442.01, posting and mailing on an affidavit of diligent efforts) is paired with an express bar on a money judgment in a DIFFERENT section (§ 76-1446). Many states have a posting-and-mailing or nail-and-mail route for possession actions, and a bar on in personam relief on constructive service is the normal due-process consequence - but it will usually be written in the trial or judgment section rather than the service section, so a library that researched service alone would miss it. Every state row on eviction procedure should be checked for where that bar lives.

### From `late-fee-limit`

Two points. (1) The library has twenty rows on this topic and the useful content in an uncapped state is not the absence but the SUBSTITUTE limit, which is always the liquidated-damages-versus-penalty doctrine and is almost always judge-made. A row that says only 'no cap' leaves the landlord with the impression that any figure is safe. Worth adding a sentence of the same shape to each uncapped state's row. (2) The most transferable Nebraska finding is the sibling act: § 69-2110(1)(d) caps late fees on a rent-to-own agreement at five dollars monthly and three dollars for shorter periods, with business-day grace periods and a once-per-payment rule. Rental-purchase acts of that model exist in most states and are nearly always more prescriptive than the residential landlord-tenant code. In any state recorded as having no residential late-fee cap, that act is where a legislature's own view of a reasonable late fee is written down - which is both a drafting benchmark and, for a library, proof that the residential silence is deliberate.

### From `law-enforcement-cooperation`

The most transferable finding in this batch. Nebraska's two landlord-assistance duties sit in the state's WIRETAP and PEN-REGISTER articles, which are near-verbatim adoptions of the federal model at 18 U.S.C. 2518(4) and 18 U.S.C. 3124 - and the federal text likewise names 'a provider of wire or electronic communication service, LANDLORD, CUSTODIAN, or other person'. Almost every state that enacted a state wiretap act copied that phrase. So in most states there is an express, compensated, court-order-gated landlord duty to assist law enforcement sitting in the criminal-procedure or telecommunications chapter, invisible to any landlord-tenant search, and no row in this library appears to carry it for any state. Three things to check in each: whether the compensation standard is 'prevailing rates' (Neb. § 86-293(5)) or 'reasonable expenses' (Neb. § 86-2,101(3)); whether the immunity and good-faith defence extend to the landlord or only to a 'provider' (Nebraska's pen-register section covers 'other specified persons', its wiretap section gives the motion-to-quash right to a provider ALONE, which is a real asymmetry); and whether the duty is gated on a court order, as both Nebraska sections are. Separately, § 28-417(1)(e)'s 'knows or should know is resorted to' drug-premises offence is also a common model provision (it descends from the Uniform Controlled Substances Act), so the constructive-knowledge criminal exposure with no landlord safe harbour is likely to exist in most states and is worth a row in each.

### From `lead-safe-certification`

A transferable research method, not a finding about another state's law: § 71-2518 and § 81-1211 both sit in chapters this pass does not hold, and both were recovered in full from 2025 slip laws because a Nebraska slip law prints the entire amended section rather than a diff. Any state whose session laws are published the same way (most are) can have an out-of-corpus section recovered the same way whenever it was amended recently, which is cheaper and more reliable than a mirror site. Substantively, the point worth carrying to the other twenty states on this topic is the question to ask rather than an answer: a state lead programme can look like a landlord regime from its catchline and bind only the health department, and the way to tell is whose name appears in the operative verb. Nebraska's reads 'the Division of Public Health ... shall establish', and that settles it. The second question worth asking everywhere is where the state's lead MONEY points - Nebraska's grant fund is confined to 'owner-occupied properties' (§ 81-1211), and a state whose fund reaches rental units may well have attached conditions to landlords who take it.

### From `lead-state-notices`

A reusable test, drawn from § 71-2518(1)(b), for the twenty other states on this topic. A state lead statute very often contains a pamphlet or educational-materials sentence, and the question that decides the topic is grammatical, not substantive: whose name is the subject of the obligating verb. Nebraska's reads 'the Division of Public Health ... shall establish' a program whose plan shall 'include the development of appropriate educational materials targeted to ... owners and tenants of residential dwellings' - the landlord is the audience, not the obligor, and the delivery channel is the agency's own website. A library that screened for the words 'lead' and 'pamphlet' near 'owner' would have scored that as a landlord notice duty. Conversely, a state whose equivalent sentence reads 'the owner shall provide the materials developed under this section' has a real duty hiding in a public-health chapter that a landlord-tenant-code search will never reach. Worth re-checking in the states already marked absent on this topic.

### From `lease-content-requirements`

A method point for the twenty-two other states on this topic. Nebraska's answer turns on a distinction the library's framing does not draw: between what a lease must CONTAIN and what a landlord must DISCLOSE in writing at or before commencement. § 76-1417(1) is the second kind, and a row that treats it as the first overstates the duty (a separate sheet complies) while a row that treats the absence of a contents list as the whole answer understates it (the disclosure is mandatory and its sanction, implied agency under § 76-1417(3), is severe). That disclosure is 1974 URLTA § 1.402, so every URLTA state has a near-identical section, and each should be checked for the same 'in writing at or before the commencement of the tenancy' wording and the same implied-agency sanction - which is a more unusual remedy than a penalty and is easy to miss. Second, the four Nebraska sibling statutes with prescribed contents (self-service storage, mobile home space, rental-purchase of goods, equity purchase) are all common model acts; in any state recorded as having 'no lease content requirements', those four are the places a real contents rule is most likely hiding for the subset of lettings they cover.

### From `lease-copy`

The tagged clause now reads HI,GU,VI,AS,MP,KS,NE. One caution for the five states already on it and for any state added later: in Nebraska the clause earns its place mostly through the RULES limb, not the copy limb, because § 76-1422(6) makes a house rule enforceable only if the tenant had notice of it when the rental agreement was entered into. That condition is 1974 URLTA § 3.102(1)(f) and exists in substantially the same words in every URLTA state, so in all of them this clause is the cheapest available evidence on the one issue that decides whether house rules bind at all. Worth stating in the clause's own notes rather than leaving it as a Hawaii-specific point about HRS § 521-52(a)(1). Second: where a state has a separate manufactured-home or mobile-home act, check it before tagging - Nebraska's § 76-1481 imposes a two-way copy duty with a material-noncompliance consequence that this clause's acknowledgment would misdescribe, and that pattern (the copy duty living in the mobile-home act only) is likely to repeat.

### From `lease-notice-initial-requirement`

The library has eight rows on this topic and seven of them are 'no initials requirement' absences, which suggests the North Dakota rule is genuinely unusual. Two transferable points. (1) The productive question in a state that lacks an initialing rule is not 'must anything be initialed' but 'must anything be in a SEPARATE DOCUMENT' - Nebraska's § 76-1419(3)(a) requires a maintenance-duty shift in a multi-unit building to be 'set forth in a separate writing signed by the parties', which is 1974 URLTA § 2.104(c)(1) and therefore exists in substantially those words in every URLTA state. A landlord told only that no initials are required will still put that agreement in the lease and lose it. Worth adding to the seven absence rows. (2) An arbitration-notice statute like Neb. § 25-2602.02 sits in the civil-procedure or arbitration chapter, reaches 'any standardized agreement', and will never be found by a landlord-tenant search - and the Nebraska annotations show both its force (strict compliance, clause voidable) and its limit (displaced where federal arbitration law governs). Both halves should be checked in the other states before an absence on lease formatting is recorded.

### From `lease-registration`

The library has only five rows on this topic (AS, MP, CO, WY, KS), which looks like a thin topic and is probably an under-screened one. Nebraska's answer came entirely from the deeds-and-conveyances article, whose six governing sections are captioned 'Deeds; ...' and mostly do not contain the word 'lease' at all - they reach leases because one section (§ 76-211) says 'or any interest therein' and another (§ 76-201) defines real estate to embrace chattels real except short leases. Any state screened for this topic by searching 'lease' plus 'record' will return a false absence for the same structural reason. Two specific things to look for elsewhere: a sentence of the § 76-238(1) kind ('valid between the parties') that answers the landlord's real question, and a relatives-only anti-fraud rule of the § 76-238(2) kind, which is unusual and which the Nebraska Legislature added in 2004 and amended twice since - a state with agricultural land is a likely place to find a counterpart.

### From `lease-term-limitation`

Two points for the other twenty states on this topic. (1) The library's framing question for this topic asks about a seal, the owner's own signature or a power of attorney - the D.C. and Northern Mariana Islands models. Nebraska has none of those, and the formality that actually bites is ACKNOWLEDGMENT: § 76-211 sends any lease over a year to §§ 76-216 to 76-237, and § 40-104 makes a homestead instrument void unless 'executed AND acknowledged by both spouses'. A state screened only for seals, powers of attorney and spousal CONSENT can carry a homestead or dower acknowledgment rule that the screen never sees, because the operative word is 'acknowledged' and the statute lives in a homestead or marital-property chapter rather than a landlord-tenant one. Worth re-screening the states already marked absent. (2) Nebraska's one-year statute-of-frauds line is drawn in four places with four different consequences - validity (§ 36-105), writing for creation, assignment and surrender (§ 36-103), execution and recordability (§ 76-211), and the definition that pulls a long lease into the conveyancing article (§ 76-201). Most states have the same cluster inherited from the same nineteenth-century model, and a row built on the validity section alone will miss the surrender point, which is the one landlords actually trip over.

### From `lease-type-parity`

The library's framing question for this topic looks for a Washington-style parity statute and will return 'absent' almost everywhere. Two better questions, both answered affirmatively in Nebraska from provisions no parity search would surface. (1) Every URLTA state has 1974 URLTA § 3.102(1)(c) - Nebraska's § 76-1422(3), 'applies to all tenants in the premises in a fair manner' - which is a genuine even-handedness requirement on house RULES even where lease terms and rent are unregulated. It is the practical answer to 'can I treat my month-to-month tenants differently', and the twenty-three other states on this topic should each be checked for it. (2) Nebraska's § 20-322(6), added by Laws 2025, LB150, expressly permits 'providing favorable conditions of loans, leases, mortgages, or contracts' limited to veterans or servicemembers. Several states added military or veteran status to their fair-housing lists in the same period, and a landlord-facing library should record whether the state coupled that addition with a safe harbour for veteran-favourable lease terms - without it, a veteran discount is a terms-and-conditions distinction on a newly protected ground.

### From `lease-type-size`

The library has eight rows on this topic, seven of them absences. A method point that would change some of them. The question 'is there a minimum type size for a lease' is almost always answered no, and it is the wrong question; the productive one is 'does any statute condition this document, or any clause in it, on how it is formatted'. Nebraska answers no to the first and YES to the second, twice: § 25-2602.02 reaches 'any standardized agreement' making arbitration the sole remedy and requires capitalized underlined type adjoining the signature block, with the clause voidable on strict-compliance failure (Kramer) but displaced where federal arbitration law governs (Aramark); and § 76-1605(3) requires a bold-type lien recital in a self-service storage rental agreement. Statutes of the first kind sit in arbitration or civil-procedure chapters and reach leases only through a generic noun like 'standardized agreement', so a landlord-tenant search never finds them - and they are common. Any state row asserting no formatting requirement should be scoped to point size, as this one is, or re-checked against its arbitration-notice statute.

### From `limitation-of-actions`

Nebraska's part-payment revival rule (§ 25-216) is not a tolling rule but a fresh-accrual rule, and it applies 'In any cause founded on contract' - so in any state with a comparable general revival statute, the single most valuable sentence to put in a landlord-facing limitation row is that accepting a partial payment on an old balance restarts the whole period rather than merely pausing it. The library's existing limitation rows (AR, MS, DC, PR, GU, VI, AS, MP) cover the eight jurisdictions whose own statutes say so expressly; the Nebraska route shows the same answer can come from a general chapter-25-style revival section with no landlord-tenant wording in it at all, which is worth probing in the remaining states before an absence is recorded.

### From `liquidated-damages`

CONFIRMATION OF A BRIEF CORRECTION, WITH ONE ADDITION, offered because the brief asks for the command output. Brief §14's third round corrects both the brief and the salvage record on §§ 25-21,275 to 25-21,278, and the correction is right: § 25-21,276(1) gives the action only 'when such act results in damages to the utility', and § 25-21,276(2) makes the measures available only 'upon proof of willful or intentional' conduct. Read section-open on this run, the section carries a THIRD gate the correction does not mention: subsections (2)(a) and (2)(b) are ALTERNATIVES, and the $750 is available under (2)(b) only 'if the amount of actual damage or loss is NOT SUSCEPTIBLE OF REASONABLE CALCULATION' - (2)(a) governs whenever it is. So the $750 is a fallback for unquantifiable loss, not a floor. The fee recovery in the closing sentence is also limited to 'cases within the scope of section 25-1801', which brief §14 separately records as carrying a ninety-day condition precedent. For other states: this is the general shape to expect wherever a statute fixes a liquidated sum, and it is the same shape the common-law doctrine takes - an agreed sum is tolerated where actual loss cannot reasonably be calculated. A library row that offers a liquidated-damages clause in any state should be checked for whether it says that.

### From `lockout-for-rent-delinquency`

Two points for the twenty-one other states on this topic. (1) The decisive drafting feature of Nebraska's prohibition is the phrase 'by action or otherwise' in § 76-1436 (1974 URLTA § 4.207) coupled with 'including willful diminution of services ... by interrupting OR CAUSING THE INTERRUPTION of' utility service. 'Causing the interruption' reaches the landlord who simply stops paying the master account, which a prohibition drafted only against 'interrupting' would not. Worth checking in each URLTA state, because the lockout rows in this library are likely to describe the physical lockout and omit the constructive one. (2) The remedy's ARITHMETIC is what makes the prohibition bite, and it is routinely misdescribed as a cap. Nebraska's § 76-1430 awards 'an amount equal to three months' periodic rent as liquidated damages' - a fixed sum with no proof of loss - whereas the holdover and diminished-rent sections in the same act are ceilings with a greater-of alternative. Any state row that calls its ouster remedy a maximum should be re-read against the statute's own words; the distinction changes the landlord's risk assessment completely.

### From `maintenance-duty-shift`

The structural point here is 1974 URLTA § 2.104(b) and (c), so it repeats in every URLTA state and in Nebraska's own mobile-home act, and the library's nineteen rows on this topic should each be checked against it in the same way. The test that does the work is purely textual: does the state's equivalent of subsection (2) ENUMERATE the subdivisions it permits to be shifted, and does the equivalent of subsection (3) enumerate none? Where that drafting pattern holds, the listed duties are shiftable only in the single-family case and nothing is shiftable in a multi-unit building beyond discrete tasks - which is a materially narrower answer than 'the lease can delegate maintenance with conditions'. Three further details worth copying into the other rows where the statute supports them: the separate-writing requirement applies only to the multi-unit case, so a single-family lease clause suffices; the consideration standard differs between the two subsections in Nebraska ('good' versus 'adequate'); and the employ-the-tenant permission (Neb. § 76-1419(4), URLTA § 2.104(d)) is an unconditional alternative that most landlord-facing material omits entirely.

### From `meter-conservation-charge`

Three points. (1) A correction the brief asked to have confirmed with output, now confirmed from the section itself: §§ 25-21,275 to 25-21,278 do NOT price a landlord's submeter at $750. § 25-21,276(1) requires that the act 'results in damages to the utility'; § 25-21,276(2) requires 'proof of willful or intentional' conduct; and (2)(a) and (2)(b) are ALTERNATIVES, with the $750 available under (b) only 'if the amount of actual damage or loss is not susceptible of reasonable calculation'. That third gate is not in the brief's correction and should be added to it. The closing sentence also limits fee recovery to 'cases within the scope of section 25-1801', which carries its own ninety-day condition precedent. (2) Utility-diversion statutes of this model exist in most states, and the same three-gate structure should be expected; any state row that describes a diversion statute as a bar on landlord submetering is likely to be overstating it in the same way. (3) The research point: the question 'does the state regulate submetered water' usually cannot be answered from the landlord-tenant code at all. In Nebraska the answer sits partly in a definitional section of the Power Review Act (§ 70-1001.01(7), 'any legal entity supplying, producing, storing, or distributing electricity within the state for sale at wholesale or retail'), partly in municipal utility tariffs, and partly nowhere. A library that records an absence for this topic without saying which bodies of law it searched has recorded nothing, and the honest shape of the answer is the one this row takes - state the lease-as-only-governor rule, state the cautious course, and name the regime that was not read.

### From `military-air-zone-disclosure`

Two points worth carrying. (1) The closed-list test is a cheap and strong way to prove this absence in any state that has a statutory seller property condition disclosure form: if the form's contents are enumerated and military proximity is not among them, the legislature considered the disclosure question for that property and answered it without military zones. (2) Nebraska's s 76-2,120(2) extends a SELLER disclosure duty to 'any lease with the option to purchase'. Any state with a seller-disclosure statute should be checked for the same extension, because it converts a lease-option landlord into a statutory seller - and a library that files seller disclosure under sales topics will miss it.

### From `minor-tenant-filing`

s 25-1317's shape is worth checking in every state with a Field Code civil procedure chapter (which is most of the Midwest and West): a judgment against a minor that may be reopened for a year after the minor reaches majority, WITHOUT the judgment having to reserve the right, is a sleeper exposure that a minor-tenant row framed only around 'may a minor be a defendant' will miss entirely. Likewise the 'defense of an infant must be by a guardian for the suit, appointed only AFTER service' sequencing is Field Code text and will recur; in a summary eviction action it is a timing problem for the landlord, not a protection the court manages on its own.

### From `municipal-utility-lien`

s 18-509's drafting shape is worth carrying: the lien attaches to 'the property served' and collection is expressly disjunctive ('either from the owner or the person, firm, or corporation requesting the service'). Where another state's row says a municipal utility lien reaches the owner, check whether the statute says 'owner' alone or 'owner or the person requesting the service' - the disjunctive version means the city need not exhaust the tenant first, and an owner-protection proviso in one of a state's utility-lien statutes (the West Virginia pattern the topic names) does not carry across to the others.

### From `nonpayment-notice`

The door-posting point generalises and is worth a check in every URLTA state. 1972 URLTA s 1.202 (Nebraska's s 76-1413) defines RECEIPT by a closed list that does not include posting, while many of the same states separately authorise posting for SERVICE OF THE SUMMONS in the summary possession statute. A landlord who reads the summons-service provision and applies it to the pre-suit notice gives a notice the statute does not recognise. Where a state's row says a notice may be posted, check whether the authority quoted is the summons-service section rather than the notice-receipt section - and whether, as in Nebraska's s 76-1446, posted service costs the plaintiff the money judgment.

### From `nonrefundable-deposit-notice`

RULE 26 - nonrefundable-fees-wv (6 states: WV,MS,PR,VI,AS,MP) was read in full and is NOT tagged for Nebraska, on two of the four rule-26 failure grounds. (1) It relies on another state's rule. Its operative sentence - 'Landlord and Tenant expressly agree that the following fees are nonrefundable' - does work in West Virginia because W. Va. Code s 37-6A-1(14) takes a pet or application fee outside the statutory definition of a security deposit IF the parties expressly agree in writing that it is nonrefundable. Nebraska's s 76-1416(1) has no such carve-out and instead reaches 'security, however denominated', so the same sentence has no legal effect here. (2) It carries a blank whose value would be unlawful. The blank invites 'a nonrefundable pet fee of $___', and in Nebraska that money is security: it must fit inside one month's periodic rent, and if it is pet money, inside one-fourth of one month's periodic rent as well. A figure chosen on the assumption that the designation removes it from the cap would breach s 76-1416(1). The clause's second sentence ('Any other money Tenant gives Landlord to secure Tenant's performance ... is part of the Security Deposit') is correct for Nebraska but is the statute's default anyway, so tagging would import the harmful half for the sake of the harmless half. MORE GENERALLY, and worth checking in every state the clause is already tagged into: whether a nonrefundable designation works turns on whether the state's DEFINITION of security deposit has an express-agreement carve-out. Where the statute instead says 'however denominated', 'by whatever name' or similar, the clause is not merely ineffective but a trap, because it invites a figure chosen outside the cap.

### From `nonrefundable-deposit-separate-notice`

The internal-contrast technique used here is portable and cheap: before writing 'state X has no separate-notice requirement for nonrefundable fees', search the state's landlord-tenant act for its own separate-writing or separate-instrument device. Most URLTA states carry 1972 URLTA s 2.104(b)'s maintenance-delegation provision, which in Nebraska is s 76-1419(3)(a) and requires 'a separate writing signed by the parties and supported by adequate consideration'. A state that uses the device there and not in its deposit section has made a visible drafting choice, which is stronger evidence than a keyword zero.

### From `nonresident-owner-agent`

Two transferable points. (1) 1972 URLTA s 2.102 (Nebraska's s 76-1417) is the reason most URLTA states have NO nonresident-agent statute: the disclosure already names a person for service of process, and the sanction is that the non-discloser becomes the landlord's agent for performing the landlord's obligations and for spending the rent. Before writing a nonresident-agent absence for a URLTA state, read its s 2.102 analogue - the answer is usually there, and the sanction subsection is the part existing rows tend to miss. (2) s 25-528's shape - an optional recorded appointment of a resident agent whose benefit is immunity from service by publication - is old Field Code real-property procedure and is likely to exist in other Field Code states under a catchline about service rather than about landlords. It is a landlord PROTECTION, which is the category the project's 'not a tenant protection, therefore reject' habit tends to drop.

### From `notice-service-fee`

Nebraska's s 76-1415(1)(c) is a deliberate change from 1972 URLTA s 1.403(a)(3), which bars only a term by which the tenant agrees to pay the LANDLORD's attorney's fees. Nebraska added 'or tenant's', so a mutual or prevailing-party fee clause is prohibited here and may be permitted in other URLTA states on the uniform text. Any shared row offering a reciprocal fee clause as the safe compromise should carry that distinction, and any notice-fee clause tagged into a URLTA state should be checked for whether the fee is in substance an attorney charge.

### From `notice-to-quit-waiver`

Two transferable points. (1) The jury-waiver clause is dead weight in any URLTA state whose summary possession section says the action is tried by the court without a jury (Nebraska s 76-1446). Before a jury-waiver clause is written or tagged into a state, check the possession section, not the general civil procedure chapter - and note that Nebraska's OLD forcible-entry section (s 25-21,219) does contemplate a jury, so a state that retains both regimes can look as if it has jury trials in eviction when its residential act does not. (2) A non-application clause inside one section of an older eviction chapter does not disapply the chapter. Nebraska's s 25-21,219 says 'This section shall not apply'; the three-day notice in s 25-21,221 fails to attach for the separate reason that its own trigger is an action under that range. Any state row reasoning from a single non-application sentence to a whole chapter should be re-checked section by section.

### From `notice-to-vacate-additional-terms`

Two points. (1) The everyday word 'uninhabitable' is a paraphrase trap across the URLTA states: the uniform phrase is 'fit and habitable' (Nebraska s 76-1419(1)(b)), and 'uninhabitable' returns zero in all twelve Nebraska chapters searched. A battery on the everyday word will produce a false absence on the habitability duty itself, not only on the pending-notice question. (2) Where a state has no pending-notice alteration ban, the substitute exposure is its ouster-and-diminution-of-services remedy, and the MEASURE matters: Nebraska's s 76-1430 (1972 URLTA s 4.107) is a FIXED three months' periodic rent plus fees with no proof of loss, whereas its holdover and failure-to-deliver measures (ss 76-1437(3), 76-1426) are ceilings with a greater-of alternative. A row that calls all of them 'caps' understates the self-help exposure by a wide margin, and that distinction should be checked in every URLTA state before a row describes the remedy.

### From `nuisance`

Three transferable points. (1) The old obscenity-nuisance abatement acts (Nebraska ss 28-807 to 28-829) exist in near-identical form in many states and are routinely overlooked because their catchlines are about obscenity. The landlord-relevant parts are the closing order and the OWNER's bond in the full value of the property to obtain release - an owner-side exposure, not a tenant protection, and therefore in the category state passes tend to reject for the wrong reason. (2) Where a state has both a criminal drug-premises statute and a civil forfeiture statute, compare their knowledge standards: Nebraska's s 28-417(1)(e) uses 'knows or should know' while its forfeiture innocent-owner defence at s 25-21,302(2) turns on 'actual knowledge or consent'. A landlord can be safe from forfeiture and still chargeable, and a row that states one standard for both is wrong. (3) A self-help entry power buried in a criminal chapter (Nebraska's s 28-826) will collide with the URLTA ouster remedy in every URLTA state that retains the older provision. Before any state row describes a conviction-based repossession right, check whether the state's URLTA s 4.107 analogue displaces it, and state the cautious course rather than the literal text.

### From `optional-lease-terms`

The 'unless otherwise agreed' census is a cheap, repeatable drafting test for every URLTA state and gives a defensible answer to 'may the lease vary this?' without needing case law. Run it over the state's landlord-tenant chapter, list the sections that carry the phrase, and treat the rest as mandatory. In Nebraska it yields eleven sections and excludes the termination, notice, remedies and casualty sections. It also exposes the opposite error: a shared clause that varies a provision the state's own drafting marks as non-default will be void in that state while valid in a state whose analogue does carry the phrase, so the census should be run before a variation clause is tagged into a new state rather than after.

### From `ordnance-demolition-meter-disclosures`

The shared-meter point is the transferable one and it is a landlord exposure in every URLTA state, not a Nebraska quirk. 1972 URLTA s 2.104(a)(6) (Nebraska s 76-1419(1)(f)) excuses the water-and-heat duty only where the installation is in the tenant's EXCLUSIVE CONTROL and supplied by a DIRECT public utility connection - two requirements a master-metered or shared-metered unit fails - and s 2.104(c) (Nebraska s 76-1419(3)) does not extend the agreed-shift option to that duty for anything other than a single-family residence. So a bill-through or allocation clause on a shared meter is unenforceable in the URLTA states as to water, hot water and heat, whatever the state's disclosure law says. The salvage record already flags the same defect in the shared row utilities-responsibility; this adds that a state with NO shared-meter disclosure statute is not thereby a state where allocation is permitted.

### From `other-landlord-facilities`

This is a URLTA-wide finding that a facilities-list search cannot reach. 1972 URLTA s 1.301(10) (Nebraska s 76-1410(12)) defines 'premises' to include 'facilities held out for the use of tenants generally or whose use is promised to the tenant', and s 2.104(a)(4) (Nebraska s 76-1419(1)(d)) imposes the maintenance duty on facilities 'supplied or required to be supplied'. Together they mean that in EVERY URLTA state an advertised or promised amenity becomes part of the statutory premises and acquires a statutory maintenance duty, with no state-specific facilities statute needed. A row that answers 'other landlord facilities' with a flat absence because the state has no amenity list is therefore wrong in substance, not merely thin. The salvage record notes the 'required to be supplied' phrase is missing from Nebraska's own habitability rows; the definitional half appears to be missing everywhere.

### From `owner-move-in-reservation`

The clause's closing sentence ('Landlord may regain possession only through a court eviction') is doing more work than it looks in the URLTA states, where 1972 URLTA s 4.107 fixes the self-help price. In Nebraska that is s 76-1430 and the figure is a FIXED three months' periodic rent plus fees with no proof of loss, not a ceiling. Worth noting for the states this clause is already tagged into: Arkansas and Kansas are not URLTA s 4.107 states in the same terms, so the sentence is a drafting courtesy there and a restatement of a hard statutory penalty in a URLTA state. Also, the clause's 30-day blank should be checked against each state's month-to-month notice period before it is tagged into a new state; where that period is longer than 30 days (several states use 60), the clause's own floor is below the figure a tenant would expect and the blank invites a number that reads as evasion even if the fixed-term analysis holds.

### From `parking-rules-notice`

Two points. (1) 1972 URLTA s 3.102(a)(6) (Nebraska s 76-1422(6)) makes a rule enforceable only if 'the tenant has notice of it at the time he enters into the rental agreement'. That is a PRE-EXECUTION DELIVERY requirement for parking rules in every URLTA state, reached through the rules section rather than a parking statute - so a state row that answers 'no parking-rules notice requirement' without citing its rules section understates the law. (2) The accessible-parking statutes are a cross-state blind spot of the same kind found here: they bind 'any person in lawful possession of any offstreet parking facility' and typically contain no landlord, lessor or tenant reference at all, so no landlord-keyword sweep reaches them, and the duties they impose (a conforming sign at each space, a separate tow-in-zone sign, and notification of law enforcement before removal) fall on an apartment-complex lot. Worth a title sweep for 'handicapped' or 'accessible parking' in every state's municipal-powers chapter.

### From `part5-nonwaivable`

The remedy-boundary point is a URLTA-wide drafting fact, not a Nebraska quirk: 1972 URLTA s 1.403(b) keys its knowing-use penalty to 'a provision prohibited by subsection (a)'. Any URLTA state whose row lists several sources of void terms together should check whether its penalty subsection is similarly keyed, because electronic-delivery and UETA prohibitions sit outside it. Separately, s 86-632(3) and s 86-635(4) are uniform UETA text, so the view-only-portal consequence (an electronic record the sender prevents the recipient from printing or storing is not enforceable against the recipient, and that cannot be varied by agreement) is available in every UETA state.

### From `periodic-services-entry`

RULE 26 - scheduled-services-entry-la (8 states: LA,AR,MS,VI,AS,MP,CO,KS) was read in full and is NOT tagged for Nebraska, on three of the four rule-26 grounds. (1) It relies on another state's rule. Its notes state the basis outright - 'Louisiana has no entry statute ... so a scheduled-services entry right exists only by contract' and 'It is lawful because no statute limits entry notice or hours'. Nebraska has an entry statute whose s 76-1423(4) says the landlord 'has no other right of access except by court order, as permitted by subsection (2) of section 76-1432, or if the tenant has abandoned or surrendered the premises', so the no-statute premise fails here. (2) It carries blanks whose values would be unlawful in Nebraska. 'at least [state notice, for example 24 hours] in advance' invites any figure, and anything under 24 hours breaches s 76-1423(3)(a); the clause also does not require the notice to state the purpose and a reasonable anticipated entry window, which s 76-1423(3)(a) requires on its face. (3) Its delivery blank is unlawful here as written. '[state method, for example text message, e-mail or A NOTICE POSTED ON THE DOOR]' offers two methods Nebraska does not allow for this notice: door-posting is not among s 76-1413(2)(c)'s three receipt methods, and fixing text or e-mail in the lease is requiring the tenant to accept electronic delivery as part of the rental agreement, which s 76-1413(9) prohibits outright (Laws 2025, LB185). THE GENERAL WARNING, worth carrying to the other seven states: this clause's lawfulness depends on the state having NO entry statute. Before it is tagged into another state, check (a) whether an entry statute exists and whether its no-other-right-of-access sentence is exhaustive, (b) the statutory minimum notice and whether content (purpose, time window) is prescribed, and (c) whether the state has an electronic-delivery consent statute that makes the lease's choice of text or e-mail unlawful. The door-posting option in particular should probably come out of the shared clause in every URLTA state, since 1972 URLTA s 1.202's receipt list does not include posting.

### From `pest-control-notice`

The transferable point is that in a URLTA state the pesticide-notice question is partly answered by the ENTRY section and rows tend to miss it. Nebraska's s 76-1423(3)(a), as amended in 2021, requires the entry notice to 'include the intended purpose for entry and a reasonable period during which the landlord anticipates making entry'. Where a state's URLTA s 3.103 analogue carries a purpose requirement, a landlord treating a unit must say the entry is for pest treatment - which is a de facto pre-treatment notice even where the state has no pesticide statute reaching landlords. Any 'no pest-control notice requirement' row should be checked against the state's entry-notice CONTENT requirement before it is written as a flat absence. Separately, the place to look for a real pesticide notice duty in most states is the administrative rules under the pesticide act (applicator posting and re-entry intervals), not the statute, which is a channel most of these passes do not hold.

### From `pet-eviction-fact-sheet`

Transferable: the pet-fact-sheet topic is really two questions, and the eight existing education rows answer only one. (a) Is there a state-issued fact sheet? (b) Does the state's security-deposit statute reach a pet deposit? Nebraska answers (a) no and (b) yes, and a state that answers (a) no may still constrain pet money. Any state row that says "no pet rules" should be checked against its own deposit statute's "however denominated" language before it is read as a free hand on pet charges.

### From `pet-fees`

Transferable test, and it sharpens the one batch 07 recorded. A "nonrefundable pet fee" is safe only where BOTH are true of the state's deposit statute: (i) its definition of security deposit has an express-agreement or fee carve-out (W. Va. Code Sec. 37-6A-1(14) style) rather than "however denominated"; and (ii) the state does not separately define rent as every payment under the rental agreement. Nebraska fails (i) and satisfies (ii) in the direction that makes the characterisation ambiguous rather than clearly unlawful -- Sec. 76-1416(1) says "however denominated" while Sec. 76-1410(13) says rent is "all payments to be made to the landlord under the rental agreement," and the two readings cannot both be right. Any URLTA state has both sentences, because they are 1974 URLTA Secs. 1.301(14) and 2.101(1), so this ambiguity is probably library-wide and not Nebraska-specific; the eight single-state pet-deposit education rows should be checked for which of the two sentences they relied on. Separately: Nebraska's quarter-month pet allowance is an ADDITION to the general cap, not an exclusion from it -- a shape distinct from both the Colorado-style pet cap and the Idaho/Missouri-style exclusion, and worth a third option in any cross-state pet-fee comparison.

### From `plain-language`

Transferable test for every "no plain-language law" row in the library: the question is not whether the state has a plain-language ACT but whether it has ANY formatting rule whose non-compliance voids a lease term. Nebraska has no act and still has one such rule (Sec. 25-2602.02), reached only by searching for the prescribed sentence rather than for the doctrine's name -- 'plain language' returns 34 hits, all the interpretive canon, and the title sweep returns 0. So the eight single-state rows that say "no plain-language rule" should each be re-screened for an arbitration-notice or signature-block formatting statute outside the landlord-tenant title before they are relied on. Also worth carrying: a state-law formatting rule of this kind may be displaced where the FAA governs the contract (the Aramark lead), which limits the exposure in every state that has one.

### From `plain-language-consumer-statement`

Transferable, and it reframes the topic. A "statement of consumer restrictions" requirement is a DISCLOSURE response to unenforceable lease terms; a URLTA prohibited-provisions section (1974 URLTA Sec. 1.403, Nebraska's Sec. 76-1415) is a VOIDNESS response to the same risk. The two are substitutes, so in any URLTA state the right answer to this topic is almost certainly "no statement required, and here is the prohibited-provisions section instead" rather than a bare absence -- and a row that reports only the absence leaves the landlord without the rule that actually governs. Worth checking the seven existing "no plain-language consumer statement" education rows (MD, MA, RI, NH, ME, VT, DE) for whether each names its own state's prohibited-provisions section; MA, RI, NH, ME, VT and DE are not URLTA states in the same way, so the substitute may differ. Second transferable point: a multistate lease form carrying a Pennsylvania-style consumer-restrictions page into a URLTA state can be affirmatively harmful, because listing waivers the state voids is evidence of the "deliberate use" that triggers the penalty (Nebraska Sec. 76-1415(2): actual damages and reasonable attorney's fees).

### From `political-access`

Transferable, and it probably affects several of the eight existing rows on this topic. A candidate-access statute is normally in the ELECTION code, not the landlord-tenant code (Minn. Stat. Sec. 211B.20 is the model; Maryland's voter-information-area duty is the other shape). Any "no candidate access rule" row researched only within the state's landlord-tenant title is therefore unproven, and the search has to be run over the election title. Second point, which no row on this topic appears to carry: in a state whose criminal-trespass statute turns on being "licensed or privileged" and which lets the TENANT license a visitor, the landlord's no-solicitation rule is enforceable in the common areas and unenforceable as to a visitor invited into the unit. That split is the practical answer to the topic in every such state and does not depend on whether an access statute exists.

### From `pool-safety`

Two transferable points. (1) A pool-safety search confined to the landlord-tenant title and the health title will miss the rule in a state that files its pool programme under an environmental or sanitation act -- Nebraska's is in the Environmental Safety Act in chapter 81, beside solid waste and water quality, and the words 'swimming pool' appear nowhere in its landlord-tenant act. Washington's WAC 246-260 and Kentucky's KRS 211.203 are health-title placements; Nebraska is a third placement, and any "no pool rule" row for a state should be checked against its environmental or sanitation title before it is trusted. (2) The barrier question is almost never answered by statute. Nebraska's statute delegates design and construction standards to regulation and, since 2026, delegates adoption and enforcement to local government -- so the useful library answer in a delegating state is "state statute sets no fence specification; the standard is the state's administrative code plus the local ordinance," and rows that assert a specific fence height from a statute should be re-checked for whether that figure is statutory or regulatory. The existing edu-no-pool-barrier-requirement-ks row is the one most worth re-screening on both points, since Kansas files its public-pool programme outside its landlord-tenant act too.

### From `portable-cooling-device`

Transferable drafting test, available in every URLTA state because the sentence is 1974 URLTA Sec. 2.104(1)(d) and (f): the act's fitness section names HEAT expressly and does not name COOLING, while the maintain-in-working-order limb reaches air conditioning only where it is "supplied or required to be supplied" by the landlord. So in any URLTA state the answer to both the portable-cooling topic and the "is a hot apartment uninhabitable" question is read off the same subsection, and a row asserting a cooling duty in a URLTA state should be checked for whether the state amended (1)(f) or is relying on (1)(d) plus a supplied unit. Second point, worth carrying to WA and OR: the real consequence of permitting a window unit is not the right to install but who owns the maintenance of it afterwards, and the two portable-cooling-device clause rows should be screened for whether they allocate maintenance, removal and window repair -- in a (1)(d) state a landlord-supplied unit becomes a statutory maintenance obligation that no lease in a non-single-family unit can shift.

### From `portable-cooling-device`

Probably a multi-state item the library carries for nobody. A state statute that authorises MUNICIPAL trade licensing for HVAC, electrical or plumbing work, with an exemption written for an owner-occupant rather than for an owner, puts a hands-on landlord on the wrong side of a criminal provision while being invisible to every landlord-tenant search. The test to run in each state: find the owner-does-own-work exemption in the trade-licensing statute and read whether it says "owner" or "the property in which the homeowner resides" -- Nebraska's Sec. 18-2308 says the latter, and the difference is the whole exposure. Second transferable point: Nebraska's Sec. 18-2314 sends the non-compliance and removal notice to "the owner", so in a delegating state the landlord is the person on the hook for work a contractor did badly.

### From `portable-solar`

A distinction worth imposing on this whole topic, because the four dossier questions conflate two different statutes. (A) An INSTALLATION RIGHT (Virginia's small-landlord provision, Vt. 30 V.S.A. Sec. 256(g), Me. 35-A Sec. 3475) creates a tenant entitlement and confines the landlord to reasonable restrictions. (B) A SOLAR-RESTRICTION-VOIDING statute invalidates a prohibition in a deed, covenant or other instrument and may or may not reach a lease. A state can have (B) and still leave the landlord free to refuse, because voiding a prohibition is not the same as granting a right to install, and a lease is a term-limited possessory instrument rather than a servitude. Each of the eight existing rows on this topic should say which of (A) and (B) its state has; a row resting on (B) and reported as a tenant right is probably overstated. Third point, and it is the Nebraska-specific one with cross-state reach: a statute barring severance of the wind or solar resource from the surface estate (Nebraska Sec. 76-3004) limits the DEAL STRUCTURE rather than the lease term -- a rooftop-solar arrangement in such a state has to be a lease, licence or easement over the surface estate, never a conveyance of the resource. Several plains states enacted anti-severance provisions alongside wind development, so this is worth screening for in CO, WY, KS, SD and ND before any rooftop-solar row is written.

### From `portfolio-thresholds`

A taxonomy this topic needs and no existing row appears to state: a counted threshold in landlord-tenant law is one of four kinds, and they are not interchangeable -- PER PORTFOLIO (doors the landlord owns, the Virginia and Ohio shape), PER BUILDING (units in the structure, Nebraska Sec. 20-319(6) and the federal accessible-design rule), PER COMPLEX (units offered under one promotional plan, Nebraska Sec. 76-1302(2)), and PER UNIT (what this dwelling is, Nebraska Sec. 76-1410(16)). The dossier's own framing ("duties tiered by the landlord's portfolio size") assumes the first kind, and a researcher who finds a "four or more units" line and files it as a portfolio threshold has probably mis-sorted a per-building rule. Second, the conjunctive point generalises and is worth checking in every state: an own-home or owner-occupied exemption usually has two limbs (occupancy AND a count), and Nebraska's Sec. 20-322(3) loses the exemption on either limb -- "this exception shall not apply to any person who makes available for rental or occupancy more than four sleeping rooms to a person or family within his or her own home." Third: the federal Fair Housing Act's 42 U.S.C. 3603(b)(1) three-or-fewer-single-family-houses exemption is a true portfolio threshold that reaches landlords in EVERY state, and a state row that reports "no portfolio thresholds" without saying whether the state act mirrors or omits that federal exemption is incomplete. Nebraska omits it.

### From `possession-bond`

"Possession bond" names two incompatible devices and the library should not let one row cover both. (A) The TENNESSEE shape: an end-of-term bond in or alongside the lease carrying a confessed judgment for possession -- i.e. a LEASE TERM. (B) The TEXAS shape: a bond the LANDLORD posts with the court to obtain possession before judgment -- i.e. a PROCEDURAL step with no lease footprint. A state can forbid (A) and still offer (B), or neither. The discriminating question for (A) in any state is whether the state prohibits confession of judgment in a rental agreement; every URLTA state does, because it is 1974 URLTA Sec. 1.403(1)(b) -- Nebraska's Sec. 76-1415(1)(b) is verbatim -- so in a URLTA state (A) is not merely absent but void, and a multistate form carrying a cognovit clause is an affirmative exposure rather than dead weight. Separately, and worth checking in every state before a row says a tenant's appeal stops the eviction: the stay is often conditional on a deposit or bond PLUS continuing monthly payments into court (Nebraska Sec. 76-1447), and the condition is where the landlord's leverage sits. Also note Nebraska's two-track appeal: Sec. 76-1447 for a URLTA possession action with its bond condition, and Sec. 25-21,233 for a non-URLTA forcible entry and detainer with no bond provision at all -- a two-track structure other states are likely to share and that a single-row answer would flatten.

### From `post-eviction-property`

Three transferable tests. (1) THE BRIDGE SENTENCE. The question "does the abandoned-property statute apply after a writ, or only to voluntary abandonment?" is usually answered not in the abandoned-property statute (whose trigger is normally "vacated by the tenant") but in the TRIAL-AND-WRIT section of the possession act. Nebraska's bridge is the last sentence of Sec. 76-1446. A library that researched only the abandoned-property statute will have a gap on exactly the fact pattern landlords face, and every post-writ row should be checked for whether it found its state's bridge sentence or assumed one. (2) THE IMMUNITY IS TIERED, NOT FLAT. Nebraska Sec. 69-2309 gives absolute immunity only for release to the FORMER TENANT; release to a believed owner and disposal by sale leave a residual exposure to an un-notified claimant who can prove the landlord should have known of their interest AND should on reasonable investigation have known their address. Rows that say "the landlord has statutory immunity" without the tier structure overstate it, and the drafting point is that the shield also fails for property omitted from the notice. (3) THE SECOND, TENANT-INITIATED ROUTE. Nebraska runs TWO mechanisms in parallel -- the landlord's notice-and-sale track (Secs. 69-2303 to 69-2310) and a tenant's written-request track with its own fourteen-day, five-day and seventy-two-hour clocks (Sec. 69-2311) -- and the damages section (Sec. 69-2312) is keyed to the second. A state whose statute has a tenant-request provision will have the same two-track structure, and a row describing only the landlord's track misses where the liability actually arises. Also worth noting for the ejectment question in the dossier: Nebraska's Sec. 69-2314 makes the Act non-exclusive, and Secs. 76-301 to 76-309 (occupying-claimant reimbursement for improvements) are a separate body of law from the detainer route, but neither provides a warehouse-storage option, so Nebraska has no analogue to the ejectment/warehouse split the dossier asks about.

### From `post-eviction-property`

This is probably a fifty-state item the library carries for three states and denies for two. The test to run in each state is a single one: does the animal-cruelty statute's definition of "owner", "custodian" or "person responsible" include someone who KNOWINGLY PERMITS AN ANIMAL TO REMAIN ON PREMISES THEY OWN OR OCCUPY? Nebraska's Sec. 28-1008(9) does, in those words. Where it does, a landlord who takes possession and leaves an animal is inside a criminal statute regardless of whether the state's landlord-tenant act mentions animals, and a "no post-writ animal duty" row (ND, SD) is wrong as written -- it is answering a question about the landlord-tenant act and reporting it as an answer about the law. Three features to record per state: whether the mental element includes recklessness (Nebraska's does, Sec. 28-1009(1)); whether there is any notice-and-wait or safe-harbour period for a landlord (Nebraska has none); and whether the state gives animal control a warrant-based entry power the landlord can invoke (Nebraska Sec. 28-1012(1)), which is the only clean exit. Also worth carrying: a state's abandoned-property statute will usually define "personal property" in terms that cannot accommodate a living animal (Nebraska Sec. 69-2302(6)), so the gap between the two statutes is structural rather than a Nebraska quirk.

### From `private-well-testing`

Transferable, and it separates two duties the dossier's single topic line runs together. (A) A TESTING duty (test the well on a cycle) and (B) a DELIVERY duty (give the tenant the results). New Jersey has both; a state can have (B) without (A) by requiring delivery only of tests the landlord happens to have, which is a much weaker rule and much easier to comply with. Each of the eight existing rows should say which it has, and whether the duty is triggered at lease signing, on a cycle, or on a request. Second point: the duty is almost never in the landlord-tenant act -- it is in the health or water title -- so a row researched only in the landlord-tenant act is unproven, and the search terms that work are the CONTAMINANT names (nitrate, coliform, arsenic) and "private well", not "water". Third, and this is the Nebraska-specific one worth checking in CO, WY, KS, SD, ND and IA: a state may require a well-related notice on a TRANSFER OF OWNERSHIP (Nebraska Sec. 76-2,124) and nothing on a lease. Finding that conveyance notice and reporting it as a landlord duty would be an error, and the discriminating words are "transferring ownership" and "transferee".

### From `prohibited-acts-renter`

Recommendation for the ten states already on prohibited-acts-renter-wy (WY, AK, HI, AR, MS, DC, GU, AS, MP, CO). The row's notes carry a WY-scoped absence finding -- "WY has no statutory advance-notice-for-entry requirement -- this clause only bars the tenant from unreasonably refusing entry, it does not itself establish a landlord notice obligation" -- and that sentence is true of Wyoming and FALSE of most of the other states on the row. Alaska, Hawaii, Arkansas (in part) and the District of Columbia are URLTA or URLTA-derived jurisdictions whose access sections do impose advance notice, and Colorado's position differs again. The sentence is already labelled "WY", so it is not an error in the row, but anyone reading the row's notes as a general statement about the clause will get the entry question backwards. Worth a one-line scope marker at sync. Second, transferable and more useful: the limb that should be screened in every state is the third one. A clause barring the tenant from refusing entry is safe only where it is tied to UNREASONABLE refusal, because in a state with a statutory notice requirement an unqualified duty to admit the landlord is an agreement to forego a right under the act (Nebraska Sec. 76-1415(1)(a); 1974 URLTA Sec. 1.403(1)(a) in every URLTA state). The word "unreasonably" in this clause is what makes it portable, and it should not be edited out. Third: the clause's purpose list is narrower than the URLTA's (it omits decorations, alterations, improvements and the supply of necessary or agreed services), so in a URLTA state the clause understates the landlord's own access purposes -- harmless, since the statute governs, but a candidate for widening if the clause is ever revised.

### From `promises-to-repair`

Transferable, and it inverts the topic for an entire class of states. The Wisconsin question is "what formality does a repair promise need to be ENFORCEABLE?" In a URLTA state the question is the opposite one, because 1974 URLTA Sec. 1.301(12) -- Nebraska's Sec. 76-1410(14) -- defines "rental agreement" to include ORAL agreements, and the landlord-noncompliance section keys its remedies to "the rental agreement". So in every URLTA state an unwritten repair promise is presumptively enforceable and the drafting problem is containment, not formality. Two consequences for the library. (1) Each of the eight existing rows on this topic should say whether its state's definition of rental agreement includes oral agreements; a row that reports "no promise-to-repair rule" in a URLTA state is reporting the absence of a formality while the promise is in fact enforceable, which is the wrong half of the answer. (2) The `promised-repairs-wi` clause is probably portable to URLTA states as an affirmative schedule with completion dates, and is worth offering there for the evidentiary reason rather than the regulatory one -- but a companion DISCLAIMER clause is not portable, because the URLTA's prohibited-provisions section (Sec. 1.403(1)(a)) is in every one of them.
