Third, and checkable without new research: the phrase to look for in any state's fitness section is "supplied or required to be supplied" (Nebraska Sec. 76-1419(1)(d)) -- those five words are what pull a voluntarily supplied amenity into the statutory maintenance duty, and they appear in the URLTA original.

### From `prop65-rental-warning`

Two transferable points. (1) The search that proves this absence is the PHRASE search, not the word search. Proposition 65's operative language is "known to the State to cause cancer"; the everyday word "warning" returns noise in every state code (22 sections here, none on point) while "known to the state" returns zero. Any "no Prop 65 analogue" row should record which of the two it ran, because a row resting on "warning" alone has not tested the right term and a row resting on "carcinogen" alone could miss a state that wrote the duty in terms of "hazardous substances". (2) The affirmative half of this topic is the one worth standardising: in a state with no chemical-warning statute the landlord's real duties are the FEDERAL lead-paint disclosure plus whatever alarm statutes the state has, and the residual exposure is habitability and tort. Nebraska makes the tort point explicit -- Sec. 76-1419's closing sentence says "[t]he obligations imposed by this section are not intended to change existing tort law in the state" -- which is 1974 URLTA Sec. 2.104 language and therefore present in every URLTA state. That sentence is the reason a chemical hazard is a repair-and-liability problem rather than a disclosure problem in all of them, and it is worth quoting in each state's row rather than asserting the conclusion. Third, a drafting recommendation: the eight existing rows all say "no Prop 65 rule". None appears to say "and remove the imported warning block", which is the actionable half for any landlord using a California-origin form.

### From `property-tax-rent-disclosure`

The transferable test is a one-step screen that decides this topic for any state without reading its landlord-tenant act at all: DOES THE STATE DELIVER PROPERTY TAX RELIEF TO RENTERS? If it does -- a circuit-breaker, a renter's credit, a "rent constituting property taxes accrued" formula -- there will be a landlord statement or certification duty somewhere, because the tenant cannot claim without a number from the landlord. If relief is delivered as a credit against the tax bill itself (Nebraska's Property Tax Credit Act, Sec. 77-4212) or as an owner-occupant homestead exemption, there is nothing to certify and the absence is structural rather than accidental. That explains the pattern in the existing rows: Nevada and West Virginia have renter-side relief and therefore statements; Maryland, Massachusetts, Connecticut, Rhode Island, New Hampshire and Maine are reported as having none. Each of those six rows would be stronger for naming the state's relief mechanism, because an absence with a reason behind it does not need re-verifying every session. Second, practical and portable: the phrase to search is "rent constituting property taxes" (and "portion of the rent"), not "property tax" -- the latter returns 38 sections of noise in Nebraska and nothing on point. Third: in any state where the relief IS owner-side, the only live landlord-tenant question is whether a tax escalator may be passed through to the tenant, which turns on the state's definition of rent rather than on any disclosure statute.

### From `purpose-limitation`

Three transferable points, and the first is the one most likely to produce a wrong row elsewhere. (1) A LEASE-VOIDING CRIMINAL STATUTE USUALLY CARRIES A SELF-HELP SENTENCE, AND IN A URLTA STATE THAT SENTENCE IS A TRAP. Nebraska Sec. 28-826 and Rhode Island Secs. 11-19-23 and 11-30-6 are both of the nineteenth-century "void at the option of the owner, immediate entry without further process" type. Any state with such a statute also has an access section and an unlawful-exclusion remedy, and the two cannot both be right. The test to run per state: does the possession act's access section purport to be EXHAUSTIVE (Nebraska Sec. 76-1423(4): "[t]he landlord has no other right of access except by court order ..."), and is the unlawful-exclusion remedy a fixed sum or a proven-damages measure? Where it is a fixed sum, acting on the self-help sentence is expensive even if the landlord is eventually right. Nebraska's is fixed at three months' periodic rent plus fees, which is why the cautious course here is to elect the forfeiture and still go to court. Rows for RI, ND, NH, ME and DE should each be checked for whether they warn against the self-help sentence or merely report the voiding. (2) READ THE SECTION RANGE, NOT THE SENTENCE. Nebraska's provision is triggered by a conviction under Secs. 28-807 to 28-829, which sounds broad and is in fact only the obscenity article; drug and prostitution offences are outside it. A row reporting "criminal use voids the lease" without checking what the cross-referenced range actually contains will overstate the statute badly, and the fix costs one title sweep. (3) THE NUISANCE-ABATEMENT CLOSING ORDER IS THE REAL EXPOSURE AND NO ROW ON THIS TOPIC APPEARS TO CARRY IT. Nebraska's Secs. 28-822 to 28-825 let a local prosecutor close the PLACE for a year and put the cost on the owner, with an innocent-owner escape available only on a bond in the full value of the property, filed before the permanent-injunction hearing, and with "[e]very defendant in the action ... presumed to have had knowledge of the general reputation of the place." Red-light-abatement statutes of this shape exist in most states and are usually filed under nuisance rather than landlord-tenant, so they are invisible to a landlord-tenant search. The per-state questions are: how long is the closing order, what does the owner's release bond cost, and when does the window close.

### From `recycling-notice`

The transferable point is a delegation test that applies in every URLTA state and is easy to get wrong in both directions. 1974 URLTA Sec. 2.104(1)(e) is the waste-receptacles-and-removal duty and Sec. 2.104(2) and (3) are the delegation provisions; the question for any state's recycling or refuse row is WHETHER THE STATE'S VERSION OF (2) ENUMERATES (1)(e) AND WHETHER (3) DOES. In Nebraska (2) names (1)(e) and (1)(f) and is confined to a single-family residence, while (3) names no subdivision at all -- so refuse arrangement cannot be delegated in a multi-unit building by any instrument. A state that amended (3) to enumerate subdivisions, or that dropped the single-family confinement from (2), gets the opposite answer, and a row saying "the lease can make the tenant responsible for trash" needs the state's own (2)/(3) text behind it. Second: an affirmative recycling-notice duty (Oregon ORS 90.318) is a different animal from an apartment recycling MANDATE (Maryland, Massachusetts), and the latter is usually municipal or county rather than state -- so each of the eight rows should say which level of government the rule comes from, because "no state rule" is not "no rule" for a landlord in a large city. Third, and cheap to carry: in any state whose definition of rent is "all payments to be made to the landlord under the rental agreement" (Nebraska Sec. 76-1410(13)), a hauler's contamination or overage charge is collectible from the tenant only if the lease says so, and is then collectible as rent -- which means it is also inside the state's nonpayment-termination machinery, a consequence worth stating wherever a trash-charge clause is offered.

### From `redemption`

This topic is really four questions and the library's rows mix them. Worth splitting per state: (1) IS THERE A DEADLINE -- a point measured back from the eviction (Virginia's forty-eight hours) or forward from the judgment, by which a tenant may pay and stay? (2) IS LEVY BARRED ONCE THE JUDGMENT IS PAID, even though the landlord need not accept the payment (Massachusetts ch. 239, Sec. 3)? That is a bar on the OFFICER, not a duty on the landlord, and a state can have it without any redemption right. (3) IS A THIRD PARTY'S PAYMENT PROTECTED -- does a charity's or agency's cheque count as the tenant's, and may the landlord restrict the method (Delaware 25 Del. C. Sec. 5716A(b)(4), (7))? (4) IS RESERVATION WORDING MANDATED when partial rent is accepted? Nebraska answers no to all four. The transferable test that matters most, though, is the interaction nobody's row appears to state: in a URLTA state the waiver-by-acceptance section (1974 URLTA Sec. 4.207; Nebraska Sec. 76-1433) turns on the LANDLORD's acceptance of rent with knowledge of the default and says nothing about WHO TENDERED IT. So in every URLTA state a third party's or an assistance agency's payment, accepted with knowledge of the default, is as capable of waiving the termination as the tenant's own -- which means a state with no Delaware-style protection still has a third-party-payment problem, just one that runs against the landlord instead of for the tenant. That is worth adding to each waiver-by-acceptance row. Second portable point: where a state's only money-stops-the-writ route is an APPEAL bond (Nebraska Sec. 76-1447), the tenant's practical off-ramp is conditioned on continuing monthly payments into court, and the landlord's leverage is the file -- check for the deposit and for each month's payment. Rows asserting that an appeal halts an eviction should carry the conditions.

### From `religious-cultural-display`

Transferable test for the 22 states with a row on this topic: a religious-display row that leans on a state religious-freedom-restoration act must check whom that act binds. Nebraska's First Freedom Act looks broad because § 20-702(2) defines "Person" to include corporations and associations, but § 20-703's chapeau restricts only "state action" and § 20-702(5) defines that as government action - so the Act reaches no private landlord. Any state RFRA-style row stating or implying a landlord duty should be checked against its own chapeau and its own definition of the regulated actor, not against its definition of "person".

### From `rent-concession`

Worth carrying to the other 18 states on rent-concession-wi: § 87-303.07 is Nebraska's enactment of 1966 Uniform Deceptive Trade Practices Act § 3-type relief, and states with the same provision give a misdescribed concession a far larger consequence than a damages claim - the lease becomes unenforceable by the landlord and the tenant may keep the benefit without paying. Any state whose deceptive-practices act contains an "induced ... to enter into a sale or lease" rescission section should have that cited in this clause's notes rather than only an advertising prohibition, because it converts a marketing problem into a possession problem. Also, Nebraska's annotation limit is worth testing elsewhere: Lindsay Internat. Sales & Serv. v. Wegener, 301 Neb. 1 (2018) holds § 87-303.07 does not reach guarantors, so a co-signer gets no rescission - check whether the equivalent section in each state is likewise limited to "buyer or lessee".

### From `rent-demand-bar`

A test the 22 states on this topic can be checked against, and it is a drafting test rather than a guess: a rent-demand-bar row should say whether the state's bar is a BAR (the landlord may not demand or collect) or an OFFSET (the tenant may subtract), because the two have different procedural homes. Nebraska is purely the second, and the giveaway is § 76-1427(2)'s election clause - "[i]f the tenant proceeds under this section, he may not proceed under section 76-1425 as to that breach" - which is 1972 URLTA § 4.104(2) and therefore present in every URLTA state. Any URLTA-state row that lets a tenant stack an essential-services deduction on top of the § 4.101 (Nebraska § 76-1425) damages route is wrong in that state too. Second transferable point: § 76-1427(1)(c)'s substitute-housing rent excusal is 1972 URLTA § 4.104(1)(c) and is the provision most likely to be missed by a row that searched for "rent abatement" or "withhold rent" - the uniform text says "excused from paying rent", so a battery on the everyday words returns a false zero in every URLTA state.

### From `rent-escalation`

A transferable test for the eight states already on rent-escalation-la and the seven on rent-increase-midterm-ky. 1972 URLTA § 5.101(2) - Nebraska's § 76-1439(2) - carries an express proviso that "[n]othing in this section shall be construed as prohibiting reasonable rent increases", so in every URLTA state the retaliation section itself answers the "is a lease clause the only route to a mid-term increase" question NO. A row in a URLTA state that says the escalation clause is the only lawful route should be checked against its own § 5.101(2) analogue. Separately, rent-increase-midterm-ky's retaliation sentence is drafted to the broadest possible standard ("any complaint, request or other conduct the law protects") and should be narrowed state by state to that state's actual trigger list: in a 1972 URLTA state the triggers are a code complaint to a government agency and tenants'-union activity only, and promising more is a contractual expansion the landlord did not have to make. Finally, worth checking in the other 26 states on this topic: most "60-day rent increase notice" figures attributed to a state turn out to be its mobile-home or manufactured-housing act, as Nebraska's § 76-1490 is.

### From `rent-increase-notice`

Two tests the 50 states on this topic can be checked against. FIRST, and it is the dossier's own suspicion confirmed for Nebraska: when a state is reported to require sixty days' notice of a rent increase, check whether the cited section sits inside the mobile-home or manufactured-housing act rather than the residential one. Nebraska's is § 76-1490, enacted by Laws 1984, LB 916, § 41, and it lives in §§ 76-1450 to 76-14,111 - a different act from §§ 76-1401 to 76-1449, with its own definitions. The tell is that the mobile-home act usually ALSO has a sixty-day figure for something else and the residential act has none. SECOND, a delivery test: a rent-increase notice row that offers "post it on the door" as a delivery method should be checked against the state's URLTA § 1.202 receipt list. Nebraska's § 76-1413(2)(c) gives three methods for a tenant - in hand, mail to the held-out or last-known address, electronic - and posting is not among them, which is the same defect already recorded against scheduled-services-entry-la. Since § 1.202 is uniform, the door-posting option is probably wrong in every URLTA state, not just Nebraska.

### From `rent-installments`

A transferable test for the 20 states on rent-installments-or and the 23 on this topic. The clause's second sentence - "Installments paid on this schedule are not partial payments of Rent" - is load-bearing only where the state HAS a statutory partial-payment doctrine or a waiver-by-acceptance section; where it has neither, the sentence is inert, and where the state's waiver section says what Nebraska's § 76-1433 says, the sentence works but not for the reason Oregon's notes give. The specific thing to check in each URLTA state is 1972 URLTA § 4.207's analogue: Nebraska's § 76-1433 permits a contrary agreement only "after the breach has occurred", so a lease-side non-waiver reservation does nothing. Any state row that relies on a lease non-waiver sentence to preserve termination after accepting a partial or late payment should be checked against that "after the breach" wording, because it is uniform text and the same defect will be present. Second point, for the late-charge sentence: it cross-references "this Lease's late charge provision", which in Nebraska is late-fee-ne - a shared row whose lease_clause_basis is CONSTRAINED_TERM although no Nebraska statute constrains a residential late fee; that mismatch is already recorded in the brief and is not re-reported here.

### From `rent-into-court-counterclaim`

Three tests for the 27 states on this topic. FIRST, the mandatory/permissive split is the whole topic and it is readable off one word: Nebraska's § 76-1428(1) says the court "MAY order the tenant to pay into court", so a deposit is never a condition of being heard, and § 76-1445 lets the tenant assert "any legal or equitable defense, setoff, or counterclaim" without qualification. A row that describes a state's rule as "the tenant must deposit rent to raise any defense but payment" should be checked against both sections, because 1972 URLTA § 4.105 is permissive and the mandatory-registry rule is usually a NON-URLTA statute bolted on elsewhere in the state's code. SECOND, answering the dossier's Maryland question for every URLTA state: look at the CONTINUANCE section, not the trial section. Nebraska's § 76-1443 carries a separate deposit power for "any subsequent continuance extending the initial trial date into the next periodic rental period", and it was added or reworked by Laws 2021, LB320, § 9 - a row that researched only the counterclaim section will miss it, and every URLTA state has a § 4.105 analogue and a continuance section. THIRD, and this is worth carrying before any jury-related clause is written or tagged anywhere: § 76-1446's "[t]he action shall be tried by the court without a jury" means a possession-scoped jury-waiver clause does nothing in Nebraska, and the equivalent sentence is in most summary-possession statutes.

### From `rent-receipt-anti-waiver`

A concrete, checkable test for the 20 states on this topic, and it is the most transferable thing in this row. The provision being looked for is 1972 URLTA § 2.104(1)'s companion rule - some states enacted it, Nebraska did not for residential tenancies but DID for mobile home parks at § 76-1478, in words that track the uniform formula exactly: "A rental agreement, assignment, conveyance, trust deed, or security instrument may not permit the receipt of rent free of the obligation to comply with [the landlord-duty section]." So the search in any state is for that five-instrument list, not for the words "anti-waiver" or "receipt of rent" alone, and it should be run across the state's MOBILE HOME act as well as its residential one. Two states' rows in this library already carry a positive version (edu-rent-receipt-anti-waiver-ks and edu-rent-receipt-anti-waiver-ak), so the uniform wording is available to compare against. Second transferable point: where the rule is ABSENT, the real exposure is the state's assignment-of-rents statute, because that is what lets a secured party take rents without becoming the landlord - Nebraska routes it through § 76-276 to §§ 52-1701 to 52-1708. Any ABSENT row on this topic that does not name its state's assignment-of-rents act has not reached the live question.

### From `rent-receipts`

A search test for the 45 states on this topic, and it is the kind that turns a guess into a demonstrated absence. Where a state has no rent-receipt statute, look for the receipt duty in its CONSUMER RENTAL-PURCHASE or rent-to-own act before calling the absence a gap: Nebraska's § 69-2106 is a request-triggered itemised cash-receipt duty, and § 69-2103(10)'s definition of covered property as "any property that is not real property" is the express exclusion that makes the residential silence a legislative choice. Those acts are near-uniform across the states (most derive from the same 1980s model), so the same contrast is available almost everywhere and is stronger evidence than a zero-hit search. Second, more cautionary point: the two evidence-code questions in this topic's list (Puerto Rico's art. 1130 and Guam's 6 GCA § 5107(10) presumptions that a receipt for later rent presumes earlier rent paid) sit in the EVIDENCE code, not the landlord-tenant act. Nebraska's evidence rules are chapter 27 and were outside the corpus here, so this row could not close that limb - any state row asserting that no such presumption exists should say whether it searched the state's evidence code, because a landlord-tenant-act search cannot see it.

### From `rent-reporting`

A test for the 28 states on this topic. A rent-reporting row that answers only "does the state require or regulate rent reporting" stops one step short: the live duty in most states is the data-security flow-down contract requirement, because sending a tenant file to a reporting service is a disclosure of personal information to a nonaffiliated third-party service provider. Nebraska's is § 87-808(2)(a), added by Laws 2018, LB757, § 7, and roughly thirty states enacted the same third-party-contract clause in the same wave of amendments to their breach-notification acts - so the question to run in each state is whether its breach-notification act has a reasonable-security plus service-provider-contract section, and whether (as in Nebraska's § 87-805) a waiver of it is void. A second, narrower check: Nebraska's § 87-808(2)(b) grandfathers contracts entered into before July 19, 2018 but catches them on renewal, and that kind of date-plus-renewal clause is common in the same family of statutes, so a row should say whether the state's version has one.

### From `rent-reporting`

This is probably a near-50-state item that the library carries for nobody, and it is checkable rather than a guess. Nebraska's § 87-808 has two halves that were added to state breach-notification acts in a well-documented wave: a reasonable-security duty on anyone owning, licensing or maintaining computerized personal information, and a requirement to impose security obligations BY CONTRACT on nonaffiliated third-party service providers. Both bind "an individual or a commercial entity that conducts business" in the state, so a landlord is inside them in every state that has them, and none of those acts uses the word "landlord" - which is exactly why a keyword-driven canvass misses it. Three things differ by state and should be stated per state rather than assumed: whether the reasonable-security duty exists at all or only the breach-notice duty; whether the third-party-contract clause exists and whether it has a grandfather date like Nebraska's July 19, 2018; and whether a waiver is void (Nebraska's § 87-805 is unusually blunt - "contrary to public policy and ... void and unenforceable" - and that sentence also belongs in each state's prohibited-lease-terms row, because it is a source of lease-term ineffectiveness independent of the landlord-tenant act). One further per-state item Nebraska settles expressly and most states do not: § 87-806(2) both channels enforcement into the state's UDAP act and bars a private cause of action. A row in another state should say which of the two it has, because a state with the deeming clause and no private-action bar gives the tenant a UDAP claim for a vendor data failure.

### From `rent-tax`

A method point that applies beyond Nebraska and a substantive one. METHOD: the right way to answer a rent-tax topic is to read the state's IMPOSITION section and check whether the lease of real property is on its list, not to search the landlord-tenant act or to search for the word "exempt". Nebraska's § 77-2703(1) is a closed enumeration and renting a dwelling is simply absent from it, which is a stronger and shorter answer than any exemption would be - and it is why six of this topic's existing rows are framed as exemptions when the real answer in most states is non-inclusion. SUBSTANTIVE, and worth checking in all 39 states on this topic: the taxable line is almost always drawn at a DURATION, and the duration in the tax code may not match the duration in the short-term-rental or landlord-tenant code. Nebraska's § 18-1758(1)(b) draws it at "not longer than thirty consecutive days" for municipal regulation and taxation, while this topic's own question list records Massachusetts at 90 days (ch. 64G, § 1), Rhode Island at a 12-month written lease (§§ 44-18-7.1, 44-18-18) and Arkansas at "less than month-to-month" (§ 26-52-301(3)(A)). A row should state which code its duration comes from, because a letting can be long enough to escape the lodging tax and short enough to be regulated as a short-term rental, or the reverse.

### From `rental-inspection`

Two transferable items for the 34 states on this topic. FIRST, answering the dossier's question in a form other states can use: in a URLTA state the answer to "can the lease authorize a housing inspector to enter" is almost certainly NO, and the proof is in two sentences of uniform text. 1972 URLTA § 3.103(1), Nebraska's § 76-1423(1), lists the persons the unit may be exhibited to - "prospective or actual purchasers, mortgagees, tenants, workmen, or contractors" - and a government inspector is on no state's version of that list; and § 3.103 has no residual access clause, which Nebraska makes explicit at § 76-1423(4) ("The landlord has no other right of access except by court order"). Any row in a URLTA state that offers an inspector-access clause should be checked against both, and against the state's waiver bar. SECOND, a drafting consequence that reaches every state with a local housing code: Nebraska's § 76-1419(1) closing sentence makes the local minimum housing code the CEILING on the landlord's statutory habitability duty ("the landlord's maximum duty under this section shall be determined by subdivision (1)(a)"), and § 76-1410(3) narrows "minimum housing code" to provisions "dealing specifically with health and minimum standards of fitness for habitation" - narrower than the same subdivision's "building and housing codes". That ceiling sentence is in the 1972 uniform text, so in every URLTA state a habitability row that treats the local code as a floor added on top of the statutory list has the relationship backwards, and the two-definition split is the thing to check.

### From `renters-insurance-rules`

A drafting test for the 33 states on this topic, and it is the most reusable thing here. An additional-insured requirement in a residential lease should be scoped to liability arising from the TENANT'S acts, because in any state with a URLTA § 1.403(1)(d)-type bar an unqualified additional-insured clause operates as an indemnity for the landlord's own negligence and is void in that band. Nebraska's bar is § 76-1415(1)(d) and it is unusually precise - "active and actionable negligence" - and the model wording for the scoped version is sitting in Nebraska's own Mobile Home Act at § 76-1475(2): "insurance that protects the landlord from negligence on the part of the tenant and any invitees or guests of the tenant." That phrase is worth lifting into the shared renter's-insurance clauses in every state, because it does the narrowing without needing state-specific language. Second point, for the states whose rows describe a force-placement scheme (tenant fails to show proof, landlord buys cover and bills it with a capped admin fee): check whether the state actually has a statute authorising it, or whether the row has borrowed the structure from a state that does. Nebraska has none - 'force.?plac' returns zero across all twelve held chapters - so in Nebraska every element of force-placement, including the fee, rests on the lease and on nothing else, and the billed amount becomes "rent" by definition.

### From `repair-cost-termination`

Two items for the 22 states on this topic. FIRST, a reading test that applies to every URLTA state: the casualty section (1972 URLTA § 4.106, Nebraska's § 76-1429) grants rights to the TENANT only, and a row that describes it as a mutual or landlord-side termination right has misread it. The giveaway is the opening - "the tenant may" - and the absence of any landlord branch. Several of this topic's existing rows are correctly framed as absences; the ones to check are any that offer a landlord casualty termination on statutory authority rather than on the lease. SECOND, and more useful, a drafting test for whether the lease can vary the casualty rule at all: count the sections in the state's act that open "unless otherwise agreed". In Nebraska there are exactly eleven in chapter 76 and the casualty section is not one of them, while sections that ARE variable say so in terms - so the omission is a deliberate drafting signal rather than an inference from the waiver bar alone. That test is cheap to run in any state and settles a question that otherwise gets argued from policy. THIRD, for any state with a condominium act modelled on the Uniform Condominium Act: its insurance section will contain a no-rebuild route (Nebraska's § 76-871(h): termination, illegality, or an eighty percent owner vote), and it is the right contrast to cite in a repair-cost-termination absence row, because it shows the legislature declining to use cost as a trigger where it had the chance.

### From `repair-escrow-exemption-notice`

A structural test for the 21 states on this topic, and it saves work. An exemption-notice topic has TWO predicates - the remedy and the exemption - and a state can be absent at either level. Nebraska is absent at the first: there is no rent-escrow remedy, so the exemption question never arises, and a row that says only "no small-landlord exemption notice" understates the answer. The quick way to tell which level a state is absent at is to run the state's act for the escrow remedy and separately for ANY unit-count or owner-occupancy threshold; in Nebraska the second search returns nothing in the residential act at all, which is itself notable because the fair housing act (§ 20-322) and the condominium act do have such thresholds. SECOND, and worth carrying to every state: Nebraska's § 76-1408 exclusion list is gated by "[u]nless created to avoid the application of" the Act - 1972 URLTA § 1.202's anti-avoidance preamble - so in any URLTA state a row describing the exclusions without that preamble has left out the part that defeats a structure built to fit one. The salvage record already records that omission against edu-five-year-lease-exclusion-ne for Nebraska; the same check is worth running on every state's scope row.

### From `repair-notice`

A drafting defect this clause avoids and that is worth checking in the 23 states on this topic: a repair-request clause that names only an electronic channel (a portal, an app, an email address) is at risk in any state that has adopted an electronic-notice consent regime for leases. Nebraska's is § 76-1413, added by Laws 2025, LB185, § 2, and its (9) is blunt - "[a] landlord shall not, as part of a rental agreement or as a condition of entering into or renewing a rental agreement, require a tenant to accept delivery by electronic means." Several states passed near-identical consent-plus-withdrawal provisions in 2023-2025, so the fix is uniform: always pair the portal with a physical address in the lease text itself. Second item: the savings sentence at the end ("a request in this form is not the only way Landlord can be given notice") is not boilerplate in a URLTA state - it is what keeps the clause clear of the § 1.403(1)(a) waiver bar where the state's habitability section accepts actual notice. Check each state's habitability section for the phrase "written or actual notice"; where it appears, an exclusive-written-notice clause is void in that band and the savings sentence should be added.

### From `repair-notice`

This is a checkable 50-state test and it answers the dossier's own question for every state at once. The 1972 URLTA § 2.104(1)(a) and (b) contain NO notice precondition; Nebraska's § 76-1419(1)(a) and (b) add "after written or actual notice", and Laws 2001, LB 7, § 14 is the amendment carrying the current text. So for each state the question is a two-parter: does the habitability section carry a notice precondition at all, and if it does, does it accept ACTUAL notice? Where it accepts actual notice, a lease term requiring written repair requests cannot limit the tenant's defenses that turn on the landlord's knowledge, and the row should say so; where the section has no precondition, the duty is continuous and a written-request clause is purely administrative. A third variant exists and should not be assumed away: a state whose precondition says "written notice" only, in which case the written-request clause does real work. Also worth carrying: Nebraska's § 76-1413(1) defines having "notice of a fact" to include "reason to know that it exists" from all facts and circumstances - 1972 URLTA § 1.302's definition - so in every URLTA state the notice concept is already constructive, and a row that treats notice as requiring delivery has the wrong standard.

### From `required-disclosures`

Three items for the 26 states on this topic. FIRST, and it answers one of the dossier's questions in a form every URLTA state can use: the owner-identity disclosure (1972 URLTA § 2.102, Nebraska's § 76-1417) is a TIMING rule, not a lease-content rule. Nebraska's words are "in writing at or before the commencement of the tenancy", which means a separate sheet complies and a lease signed after move-in may not - so a row that satisfies this duty by pointing at a lease clause has not checked whether the lease is always signed before commencement. That cuts the same way in every URLTA state, because the uniform text has the same phrase. SECOND, a place to look that most canvasses miss: the state's REAL ESTATE LICENSE act. Nebraska's § 76-2421(1)(a) imposes a commission-approved pamphlet duty running to a "seller, landlord, buyer, or tenant", so whenever a licensed property manager handles the letting there IS a mandatory pamphlet in the transaction - it just binds the licensee rather than the owner. Every state with a brokerage-relationships disclosure act will have an analogue, and a "no state pamphlet" row should be scoped to the owner rather than the transaction. THIRD, for the states whose rows describe no disclosure regime at all: the strongest way to show the silence is deliberate is the state's rent-to-own or consumer rental-purchase act, which almost always carries a long itemised pre-contract schedule (Nebraska's § 69-2104, twelve items) and a fee cap (§ 69-2110). That contrast is available in nearly every state and is better evidence than a zero-hit search.

### From `required-fees`

Two transferable items for the 26 states on this topic. FIRST, a test for the "all of the fees" sentence, which is the risky half of this clause: it is a promise, so the omission of a real charge bars collecting it. In a state where the statute defines rent as every payment under the agreement - Nebraska's § 76-1410(13), which is 1972 URLTA § 1.301(13) and therefore present in every URLTA state - the omitted charge is also not recoverable as "rent", so there is no fallback. Any state's version of this clause should pair with that state's rent definition, and the drafting note should say the list must be complete rather than indicative. SECOND, and this is the one worth circulating: a clause that offers a NONREFUNDABLE designation for a fee works only where the state's definition of security deposit has an express-agreement carve-out. Where the definition says "however denominated" - Nebraska's § 76-1416(1), 1972 URLTA § 1.301(14)'s formulation - the designation is not merely inert, it is a trap, because the charge still counts against the one-month ceiling and exceeding the ceiling is itself the violation. That is the same test the brief already records for rejecting nonrefundable-fees-wv, and it should be run in all six of that row's states. THIRD, a benchmark other states can use rather than inventing one: where a state has no residential late-fee cap, its consumer rental-purchase act usually contains the legislature's own view of a reasonable late fee - Nebraska's § 69-2110(1)(d) gives $5 monthly / $3 more-frequently, a 5 or 3 business-day grace period, once per accrued payment, and an express bar on charging a fee against a timely payment. Citing that in a late-fee row is stronger than citing nothing.

### From `rights-responsibilities-guide`

A search test for the 15 states on this topic, and it is one that produced a real find here. Run the EVERYDAY WORD alone as well as the term of art: 'rights and responsibilit' plus 'tenant guide/handbook/pamphlet' returned nothing useful in Nebraska, while a bare '\bpamphlets?\b' sweep returned § 76-2421(1)(a) - a state-commission-prepared pamphlet that must be given to "a seller, landlord, buyer, or tenant" - sitting in the real estate LICENSE act, where no landlord-tenant canvass would look. Every state with a brokerage-relationships disclosure act will have an analogue, so a "no state guide" row should be scoped to the owner's duty rather than stated as an absence of any mandatory pamphlet in the transaction. Second, for the one state in this library with a positive rule (rights-guide-receipt-de, 25 Del. C. § 5124): the thing to check in each other state is whether the guide duty is attached to the ACT (a summary of the landlord-tenant law) or to a PROGRAMME (a registration, subsidy or age-restricted regime). Nebraska has nothing of the first kind and something of the second kind that may or may not reach an ordinary age-restricted complex, which is a different answer from "none" and should be recorded as such.

### From `sanitary-code-variance`

Transferable test for the 21 states on this topic: a code-variance disclosure duty is worth searching for only where the STATE has a sanitary or housing code of its own. Nebraska's § 76-1419(1)(a) refers to "applicable minimum housing codes" and § 18-2146 leaves adoption to the municipality, so the variance question has no state-level object. Second, more general point: in any URLTA state whose § 2.104 analogue carries Nebraska's closing sentence — "If there exists a minimum housing code applicable to the premises, the landlord's maximum duty under this section shall be determined by subdivision (1)(a)" — a municipal variance is not merely paperwork, it moves the statutory ceiling on the repair duty, and a row that treats a variance purely as a tenant-notice question misses the landlord's side of it.

### From `seasonal-tenancy`

Transferable test for the 19 states on this topic, and it has two halves. (1) A seasonal-tenancy question is really a question about the state's EXCLUSION LIST, not about a seasonal statute: ask whether the list is closed, whether it has a vacation or seasonal item, and whether it carries URLTA § 1.202's anti-avoidance chapeau ('unless created to avoid the application of this act'). Nebraska's § 76-1408 is closed, has no seasonal item, and does carry the chapeau — so in every URLTA state with that chapeau a seasonal label is legally inert and a row that offers a seasonal form as an escape from the act is wrong. (2) Do not conflate a short-term-rental preemption statute with a seasonal-tenancy rule. Nebraska's § 18-1758 protects only stays 'not longer than thirty consecutive days', so it does not reach a three-month let at all; any state row that cites a short-term-rental statute as authority about seasonal tenancies should be checked against that statute's own day count.

### From `security-deposit-holding`

Two transferable tests for the 39 states on this topic. (1) A deposit-holding row should be written in two layers, because the duty often does not live in the landlord-tenant act at all: ask separately what the residential statute says about custody, and what the state's real estate licensing act says about a broker or property manager holding the funds of others. Nebraska has nothing in the first and a separate-trust-account duty in the second (§ 81-885.24(5)), and a library that researched only the landlord-tenant act would record a flat absence. That is exactly the shape of the Puerto Rico question in this topic (Ley 10-1994, arts. 2(h), 21), which is a brokerage rule rather than a tenancy rule. (2) Where a state's broker trust-account rule carries a consent carve-out — Nebraska's is "unless all parties having an interest in the funds have agreed otherwise in writing" — the operative document is the MANAGEMENT AGREEMENT, not the lease, and a row that only tells the owner to insist on escrow is pointing at the wrong paper. Also worth carrying: Nebraska's escrow-or-$50,000-surety-bond architecture exists, but in the Time-Share Act (§ 76-1715(3)), so a sibling-act contrast is available in states that look superficially silent.

### From `security-deposit-nonwaiver`

Transferable test for the 22 states on this topic, and it sharpens a rejection the brief already records. The nonrefundable-deposit question turns entirely on whether the state's definition of security deposit has an EXPRESS-AGREEMENT CARVE-OUT (as W. Va. § 37-6A-1(14) does, which is why `nonrefundable-fees-wv` fails in Nebraska) or says "however denominated" (as Neb. § 76-1416(1) does). Second, and this is the part most non-waiver rows omit: a non-waiver statute almost never bars SETTLEMENT of an accrued claim. Nebraska's URLTA § 1.106 analogue, § 76-1406, permits it in one sentence, so the real distinction is INSTRUMENT AND TIMING — a waiver in the rental agreement is void and penalised, a post-termination settlement of a claim that has arisen is lawful. Every URLTA state has a § 1.106 analogue, so the same two-sentence pairing should be checked in each; a row that says deposit rights "cannot be waived" full stop is incomplete, and it is incomplete in the direction that costs the landlord a lawful move-out settlement. Third: check whether the state's prohibited-terms list separately bars a fee-shifting clause. Nebraska's § 76-1415(1)(c) bars it in BOTH directions, which is unusual and means a landlord there cannot neutralise the deposit fee award by contract.

### From `security-deposit-on-sale`

Transferable test for the 42 states on this topic. A deposit-on-sale row usually states only the successor's liability, which is the tenant's half of the rule. Nebraska shows there are normally TWO halves and the landlord's half is the one with a procedure in it: URLTA § 2.105 (Neb. § 76-1420(1)) relieves the conveying landlord of post-notice liability, and relieves him of DEPOSIT liability as well only if he ASSIGNS the deposit to the purchaser AND gives the tenant written notice. So in any URLTA state the question to ask is not merely "is the buyer bound" (it almost always is — Neb. § 76-1416(5) is URLTA § 2.101(5)) but "what two acts must the seller perform to get out", and whether the state's notice-receipt provision lets the landlord fix the tenant's notice address in the lease. Second point, newer and worth carrying everywhere: Nebraska's 2025 electronic-delivery rewrite (Laws 2025, LB185, § 2) bars a landlord from REQUIRING a tenant to accept electronic delivery as a term or condition of the lease (§ 76-1413(9)), so any shared clause that designates e-mail or an online portal as the method for a statutory notice is void in Nebraska even though the same text is ordinary practice elsewhere.

### From `security-deposit-standards`

Transferable test for the 23 states on this topic. A deposit-standards disclosure duty is a function of a UNIT-COUNT THRESHOLD, and the threshold question should be asked of the whole deposit statute before the disclosure question is asked at all: if the state's deposit section has no unit-count line, it almost certainly has no standards-posting duty either, and the row can be written from one reading. Nebraska's § 76-1416 has no unit count — its single carve-out is institutional (public housing agencies) — which is the inverse of the states that switch escrow, interest and list duties off below a threshold. Second: where a shared row ties a deposit-standards duty to "adjoining units", that phrase is a known false-positive magnet in a property code (Neb.: 1 hit, a disability design-standards section), so the figure behind such a row should be re-run \b-anchored before it is relied on in any state.

### From `security-devices`

Transferable test for the 36 states on this topic, and it reframes the question. A security-device row usually asks "what must the landlord install?" The more consequential question in a URLTA state is "what happens once he installs it?" — because URLTA § 2.104(1)(d) (Neb. § 76-1419(1)(d)) attaches the maintenance duty to facilities "supplied OR REQUIRED TO BE SUPPLIED", which makes a voluntarily fitted deadbolt a statutory duty for as long as it is there. Every URLTA state with that phrase has the same supply-triggered exposure, and a row that reports only "no device mandate" tells the landlord the half that does not matter. Second test: where a state HAS a device mandate, check whether the delegation provision can shift it. Nebraska's § 76-1419(2) ENUMERATES the shiftable subdivisions ((1)(e) and (1)(f)) and is confined to a single-family residence, while (3) enumerates none and reaches only "specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations, or remodeling" — so in Nebraska a lock REPAIR can be delegated by separate signed writing but the underlying supply duty cannot, and the (2)-versus-(3) good/adequate consideration split is worth checking in each URLTA state because it is easy to read as one rule.

### From `self-help-eviction`

Two transferable tests for the 51 jurisdictions on this topic. (1) Read the self-help ban for the words "BY ACTION OR OTHERWISE". URLTA § 4.207 (Neb. § 76-1436) is usually adopted with that phrase, and it means the ban is not only about physical self-help: a possession action brought under the state's general forcible-entry or unlawful-detainer article, rather than under the URLTA's own possession sections, is itself outside the exception. Nebraska makes that explicit from the other side — § 25-21,219's final sentence disclaims URLTA premises — and any state whose landlord-tenant act has its own possession article should be checked for the same carve-out, because a shared eviction-procedure clause pointed at the wrong article is wrong everywhere it is tagged. (2) An abandonment exception is usually also an abandonment DUTY. Nebraska's § 76-1432(3) says the landlord "SHALL take immediate possession and SHALL make reasonable efforts to rent it at a fair rental", and early re-letting terminates the agreement — so the same subsection that lets the landlord in caps what he can recover. A row that states abandonment only as a permission is incomplete in the landlord's favour, which is the error direction rule 55's second limb warns about. Note also Nebraska's day count: "one full rental period or thirty days, WHICHEVER IS LESS", which is shorter than a flat thirty days on any tenancy with a period under a month.

### From `senior-housing-work-card`

Transferable test for the 21 states on this topic, and it is worth more than the work-card answer. A work-card row answers "must my staff be carded?", which is almost always no outside Nevada. The question that actually bites in senior housing is whether the state's ADULT PROTECTIVE SERVICES mandatory-reporter list reaches the operator or its employees, and that turns on two definitions rather than on the housing label: how broadly the state defines CAREGIVER (Nebraska: "assumed the responsibility for the care of a vulnerable adult voluntarily, BY EXPRESS OR IMPLIED CONTRACT" — § 28-353), and whether the list's institutional limb is tied to STATE LICENSURE (Nebraska: "any facility licensed by the department" — § 28-372(1)), which an unlicensed 55+ complex escapes. Where the caregiver definition includes implied contract, a landlord that provides services can be swept in without ever being licensed, and the penalty is criminal (Neb. § 28-384, Class III misdemeanor). Second, narrower point: a state that conditions its 55+ fair-housing exemption on providing "significant facilities and services specifically designed to meet the physical or social needs of older persons" (Neb. § 20-322(4)(b)(iii)(A), tracking the federal HOPA factors) creates a tension worth checking in every such state — the services that qualify you for the housing exemption are the same services that can create the caregiver relationship.

### From `sex-offender-disclosure`

Transferable test for the 28 states on this topic, and it is the question these rows usually skip. Every state's registry statute says the information is public; the question that decides whether a landlord should repeat it is WHO THE IMMUNITY PROVISION COVERS. Nebraska's § 29-4012 immunises "[l]aw enforcement officials, their employees, and state officials" and nobody else, so a Nebraska landlord who republishes registry data does so bare. Several states extend good-faith immunity to "any person" who discloses registry information; in those, a disclosure clause is low-risk, and in states like Nebraska it is not. A disclosure row should name its state's immunity class rather than assuming public data is safe to repeat. Second test: read the registry statute's CONFIDENTIAL-ITEM list, because it is usually narrower than "everything is public" and it often includes items a landlord would naturally pass on — Nebraska's § 29-4009(1)(h) withholds "[t]he name of any employer of a sex offender", which is precisely what a landlord verifying income might learn and mention. Third: where a state has an ACCESS list for fuller notification data, check whether private landlords are on it. Nebraska lists "any public housing agency" and not private landlords (§ 29-4013(4)), which means a public and a private landlord in the same town are not similarly placed — a distinction no multistate row appears to carry.

### From `sex-offender-occupancy`

Transferable test for the 35 states on this topic. These rows are almost always written as "does the state restrict where offenders may live, and does that create a landlord duty?" Nebraska shows there is a THIRD possibility that changes the answer completely: a state can legislate to CAP local restrictions and void the non-conforming ones (§ 29-4017(3) voids them "regardless of whether ... adopted prior to, on, or after July 14, 2006"), in which case the correct advice to a landlord is the opposite of caution — a local ordinance wider than the state cap is unenforceable. Before recording a state as having "no statute", check whether its statute is a preemption. Second test, and it is the operationally useful one: where a residency restriction exists, look for a FIRST-IN-TIME carve-out. Nebraska's § 29-4017(2)(c) disapplies the restriction where the school or licensed child care facility was established after the resident was, so the distance measurement alone never answers the question. Third: check how narrowly the restricted class is drawn. Nebraska restricts only "sexual predators", defined at § 29-4016(5) by THREE cumulative conditions, so the great majority of registered offenders cannot be reached by any Nebraska ordinance — a row that says "Nebraska allows 500-foot restrictions" without that narrowing overstates the restriction substantially.

### From `sfr-occupancy-disclosure`

Transferable test for the 23 states on this topic. A "no lease font rules" row is almost always measured with a POINT-SIZE pattern, and that is the wrong net. Nebraska's one formatting rule that reaches an ordinary standardized lease (§ 25-2602.02) specifies no point size at all — it specifies CAPITALS, UNDERLINING and POSITION ADJOINING THE SIGNATURE BLOCK — so a point-size battery returns a clean zero while a real, strictly-enforced formatting mandate sits in the arbitration article of the civil procedure code. Two consequences for other states. (1) Any row asserting "no typographic requirement" should be scoped to point size unless the state's arbitration-notice, consumer-contract and plain-language statutes were also swept; the words to search are capitalized, underlined, bold, conspicuous, adjoining, and "first page", not points. (2) The arbitration-notice rule is a near-universal consumer-protection pattern, it is usually triggered by arbitration being the SOLE remedy, and the penalty usually falls on the arbitration clause rather than the contract — so every state's shared arbitration clause in this library should be checked against its own notice statute, and against whether federal law displaces it (which Nebraska's annotation says it does, Aramark, 276 Neb. 700).

### From `shoreline-access-disclosure`

Transferable test for the 19 states on this topic, and it generalises past shorelines. Rhode Island's rule is a LEASE disclosure; Nebraska's only water disclosure (§ 76-2,124) is a CLOSING disclosure owed by a transferor of ownership to a transferee. Before recording a water, well or access disclosure as reaching a tenancy, read its trigger verb: "transferring ownership", "seller", "at or before closing" and "transferee" all confine it to a sale, and the project has already seen this error twice (§§ 18-3513 and 31-727.03, purchaser-side only, and § 76-2712's "homeowner's principal place of residence"). Second, narrower point worth carrying: a state's water-disclosure duty may be geographically scoped rather than universal — Nebraska's reaches only property "not inside the corporate limits of a municipality" — so a row that states such a duty without its geographic limit overstates it for every urban property in the state.

### From `showing-notice-waiver`

RULE 26 REJECTION WITH A TRANSFERABLE TEST, offered for the other eight states on `showing-notice-la` (LA, AR, MS, VI, AS, MP, CO, WY, KS). The clause works only where the state sets NO statutory entry-notice period, because it substitutes a shorter notice for "the notice required by the Landlord's Right of Entry section". Three questions decide it in any state, and they should be asked in this order. (1) Does the state fix a period? If yes, the clause is a waiver, and in every URLTA state the § 1.403(a)(1) analogue (Neb. § 76-1415(1)(a)) voids a rental-agreement waiver of rights under the act — so the clause is not merely inert, it is a penalised term. Colorado and Kansas are both on the tag list and both have entry statutes, so the clause should be re-examined there specifically. (2) Does the state's notice have MANDATORY CONTENT? Nebraska's § 76-1423(3)(a) requires the intended purpose and the anticipated window; a clause whose only blank is "hours" cannot satisfy a purpose-and-window requirement, and the stated-hours blank is a different animal from a statutory anticipated period. (3) Does the state regulate the DELIVERY CHANNEL? Nebraska's 2025 amendment (§ 76-1413(9), Laws 2025, LB185) bars a landlord from requiring a tenant to accept electronic delivery as a lease term, which kills the clause's "telephone or text message" option on its own — and that kind of provision is spreading, so the channel question now needs asking in every state rather than assumed. Separately, and consistent with the recommendation already made in this pass about door-posting: a shared showing clause would be safer rewritten as a STANDING-SCHEDULE clause — one proper notice covering a defined series of showings with stated purpose and window — which is lawful in a state with mandatory-content notice and does not depend on the tenant waiving anything.

### From `shutdown-rent-protection`

Transferable test for the 28 states on this topic. A shutdown-protection row is really a question about THREE separate levers, and states legislate different ones: the nonpayment notice period, the late fee, and the court's continuance power. Checking only the first produces a false absence. Nebraska has no shutdown statute at all, but it has a generic good-cause continuance (§ 76-1443) that a tenant can use for a pay delay and that carries a LANDLORD-SIDE protection most rows omit — on a subsequent continuance extending trial into the next rental period, the court "may require a tenant to deposit with the clerk of the court such rental payments as accrue during the pendency of the suit." Every state's eviction article should be checked for that rent-into-court sentence, because it is the answer to any continuance-based delay and it is useful whatever the cause. Second test: where a state HAS a shutdown statute, read whether it suspends the fee, the notice clock, the judgment, or only the fee — these are commonly conflated, and a row that says "protected" without saying which lever moved cannot be applied.

### From `single-family-zone-lease-limit`

Transferable test for the 22 states on this topic, in two parts. (1) A single-family-zone lease limit is almost always LOCAL, and where a state has one it is usually local-in-statute — Kentucky's KRS 383.199 is scoped to Jefferson County. So the question to ask of each state is not "is there a statute" but "is there a statute that applies to one named jurisdiction", and a row recording a flat state-level absence should say that local ordinances were not read, because that is where the restriction lives. (2) The more useful cross-state finding is the inverse pattern Nebraska shows: states are legislating to PREEMPT local restrictions on rental use (Neb. § 18-1758(2) and (6) for stays of thirty days or less; §§ 19-5501 to 19-5507 requiring middle housing where a city fails to plan). A library row that only answers "may the state stop me renting?" misses the clause-relevant half — whether the state stops the CITY stopping you — and that half is a landlord protection. Also carry Nebraska's owner-occupancy warning, which generalises: where a state exemption is drafted as "a dwelling the owner occupies" or "in his or her own home", renting the whole unit out destroys the exemption, and two Nebraska examples point the same way (§ 20-131.02(1) and § 71-6318.01(2)). A landlord's instinct that owner-occupancy language helps them is usually backwards.

### From `smart-access`

Three transferable tests for the 23 states on this topic, and the first one reframes the question. (1) In a state with no smart-access statute, the operative rule is the SELF-HELP EVICTION ban, because remote credential revocation is the easiest lockout ever invented and the statutes that price a lockout are indifferent to the mechanism. Nebraska's § 76-1430 is URLTA § 4.207's remedy limb and fixes liquidated damages at three months' periodic rent plus fees with no proof of loss; § 76-1436 bars taking possession "by action or otherwise". Every URLTA state should have a smart-access row that leads with its own § 4.207 figure rather than with the absence. (2) The second operative rule is the MAINTENANCE duty, through URLTA § 2.104(1)(d)'s "supplied or required to be supplied" formula (Neb. § 76-1419(1)(d)) — a voluntarily installed smart lock becomes a statutory duty for as long as it is there, and it is an electrical facility. (3) A master-key statute written in the era of cut metal may or may not reach a digital credential, and the wording to look for is whether the definition requires a key to be "planned and cut" (Neb. § 28-1315(4)) and whether it separately sweeps in "overriding" or "emergency" keys without that qualifier. Whatever the answer for the digital side, a keyless lock's PHYSICAL OVERRIDE cylinder is a mechanical emergency key and sits squarely inside such a statute — a point that applies in every state with a key-duplication offence and that no smart-access row in this library appears to carry.

### From `smoke-drift-waiver`

Two transferable tests for the 23 states on this topic. (1) A smoke-drift waiver should be tested against the state's prohibited-terms section on TWO grounds, not one. The usual analysis is waiver-of-statutory-rights (URLTA § 1.403(a)(1); Neb. § 76-1415(1)(a)). The second ground is the EXCULPATION/INDEMNITY limb, which Nebraska writes as § 76-1415(1)(d) covering a limitation of liability "arising due to active and actionable negligence of the landlord" and indemnity for the same — and a smoke-drift waiver almost always reaches the landlord's own negligence in maintaining shared ventilation, so it fails on that limb even where the drift itself is another tenant's conduct. Any state's smoke-drift clause should be checked against its exculpation provision as well as its waiver provision. (2) The GOING-SMOKE-FREE question is governed by the rules-and-regulations section, not by the lease, and in every URLTA state that section carries URLTA § 3.102's closing sentence: a rule adopted after the tenant enters the agreement binds the tenant only on reasonable notice AND if it "does not work a substantial modification of his bargain" (Neb. § 76-1422). A mid-tenancy smoking ban on a sitting smoker is the paradigm case, and no state row in this library appears to raise it. The conservative multistate advice — smoke-free at new tenancy and at renewal, in the lease, with a separately consideration-supported addendum for sitting tenants — is portable to every URLTA state. (3) A THIRD transferable test, which Nebraska now supplies in quotable form: a state's clean-indoor-air or workplace-smoking act may impose an affirmative duty on the LANDLORD as "proprietor" over a multi-unit building's enclosed common areas, entirely outside the landlord-tenant title, and the question turns on two drafting details rather than on anything residential. First, HOW THE RESIDENTIAL CARVE-OUT IS WORDED and WHERE IT SITS: Nebraska's § 71-5726 writes it into the DEFINITION of "public place" as "[a] private residence is not a public place", which takes the dwelling unit out and leaves the common areas in. A state that instead exempts "a residential building" or "residential property" takes the common areas out too, and a state that puts the carve-out in the exemption LIST rather than the definition may have drafted it narrowly on purpose. Second, WHETHER "OWNER" IS NAMED IN THE PROPRIETOR DEFINITION: Nebraska's § 71-5725 names "owner" expressly, so the duty reaches a landlord who employs nobody on site. Check the penalty section for the two multipliers that make this worth a row rather than a footnote — Nebraska's § 71-5733(3) makes each day a separate violation and (4) deems an employee's or agent's omission the proprietor's own — and check whether the act addresses WAIVER, as Nebraska's § 71-5732 does, since that is what defeats a lease term purporting to permit common-area smoking. Finally, note the structural trap this is the second or third instance of in Nebraska: a "private residence" exemption written for an owner-occupier that a landlord instinctively reaches for and cannot use (the same pattern appears in § 71-6318.01(2) in the lead act and § 81-15,264(4) in the swimming-pool definition). Any state's smoke row should be checked against its own private-residence exemption with that in mind. Keep the two limbs separate in every state: the common-area duty is a clean-indoor-air question, while a mid-tenancy in-unit no-smoking rule remains a rules-and-regulations question under URLTA § 3.102, and the clean-indoor-air act does not answer it. One addition to that third test, which is where a canvass of this topic goes wrong: the EXEMPTION LIST is precisely where a state most plausibly WOULD put a residential carve-out, and Nebraska's § 71-5730 does not have one — the carve-out lives in § 71-5726's DEFINITION of "public place" instead. So a canvasser who reads only the exemption list and not the definition reaches the wrong answer in BOTH directions: they miss the private-residence carve-out and conclude the Act reaches the dwelling unit, and they see no residential exemption and conclude nothing residential was considered. Read the definition and the exemption list together in every state, and treat neither as complete on its own. Nebraska also supplies a currency lesson attached to the same section: §§ 71-5725, 71-5726, 71-5731 and 71-5733 are unamended 2008 text, but § 71-5730 has been amended four times (most recently Laws 2020, LB840, § 7), so in any state the exemption list is the part of a clean-indoor-air act most likely to have moved, and a row resting on an exemption list's closedness should date that proposition to the list's own latest amendment rather than to the act's enactment.

### From `social-security-defense`

Three transferable tests for the 23 states on this topic. (1) A benefit-delay defense, where it exists, usually lives in the EVICTION PROCEDURE article rather than in the landlord-tenant act's substantive provisions, and its catchline rarely mentions benefits — Massachusetts puts it in ch. 186, §§ 11-12. So the search should be a title sweep of the possession article plus a read of the state's only defense/counterclaim section, not a keyword battery on "benefit" or "social security". Nebraska's § 76-1428 is captioned "Landlord's noncompliance as defense to action for possession" and no keyword for benefits would reach it. (2) Every URLTA state has a § 4.105 counterclaim analogue, and its GATEWAY wording decides this question: Nebraska's § 76-1428(1) admits only a claim "which he or she may recover under the rental agreement or the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act", which excludes a third party's late payment on its face. A row should quote that gateway rather than reporting a bare absence, because the gateway is the reason. (3) The genuinely portable point is the collection one: in any state, a judgment against a benefits-only tenant runs into the federal anti-attachment rule for Social Security (42 U.S.C. 407, not read here), and the state's own garnishment statute will typically reach only "disposable earnings" — Neb. § 25-1558, with its unusual FIFTEEN PERCENT cap for a head of a family alongside the usual twenty-five percent. A library that advises on the defense without advising on collectibility answers the smaller half of the landlord's question.

### From `special-district-representation`

A transferable test for the eight states on this topic, and it is a test about WHO the franchise belongs to rather than about disclosure. Every special-district row should be screened for a lessee-deeming sentence inside the district's own election section, because that is where a tenancy can acquire or lose a public vote, and it is always buried in a subdivision about condominium apartments and joint ownership rather than in anything captioned for leases. Nebraska's trigger is cumulative and lease-written: an initial term of at least twenty years AND a lease requiring the lessee to pay taxes and special assessments (§ 18-3514(2)(c); identically § 31-735(2)(c)). Where a state has such a sentence, a long-term net lease silently transfers the owner's district vote and the special-assessment clause is the switch, so the drafting instruction belongs in the row. Second, and this cuts across the CO, KS and WY rows on this topic: a district-disclosure statute addressed to a "purchaser" is not evidence that the state declines to protect tenants — it is evidence that the legislature wrote a conveyancing rule, and the tenant-side absence has to be proved separately. Nebraska's § 18-3513(2) names the broker "or, if none, the owner", which means in a for-sale-by-owner the landlord personally carries the duty; any state row stating the duty as the broker's alone should be checked for that fallback. Third, Nebraska's exclusive-remedy sentence (§ 18-3513(4): damages only, "shall not affect title to the real estate or the validity of the conveyance") is the kind of provision whose absence elsewhere leaves a conveyance attackable, so it is worth asking of each state whether the remedy is capped.

### From `sprinkler-disclosure`

Two transferable tests for the 23 states on this topic. (1) A sprinkler-disclosure row should be screened against the state's own ALARM statute before it is written as a flat absence, because the two live in the same drafting decision: a state that wrote a trigger-based carbon monoxide or smoke alarm duty for rentals and no sprinkler duty has demonstrably chosen, while a state with neither may simply have left fire protection entirely to its building code. Nebraska is the first kind — §§ 76-603 and 76-606 against a complete sprinkler silence — and that turns a bare absence into an argued one at no research cost. (2) The more useful test is the one that runs the other way: where a state DOES require a sprinkler statement, check whether the statute makes the required text a disclosure or a WARRANTY. New York's and Connecticut's rows should be read for whether a landlord who states "no sprinkler system" accurately is thereby safe, or whether a landlord who states one exists has warranted its condition — because in a state with no disclosure statute at all the only sprinkler exposure a landlord has is the overstatement one, and it arrives through the deceptive-practices act rather than the lease. Nebraska's route is § 87-303.07, which makes a lease induced by a § 87-302 violation "unenforceable by the seller or lessor" with a tenant right to rescind — a possession consequence rather than a damages one, and worth checking in every state whose deceptive-practices act carries an "induced ... to enter into a sale or lease" section. Finally, a caution for any state row that quotes NFPA 13 or NFPA 101 as the operative sprinkler standard: Nebraska's § 81-503.01(2) requires its fire code only to "conform generally" to the 2012 editions "but not when doing so would impose an unduly severe or costly burden", so the NFPA text is not the law even where the statute names it. Check each state's incorporation clause for a conformity qualifier before quoting a pamphlet as a requirement.

### From `statute-of-frauds-lease-term`

Four transferable tests for the 35 states on this topic, each of which Nebraska answers and most state rows appear not to ask. (1) WHO MUST SIGN. Nebraska's § 36-105 requires only "the party by whom the lease ... is to be made" — the lessor — and the annotations are emphatic that the lessee need not sign. A row that says "signed by both parties" is stating practice, not the statute, and in a state with Nebraska's wording the landlord's own signature is the one that decides the case. Worth checking in every state whose statute descends from the 1677 English act, because the one-sided wording is the original wording. (2) THE DOSSIER'S GUAM QUESTION HAS A GENERAL ANSWER AND IT IS IN A DIFFERENT SECTION FROM THE ONE PEOPLE CITE. Whether an ASSIGNMENT or SURRENDER of a lease over a year must be written is almost never answered by the headline statute-of-frauds section; in Nebraska it is § 36-103, the create-grant-assign-surrender-declare section, which sits two sections before § 36-105 and uses a different threshold formula ("for a term of one year from the making thereof" rather than "for a longer period than one year"). Any state row built only on its sale-of-lands section should be checked for a sibling creation-of-interests section. (3) THE DOSSIER'S MASSACHUSETTS QUESTION — recording rule or validity rule? — is the right question and the answer is usually BOTH, at different thresholds. Nebraska's validity threshold is one year (§§ 36-103, 36-105) and its acknowledge-and-record threshold is also one year (§ 76-211), with the consequence of non-recording confined to creditors and good-faith purchasers while the lease stays "valid between the parties" (§ 76-238(1)). Massachusetts' seven years and the Northern Marianas' acknowledgment rule are the recording half; the test is to find each state's two thresholds separately and never let the recording threshold be reported as the validity threshold. (4) A SHARPER VERSION OF THE SAME POINT, AND ONE NO ROW IN THE LIBRARY APPEARS TO CARRY: the AGENT'S WRITTEN AUTHORITY. Nebraska's § 36-409 lets an agent subscribe "authorized by writing" — so a management company signing long leases without a written management agreement is signing void leases. Equivalent provisions are standard in statute-of-frauds articles, and because property managers sign most leases in practice this is the single most likely real-world failure of the formality in any state. Also: a state with a UETA electronic-acknowledgment section (Neb. § 86-638) has quietly removed the notarization obstacle to recording a long lease, which several state rows may still treat as a reason not to record.

### From `statutory-caps`

A CORRECTION TO THIS PROJECT'S OWN FIGURE TAXONOMY, offered because it is transferable to all 21 states on this topic. The salvage record sorts Nebraska's figures into ceilings (§§ 76-1426, 76-1437(3)) and fixed sums (§ 76-1430); the brief's seventh round added a third shape, the floor (§ 76-1438(2)). Reading all six money sections whole shows the taxonomy needs FIVE entries, not three, and two of the existing entries need their wording repaired. (a) A CAP ON WHAT MAY BE DEMANDED is a separate shape from a cap on what may be recovered, and § 76-1416(1) is the only one Nebraska has. (b) §§ 76-1426 and 76-1437(3) are not "three-month ceilings": the words are "not more than three months' periodic rent OR threefold the actual damages sustained by him, WHICHEVER IS GREATER", so the ceiling floats up with treble actual damages and the three-month figure binds only where the loss is small. Describing them as three-month caps understates the exposure in exactly the cases where it matters. (c) § 76-1416(3) is a FIXED SUM, not a ceiling — "an amount equal to one month's periodic rent or two times the amount of the security deposit, whichever is less" — so the lesser-of formula sets the number rather than capping it, and the salvage taxonomy does not place it at all. (d) § 76-1427(1)'s substitute-housing measure is a one-month CEILING inside a remedy section, which neither the brief nor the salvage records. THE GENERAL TEST, usable on any state's row: for each statutory figure, read the five words before the number. "Not more than" is a ceiling; "an amount equal to" is a fixed sum; "not less than" is a floor; "may not demand or receive ... in excess of" is a cap on conduct rather than on recovery; and where a disjunct follows the number, read whether it says "whichever is greater" or "whichever is less", because that single word decides whether the figure is the exposure or merely the minimum of it. A second transferable point for the OH, CT, RI, NH, ME, VT, DE and AK rows on this topic: a state's money limits are almost never variable by the lease, and the cheapest proof of that is the state's own contrary-agreement formula. In Nebraska eleven chapter-76 sections open "unless otherwise agreed" and not one money section is among them, so the list doubles as a variability index; most URLTA states carry the same § 1.403-style waiver bar plus the same scattered "unless otherwise agreed" openings, and the same one-command check should work.

### From `statutory-early-termination`

Four transferable tests for the 31 states on this topic. (1) COUNT THE CLOCKS, NOT THE GROUNDS. Every one of Nebraska's six grounds has a different notice architecture — thirty days after RECEIPT with a fourteen-day cure (§ 76-1425(1)), five days with no cure (§ 76-1426(1)), vacate-then-notify within fourteen days with the termination back-dated to the vacating (§ 76-1429(1)(a)), immediate election on ouster (§ 76-1430), election as an alternative to an injunction (§ 76-1438(2)), and a fourteen-to-thirty-day forward window (§ 76-1431.01(2)(b)(i)). A row that reports a state's early-termination rules as one notice period is almost certainly reporting only the material-noncompliance section. The casualty shape in particular — vacate first, notify after, termination relates back — is uniform URLTA text (§ 4.106) and is the one most often mis-stated as requiring notice before vacating. (2) THE RECURRENCE RULE IS THE SLEEPER. § 76-1425(1)'s six-month repeat clause removes the landlord's cure right entirely, and it is uniform URLTA § 4.101(1) text present in every URLTA state. A library that states the cure period without the recurrence rule is telling landlords they always get fourteen days, which is wrong in every one of those states on the second occurrence. (3) THE DOSSIER'S NORTH DAKOTA QUESTION — termination for the landlord's fraudulent misrepresentation — has a structural answer worth carrying: the URLTA does not contain such a ground, so a state that has one has bolted it on, and in a pure-URLTA state the misrepresentation route runs through the consumer-protection act instead. In Nebraska that route is WORSE for the landlord than a termination right, because § 87-303.07 makes the lease "unenforceable by the seller or lessor" with a tenant right to rescind rather than merely ending it prospectively. So the absence of a fraud-termination ground should never be written up as a landlord protection. (4) THE DOSSIER'S TEXAS QUESTION — an omitted lease statement forfeiting accrued money — identifies a shape worth screening for everywhere: a prescribed-sentence requirement whose sanction is the RELEASE OF DELINQUENT RENT rather than the voiding of a term. Nebraska has nothing of the kind and prescribes no lease statements at all, so the screen is cheap. Finally, one Nebraska provision worth lifting into every state's domestic-violence release row: § 76-1431.01(4)(b) says the released tenant is "not subject to any fee solely because of termination of the rental agreement". That single phrase defeats early-termination fees, re-letting charges and liquidated-damages clauses in one stroke, and a state release statute that lacks it leaves those charges arguable.

### From `steam-radiator-covers`

Two transferable tests for the 23 states on this topic. (1) A RADIATOR-COVER ABSENCE SHOULD BE PAIRED WITH A SCALD-DEVICE SEARCH, because the two are the same legislative subject — preventing burns from a heating or plumbing system in a dwelling — and states that declined to legislate about radiator surfaces frequently did legislate about water temperature. Nebraska's § 18-1920 is the shape to look for and it is nearly invisible: a one-sentence section in a MUNICIPAL PLUMBING article whose entire content is that a local ordinance cannot exempt anyone from the state scald-prevention sections. A keyword battery on "radiator" would never find it; only a title sweep does. Any state row recorded as a flat absence on radiator covers should be re-screened for an anti-scald or water-temperature provision before it is relied on, and the search term is "scald", not "radiator". (2) THE DELEGATION TEST, which generalises past this topic. In every URLTA state the shiftability of a maintenance duty is a purely textual question answered by comparing the state's § 2.104(b) and (c) equivalents: Nebraska's § 76-1419(2) ENUMERATES the shiftable subdivisions ((1)(e) and (1)(f)) and is confined to a single-family residence, while (3) enumerates none and reaches only "specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations, or remodeling". So a clause making the tenant responsible for the heating system as a class fails in a multi-unit building in every state with the uniform text, and a state row that says "the lease may delegate maintenance" is over-broad. Also worth carrying to every habitability row in a URLTA state: the closing sentence of § 2.104(a) makes a local minimum housing code the CEILING on the statutory duty rather than an addition to it, which means a state's radiator rule, if one exists, is far more likely to be municipal than statutory — and a library that searched only state statutes will record an absence that is true of the statutes and silent about the law that actually applies.

### From `stigmatized-property`

Three transferable tests for the 44 states on this topic, plus one finding that is not about stigma at all. (1) SEPARATE THE DUTY FROM THE IMMUNITY, BECAUSE THEY ARE DIFFERENT STATUTES AND A STATE CAN HAVE EITHER, BOTH OR NEITHER.
