A stigmatized-property row should state four things independently: is there a duty to disclose; is there an immunity for not disclosing; is there a duty to ANSWER A DIRECT QUESTION (a weaker, separate obligation, which is what the dossier's Mississippi question is); and is there a bar on using particular information. Nebraska has none of the four, which is a materially worse position for a landlord than a state with an immunity provision, and a row that reports only "no disclosure duty" reads as reassurance when it is the opposite. The AZ row in this topic should be checked for whether its provision is an immunity or merely a non-materiality declaration, since those behave differently against a concealment claim. (2) THE PRESCRIBED-FORM TEST IS THE CHEAPEST PROOF OF ABSENCE AVAILABLE AND IT WORKS IN EVERY STATE WITH A SELLER-DISCLOSURE FORM. Read the statutory contents list item by item and count what is there; a legislature that enumerated the sewer system and a carbon monoxide alarm and omitted deaths and crimes has chosen. That turns a keyword zero into an argued absence at the cost of one section read. (3) THE REGISTRY HALF IS ANSWERED BY THE CONFIDENTIALITY SECTION, NOT BY A HOUSING SECTION. Neb. § 29-4009(1) makes the information non-confidential with a short law-enforcement-only list, and § 29-4013(4)'s access list names "any public housing agency" — a public-private split that is worth checking in every state, because where a state gives PUBLIC housing agencies privileged registry access and says nothing about private landlords, the implication a landlord might draw (that they too have a role) is unsupported. AND THE FINDING THAT IS NOT ABOUT STIGMA: Neb. § 76-2,120(1)(d) and (2) extend the full seller-disclosure statement to "any lease with the option to purchase residential real property", with mandatory attorney's fees on failure (§ 76-2,120(12) and the Pepitone and Nelson annotations). Any state with a seller-disclosure act should be screened for whether its "seller" definition reaches a lease-option, because rent-to-own landlords are the population least likely to know they are inside a conveyancing statute, and the library appears to carry no lease-option disclosure row for any state.

### From `stove-refrigerator`

Two transferable findings for the 21 states on this topic, and the first is a general method point that this topic is the cleanest example of. (1) A DEFINITIONAL APPLIANCE LIST IS ALMOST NEVER A SUPPLY MANDATE, AND THE WAY TO PROVE IT IS TO COUNT WHERE THE DEFINED TERM IS USED. In Nebraska "refrigerator, stove, or sink" appears in § 76-1410(15) and the defined term "roomer" appears in exactly two sections of the chapter — the definition and § 76-1414(4). Two sections is a figure a row can state, and it closes the question in one command. Every URLTA state has the same § 1.301(12) roomer definition with the same three appliances, so every URLTA state has the same trap, and a row built on a keyword hit for "refrigerator" in any of them is probably built on this definition. (2) AND THE CONSEQUENCE IS WORTH CARRYING TO ALL OF THEM, BECAUSE IT IS A LANDLORD ADVANTAGE NOBODY SEEMS TO HAVE WRITTEN DOWN. Uniform § 1.401(c) — Nebraska's § 76-1414(4) — makes the default tenancy WEEK TO WEEK for a roomer who pays weekly rent, which in turn selects the short termination notice under uniform § 4.301 (Nebraska's § 76-1437(1): seven days, against thirty for month-to-month). So in every URLTA state the kitchen fittings of a shared-facility building, combined with weekly rent and no fixed term, determine the notice period. Both conditions are necessary and both are in the subsection, which is the limit a row must state so landlords do not over-read it. (3) A smaller point for the CA row and any other state with a real supply duty: check whether the duty is to SUPPLY or merely to MAINTAIN WHAT IS SUPPLIED, because the uniform text does the second and only the second. Nebraska's § 76-1419(1)(d) reaches appliances "supplied OR REQUIRED TO BE SUPPLIED", and in a state with no supply statute the only things that can make an appliance "required to be supplied" are the lease — which in every URLTA state includes ORAL agreements by the § 1.301 rental-agreement definition — and the local housing code. That is the sentence a state row should carry instead of a flat "no duty to supply".

### From `student-housing`

Three transferable tests for the eight states on this topic. (1) THE STUDENT-HOUSING QUESTION IS USUALLY ANSWERED BY THE ACT'S EXCLUSIONS SECTION, NOT BY A SEARCH FOR THE WORD "STUDENT". Every URLTA state has Nebraska's § 76-1408 equivalent (uniform § 1.202), and two of its eight items do the work: institutional residence "incidental to ... educational ... service" and occupancy by a member of a fraternal or social organization in a structure operated for the organization's benefit. A row that reports "no student-housing statute" without quoting those two is leaving out the only provisions on the subject, and worse, is leaving out the fact that THEY DO NOT COVER A PRIVATE LANDLORD — which is the inference a landlord letting a student house will otherwise draw. (2) QUOTE THE ANTI-AVOIDANCE CHAPEAU WHEREVER THE EXCLUSIONS ARE CITED. Nebraska's reads "Unless created to avoid the application of the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act", and it is uniform text. Any state row that lists the exclusions as available structures, without that opening clause, is inviting a landlord to paper around the Act. (3) THE REAL STUDENT-HOUSING LAW IS AN OCCUPANCY CAP AND THE STATE STATUTE THAT MATTERS IS THE FAIR-HOUSING SAVING CLAUSE. Neb. § 20-322(4)(a) preserves "any reasonable local restrictions regarding the maximum number of occupants permitted to occupy a dwelling" — the federal Fair Housing Act has the same saving clause at 42 U.S.C. 3607(b)(1), and most state acts copy it. So in every state the answer to "how many students may I put in this house" is municipal, and the state-law content of the topic is the saving clause plus the familial-status prohibition that the saving clause does NOT displace. That distinction — cap lawful, family exclusion not — is the one a student-housing row should carry in every state. Also worth checking in any state: whether the state's own-home room-rental exemption has a numerical limit (Nebraska's § 20-322(3) stops at more than four sleeping rooms) and whether any HIV/AIDS letting prohibition sits OUTSIDE the fair-housing act, as Neb. § 20-168 does, since such a provision survives every exemption a landlord would reach for.

### From `subsidized-inspection-refusal`

Three transferable tests for the 23 states on this topic. (1) THE SUBSIDY-INSPECTION QUESTION IS AN ENTRY-NOTICE QUESTION IN DISGUISE, AND THAT IS WHERE EVERY STATE ROW SHOULD LAND. Whatever the programme requires, the landlord still has to get lawfully into an occupied unit, and in a URLTA state that means the state's § 3.103 equivalent. Nebraska's § 76-1423(3) is unusually demanding — twenty-four hours, written, "provided to each individual unit", stating the purpose and a reasonable anticipated window — and § 76-1423(4) makes the access list exhaustive ("no other right of access except by court order"), so a housing assistance payments contract confers no entry right at all. A row that answers only "no statute on subsidy inspections" leaves the landlord with the practical problem unaddressed and the one-month floor in § 76-1438(2) unmentioned. (2) SCREEN THE STATE'S PUBLIC-HOUSING-AGENCY LAW BEFORE CALLING THE ABSENCE COMPLETE, BECAUSE THAT IS WHERE SUBSIDISED-HOUSING INSPECTION LAW ACTUALLY LIVES, AND IT WILL BE IN A CHAPTER A LANDLORD-TENANT CANVASS NEVER OPENS. Nebraska's 2026 LB1114 created a code-enforcement, complaint-inspection, rental-registration, penalty and reporting regime for metropolitan-class housing agencies (§ 14-102(40)) and rewrote the agency complaint process (§ 71-15,169) — all of it binding the agency as landlord and the city as regulator, none of it a private landlord. Finding it converts a bare keyword zero into a demonstrated legislative choice, and the same split (agency regulated, private landlord not) is very likely to hold in most states. (3) A CHEAP, DECISIVE CONTROL FOR ANY SUBSIDY TOPIC IN ANY STATE: run "housing assistance payment", "housing choice voucher" and "rental assistance" as phrases rather than searching "voucher" or "subsidy". In Nebraska the three phrases return zero while "voucher" returns a plumbing-inspector compensation section and a probation programme, and "subsidized" returns two municipal bond sections. The phrase searches are the ones that mean something; the single words are noise in every state's code.

### From `subsidy-habitability-proration`

Two transferable findings for the 20 states on this topic, and the first is a question every one of those rows should be asked. (1) THE PRORATION QUESTION IS DECIDED BY THE STATE'S DEFINITION OF "RENT", NOT BY ITS HABITABILITY SECTIONS. In Nebraska the two definitions do the work and they point in opposite directions: § 76-1410(13) makes rent "all payments to be made to the landlord under the rental agreement", while § 76-1410(14) confines a rental agreement to agreements "between a landlord and tenant" — which arguably excludes the housing assistance payments contract and with it the subsidy. Both definitions are uniform URLTA text (§ 1.301(10) and (12)), so THE SAME AMBIGUITY EXISTS IN EVERY URLTA STATE and none of the state rows on this topic appears to have identified it. The test to apply to each: read the state's rent definition and its rental-agreement definition together and ask whether a payment made by a third party under a separate contract is inside or outside. Where a state has resolved it — Colorado apparently has — the row should say which definition it resolved it in, because that is the provision other states would need to copy. (2) AND A STRUCTURAL POINT THAT MAKES THE ABSENCE EASY TO MISSTATE: the uniform habitability remedies are written as fractions of the WHOLE unit's fair rental value (Nebraska's §§ 76-1427(1)(b) and 76-1429(1)(b): "the diminution in the fair rental value of the dwelling unit"), which is a measure of the PREMISES and not of the tenant's outlay. A row that says a state "has no proration rule" without noting that its remedies are drafted against the unit's value rather than the tenant's payment is understating how the default is likely to run. Finally, a drafting warning worth carrying everywhere: a lease clause limiting abatement to the tenant's portion is, in every URLTA state, a term by which the tenant forgoes a remedy under the act (Nebraska's § 76-1415(1)(a)), so the apparently obvious private fix is unavailable and the question has to be answered by law.

### From `subsidy-late-fee`

Three transferable findings for the 22 states on this topic. (1) THE QUESTION IS NOT "MAY A LATE FEE BE CHARGED" BUT "WHOSE DEFAULT IS A LATE SUBSIDY PAYMENT", AND THE ANSWER IS IN THE LEASE, NOT THE STATUTE. Every state row on this topic should state whether the state's law obligates an assisted tenant to the whole contract rent or only to the tenant's portion — and in a state with no statute, as Nebraska, the answer is whatever the lease says, which makes the drafting instruction the entire content of the row. The uniform definitions make this ambiguous rather than clear: Nebraska's § 76-1410(13) defines rent as "all payments to be made to the landlord under the rental agreement" while § 76-1410(14) confines a rental agreement to agreements "between a landlord and tenant", so whether the assistance payment is "rent" at all is open on the text. That is uniform URLTA language and the same ambiguity sits in every URLTA state. (2) A STATE WITH NO RESIDENTIAL LATE-FEE STATUTE USUALLY HAS ONE SOMEWHERE ELSE, AND IT IS THE BEST BENCHMARK AVAILABLE. Nebraska's legislature wrote $5 / $3 fees, 5 / 3 business-day grace periods, one fee per accrued payment, and an express bar on assessing a fee "against a payment that is timely made even though an earlier late fee has not been paid in full" — all in the Rental-Purchase Agreement Act, § 69-2110(1)(d). The last of those four is the one worth lifting into every state's late-fee clause whatever the state's law, because the practice it forbids (applying this month's payment to last month's fee and calling this month's rent late) is how a fee dispute becomes an eviction, and it is the specific mechanism by which an assisted tenant who always pays on time ends up in default. Look for the analogous consumer-leasing or retail-instalment act in any state recorded as having "no late fee rule". (3) THE WAIVER-BY-ACCEPTANCE SECTION IS WHERE SUBSIDY TENANCIES BITE HARDEST AND NO ROW APPEARS TO SAY SO. Uniform § 4.207 — Nebraska's § 76-1433 — turns on the landlord's acceptance with knowledge of the default and is silent as to who tendered, so a housing authority's or charity's payment waives the termination exactly as the tenant's would. In an assisted tenancy a third-party payment arriving mid-notice is the normal case rather than the exception, which makes this the single most consequential sentence in the topic for a landlord in any URLTA state.

### From `substandard-property-receivership`

Four transferable tests for the 27 states on this topic. (1) THE RECEIVERSHIP QUESTION IS ANSWERED BY THE STATE'S GENERAL RECEIVERSHIP-GROUNDS SECTION, AND THE ANSWER IS USUALLY IN ITS "SPECIAL STATUTES" CATCH-ALL. Nebraska's § 25-1081 lists nine grounds and the only route a housing receivership could take is (8), "in all cases provided for by special statutes". So the research question in every state is not "is there a receivership statute" but "is there a SPECIAL statute feeding the general grounds section", and the cheapest way to answer it is a PROXIMITY battery — receiver within a couple of hundred characters of housing, dwelling, habitable or minimum standard — rather than a search for "receiver", which in any state's code returns the bank, insurance, attachment and judgment-debtor receivers and buries the answer. (2) WHERE A STATE HAS NO RECEIVERSHIP, NAME WHAT IT HAS INSTEAD, BECAUSE THE SUBSTITUTE IS USUALLY A RECORDED INSTRUMENT AND THAT IS WORSE FOR A LANDLORD THAN A REPAIR ORDER. Nebraska's § 18-1722.01 makes it the municipality's MANDATORY duty to post the property and record the unsafe-or-unfit determination with the register of deeds, with a free release on cure. A recorded determination is a title defect that will surface at refinance or sale long after the violation is forgotten, and it is the kind of provision a landlord-tenant canvass never finds because it sits in a municipalities chapter and uses the verb "post the property" rather than the noun "placard". (3) SCREEN FOR A COST-RECOVERY LIEN SEPARATELY FROM THE REPAIR POWER. Nebraska's § 18-1722 gives the city an election between a special assessment that "shall be a lien on the real estate" and a civil action against the owner — two different exposures with different time limits and different consequences on sale, and a row that reports only "the city may abate at the owner's expense" has not told the landlord which. (4) AND A PROVISION WORTH LOOKING FOR IN EVERY STATE'S DEPOSIT SECTION, BECAUSE IT IS IN THE LAST PLACE ANYONE WOULD SEARCH FOR IT: Neb. § 76-1416(4) bars holding a tenant liable "for damages directly related to the tenant's removal from the premises by order of any governmental entity as a result of the premises not being fit for habitation due to the negligence or neglect of the landlord". That is a condemnation-displacement rule hiding inside a security-deposit section. It defeats lost-rent, re-letting and early-termination charges against a displaced tenant, and any state row about code enforcement or condemnation should be checked for an equivalent sentence wherever it may be buried — it is NOT part of the 1972 uniform text, so its presence or absence is a real state-by-state divergence.

### From `tax-escalation`

Three transferable points for the eight states already on tax-insurance-escalation-la, and one for the single-state rows on this topic. (1) THE TEST THAT DECIDES WHETHER THIS CLAUSE NEEDS STATE-SPECIFIC WORK IS NOT WHETHER THE STATE REGULATES TAX ESCALATION — most do not — BUT WHETHER THE STATE'S RENT DEFINITION SWALLOWS THE TAX SHARE. Where it does, as Neb. § 76-1410(13) does ("all payments to be made to the landlord under the rental agreement"), three things follow automatically and none of them is in the clause: non-payment of the share becomes non-payment of rent with the state's short nonpayment notice attached; the share may count toward any figure the state measures in "periodic rent" (deposit caps, liquidated-damages multiples); and the state's acceptance-of-rent waiver section is engaged every time the landlord banks the base rent while the share is outstanding. That last one is uniform URLTA § 4.207 text and it runs against the landlord in every URLTA state. A single sentence in the clause's notes — "the tenant's share is rent for all purposes of the Act" — would carry the point to all eight states. (2) THE DOSSIER'S MASSACHUSETTS QUESTION IDENTIFIES THE RIGHT SHAPE AND THE CLAUSE ALREADY SATISFIES IT. Mass. ch. 186, § 15C requires the clause to state the tenant's exact share and to refund any abatement; this clause does both, by its "[percent] percent of the increase, which is the Property's share" and by its closing credit-or-refund sentence. So the clause is probably taggable in Massachusetts too, subject to whatever § 15C says about the FORM of the statement, which was not read here. (3) THE DOSSIER'S NEW HAMPSHIRE QUESTION GENERALISES INTO A USEFUL SCREEN: where the deposit statute permits a deduction for the tenant's share of a tax increase ONLY IF THE LEASE REQUIRES IT, the clause is not merely optional but load-bearing — omitting it forfeits a statutory right. That is the opposite of the usual rule-54 analysis, in which an omitted optional clause costs nothing, and it is worth asking of every state's deposit statute before this clause is described as purely optional. (4) FINALLY, A SCREEN FOR THE REFUND LIMB'S VALUE RATHER THAN ITS LAWFULNESS: ask whether the state delivers property-tax relief to RENTERS. Where it does, a tenant paying a tax share may have an independent claim and the contractual refund is a second route; where relief is a credit against the owner's tax bill or an owner-occupant exemption, as in Nebraska, the contractual refund sentence is the tenant's ONLY route and is therefore the part of the clause most likely to be fought over. The brief records the search term for this: "rent constituting property taxes", not "property tax".

### From `telecom-access`

Four transferable points for the 31 states on this topic. (1) THE CONTROLLING LAW ON A TENANT'S DISH IS FEDERAL IN EVERY STATE, AND THE LIBRARY APPEARS TO CARRY IT FOR NONE. 47 C.F.R. 1.4000 limits a landlord's power to prohibit a small satellite dish or television antenna in an area within the tenant's exclusive use or control. A state row that reports "no state telecom access rule" and stops is accurate and dangerous, because a flat no-dishes clause is then the most likely unenforceable term in the lease for a reason the row never mentions. Every alterations or antenna clause in the library should cite the federal rule; that is a one-line addition with 50-state effect. (2) SEPARATE THE FOUR QUESTIONS, BECAUSE A STATE CAN ANSWER THEM DIFFERENTLY. (a) Must the landlord admit a provider to the building; (b) may the landlord sign an exclusive-provider agreement; (c) may the landlord charge a subscriber a different rent or a wiring or roof fee; (d) must the landlord provide or maintain a service. Nebraska answers all four with silence; New York's mandatory-access and compensation regime answers (a) and (c); the dossier's "no rent differential for subscribers" question is only (c). A single-verdict row conflates them. (3) THE MAINTENANCE QUESTION IS ANSWERED BY FOUR WORDS OF UNIFORM TEXT AND NOT BY A TELECOM STATUTE. Nebraska's § 76-1419(1)(d) reaches "other facilities and appliances ... supplied OR REQUIRED TO BE SUPPLIED", which is uniform URLTA § 2.104(a)(4) language, and in every URLTA state the trigger is therefore the landlord's own promise — including an ORAL one, because the uniform rental-agreement definition covers "all agreements, written or oral". So "internet included" in an advertisement creates a maintenance duty in every URLTA state with no telecom statute at all, and no row on this topic appears to say so. (4) A BATTERY TRAP WORTH PUBLISHING, because it will fire in every state's code: UNANCHORED 'cable' MATCHES 'APPLICABLE'. Measured here over all 7,208 sections, the unanchored proximity battery returned 17 sections — six of them URLTA sections matching on "applicable" — and the unanchored title sweep returned 89, roughly half of them captions ending "provisions applicable" or "laws applicable". The anchored forms ('cable television', 'cable service', 'cable system') return 0 and 40 respectively. Any state row resting on a "cable" search without that anchoring should be re-measured.

### From `telecom-access`

Two transferable points, and the first is a research instruction rather than a rule. (1) THE "OWNER WITHOUT THE WORD LANDLORD" BLIND SPOT HAS A WHOLE FAMILY OF INSTANCES IN UTILITY-EASEMENT LAW, AND IT IS WORTH A DELIBERATE SWEEP IN EVERY STATE. Neb. §§ 86-5,105 to 86-5,107 contain ZERO occurrences of "landlord", "lessor", "tenant" or "rental" on a direct count, yet they impose a ninety-day written-claim deadline and a two-year limitation on a PROPERTY OWNER, with the interpretive rule that "[a]n electric utility easement shall be liberally construed in favor of its use for commercial broadband facilities". Nebraska enacted this in 2020 as part of a national wave of electric-cooperative broadband enabling statutes, so most states will have a near-counterpart, and in every one of them it will be invisible to a landlord-keyword canvass. The sweep that finds it is an ANCHORED title sweep on "broadband", not a search for an owner or a lease. (2) THE SHAPE TO LOOK FOR, which makes a state's version easy to assess once located: a notice provision specifying WHICH addresses the notice goes to (Nebraska requires BOTH the utility's last-known address and the county assessor's address, and sending is what starts the clock); a short written-claim window; a longer outside limitation; and a list of claim types that survive the cut-off. Nebraska's survivors are physical damage to property, injury to natural persons, and breach of the written easement's own terms — the third being the most valuable, since it converts the owner's recorded easement into a continuing enforceable restriction (an underground-only covenant bars aboveground broadband attachments under § 86-5,105(3)). A state version lacking that third carve-out leaves the owner's recorded easement terms unenforceable after the cut-off, which is a materially different outcome and the right question to ask of each state's statute. Practical cross-state advice worth putting in any owner-facing row: keep the county assessor's owner address current, because in a statute of this shape it is a service address the owner does not control and cannot later disclaim.

### From `tenancy-at-will`

Three transferable tests for the 27 states on this topic. (1) BEFORE WRITING A TENANCY-AT-WILL ROW, CHECK WHETHER THE STATE'S LANDLORD-TENANT ACT SUPPLIES A PERIODIC DEFAULT, BECAUSE IF IT DOES THE AT-WILL TENANCY CANNOT ARISE AND THE TOPIC'S ANSWER IS AN ABSENCE WITH A SUBSTITUTE RATHER THAN A GAP. Nebraska's § 76-1414(4) is uniform URLTA § 1.401(c) text — "[u]nless the rental agreement fixes a definite term, the tenancy shall be week to week in case of a roomer who pays weekly rent, and in all other cases month to month" — so EVERY URLTA state has the same default and the same consequence, and a row in a URLTA state that describes a tenancy at will arising from an unwritten arrangement is describing pre-URLTA common law. The states on this topic with real at-will statutes (MA, MD, WI, KY, WV, MN, SD) are mostly NON-uniform states, and that split is the structure of the topic. (2) WHERE THE AT-WILL CATEGORY SURVIVES OUTSIDE THE ACT, THE LIMITATION PERIOD IS THE SLEEPER AND IT IS USUALLY FAR SHORTER. Nebraska runs ONE YEAR on a forcible entry and detainer action (§ 25-203) against TEN YEARS on a possession action under the Act (§ 25-202, per the Blankenau annotation printed with § 76-1437). A library that records the notice period for each route and not the limitation period has captured the less consequential of the two numbers, and the ratio here is ten to one. Ask of every state: what is the limitation period on the summary possession action, and is it different from the general real-property possession period? (3) THE SERVICE ROUTE DIFFERS BETWEEN THE TWO PROCEDURES AND THE OLDER ONE IS USUALLY MORE GENEROUS TO THE LANDLORD. Nebraska's § 25-21,221 permits service of the three-day notice to leave "by leaving such notice at or posting it on the detained premises" where the defendant and the usual place of abode cannot be found in the county — a posting route that the URLTA's own receipt list (§ 1.202, Nebraska's § 76-1413(2)(c)) does not contain. The brief's seventh round already records the recommendation that door-posting come out of shared entry clauses in URLTA states for that reason; the same asymmetry is worth checking on NOTICE clauses, because a state's old summary-possession statute may permit posting while its landlord-tenant act does not, and which statute governs depends on which premises are involved.

### From `tenant-bankruptcy`

Three transferable findings for the 19 states on this topic. (1) THE ABSENCE IS STRUCTURAL IN EVERY URLTA STATE AND THERE IS A SECTION THAT PROVES IT, WHICH TURNS A BARE KEYWORD ZERO INTO AN ARGUED CONCLUSION AT THE COST OF ONE SECTION READ. Uniform URLTA § 1.103 — Nebraska's § 76-1403 — provides that "[u]nless displaced by the provisions of" the act, "the principles of law and equity, including the law relating to ... BANKRUPTCY, or other validating or invalidating cause, supplement the act's provisions." So the uniform act names bankruptcy as imported law. Every state row on this topic should cite its own § 1.103 equivalent rather than reporting a silence, because the silence is the drafters' decision and the section says so. The same sentence does the same work for capacity to contract, estoppel, fraud, misrepresentation, duress, coercion and mistake — so it is the citation for a whole family of "no state rule on X" rows, not just this one. (2) USE PROXIMITY, NOT A WORD COUNT, AND MEASURE THE WORD'S OVERALL FREQUENCY IN THE SAME BREATH. "Bankrupt" is common in any state's code — 44 sections across twelve Nebraska chapters, 8 in the property chapter alone — so a bare count proves nothing and a bare zero on a narrow phrase proves nothing either. The pairing that means something is bankrupt within a couple of hundred characters of landlord, lessor, rental agreement or tenancy, run in BOTH directions, with the overall count quoted beside it to show the zero is about the pairing. (3) A LANDLORD-SIDE PROVISION WORTH LOOKING FOR IN EVERY STATE, BECAUSE IT WILL BE IN THE UTILITIES CHAPTER AND NO LANDLORD-TENANT CANVASS WILL FIND IT: Neb. § 70-1601 bars a retail water, gas or electricity utility from denying service over unpaid bills "not collectible at law because of statutes of limitations or discharge in bankruptcy proceedings". That is a tenant-facing protection with a direct landlord consequence — it removes a reason a unit's utilities cannot be put in a new tenant's name — and it uses none of the words "landlord", "tenant", "lease" or "rental", so it is another instance of the "owner or occupant without the keyword" blind spot. Search the utilities chapter for "discharge in bankruptcy", not for a tenant.

### From `tenant-confidential-information`

Four transferable findings for the 23 states on this topic, and the first two are gaps the library appears to have everywhere. (1) SEPARATE "MAY NOT DISCLOSE" FROM "MUST SECURE", BECAUSE ALMOST EVERY STATE HAS THE SECOND AND FEW HAVE THE FIRST. A row that answers only the disclosure question records an absence and misses a live duty. Nebraska has no disclosure prohibition at all and TWO security statutes, and the operative one — § 87-808(1) — binds "an INDIVIDUAL or a commercial entity", so a sole-proprietor landlord is inside it with no entity threshold and no small-business exemption, the standard being scaled instead to "the nature and size of, and the resources available to, the business". Every state's breach-notification act should be screened for whether it reaches an individual, because that single word decides whether the topic is relevant to most of the library's users. (2) THE VENDOR-CONTRACT DUTY IS A NEAR-50-STATE ITEM WITH A GRANDFATHER CLAUSE, AND THE GRANDFATHER IS THE PART TO CARRY. Neb. § 87-808(2)(a) requires a written security undertaking from every nonaffiliated third-party service provider that receives tenant personal data — screening services, management software, payment processors, collections agencies, document storage — and § 87-808(2)(b) exempts contracts entered before July 19, 2018 while providing that any such contract "renewed on or after" that date must comply. Nebraska's provision came in the 2018 wave of breach-act amendments and most states amended in the same window, so the pattern to look for in each state is: a vendor-contract mandate, a grandfather date, and a renewal trigger that quietly ends the grandfather. Reporting the mandate without the renewal trigger tells landlords their old contracts are safe when they are not. (3) ASK WHO MAY SUE, BECAUSE THE ANSWER CHANGES THE ADVICE COMPLETELY. In Nebraska the Attorney General may "seek and recover direct economic damages for EACH AFFECTED Nebraska resident" for a notice failure (§ 87-806(1)) while a security-practices failure is a consumer-protection violation that "does not give rise to a private cause of action" (§ 87-806(2)), the 2024 Data Privacy Act likewise bars a private right of action (§ 87-1125), and any waiver of the breach act is void (§ 87-805). So the exposure is regulatory and per-resident, not a tenant suit — which means a consent clause in the lease is worthless and a written security practice is valuable. A state row that does not state the enforcer has not told the landlord where the risk is. (4) WHERE A STATE HAS A COMPREHENSIVE CONSUMER-PRIVACY ACT, READ THE SMALL-BUSINESS CARVE-OUT TO ITS LAST CLAUSE, BECAUSE IT IS USUALLY NOT COMPLETE. Neb. § 87-1103(1)(c) excludes a small business "as determined under the federal Small Business Act, as such act existed on January 1, 2024, EXCEPT to the extent that section 87-1118 applies" — and § 87-1118 bars a small business from selling SENSITIVE data without prior consent. A row that reports "small landlords are exempt" without that exception is wrong in the one scenario (selling or trading tenant data) where the penalty attaches. Also worth noting for any state: Nebraska's § 87-1130 preempts municipal regulation of personal-data processing outright, which is unusual and is a landlord protection a row should state where it exists.

### From `tenant-display-rights`

Four transferable points for the 38 states on this topic. (1) IN A URLTA STATE THE DISPLAY QUESTION IS ANSWERED BY THE RULES-AND-REGULATIONS SECTION, AND ITS CONDITIONS ARE UNIFORM TEXT, SO THE ANALYSIS PORTS WHOLESALE. Nebraska's § 76-1422 is uniform URLTA § 3.102(1), and two of its six conditions decide nearly every real dispute: the rule must "appl[y] to all tenants in the premises in a FAIR MANNER" (condition (3)), which makes selective enforcement fatal, and the tenant must have "NOTICE OF IT AT THE TIME HE ENTERS INTO THE RENTAL AGREEMENT" (condition (6)), which makes a mid-tenancy rule unenforceable against an existing tenant. The brief already records condition (6) as hollowing out any clause that leans on house rules without a delivery-and-receipt sentence; this topic is the clearest illustration, because display rules are the ones landlords most often adopt after a tenant moves in and does something they dislike. (2) CONDITION (1) IS A LANDLORD ADVANTAGE THAT NO ROW APPEARS TO USE: the uniform purpose list opens with "APPEARANCE". An aesthetic rule about what may be displayed is within the statute's own legitimate purposes in every URLTA state, so a display rule does not have to be justified on safety grounds and should not be drafted as though it did. (3) SEPARATE THE THREE DISPLAY SUBJECTS, BECAUSE STATES LEGISLATE THEM INDEPENDENTLY AND A SINGLE VERDICT HIDES THE ANSWER: a flag-display right (often enacted for homeowners and common-interest communities rather than tenants, which is the NV and UT pattern); a political-sign right; and a religious-display right. Nebraska has none of the three, and the cheapest proof is the three phrase searches plus a mezuzah/crucifix/doorpost battery, all of which return zero. (4) AND THE TRAP IN THE OTHER DIRECTION, worth checking in every state: a state's only flag statute may be a FLAG-DESECRATION offence rather than a display right. Neb. § 28-928 criminalises mutilating a flag and defines "flag" broadly enough to include a banner or a replica. A keyword search for "flag" in any state's code will surface such a section, and a row built on that hit would report a flag provision that gives a landlord nothing and a tenant no display right — and that sits in federal constitutional territory a state-statute canvass cannot assess. Any state's flag row should say which kind of statute it found.

### From `tenant-employee-housing`

Transferable test for every URLTA state: URLTA s 1.202(5) is adopted almost verbatim as Neb. s 76-1408(5), and the exclusion turns on TWO facts, not one - the occupancy right must be CONDITIONAL on the employment, and the employment must be 'in and about the premises'. A row that says 'employee housing is outside the act' without both conditions over-states the exclusion in every URLTA state, and the error runs against the landlord, who will have skipped the deposit and habitability compliance. Also note the anti-avoidance chapeau ('Unless created to avoid the application of the act'), which is uniform text and makes a declaratory 'the Act does not apply' clause worse than useless.

### From `tenant-forward-proceedings`

The CA notes describe Cal. Civ. Code s 1948's void-attornment rule as a pairing for this clause. Worth knowing before the clause is tagged into further states: a void-attornment statute is NOT general - a local-corpus sweep of 7,208 Nebraska sections for 'attornment|attorn|attorns' returns 0, so the pairing is a California feature and a row that leans on it reasons from a statute most states lack. The clause itself is fine without it.

### From `tenant-insurance-claims`

A cheap, decisive screen for every state's tenant-insurance-claims row: does the state's CONDOMINIUM act carry an insurer-waives-subrogation mandate while the residential landlord-tenant act does not? Nebraska s 76-871(d)(2) requires the association's policy to provide that 'the insurer waives its right to subrogation under the policy against any unit owner or member of his or her household', and the URLTA has no counterpart. Both acts are widely adopted uniform texts (UCIOA s 3-113 and URLTA), so most states will show the same asymmetry - which means a row that says 'nothing bars the landlord's insurer from subrogating against the tenant' is on firm ground, and a row that assumes an implied-co-insured protection is reasoning from case law, not statute.

Me. Rev. Stat. tit. 14 s 6039(5)(B) is cited in edu-tenant-insurance-claims-me for 'the surety bond is not insurance for the tenant'. Nebraska's nearest analogue is in a different act and runs the other way: s 69-2110(1)(a) of the Rental-Purchase Agreement Act permits 'an initial nonrefundable administrative fee of not more than ten dollars' and s 69-2104(1)(i) requires it disclosed. Any state's row that treats a deposit-replacement surety product as regulated should check whether the regulation sits in the landlord-tenant act or in a rental-purchase/consumer act, because the two have different remedies.

### From `tenant-portal`

A transferable screen for every tenant-portal row: a state that has adopted UETA (nearly all have) already carries s 5(b) and s 5(c) of the uniform act, which in Nebraska are s 86-632(2) and (3) - UETA 'applies only to transactions between parties each of which has agreed to conduct transactions by electronic means', and the right to refuse OTHER electronic transactions 'may not be waived by agreement'. So a lease clause routing every notice, signature and payment through a portal is partly unenforceable in every UETA state regardless of whether that state has a landlord-tenant e-delivery statute, and a row that answers 'no portal law here' without the UETA layer is incomplete everywhere. The second uniform hook is UETA s 8(c)/(d), Nebraska's s 86-635(3)-(4): inhibiting the recipient's ability to print or store makes the record 'not enforceable against the recipient' and that requirement 'may not be varied by agreement' - which is a portal-design defect, not a drafting one, and no state's lease clause can cure it.

Nebraska's s 76-1413(9) ('shall not, as part of a rental agreement or as a condition of entering into or renewing a rental agreement, require a tenant to accept delivery by electronic means', Laws 2025, LB185) is part of the 2023-2025 wave of near-identical e-delivery consent provisions the brief flags. The drafting consequence is specific and probably applies in every state in that wave: the consent CANNOT live in the lease, so a library that implements e-notice consent as a lease paragraph has built the prohibited form of it. The fix is a separate optional consent form, not different lease wording.

### From `tenant-portal`

URLTA s 2.102(3) is the uniform source of Nebraska's s 76-1414(3) ('at the time and place agreed upon by the parties'; default 'at the dwelling unit'), so in every URLTA state the lease can name the portal as the place of payment without any portal statute. A state's tenant-portal row that answers only 'no portal law' misses that the rent-payment half is already answered affirmatively by the uniform rent section.

### From `tenant-records`

Transferable test for every rent-ledger row: the answer is in the state's NONPAYMENT-NOTICE section, not in a records section. Neb. s 76-1431(2) prescribes exactly two contents (written notice of nonpayment and of the intention to terminate if unpaid within seven calendar days) and no amount or balance, which is URLTA s 4.201(2) with the state's own day count substituted. A library row saying 'the notice must state the amount owed' in a URLTA state is probably importing a non-uniform add-on from a demand-for-rent statute elsewhere in that state's code, and the error is expensive because an over-specified notice can be attacked for a defect the statute never required.

### From `tenant-records`

The brief already flags this as a probable near-50-state gap; this row adds the three screens that make another state's row checkable rather than guessed. (1) Does the state's breach act cover an 'individual' as well as a commercial entity? Nebraska s 87-808(1) says 'an individual or a commercial entity', which is what pulls in the sole-owner landlord; a state whose act reaches only businesses of a stated size does not. (2) Does it carry the 2018-wave VENDOR-CONTRACT duty (Neb. s 87-808(2)(a), 'shall require by contract'), and what is its grandfather date and renewal trigger (Nebraska: contracts before July 19, 2018 exempt, but any renewal on or after that date must comply)? (3) Is there a private right of action? Nebraska expressly has none for the security duty (s 87-806(2): 'does not give rise to a private cause of action') but the Attorney General may recover 'direct economic damages for each affected Nebraska resident' for a breach-notice violation (s 87-806(1)) - so the exposure is regulatory, and a row that frames it as tenant-suit risk mis-sizes it. Also uniform-ish and worth carrying: the act is confined to COMPUTERIZED data, so a paper-only applicant file falls outside most of these statutes.

### From `tenant-repair-remedies`

A test every URLTA state's repair-remedy row can be checked against: the state's procure-and-deduct right is almost always the ESSENTIAL-SERVICES section (URLTA s 4.104, Neb. s 76-1427(1)(a)) and not a general repair-and-deduct. In Nebraska 'repair and deduct' -> 0 across 7,208 sections while s 76-1427(1)(a) plainly allows deduction for water, hot water, heat and essential services. So a row that says 'this state has repair-and-deduct' is probably describing the essential-services remedy with the wrong scope, and a row that says 'no deduction from rent is ever allowed' is wrong for the same reason. Check the scope words, not the doctrine's name.

The rent-escrow question also has a one-command answer that other states can copy: sweep the escrow family ('\bescrows?\b|rent escrow|paid into escrow') over the whole property chapter and see whether any hit falls INSIDE the residential act's section range. In Nebraska 11 of 11 fall outside it. And note the direction of the one procedural pay-into-court power, s 76-1428(1): the court 'may order' the tenant to pay rent in, and s 76-1428(1) also gives the LANDLORD reasonable attorney's fees where the tenant's defence or counterclaim 'is without merit and is not raised in good faith' - a landlord-side provision in a tenant-remedy section that a canvass of the remedy sections alone will miss.

### From `tenant-right-to-organize`

Transferable test for every state's tenant-organizing row, and it is a two-list test, not one: (i) is the PROTECTED CONDUCT list open or closed, and (ii) is NON-RENEWAL among the prohibited acts? Nebraska's URLTA s 76-1439(1) has a closed two-item conduct list and omits non-renewal; the same state's Mobile Home Act s 76-14,106(1) has a four-item list and includes non-renewal. Because URLTA s 5.101 is the common source, most URLTA states will show the narrow form, and a library row that tells a landlord 'do not decline to renew an organizing tenant' is over-warning in those states while a row that omits the organizing trigger altogether is under-warning. Check both lists against the state's own text before tagging.

A second, cheap screen that settles the Massachusetts-style question in any state: sweep 'presum' over the property chapter and see whether any hit sits inside the residential act's range. In Nebraska it is 25 sections and none in ss 76-1401 to 76-1449, so there is no retaliation presumption and no burden-shifting - which means the tenant must prove the retaliatory motive, and a row that warns of a presumption is importing another state's rule.

### From `tenant-rights-statement`

Screen worth applying to every state's tenant-rights-statement row before it is written as an absence: sweep '\bpamphlets?\b' and 'brochure' across the property and professions chapters, not just the landlord-tenant act. In Nebraska that sweep returns 13 sections, and the only one naming both 'landlord' and 'tenant' is s 76-2421 - the real estate licensee's brokerage disclosure pamphlet, a REAL mandatory document that reaches a landlord who is licensed or who uses a licensed leasing agent, and which no landlord-tenant-act search finds. Most states license brokerage and most have an agency-disclosure pamphlet, so the same hit is likely nationwide, and the distinction a row must draw is licensee-duty versus landlord-duty. Getting it wrong in either direction is costly: called a landlord duty it invents compliance work; omitted entirely it misses the one pamphlet a broker-using landlord should confirm was delivered.

### From `tenant-statutory-duties`

A three-bucket test result other states can reuse: in a URLTA state a lease clause restating the statutory tenant duties is NOT SERVES_LANDLORD, because the uniform landlord-remedy section already names the duties section as an independent ground (Neb. s 76-1431(1) and (3), URLTA s 4.201 and s 4.202, both running on 'noncompliance with the rental agreement OR section [tenant duties]'). The clause therefore adds no remedy. Any state's row that classifies a tenant-duties restatement as a lease clause should be re-checked against that state's landlord-remedy section - if the duties section is named there, the restatement is education.

The real lease-side work in every URLTA state is the HOUSE-RULES section, not the duties section. Neb. s 76-1422(6) makes a rule enforceable 'only if ... the tenant has notice of it at the time he enters into the rental agreement', and its closing sentence allows a later rule only with reasonable notice and only if it 'does not work a substantial modification of his bargain'. This is URLTA s 3.102(1)(f) and (2), so any shared clause that leans on house rules without a delivery-and-receipt sentence is hollow in every URLTA state - and the mid-term rule change has a substantive ceiling, not just a notice requirement.

### From `term-change-notice`

A precision point that probably bites in every URLTA state and that a month-to-month notice clause can get wrong: URLTA s 4.301(b), Nebraska's s 76-1437(2), runs the thirty days to 'the PERIODIC RENTAL DATE specified in the notice', while the week-to-week twin at (1) runs seven days to 'the TERMINATION DATE specified in the notice'. So a month-to-month notice must expire on a rent date, and a shared clause or education row that says 'at least 30 days' notice' without the periodic-rental-date anchor permits a notice that is void for landing mid-period. Check the state's own words for which date the clock runs to.

Sibling-act test for every term-change-notice row: does the state have a SEPARATE mobile-home-park or manufactured-housing act with a rent-increase notice? Nebraska's s 76-1490 requires sixty days' written notice of any rent increase in a park and the URLTA has nothing, which turns the residential silence into a demonstrated choice rather than an unsearched gap. Most states have both acts, so this is a cheap way to make an absence row defensible - and it also warns that a landlord who owns a park is on a different clock in the same state.

### From `tpa-exemption-notice`

Transferable structural test for every tpa-exemption-notice row: ask whether the state's exemptions are SELF-EXECUTING or NOTICE-CONDITIONED. California's rent-cap exemption is notice-conditioned, which is why the notice exists and why failing to serve it costs the exemption. The URLTA's exclusions (URLTA s 1.202, Neb. s 76-1408) are self-executing AND carry an anti-avoidance chapeau, so in a URLTA state an exemption recital in the lease is not merely unnecessary - it is affirmative evidence that the arrangement may have been 'created to avoid the application of the act'. Any state's row on this topic should say which of the two kinds of exemption the state has, because the drafting advice is opposite in the two cases.

### From `tpa-notice`

A distinction worth checking in every state's tpa-notice and conversion row, because it is easy to state backwards: is the conversion purchase right MANDATORY or merely a price protection conditional on an offer? Neb. s 76-886(b) says the converter 'may offer to convey each unit', and the only duty is the thirty-day no-better-terms rule that follows IF an offer is made. That provision is UCIOA s 4-112, so the permissive form is likely shared by the UCIOA states, while the mandatory opportunity-to-purchase states (Maryland, D.C., Rhode Island) get it from separate non-uniform legislation. A row that tells a landlord 'you must offer the unit to the tenant' in a UCIOA state is probably importing the non-uniform rule.

### From `tpa-sunset`

Method test for every tpa-sunset row, and it is a trap worth naming: an absence on this topic must NOT be proved from a session-law search. The reason is structural and not a matter of what any particular sweep returns - a session-law corpus covers only the sessions it holds, so a zero in it tells you what those sessions did and nothing about what the code says. Nebraska makes the point twice over. A searcher who sweeps the 2025-2026 slip laws for the act's name gets 2 files (LB185, electronic delivery; LB80, the domestic-violence sections) - both CROSS-REFERENCES to the Act's name and neither a sunset - and a searcher whose tool wraps text at a fixed column gets 0 for the same query, because the act's name is long enough to straddle a line break. Either figure would support 'no recent activity, therefore no sunset risk', and that inference is unsound on either one: the Act dates from Laws 1974, LB 293, and a sunset enacted in any earlier session would appear in no 2025-26 slip law at all. CORRECTED 2026-10-29: an earlier version of this finding asserted the 0 and explained it as 'the sessions simply never named it', which is false - they did name it - so the finding now rests on the corpus's coverage rather than on a count. Prove it the other way: sweep 'sunset|shall terminate on|repealed on|cease to be effective' over the whole code with controls, and read the act's own HOW-CITED and APPLICABILITY sections, which is where a sunset has to sit. The same approach also catches the opposite signal cheaply - an act whose citation sentence was just widened to take in new sections is being expanded, not wound down.

### From `translation-duty`

Transferable test for every translation-duty row: find where the state's translation trigger LIVES before deciding its scope. In Nebraska the lease-naming translation duty is in the FORECLOSURE-RESCUE act (s 76-2727, 'Any equity purchase contract, rental agreement, lease ... signed by a homeowner'), and the advertise-in-the-language duty is in the HOME SOLICITATION SALES act (s 69-1604(3)), which s 69-1601(1) confines to 'consumer goods or services'. Foreclosure-rescue and home-solicitation statutes are both widespread, so other states probably have the same two provisions - and a keyword search for 'translation' plus 'lease' will hit the foreclosure one and look like a general lease-translation duty. Check the act's 'homeowner' or 'residence in foreclosure' definition: if it requires owner occupancy, the duty reaches only a sale-leaseback and not an ordinary tenancy.

A scope word that any 'no translation duty' row needs: California's Civ. Code s 1632 trigger is doing business in the language, and the states that copied it often copied it into a CONSUMER-GOODS act rather than into housing. Nebraska's s 69-1601(1) is the model of the limit - 'a sale, lease, or rental of consumer goods or services' - where the word 'lease' is present and still does not reach a dwelling. So a row must test the act's own subject-matter definition rather than the presence of the word 'lease' in the trigger.

### From `trespass-notice`

The decisive question in every state's trespass-notice row is not the notice methods but WHO MAY LICENSE ACCESS, and it is usually answered in the affirmative-defence section rather than in the offence. Neb. s 28-522(3) gives a defence where 'the actor reasonably believed that the owner of the premises OR OTHER PERSON EMPOWERED TO LICENSE ACCESS thereto would have licensed him to enter or remain' - Model Penal Code s 221.2(3) language, so most states have it - and the printed annotation (State v. McCave, 282 Neb. 500 (2011)) holds that a licence from ANY such person suffices and the defendant 'need not show that every owner licensed his or her presence'. A row that tells a landlord a written ban letter makes a tenant's invited guest a trespasser is wrong wherever that defence exists, which is most places. The sound advice everywhere is: ban list for non-tenant areas, tenant covenant for guests.

A second, narrower point worth carrying: Neb. s 28-521(5) escalates the offence 'if the offender defies an order to leave PERSONALLY COMMUNICATED to him or her by the owner of the premises or other authorized person'. That is an operational instruction, not a drafting one - a mailed ban letter and an in-person order to leave sit at different grades - and a row that lists only the posting and written-notice methods leaves the landlord's strongest step unmentioned. Check each state's grading provision for a defiance escalator.

### From `trespass-notice`

This clause shape is portable to every state with the Model Penal Code s 221.2(3) licence defence (Neb. s 28-522(3)) and a URLTA-style tenant-conduct duty, which is most of the library. The two lines that must be re-checked per state are the carve-out list and the enforcement hook: Nebraska's carve-out tracks s 76-1431(5)(a)(i)-(iii) (protective order, law-enforcement report, qualified-third-party domestic-violence certification) and its hook is s 76-1431(1)/(3). A state with a broader domestic-violence protection needs a broader carve-out, and a state whose landlord-remedy section does not name the tenant-duties provision needs the covenant restated as an express lease obligation rather than cross-referenced.

### From `truth-in-renting`

A truth-in-renting row should separate two things that the statutes in New Jersey and Michigan combine, because most states have only one of them: (A) a PRESCRIBED-NOTICE duty (attach or deliver a state statement) and (B) a KNOWING-USE PENALTY for including a void term. Nebraska has (B) and not (A): s 76-1415(2) gives the tenant actual damages and reasonable attorney's fees where 'a landlord deliberately uses a rental agreement containing provisions known by him or her to be prohibited', which is URLTA s 1.403(2) and therefore present in every URLTA state. So a row saying 'this state has no truth-in-renting law, nothing to worry about' is wrong about the half that actually costs money, in every URLTA state.

A scope word worth checking on every exculpation-ban citation: Nebraska's residential ban is NEGLIGENCE-SPECIFIC - s 76-1415(1)(d) reaches exculpation or indemnity for liability 'arising due to active and actionable negligence of the landlord' - while the same state's mobile-home-park version, s 76-1477(1)(c), reaches liability 'arising under law' generally and runs BOTH ways between landlord and tenant. States differ on exactly this word, and a shared renter's-insurance or hold-harmless clause calibrated to a general ban will be narrower than it needs to be in a negligence-specific state and unlawful in a general-ban state.

### From `unauthorized-occupant-removal`

A structural trap worth checking in every URLTA state's squatter or unauthorized-occupant row, because Nebraska shows it exists in the uniform text itself: the state's general forcible-entry statute may EXCLUDE premises governed by the residential act, while the residential act CLAIMS every action for possession of such premises. Neb. s 25-21,219's last sentence and s 76-1440 use the identical phrase 'any premises subject to the provisions of' the Act from opposite directions, and neither defines it. The practical consequence is the same wherever the pair exists: a landlord who files the squatter action in the general statute may be met with a jurisdictional objection, and the safe practice is to serve both notices and plead the statutory authority in the alternative. A row that names only one route in such a state is giving advice that can be dismissed for want of jurisdiction.

Two drafting-independent points other states' rows can reuse. (1) The URLTA's expedited criminal-activity route may already reach a non-tenant by its own words: Neb. s 76-1431(4) gives judgment 'against any tenant OR OCCUPANT', and it expressly overrides the general three-day notice statute ('Notwithstanding ... section 25-21,221'). Check whether the state's equivalent says 'occupant' - if it does, the fast route exists for conduct cases and no squatter statute is needed for them. (2) The cost of guessing wrong is a FIXED sum, not damages: Neb. s 76-1430 gives three months' periodic rent as liquidated damages plus a reasonable attorney's fee for an unlawful removal or exclusion, with no proof of loss required. That is URLTA s 4.107 and the figure varies by state, so every self-help warning should quote the state's own number and say whether it is a fixed sum, a ceiling or a floor.

### From `unbundled-parking`

A consequence of unbundling that every state's unbundled-parking row should check and that the California rows do not raise: does the state's security-deposit definition reach a PARKING deposit? Neb. s 76-1416(1) caps 'security, HOWEVER DENOMINATED' at one month's periodic rent with a single exception for a pet deposit, so unbundling parking and taking a space deposit eats into the dwelling deposit. The brief already records the transferable test in the other direction (a nonrefundable designation works only where the state's definition has an express-agreement carve-out; 'however denominated' defeats it), and this is the same test applied to an ancillary charge. In any 'however denominated' state, unbundling changes the deposit arithmetic.

Second-order point, and the test is a two-definition one rather than the obvious one: whether unbundling shrinks the deposit CEILING depends on how the state defines RENT, not on how it defines the deposit. URLTA s 1.301(12) - Neb. s 76-1410(13) - says 'Rent means all payments to be made to the landlord under the rental agreement', and URLTA's 'premises' definition reaches 'facilities held out for the use of tenants generally', so in a URLTA state an unbundled parking charge is still rent and the ceiling does not move. A state that defines rent as consideration for the DWELLING UNIT alone would come out the other way, and a clause splitting the charge there would quietly cut the landlord's deposit headroom. Check the rent definition before splitting a charge in any state.

### From `unpaid-damages-interest`

A test every unpaid-damages-interest row can be checked against, and it reframes the topic: in a URLTA state the interesting provision is usually NOT the general interest statute but the Act's own FEE PROHIBITION. Neb. s 76-1415(1)(c) - URLTA s 1.403(1)(c) - prohibits a term that the tenant 'Agrees to pay the landlord's or tenant's attorney's fees', so the standard 'interest plus costs plus attorney's fees' sentence is partly void in every state that adopted it unamended, and the landlord's fee recovery instead runs through the statutory willfulness provisions (Neb. ss 76-1431(3), 76-1437(3)). Any state's row that offers an interest-and-fees clause should be checked against that state's s 1.403 list before it is tagged.

A small-claims interest statute is a better answer than a general legal-rate statute for most landlord claims, and it carries conditions a general-rate analysis will miss. Neb. s 25-1801 gives six percent from thirty days after accrual plus a sliding statutory attorney's fee on any lawsuit of four thousand dollars or less - but only after a NINETY-DAY condition precedent, only if a judgment is secured (payment in full before judgment yields costs alone), and on an accrual date the statute defines and that the parties may move 'unless some different time period is expressly set forth in a written agreement'. States commonly have a small-claims or small-account fee-and-interest statute of this shape; a row that cites only the general legal rate will understate what the landlord can get and will miss the condition that forfeits it.

### From `usufructuary-lessor`

Transferable test for every common-law state on this topic: do NOT write 'no usufruct, therefore no rule'. The usufruct rows answer 'what happens to the lease when the lessor's own estate ends', and every common-law state answers it through the life estate / estate for years plus a remainderman's waste-and-trespass action. The two things to look for are (i) a statute letting the remainderman sue DURING the intervening estate (Nebraska: § 25-2132, 'notwithstanding any intervening estate for life or years') and (ii) whether the state's waste statute bars forfeiture and multiple damages but preserves a contrary covenant in the creating instrument (Nebraska: § 76-120's closing 'except in accordance with covenants, agreements or conditions binding such defendants'). A state whose waste statute lacks that carve-out gives the tenant a materially different risk profile.

### From `utility-allowance-cap`

Transferable test for `utility-allowance-cap-co`, in order. (i) HOW DOES THE STATE DEFINE RENT? Where the definition is 'all payments to be made to the landlord under the rental agreement' (Neb. § 76-1410(13), and the same words appear in every 1972-URLTA state), the clause's de-characterisation sentence costs the landlord the summary nonpayment route; where rent is defined narrowly as the periodic charge for occupancy, the sentence is harmless. The clause should be checked in all nine tag states on this one point. (ii) CAN THE LEASE SHIFT THE SUPPLY DUTY? URLTA § 2.104(2) and (3) (Neb. § 76-1419(2),(3)) permit shifting the water-and-heat subdivision only for a single-family residence; the clause's own example utility is water and sewer, so in every URLTA state it needs an express carve-out preserving the supply duty for multi-unit buildings, which it does not have. (iii) IS THE CHARGE A LIEN ON THE PROPERTY? Where municipal sewer or water charges are a lien on the property served and collectible from the owner (Neb. § 18-509(1), 'either from the owner or the person, firm, or corporation requesting the service'), a cap on the landlord's 'obligation to pay' caps nothing as against the city - so the clause should not be presented to a landlord as a cap on exposure.

### From `utility-apportionment`

Transferable screen for every state on this topic, and it takes one command: BEFORE calling an apportionment rule absent, search the state's CONDOMINIUM act and its MOBILE HOME PARK act, not just its landlord-tenant act. Nebraska's Uniform Common Interest Ownership-style § 76-873(c)(3) and its Mobile Home Act § 76-1482 both legislate on non-metered utilities while the URLTA is silent, which converts a bare absence into a demonstrated legislative choice. Second transferable point: where § 76-873(c)(3)-style text is used as a contrast in ANY state's row, it must carry BOTH of its conditions - the subsection chapeau ('To the extent required by the declaration') and the subdivision's own 'if reasonably determined' - because quoted bare it reads as a mandate and is not one.

### From `utility-deposit-return`

Transferable test, and it splits the topic in two before any research is done. (i) THE LANDLORD-HELD UTILITY DEPOSIT is governed by the state's SECURITY-DEPOSIT definition, not by any utility statute. Where the definition is 'security, however denominated' (Neb. § 76-1416(1), URLTA § 1.401-style text), a separately labelled utility deposit is security, counts against the cap, and runs on the deposit clock - and the already-recorded `nonrefundable-fees-wv` test is the same test from the other side: a state whose definition carries an express-agreement carve-out lets the label work, a state that says 'however denominated' does not. (ii) THE UTILITY-HELD DEPOSIT is governed by the state's UNCLAIMED PROPERTY act, which in Nebraska gives it a three-year dormancy from termination of service (§ 69-1304(a)) against the deposit act's fourteen days. Every state has a Uniform Disposition of Unclaimed Property Act analogue with a utility-deposit section, and a row that answers only the landlord-held half leaves the tenant's actual money unaccounted for. Checking § 69-1304's analogue is a one-section lookup in any state.

### From `utility-disclosure-attachment`

Transferable test for every 'disclosure attachment' row in the library, in order and cheap to run. (i) Does the state have the underlying disclosure duty at all? If not, every attachment, type-size and separate-signature question is moot and the row should say so in one sentence rather than reasoning about vehicles. (ii) If it does, WHERE does the statute put it - 'in the rental agreement', 'attached to', or merely 'in writing before signing'? Nebraska's two data points are opposite in form: § 76-1605(3) says the agreement 'shall contain' a statement in bold type, § 76-1482 says the landlord shall 'provide a written explanation ... before the rental agreement is signed'. The second is discharged by a handed-over sheet and the first is not. (iii) Search the FORMATTING words, not 'points': capitalized, underlined, bold, conspicuous, adjoining, 'first page'. Measured on point size alone, Nebraska looks like it has no lease formatting rule and it has one (§ 25-2602.02). This is the net-too-narrow error the brief records twice, and it will be present in any state's row whose absence claim was measured on type size.

### From `utility-disconnection-notice-authorization`

Transferable test for every `utility-disconnection-notice-authorization` row, and it is a THREE-layer question the library's rows appear to treat as one or two. LAYER ONE: does the state's utility statute itself require a third-party notice procedure? Nebraska's § 70-1607 does, mandatorily, and the designation belongs to the SUBSCRIBER - so the lease clause is the tenant's election, never a landlord right, and a clause drafted as a landlord entitlement purports to give the landlord something the statute gives someone else. LAYER TWO: does a statute authorise third-party notification without requiring a procedure (Wis. Stat. § 196.643(3))? LAYER THREE: does the tariff or the regulator's rule provide it (3 AAC 52.410(b)(10))? Where none exists the clause must require the tenant to sign the PROVIDER'S own form rather than purporting to bind a provider that is not a party to the lease. Two structural warnings for states like Nebraska. Public-power states have no public service commission in the distribution chain, so a row that looks only at the state utility commission will record a false absence wherever distribution is municipal or district-owned. And the statutory protections may be defined by ACCOUNT HOLDER rather than by premises: Neb. § 70-1602 excludes 'businesses of any nature' from 'domestic subscriber', which makes the landlord-held account the worst of the three options rather than the most controlling - read that definition in every state before recommending a landlord-held account.

### From `utility-disconnection-notice-authorization`

Transferable test, and it is the one most likely to be missed in every state. A municipal utility lien statute is usually read for the LIEN. Read it for the NOTICE and the CUT-OFF right as well: Nebraska's § 16-682 contains a duty on the city to notify a non-occupying owner at sixty days' delinquency and a right for the owner to stop the lien growing by demanding discontinuance. Then ask the second question, which is the one that makes it hazardous: does exercising that municipal right collide with the state landlord-tenant act's prohibition on the landlord 'causing the interruption' of an essential service (Neb. § 76-1430, URLTA § 4.107)? Every URLTA state has the § 4.107 analogue, and a municipal-code-derived right to demand a shutoff exists in many of them, so the collision is probably general and the library carries it for nobody. The liquidated-damages measure decides how dangerous it is: Nebraska's is a FIXED three months' periodic rent plus fees, needing no proof of loss. AND ONE MORE READING THAT SHARPENS THE COLLISION TEST: look at the state disconnection article's own EXCLUSIONS clause. Neb. s 70-1615 steps the article aside only for interruptions 'made necessary by the utility' for repair, maintenance or health and safety. Where a state's exclusions clause is drafted that way and contains no owner-requested category, a municipal-code right to demand a shutoff sits in tension with the landlord-tenant act rather than being blessed by the utility statute - which is the shape of the unresolved question here.

### From `utility-interruption-submeter`

Transferable test for every `utility-interruption-submeter` row: the question is not 'does the state regulate submetered interruption' but 'what SHAPE is the state's liquidated-damages figure for a diminution of services, and does the tenant get RESTORATION?' Nebraska answers fixed-three-months-plus-fees with no restoration remedy (§ 76-1430), and its own mobile-home act answers ceiling-of-one-and-a-half-months WITH restoration (§ 76-14,100). Three things to read off any URLTA § 4.107 analogue before writing the row: (i) is the figure a fixed sum, a ceiling or a floor - it changes whether the tenant must prove loss at all; (ii) does 'causing the interruption' appear, which is what reaches non-payment of a landlord-name account and a landlord-requested municipal shutoff; (iii) is there a restoration remedy, because its presence turns the section from a damages provision into an injunction. Separately: URLTA § 2.104(1)(d)'s 'supplied OR REQUIRED TO BE SUPPLIED' makes a voluntarily installed submeter a continuing maintenance duty in every URLTA state, which the library's submetering rows answer nowhere. FOURTH READING, added once the disconnection article could be read: check the state's disconnection statute's EXCLUSIONS section, not only its landlord-tenant act. Neb. s 70-1615 steps the article aside only for interruptions 'made necessary by the utility' for repair, maintenance or health and safety - the utility's own grounds, not the landlord's. Where a state's exclusions clause is drafted the same way, the absence of a landlord-requested ground is affirmative confirmation that no lawful landlord-side interruption exists, which is stronger than an absence found by searching the landlord-tenant act alone.

### From `utility-interruption-submeter`

Transferable test, and it is a two-statute question the library answers with one statute everywhere. Every state with a civil utility-diversion action almost certainly has a CRIMINAL meter statute as well, and the criminal one is usually (i) older, (ii) free of the civil action's damages and willfulness gates, and (iii) equipped with a presumption against the occupant or possessor. The three limbs to look for are the bypass limb, the 'knowingly permit the use' limb - which is what converts a tenant's theft into the landlord's offence - and an UNLAWFUL RECONNECTION limb keyed to the state's utility-disconnection statute, which is the one a landlord trips over in the ordinary course. Then read the presumption clause against the state's definition of what the tenant possesses: a presumption aimed at 'the person in possession of the premises' points at the tenant inside the unit and at the landlord at a master meter, so the same sentence allocates risk differently in a single-metered and a master-metered building.

### From `utility-landlord-account`

Four transferable tests for every `utility-landlord-account` row, and the first is new and probably changes several of them. (i) READ THE 'DOMESTIC SUBSCRIBER' OR 'RESIDENTIAL CUSTOMER' DEFINITION IN THE STATE'S DISCONNECTION STATUTE BEFORE RECOMMENDING OR DESCRIBING A LANDLORD-HELD ACCOUNT. Where it is written as an exclusion list naming business entities - Neb. § 70-1602: 'shall not include municipalities, cities, villages, political subdivisions, companies, corporations, partnerships, limited liability companies, or businesses of any nature' - every protection in the article turns on who holds the account, and the landlord-held account is the weakest position rather than the most controlling. Ask also whether a natural-person landlord is caught; Nebraska's text cannot settle it. (ii) IS THERE A MANDATORY THIRD-PARTY NOTICE PROCEDURE? Neb. § 70-1607 obliges every covered utility to establish one and gives the designation to the subscriber, which makes 'tenant's account plus landlord designated as third party' the superior arrangement for both sides. Look for the same provision in any state with a disconnection article. (iii) IS THERE A RECEIVERSHIP, AND WHERE WOULD IT LIVE? Do not search the landlord-tenant act alone - a rent-receivership remedy is often in the civil-procedure or municipal-code-enforcement chapter. Nebraska's measured answer is no: 'receiver' appears in seven chapter-76 sections and none is inside either landlord-tenant act. (iv) IS RENT-INTO-COURT PERMISSIVE OR MANDATORY? Neb. § 76-1428(1) says the court 'from time to time may order', which the brief already records as the URLTA pattern. And one point most rows will have backwards: whose name is on the account is irrelevant to a municipal SEWER lien - Neb. § 18-509(1) attaches it to 'the property served' and lets the city collect 'either from the owner or the person, firm, or corporation requesting the service' - so a row that frames the landlord-held account as the source of the landlord's exposure is wrong for sewer and right only for the service-continuity duty.

### From `utility-shutoff-statute`

Three transferable points, the second of which is the one that changes rows. (i) FIND THE SHUTOFF STATUTE THROUGH THE METER-TAMPERING CRIME'S CROSS-REFERENCE. A utility-disconnection regime is often numbered far from both the landlord-tenant act and the public-utilities regulation it sits beside; Nebraska's was reachable only because § 28-515.02(1)(c) names it by number. That route works in any state with an unlawful-reconnection offence. (ii) READ THE 'DOMESTIC SUBSCRIBER' OR 'RESIDENTIAL CUSTOMER' DEFINITION BEFORE RELYING ON ANY PROTECTION IN THE ARTICLE. Where it is written as an exclusion list naming business entities - Neb. § 70-1602: 'shall not include municipalities, cities, villages, political subdivisions, companies, corporations, partnerships, limited liability companies, or businesses of any nature' - every protection turns on WHO HOLDS THE ACCOUNT, which makes a landlord-held-account clause a decision about forfeiting statutory rights rather than a billing convenience. Every `utility-landlord-account` and `utility-transfer` row in the library should be checked against its state's definition. (iii) WINTER RULES ARE EXTENSIONS, NOT MORATORIA, AND THE LIBRARY'S SOUTH DAKOTA ROW ALREADY HAS IT RIGHT ('Winter adds 30 days to utility disconnection notice - an extension, not a moratorium'); a row describing a seasonal rule as a moratorium overstates it. Two further markers worth carrying: an ELECTRONIC-DELIVERY OPT-IN in the utility statute (Neb. § 70-1605 requires that the subscriber 'specifically elected' it) is the same consent pattern as the landlord-tenant electronic-notice wave, and the two arrived separately - Nebraska's utility one in 2020 (Laws 2020, LB632, § 7) and its landlord-tenant one in 2025 (Laws 2025, LB185) - so a state that has one may well have the other. And a THIRD-PARTY NOTICE PROCEDURE provision (Neb. § 70-1607) is the lawful substitute for a landlord-held account in any state that has one, because the designation belongs to the subscriber and costs the tenant nothing.

### From `utility-submetering-disclosure`

Four transferable tests for every submetering-disclosure row, and the last one is the one that is almost always missing. (i) WHICH LAYER? Statute, utility-regulator rule, or neither - and in a public-power state the second layer may be a district's rate schedule rather than a commission's rule, so 'no commission rule' is not an absence. (ii) WHAT IS THE THRESHOLD, AND IS IT THE SAME FOR EACH UTILITY? Maryland's and Texas's differ by building size and by utility; a single-threshold row will be wrong for one of them. (iii) IS THE UNPAID SUBMETER CHARGE RENT? This decides whether the charge is evictable and whether the state's late-fee rules apply to it. Nebraska's § 76-1410(13) ('all payments to be made to the landlord under the rental agreement') makes it rent and therefore evictable on seven days under § 76-1431(2), which is the exact opposite of the regulated states' 'no eviction for nonpayment' rule - so the same clause has opposite consequences in a URLTA state and in a regulated-submetering state, and a shared clause cannot carry both. (iv) THE TYPE-SIZE QUESTION MUST BE MEASURED WITH THE RIGHT NET. Search capitalized, underlined, bold, conspicuous, adjoining, 'first page' - NOT 'points'. Nebraska measured on point size looks free of lease formatting rules and is not (§ 25-2602.02).

### From `utility-transfer`

Rule 26 rejection with a transferable test: `utility-transfer-tn`'s opt-in cutoff - the landlord may cut off landlord-name utilities the tenant did not transfer within three days - is unavailable in every URLTA state and is worse than inert there, because it both fails and creates liability. The test, in order: (i) does the state have a URLTA § 4.107 analogue penalising a landlord who 'interrupt[s] or caus[es] the interruption of' an essential service (Neb. § 76-1430)? If yes, the cutoff is the prohibited act. (ii) Is the state's figure a fixed sum? Nebraska's three months' periodic rent is FIXED, so the tenant need not prove loss. (iii) Does the state void a tenant's waiver of Act rights and penalise the landlord's deliberate use of such a term (Neb. §§ 76-1415(1)(a) and 76-1415(2): actual damages plus reasonable attorney's fees)? If yes, the clause is not merely unenforceable - including it is itself the exposure. Tennessee is a URLTA state with § 66-28-301 and following, so the clause should be checked against Tennessee's own § 4.107 analogue before it is offered anywhere else. The replacement drafting, which is lawful in every URLTA state: make the transfer a positive tenant obligation with a date, make the landlord's advance recoverable AS RENT so the summary nonpayment notice reaches it, and state expressly that the landlord will not cut off or ask anyone else to cut off service. FOURTH TEST, added once Nebraska's disconnection article could be read, and it strengthens the replacement drafting: ask whether the state's disconnection statute defines its protected customer as an EXCLUSION LIST naming businesses (Neb. s 70-1602: 'shall not include ... companies, corporations, partnerships, limited liability companies, or businesses of any nature'). Where it does, a transfer-of-service clause is not merely a convenience for the landlord - it is what gives the TENANT the statutory notice period and fee cap, which makes it far easier to justify and far harder for a tenant to resist. And where the state also mandates a third-party notice procedure (Neb. s 70-1607), the clause should pair the transfer with the tenant designating the landlord, which answers the landlord's real worry - no warning before a shutoff - without the landlord holding the account.

### From `veterans-incentive`

Transferable test, and it reverses the usual shape of this topic. Every other state's row on `veterans-incentive` asks 'does the state give the landlord an incentive to rent to veterans'. The question that actually matters to the landlord is 'is veteran or military status a PROTECTED CLASS in this state, and if so is there a safe harbour for favouring veterans?' Nebraska added the class in 2025 (Laws 2025, LB150, amending §§ 20-318, 20-320, 20-322 and 76-1495) and added the safe harbour in the same act (§ 20-322(6)). In a state with the class and no safe harbour, a veterans discount is itself a fair-housing exposure and the row should say so; in a state with neither, it is simply a commercial decision.
