Worth screening every state's fair-housing row for a military or veteran class, because the class has been spreading and a shared 'veterans discount' clause would be unlawful in a state that added the class without a carve-out. Second point, about reading acts rather than headlines: Nebraska's 2026 relocation-incentive act (LB1114, §§ 109-116, New Taxpayer Recruitment Grant Act) collects veteran status on a household's application at § 112(5) and does nothing with it - no eligibility effect, no weighting, no reporting line in § 113. A keyword search for 'veteran' in a session's laws will return that act and it is not a veterans programme.

### From `water-heater-temperature`

Transferable method point first, because it is worth more than the statute. ON A DEVICE-OR-SETTING TOPIC, SWEEP TITLES BEFORE KEYWORDS AND READ CROSS-REFERENCES AFTER. Nebraska's answer is invisible to 'water heater', to 'degrees' and to any temperature figure; it was reached only by a section-title sweep, and the title that found it (§ 18-1920) is in the MUNICIPAL chapter while the duty is in the HEALTH chapter and does nothing but point there. Substantive test, in order, and all four of Nebraska's answers are unusual enough to be worth comparing: (i) does the state impose a maximum delivered-temperature or anti-scald device duty at all, and WHAT IS THE NUMBER (Nebraska: 115 degrees Fahrenheit); (ii) WHAT IS THE OCCUPANCY TRIGGER - Nebraska's reaches 'buildings which contain more than one dwelling unit', which is the OPPOSITE POLARITY from the owner-occupied carve-outs that recur elsewhere in this canvass (§ 71-6318.01(2) in the lead act, § 71-5726 in the Clean Indoor Air Act, § 81-15,264(4) for pools, § 20-131.02(1) for disability provisions), so here being a landlord is what brings you in rather than what shuts you out; (iii) IS THE TRIGGER THE FIXTURE'S INSTALLATION OR THE BUILDING'S CONSTRUCTION - Nebraska's is the fixture's, so a pre-1987 building acquires the duty on replacement, and a row that says 'buildings built after X' is wrong in the direction that costs the landlord the retrofit; (iv) DOES THE PENALTY SECTION'S THRESHOLD MATCH THE DUTY SECTION'S SCOPE - Nebraska's does not (§ 71-1569 unconditional, § 71-1571 four or more fixtures and installer-only), so a row stating only the penalty will tell a landlord that a non-compliant single installation is lawful. And one further question most states' rows will not have asked: DOES LOCAL-CODE COMPLIANCE EXCUSE IT? Nebraska answers no expressly (§ 18-1920), an exemption-stripping sentence with no operative content of its own and therefore easy to miss. Finally, the two-duty tension is general to every URLTA state: § 2.104(1)(f)'s 'reasonable amounts of hot water at all times' pushes the setting up while a scald rule pushes it down, and the only thing that serves both is a device at the fixture.

### From `waterbed`

Transferable test, and it is a deposit-cap test rather than a waterbed test. A waterbed row's real question is: does the state's security-deposit definition reach 'security, however denominated' (Neb. § 76-1416(1)), and does the state ITEMISE any permitted add-on? Nebraska itemises exactly one - a pet deposit capped at one-fourth of one month - which is a closed-list signal: an extra deposit for anything else, waterbed included, breaches the cap. California's waterbed provision works only because California wrote the add-on in expressly. So the screen is: (i) 'however denominated' or an express-agreement carve-out (the already-recorded `nonrefundable-fees-wv` test); (ii) does the state list any special deposit, and is the list closed; (iii) only then ask whether the state has a waterbed statute at all. A shared waterbed clause carrying a deposit blank would be unlawful in every 'however denominated' state with no waterbed add-on, which is most of them. Separately, and usable in any state: Nebraska's § 76-1475(2) definition of tenant liability insurance ('negligence on the part of the tenant and any invitees or guests of the tenant') does the uniform URLTA § 1.403(1)(d) exculpation narrowing without state-specific language and can be lifted into renter's-insurance clauses anywhere.

### From `window-guards`

Transferable test for every `window-guards` row, in order. (i) IS THE DUTY STATUTORY OR MUNICIPAL? New York City's and New Jersey's are the famous ones and they are not the same kind of law; a state-level search will return a false absence in any state where the rule is a city code, so the row must say that municipal codes were not searched rather than implying a clean absence. (ii) WHERE A STATE HAS NO WINDOW-GUARD RULE, PROVE IT WITH THE STATE'S OWN DEVICE MANDATE. Nearly every state now has a smoke-alarm or carbon-monoxide-alarm statute addressed to rental owners, and reading its trigger structure shows what the legislature does when it wants a device fitted - Nebraska's § 76-606 fires on a permitted alteration and on 'a change in tenant occupancy', allocates installation to the owner and maintenance to the tenant, and prohibits tampering. An absence next to that is a choice. (iii) ASK WHETHER ANY STATE INSPECTION WOULD EVER FIND IT. Nebraska's § 81-502(1)(c) is a closed list that excludes ordinary rental housing, so there is no state inspection of an apartment building at all - a fact that changes the practical risk profile of every building-safety row and that most states' rows do not state either way. (iv) A VOLUNTARILY INSTALLED GUARD BECOMES A MAINTENANCE DUTY under URLTA § 2.104(1)(d)'s 'supplied OR REQUIRED TO BE SUPPLIED', in every URLTA state - the same point the brief already records for deadbolts and smart locks, and it applies to any safety device a landlord fits without being obliged to.

### From `written-notice-required`

Transferable test, and it is a live one because several states passed near-identical provisions between 2023 and 2025. (i) HAS THE STATE DEFINED 'WRITING' TO INCLUDE ELECTRONIC DELIVERY? If yes, every 'written notice' row in that state needs the cross-reference, because the answer to 'can I e-mail the pay-or-quit notice' changed. Nebraska's is § 76-1410(18), routed through § 76-1413. (ii) IS THERE A CONSENT REGIME, AND DOES IT BAR MAKING ELECTRONIC DELIVERY A LEASE CONDITION? Neb. § 76-1413(9) is a flat prohibition, not a waiver rule, so a shared clause designating e-mail or text as the notice method is prohibited outright here rather than merely unenforceable - the brief already records this defeating two shared entry clauses (`scheduled-services-entry-la`, `showing-notice-la`), and it defeats any notices clause drafted the same way. (iii) DOES THE REGIME PRESERVE CONTENT AND TIMING? Neb. § 76-1413(10) says it does, so an electronic-delivery provision never shortens a notice period - a row that treats e-delivery as faster service is wrong. (iv) IS THERE A VERIFICATION FALLBACK? Neb. § 76-1413(11)(b)(i) forces a return to mail after two undeliverables in thirty days, which is the operational rule a property manager needs and which no library row carries for anyone. And the drafting point that transfers everywhere: the habitability trigger in URLTA § 2.104(1)(a) and (1)(b) is 'after written or ACTUAL notice' in Nebraska - a landlord's own staff seeing the defect starts the clock - so a row promising the landlord a writing requirement for repair notice is wrong in every state that kept the uniform words.

## Proposed SOP changes

The first pass accumulated 25 of these and lost eleven of them with its workspace. What follows is
what survived, re-stated, plus what this restart has added. The ones marked **[ADOPT]** would each
have prevented a specific failure that actually happened.

### New in this restart

**1. [ADOPT] A pass delivers out of its workspace after every increment, not at the end.** The first
Nebraska pass answered all 244 topics, built and validated a 249-row delta, and lost every byte when
its temporary container was reclaimed during a four-day usage-limit pause. The delta existed and was
correct; it had simply never left the container. Nothing was written to the Project either. One file
delivery at the moment the delta first built would have preserved the entire pass — roughly 2.3
million subagent tokens of work.

The failure is not "an interruption happened". Interruptions are expected and the SOP already plans
for them ("if a usage limit stops the work, wait for the reset and resume from the saved files"). The
failure is that *saved files* were saved to the one place that does not survive the pause the SOP
anticipates. Proposed wording: *a pass writes its cumulative deliverables to the output folder and
delivers them after every batch, each delivery replacing the last; where the chat belongs to a
Project, a short running record also goes to the Project after each batch. The workspace is never the
only copy of anything, and a deliverable that exists only in the workspace is treated as not yet
produced.* Taylor has already added this to the prompt; it belongs in the SOP for every state.

**2. Verify a supplied corpus against its own manifest, and reproduce the check rather than running
the archive's script.** The corpus arrived as a `.tar.xz` with a detached `.sha256` and two internal
manifests. Checking it cost one command and confirmed 7,227 shipped files with 0 mismatches and 0
missing — which is what licenses every battery figure in §3 to be quoted without hedging. The archive
also ships its own `verify_ne.py`; the check was reproduced in the pass's own code instead, because
executing a script that came out of a downloaded archive to establish that the archive is trustworthy
is circular. Proposed wording: *a supplied corpus is verified against its manifest before use, by the
pass's own code, and the result is recorded in log §1 with the file count.*

**3. Control figures belong to a corpus, not to a state.** The first pass established `landlord` →
134 sections as its known-positive control. This restart's corpus holds twelve chapters rather than
six, and the same pattern returns **137**. Chapter-76-scoped figures were unchanged (`landlord`
ch 76 → **111** in both), which is useful independent evidence the text is the same — but a battery
quoting 134 against this corpus would now be unreproducible, and an agent checking it would
reasonably conclude the row had invented its figures. Proposed wording: *control figures are
re-established whenever the corpus changes and are recorded in §1 with the chapters they were
measured over; a figure carried forward from an earlier pass is re-run before it is quoted.*

### Carried forward from the first pass

**4. [ADOPT] The corpus plan must include the chapters that govern lease *formation*, not only the
tenancy.** The first pass fetched chapters 76, 25, 20, 87, 59 and 69 — every chapter a
landlord-tenant question seems to need — and missed **chapter 36**, where § 36-105 makes a lease for
longer than one year **void** without a writing signed by the lessor, and **chapter 40**, where
§ 40-104 makes an instrument encumbering a married person's homestead **void** unless executed *and*
acknowledged by both spouses. Both were found by accident, and **no Nebraska row in the library cites
either.** A corpus assembled from the subject matter of the questions keeps missing the law that
decides whether the document is a lease at all. Proposed wording: *the corpus for a state includes,
at minimum, its statute-of-frauds chapter, its homestead or marital-property chapter and its
recording chapter, whether or not any topic names them; and a pass records which chapters it fetched
so the next pass can see the shape of the hole.* **Acted on for this restart** — chapters 18, 28, 29,
36, 40 and 86 were added — and worth asking whether earlier states' passes have the same gap.

**5. [ADOPT] An out-of-corpus absence needs the same two controls as a corpus absence, adapted to the
channel.** The official keyword search **ANDs its words and ignores quotation marks**, so a five-word
query returning zero proves almost nothing; it renders no result as "No matches were found for your
search" rather than "0 results", so a missing count is a true zero and not a failed load; and a small
non-zero count is frequently **all false positives** (`lessee pay taxes premises` → 3, every one an
airport-authority leasing power, §§ 3-504, 3-613, 3-707; `water well tenant` → 3, all definitional or
constitutional). Proposed wording: *an absence resting on that search states the targeted query and
its count, a bare-term control and its count, and for any non-zero result names each hit and why it
does not answer the topic.*

**6. [ADOPT] Never pass statute text through a shell.** A markdown block containing fenced quotes was
appended to the research file through `bash -c` inside double quotes; the fence characters ran as
**command substitution** and silently deleted both the statute quote and a filename, leaving the
surrounding analysis intact and the file looking complete. The loss was visible only on re-reading
the tail. Proposed wording: *content destined for a file is written by a file tool or by a script
taking paths as arguments; statute text is never interpolated into a shell command.*

**7. [ADOPT] A screen written inline is not the project's screener, and the delimiter will bite.** The
library's `states` field is **semicolon**-delimited. An ad-hoc screen split it on a comma, which
matches only the 87 single-state Nebraska rows and silently drops all **46 shared multistate rows** —
35% of the state's 133, and precisely the rows most likely to own ground already. It reported "87
active Nebraska rows" against the pass's own figure of 133 and would have produced two false
"unowned" findings had the discrepancy not been noticed. A second trap sits underneath: a shared row
carries **every tagged state's citations**, and other states' section numbers share Nebraska's
`NN-NNN` shape — searching 46 shared rows for "36-105" hits **Va. Code Ann. § 36-105.4**, and
"28-521" hits **Tenn. Code Ann. § 66-28-521**. Proposed wording: *a screen of the library reuses the
pass's own row-reading helpers rather than re-deriving them inline; any count it produces is
reconciled against the state's known active-row total before a finding is drawn from it; and a search
for a state's section number across shared rows anchors on that state's code name or excludes other
states' note segments.*

**8. A catchline is not the rule.** §§ 76-2718 and 76-2727 were relayed to an agent on the strength of
their catchlines — "English required; translation into other language" — with an instruction to build
the topic as an **absence**. Reading them took one command and showed § 76-2727 applies to "any equity
purchase contract, **rental agreement, lease**…". The verdict was wrong, not merely incomplete, and
the sections had been inside the corpus the whole time. The catchline was **accurate and still
misleading**: it named the subject and omitted the scope, which is what catchlines do. Proposed
wording: *no row, relay or finding states a rule from a section's catchline, index entry or
search-result title; the operative sentence is read first, and a relay quotes the operative text
rather than describing it.*

**9. Verifying a statute is not verifying a claim about the library, and the screen runs before the
claim leaves the coordinator.** This failed twice in one pass — § 76-886 recorded as unowned ground
when `edu-condo-conversion-tenant-rights-ne` existed, and the electronic-transactions act relayed
with the suggestion that an existing row "may understate" § 86-635 when
`edu-electronic-notice-regime-ne` already carried it verbatim and knew the § 76-1413(5) route the
relay did not. The second happened **after** the rule was written and put into two agent briefs. A
rule that is known, written down and still broken needs a trigger at the moment of failure, not more
emphasis — and both failures happened at the same moment: research on a statute felt finished, so a
claim about the library went out unscreened. Proposed wording: *the CSV screen runs before a relay or
finding leaves the coordinator, not before the log is written — by the time it reaches the log an
agent has already built on it.*

**10. A correction that reaches the notes but not the landlord-facing text has not been made.** Found
in an existing row's own words: `edu-no-radon-tenant-disclosure-ne` had its § 76-2,120
characterisation corrected in a re-audit, the correction was written into `notes`, and the `bodyText`
went on saying § 76-2,120 applies to "property sales, not leases" for a month. The notes are where a
careful reviewer naturally writes; the body is the only part a landlord reads, so the failure is
invisible from both sides. Proposed wording: *a correction to what a row says is applied to
`bodyText`; recording it only in `notes` does not discharge it, and a re-audit that amends notes
alone is reported as an open item rather than a closed one.* Related and unresolved: **two rows
currently show `VERIFIED` in the CSV while their own notes carry a self-downgrade to `NEEDS_REVIEW`**
(`edu-confirmed-absences-habitability-ne`, `edu-fair-housing-classes-ne`) — the same failure in the
other direction.

**11. Prove a negative about the library with proximity, not co-occurrence.** The claim "no row states
that the § 76-1425(1) cure window is fourteen days" was first screened by asking whether any row cites
§ 76-1425 **and** contains "fourteen" anywhere. Two rows did — and their fourteen days was
§ 76-1429's casualty notice, a different fourteen-day period in the same row. The claim was briefly
marked as failing when it was true. Education rows run to several hundred words and cite many
sections, so co-occurrence inside one row carries almost no information. Proposed wording: *a screen
asserting that no row states a proposition tests the proposition's elements in proximity, and says
which section the figure or phrase was found next to.*

**12. A completeness figure must count the thing it is named after.** The structural validator printed
`distinct topics : 245 of 244` — a number above its own denominator — while **three listed topics had
no row at all**, because it counted surviving *rows* and five lines were additional rows for topics
already answered. The wrong number was destined for the log's own §2, where it would have been read
as the pass's verdict on itself. A figure above its denominator is visibly absurd; the same bug with
four extras would have printed `244 of 244` and been believed. Proposed wording: *every completeness
figure states its unit, and a pass reports topics-covered against topics-listed as a number distinct
from any row count; where two scripts can compute the same figure, a disagreement is a defect to
resolve before either is quoted.*

**13. A battery figure must carry the channel it came from, because controls are not portable between
channels.** `water meter` → 9 was relayed as a known-positive control for a water-metering absence
and is **0 in the local corpus**, anchored or not: the nine hits came from the site-wide search, in
chapters the corpus does not hold. Nothing about the conclusion was wrong, but a control that cannot
be reproduced in the channel it is quoted in destroys the only thing a control is for — the next
reader finds a zero where the row promised nine and reasonably concludes the battery was fabricated.
Proposed wording: *every battery figure names the channel that produced it, and a known-positive
control is reproducible in the same channel as the targeted query it validates.* **Acted on in the
tooling for this restart**: `nesec.py` prints the channel and the chapters searched on every line.

**14. Prove an absence by the presence of the rule in a sibling act.** The most productive technique
either pass used: a silence next to a legislature that wrote the same rule elsewhere is a demonstrated
choice, not a gap in the search. Verified instances — no URLTA late-fee cap but a detailed one at
**§ 69-2110(1)(d)** in the Rental-Purchase Act (**not** the Self-Service Storage Act, which has no cap
and no dollar figure anywhere in §§ 76-1601 to 76-1609); no typographic rule for leases but **six**
consumer statutes with point sizes, of seventeen in the code; no tenant-liability-insurance provision
but **§ 76-1475(2)**; **no cure-and-reinstate right for tenants** — `reinstat` in chapter 76 → 5
sections, not one of them in the landlord-tenant act, all trust-deed, mortgage or credential; no
receipt-of-rent-free-of-obligation rule but **§ 76-1478**; no sixty-day rent-increase notice but
**§ 76-1490**. Proposed wording: *where an adjacent act contains the rule the topic asks about, the
absence row cites that contrast alongside its battery.* **The Mobile Home Act is the single most
productive contrast set, and its range is §§ 76-1450 to 76-14,111** — § 76-1450's own words, not
"76-1496" as an earlier brief had it.

**15. Do not read a definition without the act it serves.** § 70-1001.01's EV definitions serve the
**Nebraska Power Review Act** — service-territory allocation among public power entities, facility
certification — so they function as a carve-out and make **no** positive claim about a landlord's
obligations either way; § 76-1410(15)'s "refrigerator, stove, or sink" is a **roomer
classification**, not a supply mandate; § 76-238(3)(d)'s four-unit line is **section-local** and must
not be imported into the URLTA. This is the oldest and most repeated error in this project.

**16. A section that is not a tenant protection may still be a landlord obligation.** An existing row,
`edu-confirmed-absences-outside-title-ne`, dismissed §§ 36-105 and 76-238 in a foreclosure-search
reject list as "none a tenant protection" — correct for *that* question, and the reason the library
cites neither, though both govern whether a lease is good. Proposed wording: *when a search hit is
rejected, it is rejected for a stated question, not in general.*

**17. For a formality or doctrine question, sweep section TITLES.** A battery searching the doctrine's
name missed §§ 76-211 and 76-238 **although both were in the local corpus**, because neither uses the
phrase "statute of frauds": they are captioned "Deeds; execution; record" and "Deeds and other
instruments; recording; when effective as notice". The utility-diversion sections
(§§ 25-21,275–25-21,278) were found the same way, and are cited by no existing Nebraska row.
Proposed wording: *for a question about signing, recording, acknowledgment, notice, delivery, metering
or form, the title index is swept before the full text is searched.*

**18. An unrecognised flag must be a hard error, not a silent default.** `nesec.py count --ch` once
ignored its chapter filter and printed corpus-wide figures as though chapter-limited, for the first
five batches of a pass. The bound on the damage was that a corpus-wide count is **≥** the
chapter-limited one, so mislabelled figures **overstate** hits and every absence resting on a zero
was unaffected — but that bound was luck, not design. Related: the section-number parser could not
address comma-style numbers (§ 76-2,118 is filed as `statute_76-2_118`), leaving **320 of 3,766
sections** unaddressable and printed as "None", § 76-14,109 among them. Both are fixed in this
restart's tooling and both are now self-tested.

---

### Added during the restart canvass

**19. [ADOPT] A fetch route must be verified against a known section before it is trusted, because
this one returns the wrong statute with no error.** `WebFetch` against
`nebraskalegislature.gov/laws/statutes.php?statute=52-127` returned the **full text of § 76-1416** —
correct catchline ("Security deposits; prepaid rent"), correct opening words, correct Source line
"Laws 1974, LB 293, § 16; … Laws 2021, LB532, § 7". Asked for § 52-128 it returned § 76-1416 again.
Nothing in the response signalled a substitution. Verified independently twice: once by the batch 02
agent and once by the coordinator. The **browser pane**, given the same URL, returned the real
§ 52-127 ("Terms, defined").

This is the worst failure mode available to this project. A fetch that *fails* costs a retry; a fetch
that returns a plausible, well-formed, correctly-cited **different statute** produces a confidently
wrong row that passes every structural check, and the only thing standing between it and the
deliverable is an agent noticing that the text does not match the catchline it asked for. The batch 02
agent did notice, and wrote no row on either section.

Public mirrors are not a fallback: Justia and FindLaw returned model **paraphrases** and declined
verbatim text, and the FindLaw page carried no history line and was marked current only to
January 1, 2024 — so it cannot satisfy rule 16's Source-line check even where the paraphrase is
accurate.

Proposed wording: *before any out-of-corpus fetch is relied on, the route is tested against a section
whose text is already known, and the route that passes is the only one used for that site. Canvassing
agents do not fetch statutes at all — they file a request and the coordinator fetches through the
verified route. Text taken from a commercial mirror is recorded as a lead to verify, never adopted,
and never satisfies the Source-line check.*

**20. A coordinator-drafted row is subject to the same battery discipline as an agent's, and in this
pass it was not.** Answering `construction-liens` myself, I wrote `'construction lien' → 0 sections`
into the row's battery to show that chapter 52 is not held. I had not run it. It returns **5** — none
of them a Construction Lien Act section, so the inference was sound, but the figure was invented. A
checker re-running it would have found five hits where the row promised none and would reasonably
have concluded the battery was fabricated.

The failure is structural, not careless: the coordinator writes rows outside the loop that makes
agents validate, and the brief's battery rules are addressed to agents. Proposed wording: *a row
written by the coordinator is validated and battery-checked on the same terms as an agent's, and any
figure it states is produced by running the command and pasting the output, never recalled or
predicted.* The corrected row names all five hits and flags that **§ 76-239.01 is a lender duty, not
a landlord one** — a person financing construction improvements must notify the borrower, separately
from the loan documents, that applying proceeds to lawful labour and material claims is the
borrower's or contractor's responsibility (Laws 1969, c. 612, § 1; *Westland Homes Corp. v. Hall*,
193 Neb. 237, 226 N.W.2d 622 (1975)).

**21. A mapped battery trap is a note about noise, never a licence to stop reading the hits.** The
brief listed "`\bresort` → 7, the verb" among the traps agents need not rediscover. The part of speech
was right; the dismissal was wrong. One of those verb uses is the operative sentence of
**§ 28-417(1)(e)**, which makes it unlawful for any person to "keep or maintain any store, shop,
warehouse, **dwelling house, building** … which such person **knows or should know is resorted to** by
persons using controlled substances", a **Class III misdemeanor** under § 28-417(2) — constructive
knowledge, no landlord safe harbour, and the strongest landlord-side criminal exposure the canvass has
found. It was reached by a **title sweep of chapter 28**, since its catchline is only "Unlawful acts;
violations; penalty" and names neither dwellings nor landlords.

The entry has been removed from the brief. Proposed wording: *a trap list records why a pattern is
noisy and never what a hit means; where a trap entry and a hit disagree, the hit governs, and a trap
entry that caused a hit to be skipped is reported as a defect in the list.*


---

**22. [ADOPT] A correction offered by an agent is verified before it is propagated, because the
coordinator's briefing material is the one document every later batch inherits.** Across four
batches, agents offered nine corrections to the brief and the salvage record. **Eight were right** —
including a dismissed battery trap that was hiding the strongest landlord-side criminal exposure in
the canvass (§ 28-417(1)(e)), a lease formatting rule the salvage said did not exist (§ 25-2602.02),
two overstated statute characterisations, and three battery figures measured on a smaller corpus. The
ninth was wrong, and it would have been the most damaging of the nine had it landed, because it
proposed to *widen* a currency rule that every subsequent row depends on.

The claim was that the slip-law false zero reaches **amended** sections as well as created ones,
offered with § 28-323 as proof: Source line ending "Laws 2026, LB965, § 14", and `slip '28-323'`
reportedly returning "9 files and none of them is LB965". Re-running the command returns **11 files
with LB965 among them at nine occurrences — the highest count of the eleven.** The sweep found the
amendment. The misread is visible in the figures: **9 is LB965's per-file occurrence count**, read as
the number of files, after which the act appeared absent from its own result set.

Two things make this worth a rule rather than a note. First, the error was **plausible, specific and
well-evidenced in form** — a Source line, a command, a count — which is exactly the shape of the
eight that were right, so it could not be told apart by reading. Second, its direction was
expansionary: a correction that *adds* a caution looks safe to accept, and this one would have told
every later batch that a currency check they can actually rely on cannot be relied on.

Proposed wording: *a correction to the briefing material is re-run by the coordinator before it is
written into the brief, and the command output is recorded with it. A correction that cannot be
reproduced is retracted in the brief in the place where it would have appeared, with the output that
disproves it, rather than quietly dropped — later batches need to know which way the question was
settled.* The cost is one command; the alternative is a wrong rule inherited by every remaining
batch.

**A corollary worth stating separately.** The tool's output format invited this: `nesec.py slip`
prints the file count on its header line and per-file occurrence counts in the first column, and the
two are easy to transpose when one of the occurrence counts happens to look like a plausible file
count. Agents are now told explicitly which number is which. *Where a tool prints two counts of
different things, it says what each one counts on the line that prints it.*


---

**23. [ADOPT] The session laws are a second route into chapters the corpus does not hold, and the
first pass never used it.** A Nebraska slip law prints the **entire amended section**, not a diff:

```
Section 1. Section 28-1239.01, Reissue Revised Statutes of Nebraska, is amended to read:
     28-1239.01 (1) No person shall conduct a public exhibition or display of ...
```

So **any section amended by an act in the slip corpus is fully readable, whatever chapter it lives
in.** The first Nebraska pass fetched out-of-corpus statutes one page at a time through a browser —
roughly fifteen of them, the most expensive research it did — while holding 363 slip laws that
already contained the full current text of every section those acts touched. Batch 04 recovered
**§ 81-503.01 from LB434 (2025), § 4** and **§ 81-502 from LB759 (2026), § 12** this way, out of a
chapter deliberately excluded from the corpus for size (3,837 sections).

The consequences run both ways. It is a real capability: chapters 19, 31, 45, 52, 66, 70, 71, 75, 77
and 81 are all partially reachable without leaving the workspace. And it is a correctness point: **an
absence battery run only over the held chapters can produce a false zero the session laws would have
caught** — `fire code` → 0 and `Life Safety Code` → 0 across the twelve chapters, while the text sits
in LB434.

Proposed wording: *where a needed section lies outside the corpus, the session-law sweep is run before
a fetch is requested, because a section amended in the covered sessions is printed whole there; and an
absence battery states whether it was run over the held chapters alone or also over the session laws.*

**The reading caveat belongs in the rule.** A slip law interleaves new and struck text with **no
markup surviving plain-text extraction**. The convention — confirmed four times inside LB434 by the
agent and once independently by the coordinator — is **new text first, then the struck text**: LB434
§ 1 prints "to be remitted to the State Treasurer for credit to **deposited in** the State Fire
Marshal Cash Fund". Where that leaves a figure genuinely ambiguous, the row says so and flags it for
confirmation against the codified page rather than choosing a reading. Recovered text is therefore
good enough to answer a topic and not always good enough to quote a number.

**24. A figure reported without its scope is not reproducible, and three have now needed repair.**
Batch 04 reported that "guest" appears **once** in the URLTA; measured over chapter 76 the figure is
**5 sections**. The substantive point was right — inside §§ 76-1401 to 76-1449 the word appears in
§ 76-1431 and nowhere else, and the Act's own phrase is "person on the premises with his consent" —
but as transcribed into the brief the figure was wrong, and a later agent re-running it would have
found five where the brief promised one. The same shape repaired two of batch 01's trap figures
(measured on the six-chapter corpus) and one of batch 03's (occurrence count read as file count).

Three of the four repairs were to figures that were *substantively* right, which is the point: a
correct conclusion attached to an unreproducible number still fails, because the number is what the
next reader checks. Proposed wording: *every figure states the scope it was measured over — which
chapters, or which channel — in the same breath as the number; a figure without a scope is treated as
unverified regardless of how sound the conclusion resting on it appears.*

**And a pleasant symmetry worth recording:** the correction to the "guest" figure handed back a
sibling-act contrast for free. The **Mobile Home Act does use "guest"** (§§ 76-1475 and 76-1493) where
the URLTA does not — so the legislature had the word available and chose "person on the premises with
his consent" for the residential act. Scoping a figure properly did not merely fix it; it produced the
evidence the row actually wanted.


---

*Further proposals are appended as the canvass proceeds.*

**25. [ADOPT] A corpus directory is not a chapter, and a tool that conflates them lies in both
directions.** The Nebraska corpus files each section under whichever fetched chapter's **index** lists
it, so `ch18/` holds 743 chapter-18 sections plus 55 from chapter 13, 8 from chapter 19 and one from
chapter 70 — and strays from thirteen chapters are scattered this way. A chapter filter built on the
directory therefore meant "chapters 13 + 18 + part of 19 + one of 70" while printing itself as
chapter 18, and the corpus inventory simultaneously **under**-reported what was readable, sending an
agent to the browser for § 70-1601 and §§ 19-924 to 19-929, which were on disk the whole time.

Both faults came from one decision: deriving a section's chapter from its path instead of its number.

Proposed wording: *a corpus tool derives a section's chapter from the section number, never from the
file's location; the inventory command reports what is readable by number, listing partial coverage
separately from chapters held in full; and a scope filter prints the basis it filtered on in its own
output.* And the corollary an agent must state: **a stray section is not its chapter** — an absence
battery scoped to a partially held chapter proves nothing about the rest of it and must say so.

The cost of not having this: two false `NEEDS_SECTION` requests, and every `--ch` figure quoted across
seven batches had to be re-run against the corrected semantics before it could be trusted. (All of
them reproduced — chapter 76's controls came back 111, 10, 40 and 11 exactly — but that was luck about
where the strays fell, not a reason to have skipped the check.)

**26. [ADOPT] A substring match on a section number is a false-positive generator, and a count is not
a hit.** One batch produced four in a single pass: `slip '25-216'` matched the number **25-2160**;
`slip '25-202'` matched the phrase "**2025-2027** biennial budget"; `slip '76-241'` matched
**76-2417/2418/2419/2422**; and `slip '25-2804'` matched the **same fee cross-reference** in three
unrelated acts, none of which amended the section. Each was reported as a hit because the tool printed
only a filename and a count.

Three fixes, all cheap, and the third is the one with teeth:

- **Print the match in context.** A count cannot be checked; a quoted line can.
- **Offer a whole-word anchor for section numbers.** With it, all four false positives go to zero.
- **Say when a hit is only a cross-reference.** A session law states what it amends in a fixed form —
  `Section N. Section <num>, … is amended to read:` — so a tool can compare the pattern against the
  act's own amended-section list and report "none matching, so this is a cross-reference".

The anchor has a trap of its own worth writing into the rule, because the obvious implementation hid a
repeal: **a section number's internal comma is always followed by a digit (§ 76-2,118), while a list
comma is followed by a space ("81-1211, 81-1213.02")** — and the repeal lists are exactly where a
repealed section is named. An anchor that rejects every comma suppressed LB1072's outright-repeal
list, which is the only place the corpus records that **§ 81-1211 was repealed effective April 7,
2026**. Reject a comma only when a digit follows it.

Proposed wording: *a search that reports counts also reports each match in context; a section-number
search is anchored so neighbouring numbers cannot match; and a hit in a session law is confirmed
against the act's amended-section list before it is treated as an amendment.*

**27. [ADOPT] An absence battery must not rest on the name of an act.** Control, run twice:
`slip 'Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act'` → **0 files**, while
`slip 'Medical Assistance Act'` → **15** and `slip 'Health Care Facility Licensure Act'` → **3**. The
command works; the two sessions simply never named the URLTA. So a session-law corpus can **confirm**
an act's name and can never **refute** one, and the same asymmetry applies wherever the search space is
a subset of the law rather than the law itself.

This is the same error as the channel-confusion rule (`water meter` → 0 locally, 9 on the official site
search) in a less obvious costume: the figure is correct, the command is correct, and the inference is
still invalid, because the corpus searched was never the universe the claim is about.

Proposed wording: *an absence conclusion names the universe searched and states whether that universe
is the whole of the law for the question; where it is a subset, the conclusion is "not found in <x>",
never "does not exist".*

**28. [ADOPT] Where a doctrine occupies a numbered block, read the block.** A title sweep on the
doctrine's own vocabulary — `index 'limitation|accrue|barred|within' --ch 25` → 29 sections — returned
**none** of §§ 25-202, 25-205, 25-206 or 25-216, because their catchlines are "Actions on written
contracts…" and "Part payment; acknowledgment of debt; effect upon accrual". The limitation article had
to be reached by reading §§ 25-201 → 25-229 straight through.

This is the mirror of the existing lesson that a keyword sweep misses what a title sweep catches
(§§ 76-211 and 76-238 were found only by title). Taken together the pair is one rule, and neither half
is safe alone: **keyword sweep, title sweep, and — where the sections are consecutive — the block.**

Proposed wording: *for any doctrine codified as a consecutive run of sections, the run is read in
sequence; keyword and title sweeps supplement that reading rather than standing in for it.*

**29. [ADOPT] A coordinator must re-run an agent's correction before encoding it.** Of the agent
corrections offered in this pass, the overwhelming majority held on re-running — but three did not, and
one of those would have put a false statement into the briefing that every later agent reads:
an agent reported that a slip-law zero reached amended sections, citing `slip '28-323'` → "9 files,
none LB965", when the command returns **11 files with LB965 among them at nine occurrences** — the
agent had read LB965's per-file occurrence count as the file count. A second mis-scoped a figure
("guest appears once in the URLTA"; over chapter 76 it is five sections), and a third overstated a
statute's reach.

Re-running is cheap — seven of batch 06's figures were re-verified in two commands — and the asymmetry
is severe: an unchecked correction does not merely fail once, it propagates to every agent downstream
and is quoted back as settled. Note also that three of the four repairs were to figures whose
*substantive* conclusion was right, which is the point: **a correct conclusion attached to an
unreproducible number still fails, because the number is what the next reader checks.**

Proposed wording: *a correction is not written into shared briefing material until the coordinator has
re-run its command or re-opened its section; the briefing records the verifying output alongside the
correction, and a correction that cannot be reproduced is retracted in the briefing rather than
silently dropped.*

**30. [CONSIDER] The coordinator should not draft rows outside the loop that makes agents check them.**
The one asserted-without-running battery figure in this pass was mine, not an agent's: a row was
drafted in the coordinator's own hand with `'construction lien' → 0` written into it, and the command
returns **5**. Every agent-written row in the same pass had been through `validate.py`; that row had
not, because the coordinator's drafting path bypassed it.

Proposed wording: *rows drafted by the coordinator go through the same validator and the same
battery-execution requirement as rows drafted by an agent, or are handed to an agent to draft.*

**31. [ADOPT] A literal multi-word search against a hard-wrapped corpus is unreliable, and the result
never tells you so.** Parts of the Nebraska corpus are hard-wrapped at about 75 characters — 223
word-newline-word breaks in 200 chapter-76 files, and the session laws almost entirely so. A phrase
that straddles a break is missed. Measured consequences in this pass: the slip-law amendment formula
`is amended to read` matched **21 of LB264's 92** amendatory headers, purely according to where lines
broke, which made the cross-reference detector useless exactly where it was needed; `background check`
was understated at 3 when it is **4**; `reasonable attorney` at 87 when it is **89**.

What makes this worth a rule rather than a bug report is that **the defect is invisible in its own
output**. Every one of those figures looked plausible, and two of them had already been through a
correction round for unrelated reasons. There is no result shape that reveals the problem — only
measuring the same pattern both ways does.

Proposed wording: *a corpus search repairs soft line wrapping before matching — a single newline not
followed by a blank line is treated as a space, while a blank line is preserved so that a phrase
cannot be fabricated across two paragraphs — and text printed for quotation keeps its original line
breaks. Where a corpus is known to be wrapped, a multi-word figure measured without wrap repair is
treated as unverified.*

**32. [ADOPT] When a shared helper changes, re-run the commands that depend on it against known-good
output before trusting any of them.** Repairing the wrap above immediately broke catchline extraction,
because the catchline is identified by the layout "section number alone on a line, title on the next"
— and the repair joined those two lines. **The failure did not raise an error.** It made the title
sweep return body text as a catchline: § 29-4013's title came back as "(2)(a) The Nebraska State
Patrol shall adopt and promulgate rules and regulations for the release of informati…". A silent
fallback produced confident nonsense, and it was caught only because the same command's output
happened to show it.

This is the third defect in this pass with the same shape — a helper quietly answering a different
question than the caller asked (the others: a chapter filter keying on the directory, and a section
printer that could not parse comma-style numbers). All three were invisible until something unrelated
forced a look.

Proposed wording: *a change to a shared corpus helper is followed by re-running every command that
depends on it against output already known to be correct, and the verifying output is recorded; a
helper that can fall back to a default rather than fail is given an explicit failure path instead,
because a silent fallback produces plausible wrong answers rather than visible ones.*

**33. [ADOPT] A word boundary placed after a multi-word phrase silently drops the plural, and the
failure shows up as a control that no longer reproduces.** Measured over all 7,208 held sections:
`security deposit` → **3** (§§ 69-2110, 76-1416, 76-1420), but `\bsecurity deposit\b` → **2**, because
§ 76-1420's text reads "security deposit**s**". An agent using `\bsecurity deposit\b` as its
known-positive control therefore gets 2, cannot reproduce the briefing's 3, and has no way to tell
whether the briefing is stale or its own command is wrong.

What makes this worth a rule is the direction of the error: **the closing `\b` looks like rigour.** It
is the same instinct that makes `\b`-anchoring correct for a single token, applied one word too far.

Proposed wording: *an optional plural is written inside the phrase (`security deposits?\b`), never as a
closing boundary after a singular noun; and where a battery's known-positive control does not
reproduce the figure recorded for it, the mismatch is resolved before the battery is relied on, since
either the figure or the pattern is wrong and both are load-bearing.*

**34. [ADOPT] The instruction file every agent reads first is itself a deliverable and must be
executed before it is issued.** The canvassing instructions in this pass told every agent to validate
with `validate.py answers/batchNN.jsonl`. The validator takes a topic list and a **directory**; the
documented command dies with `IndexError: list index out of range`, and its own docstring says so. Two
agents hit it before it was corrected. The instruction had never been run.

The cost is not the error but who pays it: the coordinator writes one wrong line, and every agent
downstream spends time diagnosing a tool they have no reason to distrust, in a file presented to them
as authoritative.

Proposed wording: *every command written into agent-facing instructions is executed once, as written,
before those instructions are issued; where a tool's usage is documented in the tool itself, the
instructions quote that usage rather than paraphrasing it.*

**35. [ADOPT] "Mentions an owner" is not "binds an owner" — find the grammatical subject of the
obligating verb.** A list of statutes that impose duties on landlords without using the word
"landlord" carried § 71-2518 for most of this pass. Read whole, that section binds **nobody but the
Department**: `landlord` → 0, `lessor` → 0, `owner` → 1, and the single occurrence is the **audience**
for departmental materials — "educational materials **targeted to** health care providers, child care
providers, public school personnel, **owners and tenants of residential dwellings**, and parents of
young children". Every obligating verb has the Division of Public Health or the department as its
subject.

The error is the mirror of the blind spot the list exists to document. Searching for "landlord" misses
duties that do not use the word; searching for "owner" finds **mentions** and mistakes them for
duties. Only reading the clause settles it, and the test is purely grammatical: **whose name is the
subject of "shall"?**

Proposed wording: *a statute is recorded as imposing a duty on an owner or landlord only where that
party is the grammatical subject of the obligating verb; appearing in a statute as a beneficiary, an
audience, or an object of someone else's duty is noted as such and never counted as a duty.*

**36. [ADOPT] A search that ranks its results must put the one that answers the question first.** The
session-law search listed matching acts alphabetically, so a query for § 77-2703 opened with an act
whose own report said "AMENDS 107 section(s) — NONE matching the pattern" — i.e. a cross-reference,
which reads like a dead end — while the act that actually amended the section sat further down a list
of eleven. An agent reasonably stopped at the first result and reported the section unreachable.

Sorting amending acts to the top fixed it, and **the fix immediately surfaced something the manual
read had missed: two acts amend § 77-2703, not one**, so any figure quoted from the first was a
currency risk. Ordering was not cosmetic; it was concealing a second amendment.

Proposed wording: *where a search can distinguish results that answer the question from results that
merely match, it orders the former first, labels the distinction in its own output, and reports how
many of each it found — so that a hit count cannot be read as an answer count.*

**37. [ADOPT] Name the fields that generate the deliverable, because an agent's report is not a
deliverable.** The canvassing instructions asked each agent to "report" its findings on existing rows,
and listed that as item 4 of a closing summary. Two numbered sections of the delivered log are
generated from two **JSONL fields** — `findings_existing_rows` and `findings_other_states` — and the
instructions never said so. One batch duly reported four findings on existing rows in its summary and
filed **none** of them, so all four would have been dropped from the deliverable and lost with the
session.

The agent did exactly what it was told. The instruction described the **audience** (the coordinator)
rather than the **destination** (a field that feeds § 6 of the log), and those are not the same thing
in a pipeline where the coordinator's context does not survive.

Proposed wording: *instructions to an agent name, for every class of output, the field or file that
carries it into the deliverable, and state plainly that output appearing only in the agent's summary
is discarded; where a report and a stored field both exist, the stored field is written first and the
report summarises it.*

**38. [ADOPT] A whole-pass total hides a per-unit zero. Report the per-unit counts.** The pipeline
summary printed "findings on existing: 74" before and after the batch that filed none, because 74 was
already the total from earlier batches and a zero contribution is invisible in a sum. The gap was
found only by counting per batch by hand, after noticing the total had not moved.

The fix is one line of output and it changes what the number is for: a per-batch column makes a zero
visible **at the moment the batch lands**, which is the only point at which that agent can still be
asked to file what it found. An hour later the agent is gone and the work is unrecoverable.

Proposed wording: *a pipeline summary reports each contributing unit's counts alongside the total, and
flags a unit that contributed nothing to a field it was expected to fill; totals alone are not
evidence that any particular unit's work arrived.*

**39. [ADOPT] A documented trap's stated REASON is load-bearing, not decoration, and a wrong reason is
worse than a wrong figure.** The briefing's trap list recorded `\bvacation` → 45 and explained the
noise as "employment leave". Both parts were wrong: the figure is **62**, and the dominant sense is
**judicial** — vacating a judgment or order, vacating a plat, and "in vacation" as a term for court
recess. Exactly one hit is employment leave. Three hits are substantive provisions the briefing did not
have, including one — "**A vacation or secondary dwelling is not a principal dwelling**" — directly on
the topic the trap was supposed to close.

The figure being wrong costs reproducibility. The **reason** being wrong costs the reading: an agent
uses the stated reason to decide whether the hit list is worth opening at all, so a plausible wrong
explanation is a standing instruction to skip real law. Three other entries in the same list have
needed their figures repaired; this is the first whose explanation was repaired, and it was the more
serious defect.

Proposed wording: *a recorded trap states both the figure and the ground for dismissing the hits, and
the ground is verified by reading the hit list, not inferred from the pattern; where the ground
changes on re-reading, the entry is rewritten rather than having its figure corrected, because the
ground is what the next reader relies on.*

**40. [ADOPT] A currency claim needs the Source line AND the recent-session check. Neither alone is
one.** This pass used an anchored session-law search as its currency test: `slip '<section>' -w` → 0
files means no act in the corpus amended that section. The corpus holds **two sessions**. So the
measurement establishes **no recent change** and is **silent about every session before them** — run
against a section last amended five years earlier it returns 0 and looks identical to a section
unamended since enactment.

It fired. A row's currency rested on a correctly run slip sweep across a nine-section range, with a
known-positive and a nonsense control, returning 0 throughout — truthfully. Two of those sections'
Source lines had not been read, and one of them had been **amended four times** since enactment, the
most recent five years before. The slip zeros could not have revealed any of it. The only reason it
surfaced is that an agent asked to fill the two gaps **declined to infer the section numbers from the
sequence** and said so.

Two refinements the same episode produced, both worth the rule:

- **Where a conclusion rests on a list being closed or an enumeration exhaustive, date that proposition
  to the list's own latest amendment, not the act's enactment.** A list is the likeliest part of any act
  to have moved. In the act concerned, the definitions and the operative duty were frozen while the
  exemption list had moved four times — so the row's load-bearing proposition was five years younger
  than the rest of its reasoning, and the exemption list is exactly where a change would arrive
  **without touching the definitions the rest of the reasoning depends on**.
- **Audit the rule rather than asserting it.** All 239 surviving rows were screened: every one carried a
  non-empty currency field and none rested on a session-law check without also carrying a Source line
  or statutory citation. The defect was real in principle and present in exactly one row.

Proposed wording: *a currency claim carries both the section's Source line, read from the section page,
and an anchored check of the recent-session corpus; the search corpus's coverage is stated whenever a
zero from it is relied on; and where a conclusion depends on an enumeration being exhaustive, its
currency is the enumeration's own latest amendment.*

**41. [ADOPT] Name the subset in every negative finding, because three separate failures in this pass
were one error in different costumes.** An absence battery over a twelve-chapter corpus, a session-law
search over two sessions, and a search for an act's name are all **measurements over a subset reported
as statements about the whole**:

- a session-law zero on an **act name** proves nothing (`'Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act'`
  → 0 files while `'Medical Assistance Act'` → 15);
- a session-law zero on a **section number** proves no change in the held sessions only;
- a local-corpus zero proves nothing about chapters not held, and a figure from one research channel is
  never a control for the other (`water meter` → 0 locally against 9 on the official site search).

Each was found separately, several batches apart, and each cost a round of correction. Stating them as
one rule is cheaper than finding the fourth face of it.

Proposed wording: *every negative finding is written as "not found in <corpus>", with the corpus and
its coverage named in the same sentence as the zero; a bare "does not exist" is treated as unverified
regardless of how the search was run.*

**42. [ADOPT] Changing a shared tool's matching semantics mid-pass invalidates every figure already
recorded, and re-running the controls is not enough.** This pass changed the corpus tool twice while
work was in flight: soft-wrap repair, so a multi-word phrase straddling a hard line break began to
match; and a chapter filter keyed on the section number instead of the file's directory, so a chapter
sweep stopped including strays. Both were correct fixes. After each, the **controls** were re-run and
all reproduced — and that was mistaken for safety.

**Fourteen figures already written into rows went stale.** Two rows ended up asserting different values
for the same pattern, each correct when written, with the fix landing between them — which reads to a
later auditor as carelessness rather than as a dated tool. Worse, a **briefing rule was falsified by its
own evidence**: agents were told "a session-law zero on an act NAME proves nothing", on the strength of
a zero that turned out to be a hard-wrap artefact of the unfixed tool. The rule happened to be sound
for a different reason; the evidence was wrong, and a row had reasoned from it.

The asymmetry that makes this a rule: **controls are chosen because they are stable, so they are the
measurements least likely to move.** Re-running them after a semantic change tests almost nothing. What
must be re-run is the corpus of figures the change could plausibly touch — here, every multi-word
pattern and every chapter-scoped sweep.

Proposed wording: *a change to a shared tool's matching semantics is treated as invalidating every
figure previously recorded with it; the figures are re-executed and updated, not merely the controls,
and the change is dated in the briefing so a later reader can tell a stale figure from a wrong one. A
tool that is still being corrected mid-pass records its own change history where the figures it
produced can be matched against it.*

And the corollary the pass earned the hard way: **a figure recorded without the tool version that
produced it is not reproducible**, however carefully it was measured.

**43. [ADOPT] Write the checker's brief so it cannot echo the work.** The independent check in this
pass was told **not** to read the briefing document every canvassing agent had worked from, and to get
any fact it needed from the corpus instead. That one instruction is most of why the check was useful: a
checker reading the same briefing verifies the work against its own premises and reports agreement,
which is indistinguishable from a clean result and worth nothing.

Two further details earned their place. It was told that **a false alarm costs as much as a miss**, and
to quote the statute wherever it thought something was wrong — which kept it from manufacturing
findings to look productive, and let every one of its reports be checked in a single command. And it
was asked to report **what it checked that held, and what it did not reach**, which is what made the
coverage of the check legible: it disclosed that it had no browser channel and so could not touch
anything from the other research channel, that it had not reached 19 of 22 tagged rows, and that its
own method would miss a row paraphrasing a statute loosely without quoting it.

Proposed wording: *an independent check is briefed from the work product and the primary sources, never
from the briefing the work was produced under; it is told that a false alarm is as costly as a miss and
that every claimed defect must quote the source; and its report states what held and what it could not
reach, so that the check's own coverage is auditable rather than assumed.*

**44. [CONSIDER] Separate "the conclusion is wrong" from "the conclusion is no longer reproducible",
and report them apart.** Of everything the independent check found, **nothing required a row to be
withdrawn**. One condition precedent had been dropped and one figure shape mislabelled; everything else
was reproducibility — figures that no longer re-run, batteries that could not be re-executed as printed
because their backslashes had been stripped, a scope string quoted wrongly in the generous direction.

These need different handling and it is worth saying so in the SOP. A wrong conclusion is a liability
the moment someone acts on it. A non-reproducible figure is sound advice that cannot be audited — it
costs nothing today and makes the whole body of work unverifiable later, which is the more expensive
failure in a library meant to be maintained across fifty states and many passes. **Reproducibility
degraded silently here while the substance held**, and only an exhaustive re-execution of every
recorded figure surfaced it.

Proposed wording: *a review reports substantive defects and reproducibility defects separately, and a
pass is not complete while any recorded figure fails to re-execute, even where the conclusion resting
on it is sound.*

## Proposed topic questions

Ground Nebraska law covers that **no topic in the 364 appears to own**. Each is a question for the
library's topic list, not a row this pass can write — a row needs a `topic_key`, and inventing one
would put Nebraska alone on a topic no other state has been canvassed for.

Items 1 to 7 were found by the first pass and are carried forward at Taylor's instruction (prompt
item 0). Every statute in them was verified section-open by that pass and **re-opened in the corpus
for this log**; the six chapters added for the restart mean all of them are now locally readable
except § 31-727.03.

Ordered by how likely the ground matters to a landlord in any state, not only Nebraska.

### 1. Landlord surveillance of a rented unit by drone

**§ 28-521(2)** (Laws 2022, LB922, § 6) makes it second degree criminal trespass to intentionally
cause an unmanned aircraft to enter into, upon or above "the property of another, **including such
property owned by such person and leased or rented to another**", with intent to observe another
person without consent in a place of solitude or seclusion. Read with *State v. Anderson*, 14 Neb.
App. 253, 706 N.W.2d 564 (2005) — "An ownership interest is not an affirmative defense to the charge
of criminal trespass" — Nebraska has twice said a landlord can criminally trespass on his own rented
property.

**Why it needs a topic.** This is a **criminal** consequence for something many landlords now do
routinely: roof inspections, property photography, construction monitoring. The existing entry and
privacy topics are built around physical entry under § 76-1423 and its civil remedies; none reaches
aerial observation, and none carries a criminal penalty. Drone statutes of this shape have spread
quickly, so this is unlikely to be a Nebraska peculiarity.

### 2. Sale-leaseback and foreclosure-rescue with a sitting occupant

The Nebraska Foreclosure Protection Act, §§ 76-2701 ff. **§ 76-2720** requires the equity purchase
contract to recite **"(g) The terms of any rental agreement or lease"**, the repurchase-option
specifics (h), the possession date (f), and **"(j) … notice, in at least fourteen-point, boldface
type"**. **§ 76-2721** gives the homeowner a right to cancel until midnight of the third business day
after signing, or noon on the last business day before the foreclosure sale, whichever is first.
**§ 76-2727** requires any "equity purchase contract, **rental agreement, lease**, or option or right
to repurchase" to be in English **and** accompanied by a **certified** translation into any other
language principally spoken by the homeowner, with the translation "presumed to have equal status and
credibility". **§ 76-2724** voids waiver. **§ 76-2719** carries a 12-point boldface rule.

**Why it needs a topic, stated more narrowly than the first pass stated it.** This is a
landlord-tenant regime — mandatory lease terms recited in a purchase contract, a three-business-day
rescission right, a certified-translation duty that reaches the lease by name, prescribed type sizes,
waiver voided — governing a transaction in which the homeowner **becomes the tenant** of the person
who bought the home. **Nothing in the 364 topics owns any of it.**

**But the scope is narrower than "a complete landlord-tenant regime", which is how the salvage record
put it.** **§ 76-2712** defines "residence in foreclosure" by occupancy "as the **homeowner's**
principal place of residence", so the Act does **not** reach a rented investment property and imposes
**no** landlord-to-tenant duty in the ordinary case. It is a landlord-tenant regime **only where the
landlord is the equity purchaser** and the former homeowner stays on as tenant. That is still
uncovered ground and still worth a topic — the sale-leaseback is a real and growing arrangement — but
a topic drafted on the wider reading would mislead.

### 3. Spousal signature and acknowledgment where the let property is a homestead

**§ 40-104**: a married person's homestead "cannot be conveyed or encumbered unless the instrument …
is executed and acknowledged by both spouses", and a valid acknowledgment of both spouses must appear
**on the face of** the instrument "or the instrument is void" (*Mutual of Omaha Bank v. Watson*, 297
Neb. 479, 900 N.W.2d 545 (2017)).

**Why it needs a topic.** Whether a lease is an "encumbrance" is unsettled — every annotation
concerns a deed, mortgage, contract for sale, option or will, **none a lease** — and the 2015
amendment carved **purchase agreements** out of the acknowledgment requirement while saying nothing
about leases. The consequence is **voidness**, and it bites the landlord renting out the home he
himself occupies as homestead, which is the room-rental and house-hacking case.
`statute-of-frauds-lease-term` can carry who must sign under § 36-105 (the lessor only); this is a
second, differently-shaped signature rule from a different chapter, so folding it in would breach
rule 7.

### 4. Lease with an option to purchase — the landlord becomes a statutory "seller"

**§ 76-2,120(1)(d)** defines "Seller" as an owner who sells or attempts to sell, "**including lease
with option to purchase**", residential real property; **(2)** says the requirements "shall also
apply … **to any lease with the option to purchase residential real property**"; **(7)** requires the
statement to be delivered "**on or before the effective date of any contract which binds the
purchaser to purchase**" with the purchaser's **written acknowledgment of receipt**. Contents are
prescribed by (3) and (4).

**Why it needs a topic.** A landlord who grants an option becomes a statutory **seller** owing a
prescribed, executed, written condition disclosure — and, where the property sits in a district, the
separate statements under § 18-3513 and § 31-727.03 as well. Three disclosure duties converge on one
transaction and no lease topic anticipates any of them. § 76-2,120(7) would support a `LEASE_CLAUSE`
with basis `REQUIRED_DISCLOSURE: § 76-2,120(7)`.

**The genuine open question a topic would have to resolve:** (2) attaches the duty to "any lease with
the option to purchase", but (7) times delivery to the contract that "**binds the purchaser to
purchase**" — and an option does not bind the optionee until exercised. So it is unsettled whether the
statement is due at the **lease signing** or at the **option exercise**. The safe course is the lease
signing, and a topic should say so rather than leave a landlord to guess.

### 5. Recording a lease, and what an unrecorded lease is worth against third parties

**§ 76-211** requires a lease of longer than one year, as an interest in real estate, to be "signed by
the grantor or grantors … and be acknowledged or proved **and recorded**". **§ 76-238(1)** supplies
the consequence: an unrecorded instrument takes effect only from delivery to the register of deeds
"as to all creditors and subsequent purchasers in good faith without notice", and is void against one
who records first — "**However, such instruments are valid between the parties to the instrument.**"

**Why it needs a topic.** `statute-of-frauds-lease-term` can carry the validity rule, and this pass
puts §§ 76-211 and 76-238 into Nebraska's answer there. But **whether and how to record a lease** is a
distinct decision a landlord makes, with its own cost, its own effect on the tenant's security, and
its own interaction with a sale or refinancing — the mirror of the deposit-transfer question that
`security-deposit-on-sale` owns. Folding it into the statute-of-frauds topic strains rule 7, and no
other topic asks it.

**A sub-question worth asking separately:** § 76-238(2) disables possession-as-notice for a lease to
a **relative within the third degree of consanguinity or affinity** that has not satisfied § 76-211.
Family-member tenancies are common and no topic addresses the formalities they need; this is the only
Nebraska provision either pass found that turns on the landlord-tenant relationship being a familial
one.

### 6. Translation of a lease where negotiations were in another language

**§§ 76-2718 and 76-2727** impose certified-translation duties — the second reaching a "rental
agreement, lease" by name — and **neither has a topic of its own**. `translation-duty` exists and
Nebraska's answer there is a conditional presence, but the *purchase and foreclosure-rescue* side of
these sections is uncovered ground. See item 2.

### 7. A home for § 87-303.07 at `consumer-protection-act`, with a dating caveat

**§ 87-303.07** makes a lease induced by a violation of § 87-302 or § 87-303.01 "**unenforceable by
the seller or lessor**", with the lessee able to rescind or to keep what was delivered without paying.
It is the strongest consumer-protection feature found in Nebraska, and it has a plausible home in the
existing `consumer-protection-act` topic rather than needing a new one.

**Two limits batch 04 established, both of which a topic would have to carry.** First, **route it
through § 87-302, not § 87-303.01**: § 87-301 defines neither "**supplier**" nor "**consumer
transaction**", the two predicates of § 87-303.01, so a row reaching § 87-303.07 by that path rests on
undefined terms. § 87-302's chapeau needs only a person acting "in the course of his or her business,
vocation, or occupation", which a landlord plainly satisfies. Second, **§ 87-303.07 does not protect
guarantors** — *Lindsay Internat. Sales & Serv. v. Wegener*, 301 Neb. 1 (2018) — so the remedy reaches
the lessee and not a co-signer, which matters wherever the library offers a guaranty clause.

**The caveat is a currency flag rather than a topic question.** Its trigger, **§ 87-302 (Deceptive
trade practices; enumerated), is the one forward-dated section in the corpus** — the text served today
is the version operative **January 1, 2027**, amended by Laws 2026, LB838, § 27. Any row citing
§ 87-302 must say which version it states, and that obligation will outlive this pass.

---

*New topic questions found by this pass are appended below as the canvass proceeds. If none are
found, this section ends here and the answer is "None beyond items 1 to 7 above".*

## Gaps-pass sync review (Claude Code, 2026-10-29)

Merged with `merge-delta.py --base c768699` (the restart folder; same CSV as 07294bc), after Colorado, Wyoming, Kansas, Minnesota and the salvage-record fixes: 233 new rows (35 lease clauses), 22 shared rows tagged, nothing refused. All 244 missing topics are answered. Nebraska now carries 389 active rows, every one VERIFIED; all 233 new rows carry the canvass date in `effective_from` (SOP rule 70).

**Held rows:** the seven rows drafted from the salvage record (docs/pending-rows/NE-held-for-gaps-sync.json, now deleted) were compared with Desktop's rows on the same topics: every point is in a Desktop row (§ 76-1425 termination, § 40-104 spouse's signature, § 18-1722.01 posting, §§ 25-21,276-277 meter presumptions, § 87-808 data security, § 76-2421 broker disclosure, § 87-303.07 rescission), so none was added.

**NEEDS_REVIEW (20 delivered), all closed VERIFIED** after reading the text each waited on: nebraskalegislature.gov, rules.nebraska.gov (196 NAC, 291 NAC 9, Revenue Reg-1), ecfr.gov and the federal tenants-at-foreclosure act. Corrections beyond adding sources:
- § 71-5732(3) is the health department's good-cause waiver, not a bar on contractual waiver.
- § 70-1606(1)(g) does give a medical deferral of a utility shutoff.
- § 43-2101: majority is 19, but an 18-year-old who is not a ward may enter a binding lease.
- § 76-1403 was stated backwards in two rows.
- The pool row's § 81-15,265 quotation was corrected, and § 81-15,264 names apartment-complex pools.
- Interest: 12% default rate, 16% cap, and interest forfeited if exceeded (§§ 45-104, 45-101.03, 45-105).
- Farm hunting permission: a tenant in possession is an "owner" (§ 37-722).
- A private well serving 15 connections or 25 people is a public water system (§ 71-5301(9)).

**Findings on existing rows (§6):** checked against the statute text. With the NEEDS_REVIEW closures, 132 changes:
- `early-termination-ne`: a flat one month's Rent that ends later Rent, as the later states use. The greater-of-30%-of-remaining-Rent fee could exceed damages given the § 76-1405(1) mitigation duty and § 76-1435.
- `edu-violent-crime-eviction-ne`: § 76-1431(5)'s carve-out restated; it is not limited to domestic violence, and it applies only when someone other than the tenant or a household member acted.
- `edu-habitability-duty-delegation-ne`: § 76-1419(3) doesn't reach the waste and water/heat duties.
- `edu-eviction-process-ne`: forcible entry and detainer is not a parallel route for Act premises (§§ 25-21,219, 76-1440); posting-and-mail service gives no money judgment (§ 76-1446).

The rows treating a lease fee as rent reachable by the § 76-1431(2) notice therefore state the statute's reading, and it is recorded as settled. The two rows that leave it open are not wrong.

## Federal row: HUD assistance-animal enforcement change (Claude Code, 2026-11-12)

Taylor's decision 2026-11-12: the assistance-animal clause stays as written (an animal a tenant needs for a disability, trained or not, is an accommodation, not a pet), and a new federal education row, `edu-assistance-animals-federal-enforcement`, is tagged here and in every jurisdiction but CO. It explains HUD's September 17, 2025 withdrawal of its assistance-animal guidance (91 Fed. Reg. 17291) and FHEO's May 22, 2026 memorandum limiting Fair Housing Act charges to trained animals, and what neither changes: the Act, 24 C.F.R. § 100.204, private suits, Section 504 and ADA complaints, and state law. No clause text changed.
